quote: One of the best films I've recently seen, It's really a delightuful movie. The three main actors are really wonderful. I think both Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush deserve an Oscar for his marvelous performances.
A captivating movie with amazing performances and a stellar script. One of 2010's best. Colin Firth was just wonderful.

Colin Firth used to be among my least favorite actors. He just seemed so pompous and set in a certain role, usually a bit a pratt and he seemed to play the role well. Now that's he's over fifty, it's almost like Mr. Firth has caught and second wind. This is second year in a row that he's been in one of the best offerings of the season. Last year we had Tom Ford's A Single Man, and now, The King's Speech. His performance is perfect. Not only does he portray the impediment well, he captures the character perfectly too. Hands down his best work yet. Historical dramas are really hit or miss to me. Some are great, some or forgettable or just okay, and quite a few are absolutely terrible. The King's Speech definitely falls into the 'great' category. Probably the single best thing is that it doesn't focus on any one thing that much. It doesn't just focus on the politics, just on the war movement, or just on the treatment/therapy, or just on the family, or anything else. It dabbles in everything which gives us a broad scope of the situation, but also keeps the storyline from falling into needless complications that no one cares about. It leaves you with a general sort of idea of what happened with the nitty gritty details left out. We go on journey with Bertie and experience his transformation. While the characters are almost archetypes of their set roles, it is still a character driven film. It's not perfect and I think a second viewing might spoil it, but honestly, it's a very, very good film and well worth experiencing once.

I knew that King George VI had not been prepared (in either sense) to become king of his country and that he had not been a confident person, until this film came along I didn't know that he had stammered.  The effect on him as a person, as the Duke of York and as king are all explored and we learn how he was able to cope with his public duties with the help of Lionel Logue, an Australian speech therapist, a man not considered appropriate for this task by the establishment.  Most of those in the film give outstanding performances, Colin Firth was as good as everyone says, but I particularly liked the small part played by Guy Pearce as Prince David/King Edward VIII, and was amazed by the sets.

There isn't a bad performance in the lot (though I thought casting Tim Spall as Sir Winston Churchill was a bit of a reach).  An outstanding bit of cinema that is sure to garner Oscar nods for Tom Hooper, Colin Firth, Geoffrey Rush and Helena Bonham Carter.

And regardless of how many Oscars it receives or not, for me, it's the front-runner.

This is the true story of a king with a stutter and the man who helps him overcome it. I was mesmerized by his excellent performance. This challenging role presents him as a top notch actor. Geoffrey Rush.Terrific as the unorthodox Australian speech therapist. Their friendship: funny and touching, their natural charm and effortless chemistry is a big part of what makes the film so endearing. And Helena Bonham Carter, usually known for her strange, outrageous choice of characters was a treat as the supportive Queen Elizabeth. A true story with a fascinating history lesson and it is really a direct and heartfelt piece of work from all involved.

Director: Tom Hooper 

Summary: Britain's King George VI (Colin Firth) struggles with an embarrassing stutter for years until he seeks help from unorthodox Australian speech therapist Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) in this biographical drama that chalked up multiple Academy Awards, including Best Picture. Logue's pioneering treatment and unlikely friendship give the royal leader a sense of confidence that serves him and his country well during the dark days of World War II.

My Thoughts: "An emotional, inspiring, and sometimes funny tale. The King's Speech, deserved all the hype it was receiving. The movie was enthralling from start to finish. Colin Firth was fantastic in the film as was Geoffrey Rush. They were perfectly matched for this film. Helena Bonham Carter also gave a great performance as the encouraging wife. Just a great cast telling a very interesting story. Many parts of the film I loved, one being when Lionel sits in the King's chair. The argument that ensues shows King George VI coming to the knowledge that he has a voice and should be heard. Some powerful moments and some very sad one's as well. For instance when he is talking about his first nanny, that was awful. The movie is one that should be seen and one that will be remembered not only for it's performances, but for it's great story."

Sadly, this will always be regarded as the overhyped Best Film winner of 2011, and perhaps this is rightly so. Sure, this film had much beauty and simplicity to its plot and performances, but so simple a film should not have been so highly lauded. I think we all gave a chuckle or two with the ease of the comedy between the principle actors, but wit does not constitute an entire film. Yes, a man on the verge of ascending the throne who is in mortal turmoil over the abdication of his brother and the embarrassment of a crippling stutter is entertaining, but the material did not reflect this widely enough. The emotional problems of "Bertie" are highlighted by speech therapist Lionel Logue, proving that it is fixable. Adding to the drama is a war breaking out with Germany and a brother who is more interested in pursuing socialite Wallis Simpson than becoming yet another figure head. According to historians, several key details were smudged in order to heighten the suspense. I'm fine with taking liberties in small ways, but the fact that in the film is takes several years instead of the actual several months to correct George's speech, was a giant hole in the plot. It was an unbelievable script, full of other such holes, and inconsistencies. Though it ran smooth, fast for a longer film, it became tiresome to watch as Firth blunders through several speeches, and foams at the mouth while delivering a string of curse words as a therapeutic exercise. It wasn't bad, but it wasn't the perfect film we have all been led to expect.

Hopeful and inspiring.  Interesting look at history and developing technology in 1930's Britain.  Colin Firth is touching as the would be king who is afraid of speaking in public.  Geoffrey Rush is amusing as the Australian speech therapist who helps the king find his voice.  "Bertie" is stubborn and at first only wishes to work on mechanics.  The most powerful scene for me was probably when "Bertie" sits down for a stiff drink with Lionel over paint and a model airplane.  Lionel begins to become friend and counselor to "Bertie" because the death of his father brings up buried feelings of inadequacy from his childhood.  Eventually they can start dealing with the whole issue.  And there are many light-hearted quips to keep things from getting too heavy.  Still when Britain declares war on Germany in 1939, the idea of speaking to so many people across the British empire through the "wireless" is quite intimidating.  To arrive at the end and hear the King's rallying speech after so much work was very uplifting.  The entire supporting cast plays their roles admirably as well.

Director: Tom Hooper Starring: Colin Firth, Geoffrey Rush, Helena Bonham Carter, Guy Pearce Running time: 118 minutes Country: UK, Australia I was looking forward to seeing The King's Speech all year and now it is finally here! I must admit that I did actually enjoy it more than I was expecting to. It is a beautiful story that is truly inspiring and surprisingly a film that can and will make its audiences cry like it almost made me cry. Admittedly, I never really knew very much about King George VI until I saw this but he has really opened my eyes and has shown me that it is indeed Great Britain. I would naturally call The King's Speech an underdog story because Britain goes from bad to worse and then George picks this country up and fights! The film also demonstrated the passion and the pride that this country has and it is so great! I must also admit that there were some moments in The King's Speech that were pretty damn funny so yeah, this film did have its light-hearted and friendly moments aswell. I tell you what this reminded me of (not regarding the story but how the audience feel about leader of country and country itself) is Clint Eastwood's Invictus because that film demonstrated how great South Africa became because of one man. As far as awards go, this isn't the first time that a historical film involving kings and queens has been a contender for Best Picture. Let's not forget Elizabeth, A Man For All Seasons, The Private Life Of Henry VIII, The Queen and a few others but this easily surpasses all of them and I am not even sure whether any other historical film will be able to beat this one! I think most of them fail because the acting is rather weak on occasions and I just fail to feel any emotion or anything realistic about them. I mean, there are some historical royalty films that can be too complex for its audiences depending on the viewer(s) but this is quite possibly the easiest royalty story that I think I have watched. The King's Speech tells the story of the man who became King George VI, the father of Queen Elizabeth II. After his brother abdicates, George ('Bertie') reluctantly assumes the throne. Plagued by a dreaded stammer and considered unfit to be king, Bertie engages the help of an unorthodox speech therapist named Lionel Logue. Through a set of unexpected techniques, and as a result of an unlikely friendship, Bertie is able to find his voice and boldly lead the country through war. It is simple an outstanding cast! British actors Colin Firth, Helena Bonham Carter, Guy Pearce, Michael Gambon, Derek Jacobi and Australian actor Geoffrey Rush join together in front of the screen and show the nation and the world how great Britain was back then and that there is still hope for a Great Britain. All of the actors had a lot on their shoulders going into this film especially Colin Firth and Helena Bonham Carter as George and Elizabeth. Colin Firth was absolutely outstanding! It was unfortunate that he didn't win Best Leading Actor last year for A Single Man but I think he'll win it this time round. If not Colin Firth, it'll go to James Franco in 127 Hours. It goes to show that despite George VI didn't have full confidence publicly of being a king but he had the heart of one and he was and still is a fine example of great men in this country and Colin Firth showed that! I was on the journey with George and felt like a proud Englishman all the way through it. Firth's performance as King George VI is definitely one of the best male performances that I think I have ever watched. In the past, Geoffrey Rush has played supporting roles in quite a few historical films about history and films set in a historical era like this such as Shakespeare In Love, Elizabeth, Elizabeth: The Golden Age and Twelfth Night but his performance as Lionel Logue was just brilliant! I thought that the bond between Rush as Logue and Firth as George was like a firm hold from the very start to the very end and together, they both build a friendship that makes Britain strong in a dark time. Geoffrey Rush also made me laugh on occasions and he should get his rightly deserved Oscar nomination too. I was curious about Helena Bonham Carter playing Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon aka the Queen Mother seeing as Helena is perhaps the most unique and peculiar of all actresses and she's in a relationship and got children with the most unique and peculiar of all directors: Tim Burton. Anyway, I think she did an absolutely fantastic job and she made Elizabeth like a real hero because she was the one who went to Lionel Logue first for him to treat her husband George VI. I mean, yeah she did look like Elizabeth when she was younger, obviously, but she also looks like she would actually make a good Queen herself. To be honest, all three actors deserve their Oscar wins for their roles in this film. Other good performances from Guy Pearce as Edward VIII, Michael Gambon as George V, Timothy Spall as Winston Churchill and Sir Derek Jacobi as Cosmo Gordon Lang (Archbishop of Canterbury). Tom Hooper is a director who is the early stages of his career making feature films but he has almost reached the top already. He previously directed The Damned United which was a success but not like this one. He deserves all the credit that he put into this film and he had a lot on his shoulders as well seeing as he controls all what is going on on-set. Screenwriter David Seidler apparently had stuttering problems as a child as well so that is another key point that makes this film just so great! His script was solid, genuine, heartfelt and at times, hilarious! However, it will be tough for him to beat Chris Nolan's script in Inception though. Overall, The King's Speech is an absolutely magnificent film that is definitely one of the most moving and inspiring films that I have seen in a long time. It has made me feel proud to be English. As far as I'm concerned, despite The Social Network is the favourite for Best Picture and as brilliant as it is, The King's Speech along with Toy Story 3, Inception, Black Swan and 127 Hours, it completely swept it away! Her Majesty would be proud of this film and all of the actor's and maker's dedications towards the film. She may knight Colin Firth and maybe even Helena Bonham Carter for portraying her parents so amazingly! A masterpiece in every way and I would call it a tear-jerking film. I was just left speechless at the end of the film in the cinema.

This is based on the historical events of how in the 1930's Britain's sovereignty was faced with a leadership crisis. King George V (Michael Gambon) is rapidly ageing and looking for a true heir to his throne. Neither of his children are adequate candidates. His eldest son Edward VIII (Guy Pearce) is far too frivolous as he is looking to take up with an American woman who has already been divorced and remarried. The king's second son, Albert Frederick Arthur George (Colin Firth) or Bertie as his family calls him, seems like a more sensible choice but he is entirely lacking in confidence because of his terrible speech impediment. No amount of treatment has been able to cure Bertie of his condition. His wife Elizabeth Bowes Lyon (Helena Bonham Carter) seeks help from an unlikely source: a lower-class Australian speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). Bertie is initially reluctant because Lionel's unorthodox approach forces him out of his comfort zone. With the impending rise of Hitler though, Bertie begins to understand the urgency to inspire people's confidence in the British government and learns to trust Lionel. 

The King's Speech, a thoroughly entertaining slice of history, is just the third feature from director Tom Hooper. Yet it has still been crafted with a particular amount of delicacy. It's been photographed by cinematographer Danny Cohen with mostly drab colours. The overarching grey skies and dark textures of Bertie's suit are some of the subtle visual devices used to convey Britain's sense of dread and uncertainty at this time. The atmosphere is complimented by the pivotal subtext of David Seidler's intelligent screenplay, specifically the way people are won and lost on what they see and hear. Bertie's father describes how politicians are now nothing but actors because of technological improvements, like the radio and the way that this has, for better or worse, drawn the public closer to the lives of their leaders. It's an idea conveyed most extensively through the progressive friendship of Bertie and Lionel, allowing the film to succeed as a historical piece and equally as a film about social interaction. 

The sessions shared between Lionel and Bertie are the most crucial aspect of the narrative and the experience of both these terrific actors make these scenes shine. Firth, a current favourite for the Best Actor Oscar, has rarely been better. He has played critically suppressed men before, like his nominated performance in A Single Man, but his performance is distinguished through a number of extraordinary physical constraints. His stammering alone is heartbreaking to watch and listen to. Yet the way Firth struggles internally with his own body, trying to wrench the words out from his lungs, is what makes his work truly powerful. There are more poignant details revealing his isolation from his family and his rivalry with his inept brother too. But his role is enhanced most significantly by his palpable chemistry with Lionel, his antithesis. Whereas Firth is appropriately contained, Rush provides a wonderful burst of energy to the film. The script offers him endless opportunities for quiet humour and his comic timing remains impeccable. "You're peculiar", Bertie tells him, to which Lionel replies so finely: "I take that as a compliment". Lionel's charisma and humour is imperative in asserting Bertie's insecurities but also the corridor through which he will draw himself emotionally closer to the common man. There are also some unexpected angles to this friendship too, like whether Lionel is in some respects trying to influence the monarchy by coaching Bertie. In terms of writing and performances, The King's Speech is an inspired piece of historical cinema.

After the death of his father King George V (Michael Gambon) and the scandalous abdication of King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce), Bertie (Colin Firth) who has suffered from a debilitating speech impediment all his life, is suddenly crowned King George VI of England. With his country on the brink of war and in desperate need of a leader, his wife, Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter), the future Queen Mother, arranges for her husband to see an eccentric speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). After a rough start, the two delve into an unorthodox course of treatment and eventually form an unbreakable bond. With the support of Logue, his family, his government and Winston Churchill (Timothy Spall), the King will overcome his stammer and deliver a radio-address that inspires his people and unites them in battle. Based on the true story of King George VI, THE KING'S SPEECH follows the Royal Monarch's quest to find his voice.

Captivating and magnificent. Those are the words I use to describe this film. It's brilliantly crafted and well written.

For me, the film hits a deeper note. I can sympathize with the Duke of York, as I had a fear if public speaking. Everyone has to do it some time in their life, and some are better at it than others.

By taking such an epic scope of the film and narrowing it down to the perspective of one man, it makes the film more manageable when it comes to audience participation. We are seeing a Royal family struggle, but from the underdog.

As for the acting, masterful. Colin Firth is at his A game right now, giving King George VI the stammer and a little lisp when he improves. We feel his tumultuous affairs and the weight on his shoulders.  Geoffrey Rush plays the everyman, a mentor to the main character with his own goals and motivations.

Also excellent are Helena Bonham Carter, in a movie not directed by Tim Burton. She plays a mix of supportive and homeliness that is not too sappy. And Guy Pearce, he was so good I thought he was British actor Toby Stephens the entire movie, until the ending credits told me otherwise.

The film is well written. The only complaint is the transition between large periods of time, it simply cuts to a new location with a title and new year. They could have done this a bitter better since the movie says it takes place over many years, but it doesn't seem like it.

As for the pacing itself, amazing. Never a dull scene and the dialogue is exemplary. The character development is through the roof, giving humanness to a person of the past I've never even considered reading about in my spare time. It paints a nice portrait of a held back dysfunctional family in disarray over important matters.

The cinematography lends a hand into how it all plays out. There are few locations, but the camera floats in front of King George for some scenes, making it a sort of build up to the next scene. They also play around with angles a lot, giving variety to the scenes with sitting and conversation.

There is a very harmonious usage of Symphony No. 7 in A major, Op. 92, II. Allegretto by Beethoven with the climax. King George must address the nation (therefore the title) and it is used as he speaks. I've seen this done a few times before (Tarsem Singh's The Fall, Knowing) and this tops them both.

A wonderfully literate, sophisticated, and charming film, The King's Speech depicts British royalty in a fresh manner that brings warmth, humanity and humor to the proceedings. The suspense rivals James Franco's climactic moment in 127 Hours. And indeed, the Best Actor Oscar race seems to be neck and neck so far between Franco and Firth, who is heartbreaking and endearing as the reluctant King. Lovingly directed by Tom Hooper, The King's Speech not only brings to vivid life a piece of little known British history, it also illuminates a beautiful relationship between royalty and the commoner who can help. Geoffrey Rush gives a vibrant, full-bodied performance as George VI's speech therapist who teaches him more than just technique, he teaches him about heart and soul. Their scenes together are wondrous and as an actor and educator myself, I was transfixed by their characters' rapport. Driven largely by the twin historical engines of his older brother's abdication (Duke of Windsor and Wallis Simpson, an oft-told tale), and the onset of WWII and especially the Nazi threat, knowing that he was about to become King, Collin Firth's Duke goes against his instinctual and in-bred habits to surrender to Geoffrey Rush's character, an arrogant and shabby and very unorthodox speech therapist, not only a commoner but an Austrialian to boot. The interplay of class, affliction, psychology, courage and love that flows back and forth between these characters is something to behold, driven home by our knowledge that the King's radio speeches were a key part of the British spirit that helped win the War. An utterly exhilarating experience, and a guaranteed Oscar contender.

Remarkably old fashioned in its filmmaking and construction, The King's Speech shines with its perfect mix of wit, intelligence, and heart. Instead of being melodramatic and bombastic as so many period pieces, particularly those about monarchs, are, the film instead focuses on a sublime friendship that develops between two radically different men. Coupled with the utterly universal themes of inadequacy, The King's Speech is far more human and relatable than the majority of these pictures are. Director Hooper is not a showman but rather a firm and elegant filmmaker, allowing his subtle images and most of all his performers to shine. And this cast is more than up to the task. Between last year's A Single Man and now his work here, Colin Firth is slowly revealing more layers of his talent and proving to be one of the most complex and sublime actors we have. The legendary Geoffrey Rush is every bit his equal, never outshining him but working with him to form the perfect bond. Helena Bonham Carter, as cleaned up and sane as we have ever seen her, is lovely as the unwavering emotional support to Firth's Bertie/King George VI. 

Filled with a great deal of warmth, humor, and humanity, the film is a near revelation, attacking history with an unexpected spin. Never too shy to wink at what a monarchy and being a part of it entails, the film subtly explores the historical aspects of the period as well, with the inevitable start of World War II as well as the brief period in which Bertie's brother, played by the great Guy Pearce, served as King. But it is of course the aforementioned friendship as well as Bertie's attempt to overcome his impairment that makes the film work so well. 

There will, of course, be those who view the film as being too antediluvian or who often find historical work and period pieces to be boring. But for those who take a chance you will find one of the most intelligent and rewarding films of the year. And once again, Colin Firth deserves that damn Oscar.

Colin Firth gives a remarkable heart-wrenching performance as the stuttering Bertie who becomes King George VI.  Firth acts as a man who really has a speech imediment and puts his heart into the performance making it one of his best.

Geoffrey Rush plays Lionel the man who takes on the responsibility of helping Bertie overcome his stammering.  He puts emotion and humor into his portrayal capturing the average man in a bold way.

Helena Bonham-Carter uses subtle acting in her role as Bertie's wife showing mostly through facial expressions and physical mannerisms her desire for her husband to conquer his problem and also her love for him and the hurt she feels when she knows he is hurting or frustrated.

A great supporting cast including Guy Pearce and Timothy Spall, who is amazing as Winston Churchill, add incredibly to the film as well.  Tom Hooper shows in his direction that he knew exactly what he wanted to portray and made sure it came out in every scene and shot.

The photography is brilliant often showing up close shots of Bertie to help the audience feel the intensity of his frustration with his stammering or his fear of the microphone. The close ups on the mic itself imply that to Bertie the mic is in fact a character - one he is deathly afraid of as it exactly points out his major fault and does not allow him to escape it.

The editing enhances the story as does the sound. The sound mixing does an amazing job especially with the microphone scenes and the Lionel helping Bertie scenes.  The art direction and all other technical aspects of the film only enhance the overall viewing experience.

The King's Speech, in my opinion, is one of the best films of 2010 and will withstand the test of time.  It shows that no person is exempt from problems in life whether rich or poor, high position or low position.  It is an encouraging, often humorous, and hope-filled film.

"The King's Speech" does not shove exposition down your throat. Nor is its 1920s England backdrop and fancy costume made the star of the show. Even at its best, the movie, about King George VI (Colin Firth) and his encounters with a speech therapist (Geoffrey Rush) in preparation to lead his country into the throes of World War II, about morality and royalty, all of which trace to the roots of social conduct and a single morsel of existential dignity. Nope. "The King's Speech" just goes about making a buddy movie in a different way. 

Rush and Firth shine as friends in a time that doesn't feel morose, thanks largely to the direction by Tom Hooper, who allows these guys to stand out as actual characters. It's the best kind of costume drama -- one that all but ignores the costume and embraces the entertainment values of the drama. "The King's Speech" is brimming with good intentions and rich, honest humor, tacts lost in most lengthy period pieces that usually make even the people on screen cry with boredom. 

Hooper's flick is consistently brilliant from its creation of actual real-life set-ups that don't run together. It's the difference of character that the suspense derives from. And I can go into it deeper than that, but it'd be pretty much irrelevant to. The work that went into "The King's Speech", the funny and frankness, sit up front to one of the year's most surprising crowd-pleasers.

At first glance, you may think that The King's Speech is just stiff upper lip British drama. No, The King's Speech, about the real life stammering king who learned to rally his subjects, is a masterful achievement in direction, screenwriting and acting. King George VI (Colin Firth, amazing), the father of the present Queen Elizabeth II, met his match in Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), an eccentric speech therapist from Australia who helped this king discover his inner, stammer-free voice, and go on the radio in 1939 and rally his people to support Britain's declaration of war on Hitler's Germany.

The King's Speech emphasizes the power of words, not war. Screenwriter David Seidler struggled with his own stutter growing up, and his personal struggles informs The King's Speech deeply. He first conceived of The King Speech as a stage show, but went for the screen instead. He found a perfect director in Tom Hooper, the great talent who has seen Emmy love for John Adams, Elizabeth I, and episodes of Prime Suspect. Every frame is given a strong sense of urgency that transcends stuffy historical dreariness.

We first meet the king in 1925, where he is known as Prince Albert. He's attempting to speak at the British Empire Exhibition, but the words aren't coming, and his long silences fill the stadium. His embarrassment is  palpable, especially felt by his wife, Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter does more with looks and glances than words can ever hope) who discovers Logue and convinces Albert to see him. Albert dislikes being in Logue's presence, who requires that the two use first names. When Lionel calls Albert 'Bertie', his family nickname, Firth's reaction is priceless. Lionel's methods are like therapy sessions, in which he prods for details from his patients' personal life. He discovers a prince raised by a tough father, King George V (the great Michael Gambon), and a brother, Edward VIII (Guy Pearce) who has teased him all his life. Edward rocks the family when he abdicates the throne in order to marry the twice divorced American Wallis Simpson. That leaves Bertie next in line to be the new monarch.

Firth is absolutely brilliant in the role, investing this monarch with bruised nuance and beauty. An Oscar nominee for last year's A Single Man, Firth's performance is explosively marvelous, towering, and he deserves a heap of awards attention. And Rush matches him step for step. A failed actor, Lionel is prone to outrageous gestures, and Rush brings him to remarkable flesh and blood life. The two are amazing foils, Lionel the jolt willing to lay himself bare, Bertie the blue blood raised to keep all of it inside. Watching Lionel get Bertie to just lose it, whether sitting on the throne or goading him into a barrage of curse words, is hilarious and moving. And the scene in which Lionel's wife meets the king is especially rich, seeing as how the actress, Jennifer Ehle, played Firth's lover in the BBC's Pride and Prejudice.

The King's Speech isn't stuffed with pomp, it hasn't got the budget. Instead it's bursting with intimacy. Hooper directs the scene in which Lionel conducts the king as he delivers his first wartime speech marvelously. It's a salute to the human spirit and one of the best movies of 2010.

Movies are a form of entertainment that for the most part, are meant to sweep audiences away from all the negativity of the world.  Yet so few movies have been written in recent years that have managed to take audiences away quite as well as 'The King's Speech'.  It's a spectacularly written and acted period piece, that deserves every award which it's won.  Biopics are nothing new to the movie business.  But this story is less a biopic than a story about one man's personal struggles with himself and his family because of the stigma attached to stuttering.  It makes a man of great power into a relatable, human character.  That's even more obvious in his friendship with Lionel, his speech therapist.  Far too often, movies of this ilk take themselves too seriously, thus bogging them down, and making them boring.  Somehow, writer David Seidler has managed to avoid that pitfall, instead crafting a story that immerses audiences in its world.

David Seidler took a major risk in writing the script for this film.  A movie about a person with a speech disorder comes across as less than interesting on the surface.  But Seidler worked some kind of magic with the script.  He did everything right in crafting George's story.  He even managed to successfully mix in a sociological nature versus nurture discussion about the root of the stuttering disorder. It took a long time from the original release date of this movie for it to come to a theater near me, but it was well worth the wait. It's about Queen Elizabeth's father King George VI. He had a speech impediment and really hated having to speak publicly. Being the Duke of York it is impossible to avoid that once in awhile. When his older brother King Edward VIII abdicated because he wanted to marry a commoner, George found himself king suddenly. He had to speak at his coronation and had to make a radio address to the nation when England declared war on Germany (World War II). With the help of a speech therapist, he was able to overcome that handicap and give a clear and reassuring speech. I think Colin Firth should be nominated for a Best Actor Oscar for this. George was a man of many moods, often frustrated and angry at his situation, often arrogant with his commoner tutor, but loving to his daughters and capable of learning not only to speak clearly but also to develop a friendship free of condescension with his tutor. Firth played those moods and the struggle with stuttering remarkably well.  It's nice to see Helena Bonham Carter in something that's not creepy for once, and my mother says she enjoyed seeing wonderful older actors like Derek Jacobi. This is a really good movie: it deals with an important historical period, a human disability, personal struggle and strength of character in more than one character, with grace and humanity but without sentimentality.  Well worth the price of a ticket at one of the more expensive theaters.

His speech therapist (Geoffrey Rush - Shine, Pirates of the Caribbean, Shakespeare In Love) is slightly unorthodox but knows how to get results.  His treatment of the future king-of-England puts Bertie (Firth) in his place and the two form a dependable friendship that is admirable.  George's wife (Helena Bonham Carter -- Howard's End, Wings of the Dove, Alice in Wonderland) is patient and kind and stands by her man (she is the future Queen Mum of the present Queen Elizabeth II).  The trio's performances are all marvelous and have ALL been nominated for Academy Awards -- deservingly.  That the film is light on the history and it glosses over some fairly important details (King Edward's [Guy Pearce - L.A. Confidential, Memento, The Hurt Locker] Nazi-sympahtizing ways) is rather disturbing; but I was able to still enjoy the production.  It is a glorious merging together of art direction, music, costume design and production values.  It is top-notch and something to see.  Costume drama/period pieces don't tend to attrach a large-audience; but I think The King's Speech is special in that it is a movie for everyone.  Watch out for this one ... while it isn't the best picture I have seen of the year (because of its historical inaccuracies); I think it is a force to be reckoned with.  The King's Speech will have you talking about it long after you've seen it (I saw it a month ago and just got around to this review ... see I am still talking about it).

Timothy Spall and Michael Gambon both make the most out of small roles, especially Spall, whose Churchill is right on point.
Director Tom Hooper also deserves much of the credit to the success of the film, as does the art department. The old fashioned, saturated cinematography is right on point, with the colours becoming more vibrant as Bertie becomes more comfortable with his role as King George VI. One of the most surprising things I've discovered is how many people are truly terrified by the thought of public speaking. In a list of most common fears, public speaking will usually beat sickness, spiders, or even death. I personally have never had a fear of public speaking, as quiet as I am, if I need to talk to a big group of people I will, no big deal. King George VI was not like me. He had a fear of public speaking so serious that he would stutter and choke when even speaking to a single person. Even at times with his own family. And he was made King at a time when radio and mass media were newly invented means of communication. Shitty timing for him. And so forms the plot of The King's Speech.

If The King's Speech wins the Oscar for best picture in March, I won't be disappointed. Tom Hooper is no stranger to taking boring concepts and making them entertaining and accessible. The miniseries John Adams could have been a historic snore fest if he hadn't found a way to tell the story in a compelling way. And last year's The Damned United would have been just another forgettable underdog sports flick if he hadn't given it the grit and visual excitement it needed to be more.

Although I don't think it is the best picture of the year(like so many critics have stated), it is a solid good flick of 2010, and an all-around enjoyable film. "The King's Speech" deals with a historical issue in which the 6th King of Britain struggled to take the throne after the death of his tyrannical father. Faced with little hope, a speech impediment, and low odds, "Bertie's" main quest ultimately becomes curing his stammer. Colin Firth plays Bertie quite astonishingly, what with a couple of hoo's and ha's. His performance is natural which is ironic, being as Bertie is a forced character. His disability to speak publicly and even socially make it frustrating and some-what humorous for the audience to follow, but in the end it's an all around Oscar-worthy roll. With the aid of Lionel, a failed actor(portrayed by Geoffrey Rush), the King comes to his throne in the end with a rekindled sort of respect for himself, his country, and his family. It's a particularly moving film--on more parts then none. One scene Firth's character breaks into huge emotional tears, and the performance is chilling and great to watch. Helena Bonham Carter supports Firth and Rush with her subtle and sarcastic humor, and overall "royal-highness" like presence. She truly is natural at period pieces, and I feel Bonham Carter should sometimes stick to rolls like these. In the act of being more subtle, her ability to perform ultimately shines more then is has before. And seeing Geoffrey Rush perform is no chore, he also is quite a natural at playing a seemingly eccentric actor posing as a doctor for the troubled king. There are many scenes in this movie which show off how well it was made, and how much went into it. You can imagine with authentic looking costumes like the ones shown here, a lot of work must've gone into the production of this picture. I couldnâ(TM)t see any other movie winning the Oscar for best costume design or makeup. But as far as original screenplay goes, I'm not so sure. True is is original, but the fact that it was based on a true story makes that particular category name, questionable. Howver, that is beside the point. "The King's Speech" is a touching, well made film that highlights the now "spruced-up" careers of the three astonishing leads.

This morning, I was fortunate to attend an advanced screening, amongst a sold-out audience (not so fortunate: at least 150 others, qued-up down the street, around the corner, hoping for tickets, but turned away, disappointed), and ... the film was MORE THAN WELL-WORTH THE WAIT , as well as an early rise to attend on a Sunday!

Simply ... majestic.  Exquisite, flawless performances from Firth and Rush.  Both: guaranteed Oscar nods (if not, wins!).  Guy Pearce: excellent. I'm on the fence about Helena Bonham Carter; she was good, but part of me somewhat feels that she was miscast as Elizabeth (The Queen Mother).

More than a few scenes moved me to tears: 

*  the cruelty & neglect described of Bertie's (George VI) childhood.

*  David (Edward VIII) breaking-down upon the reality that he had succeeded the crown as George V died.  Attempting to seek comfort in the arms of his mother (Queen Mary), with she completely uncertain of how to even embrace her son.

*  tenderness and hands-on parenting by Bertie & Elizabeth of their daughters, Princesses Elizabeth & Margaret â" a complete contrast to what Bertie & David had known as children.

I could go-on, but this would ruin the film for others.  And this is not a film to be missed, folks.

One personal observation: Firth, Bonham-Carter, and the two young actresses whom play their princess daughters all have brown eyes.  In actuality, the late Queen Mother, the late King George VI, Queen Elizabeth II, and the late Princess Margaret all have/had BLUE eyes.

Un elemento constante en The King's Speech (2010) es el micrófono. Y cada vez que Albert "Bertie", Duque de York (Colin Firth, indiscutible ganador del Oscar a Mejor Actor este año), ve uno o se pone frente a él, entra en un estado de pánico incontenible. No es el pánico escénico común y corriente, sino un estado de ansiedad tremendo, debido al impedimento que sufre: el tartamudeo. Es un estado incapacitante para Albert quien, siendo hijo del rey Jorge V (Michael Gambon, en una pequeña participación), o sea una figura pública, está completamente expuesto a la crítica y a toda clase de burlas. Como en la escena que abre el filme, justo cuando Albert tiene que dar un discurso en un hipódromo de Wembley, a ser transmitido durante la clausura de un evento.

No es extraño que la película de Tom Hooper, realizador con una sensibilidad especial para melodramas de época (como lo mostró en la teleserie "John Adams), haya también ganado el Oscar a Mejor Director y Mejor Película. Es una feel good movie en toda la extensión de la palabra, sobre la lucha que tiene que llevar un hombre para superar una desesperante incapacidad que tiene para hablar. No es cualquier hombre, sino un presumido hombre de la nobleza británica, que tiene que mostrar su lado más vulnerable y humano para curar su tartamudeo.

After the death of his father King George V (Michael Gambon) and the scandalous abdication of King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce), Bertie (Colin Firth) who has suffered from a debilitating speech impediment all his life, is suddenly crowned King George VI of England. With his country on the brink of war and in desperate need of a leader, his wife, Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter), the future Queen Mother, arranges for her husband to see an eccentric speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). After a rough start, the two delve into an unorthodox course of treatment and eventually form an unbreakable bond. With the support of Logue, his family, his government and Winston Churchill (Timothy Spall), the King will overcome his stammer and deliver a radio-address that inspires his people and unites them in battle. Based on the true story of King George VI, THE KING'S SPEECH follows the Royal Monarch's quest to find his voice.

I'm not usually one for royal family films or really anything with corsets, hoop skirts, or tightly bound bodices.  Give me aliens sucking humans into spaceships any day (just not SKYLINE!) over a room full of people gavotting around to some godforsaken harpsichord nightmare.  So imagine my trepidation going into a film about the King of England learning how to overcome his stutter.  

Well, I'm happy to report that THE KING'S SPEECH manages to play quite wonderfully, especially to people like me.  This is a film which manages to undercut all the pomp and circumstance usually found in films of this type and get to the heart of what makes people human.  A major reason for this is that so much of the film puts our Royals into very ordinary surroundings.  We're not watching a King sitting on a throne, but instead see him in lower middle class surroundings.  I think it's why I always treasured THE PRINCE AND THE PAUPER so much as a teen.  Colin Firth, so great last year in A SINGLE MAN, is wonderful at combining his bouts of rage with his insecurities as King George VI.  Geoffrey Rush plays the speech therapist with such humor, but keeps him very vivid and strong instead of going the campy route he did in SHAKESPEARE IN LOVE.  Helena Bonham Carter, after a string of crazy cuckoo roles, returns to her upper crust roots here as the woman we would all know will become QUEEN MUM.  She gives a very sweet, controlled performance here, showing great steely nerve underneath her loving exterior.  It's quietly awesome, and I'm sure all three will get Oscar nominations.  

This film is more about class divides, and how we can and should look past them, than it is about watching a man learning how to give a speech.  It's witty, clever, heartfelt, and filmed with lots of strange fisheye lenses, off kilter framing, and enough odd tableau style master shots to trick you into thinking you're watching anything but one of those horrible Masterpiece Theater monstrosities.  And that's a recommendation!

A historical drama about the unconventional relationship between Bertie (Colin Firth), suddenly crowned King George VI of England, and his eccentric speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). Bertie's wife, Elizabeth (Helena Bonham-Carter), the future Queen, hires Logue to help him overcome a stammer. After the death of his father, King George V (Michael Gambon), his brother Edward VIII (Guy Pearce) is abdicated from the throne, following a brief reign amid a scandalous marriage, ascending Bertie to the crown. According to events presented here, Bertie must overcome a speech impediment to deliver a radio address to the British people on the brink of World War II. Written by David Seidler and directed by Tom Hooper, the material is dangerously close to Masterpiece Theater territory. The offbeat humor in detailing the class warfare between the therapist and the king helps to balance the pomposity. The filmmakers err at avoiding any mention of Nazi appeasement within the monarchy in favor of simplistic heroism. Colin Firth is terrific at drawing us into the vulnerability and inadequacy of a powerful leader; Helena Bonham Carter is a sympathetic Elizabeth; Timothy Spall seems to be impersonating Alfred Hitchcock instead of Winston Churchill but he's still effective. Fine cinematography by Danny Cohen; music by Alexandre Desplat. Won Oscars for Best Picture, Actor (Colin Firth), Director, Original Screenplay. With Derek Jacobi, Jennifer Ehle.

Here's a case where I just don't understand the hype, yet again. Maybe because its a period piece, or the subject matter, or the names, but this movie is being hailed as perfection, and I don't see it. It was a good movie, with performances that were better than the movie around them. It was inspiring and uplifting, but I guess I missed something. Watch this movie to see Colin Firth in a fine performance met by an equally fine performance by Geoffrey Rush, and also some zippy writing.
The King's Speech centers around the Duke of York who has a stammer. He struggles in public speeches, but luckily he doesn't have to worry, because he won't have to be king. But, wait, yes he will. His brother wants sex and marriage more than he wants to lead his country against the sweeping nazi forces. So, King George VI has to step in and be the figurehead against his country. With the invention of the radio, that just got way harder, especially for a stammerer.
After a slew of failures his steadfast wife sets him up with a new speech therapist, who is unconventional. Through a montage or two, and a series of sessions, not much headway is made. Anytime there is there is always a setback, like Bertie getting upset at the therapist over his pryiing int personal matters or his lack of formality, or one of the family matters in the royal family, sets him a-stammering again. Which of course leads to there unlikely friendship, and ultimate success on the greatest stage.
Its made more poignant by the fact the force he opposes is one of the greatest public speakers of all time, Hitler. They need a king who is a leader, and that is not what stammerers do best.
The acting is what saves the movie. Firth is layered as a man who struggled with the expectations of a King for a father, the weight of a country on his shoulders, the lack of friends because of the royal lifestyle, and a man hampered by a stammer. The stammering is done with care and grace, and I believe Geoffrey Rush said it best in an interview. The point isn't to try to stammer, but to try and communicate. That is what is heartbreaking, is seeing a man who is trying to say something, who has something to say, and can't.
Geoffrey Rush is all wily charm and zippy one liners as a man who refuses to give up and refuses to acknowledge formailities he thinks will hamper the therapy. All in all its a good movie, but nothing is ever in doubt, and things feel repetitive as its a cycle of small improvement, set back, fight, apologizing, improvement. I'm not slighting it for the formula at all, I jsut wanted to be more moved as I was getting there.

The Duke of York, Albert Fredrick Arthur George (or Bertie as we affectionately come to know him), has a problem. Having been neglected and mistreated all his life in the shadow of older brother Edward, the heir to their father's throne, Bertie has developed a nervous stammer that undermines him and the significance of his royal station every time he attempts to speak. His wife Elizabeth seeks the aid of Australian speech therapist Lionel Logue, who is ambitious about getting to the root of Bertie`s troubles. The mechanics of speaking is not the issue. It's poor Bertie's confidence and sense of self-worth that needs a shot in the arm, especially with WWII looming on the horizon.
Colin Firth is quite excellent as Bertie. He's able to elicit our sympathy easily enough, but it's the more rough-around-the-edge qualities like his quick temper and social elitism that bring a sense of humanity to his character. He plays very well with Geoffrey Rush (as Logue), enjoying a warm but sometimes tense chemistry from which stems the movie's heart. Themes about class distinctions and inequality are made, albeit a tad bluntly, by David Seidler's witty script, and are fleshed out even more by Eve Stewart's magnificent production design.

Albert finds another problem after his brother, The Duke of Windsor (played by Guy Pearce) who is crowned as the new Kings after the loss of their father, is planning on marrying a two times divorced woman. Intense and intimate rehearsal with Lionel makes Albert feels more comfortable and more open than before until it becomes too close and the two is having misunderstanding. And, let's start the new year with my fisrt review. Saw this movie 2 nights ago. This movie is about two things only: the acting and then direction. The latter, we'll get to that later, but, as I suspected by reading about it and going to the theater, it has all the right ingredients for Oscar gold. How many it is going to get? I don't know, but one is for sure: Colin Firth's bombastic performance as the stammering Duke of York who later turns into King George VI (the father of today's British Queen Elizabeth, in case you were wondering). Mr. Firth's performance from the moment the movie starts and reveals to us his speech impediment is an embodiment of pure work of art. He was deeply committed to this role and through the movie, he is completely mesmerizing and hypnotic just to look at. His acting is this movie is the way any actor is supposed to be acting. I can't stress enough how good he was in this movie.

And Geoffrey Rush's performance. I don't know who are going to be the lead contenders for Best Supporting Actor, but I'm positively sure, Mr. Rush will be at the top of the list. As a failed Shakespearian actor who takes on the speech therapy career, the interaction with Mr. Firth's character through the movie is seriously funny, dramatic and just a magnificent beauty just to watch. To say that in this movie he shows us why he's one of the top 5 actors alive is an understatement.

Many movies has presented us, at the core of their sotylines, couples where their relationship develop and grow under different circumstances. Whether it's love, friendship, hate or parenthood. "The King's Speech" presents us another type of couple that develop into something else, a servant making a King. Mr. Firth and Mr. Rush's relationship grows in an unusual way, which  I never seen in movies before.

Of course, we have to mention that Helena Bonham Carter's performance. She was nothing short of magnificent as the Duchess of York, also the future Queen Mother, trying to help out her husband. One thing that I loved about her performance is the fact that we finally get to see her outside of a Tim Burton movie, and she released all her potential in this one. Also, Guy Pierce and Michael Gambon were too nothing short of magnificent.

Another understatement: Tom Hooper, the director, delivered a superb movie, just in terms of acting alone. Nevermind the set, the art decoration, the costumes and the cinematography. Whatever he demanded or asked from his actors, especially from Mr. Firth anbd Mr. Rush, was right on the money and delivered in a powerful manner. Also, as many other movies before his, between the lines you can see that this movie was his own attempt to critize or take a poke at the House of Windsor. Can you blame him?

Bottom line: Go see it!!! Just for Mr. Firth's performance alone. Highly highly recommended.

"The King's Speech" is a delightful trifle. It is put together so well by director Tom Hooper and has such a splendid and humane lead performance from Colin Firth that some may mistake it for more than it is. It's a television-level story tarted up with glistening vocabulary, great sets and costumes, and solid direction. You can polish a piece of glass until it shines brilliantly, but that doesn't make it a diamond. (I was not exactly surprised when I learned that Hooper is a television director trying his hand at cinema.)

Firth plays Prince Albert, who ascended the British throne just a few years before the start of World War II. We meet him several years before this, when his father, King George V, was in his dotage. Albert and his devoted wife (beautifully and warmly played by Helena Bonham Carter) have been in a years-long struggle to cure Albert of his near-constant stammer. They finally come upon an unorthodox, peculiar speech therapist (Geoffrey Rush, injecting much humor into the role) who becomes a close confidant and aide to Albert all through his reign.

One of the many joys of this enjoyable little film is the extraordinary experience of seeing Firth, Carter and Rush on the screen at the same time. I sometimes felt I had died and gone to acting heaven. Hooper apparently coached them to bring out the humility and warmth of their characters, rather than the stoicism and scholarship that actors typically exude when they play royalty. This was much appreciated.

But it cannot be denied that the story doesn't go much beyond a celebration of self-esteem. Great acting it may be, but, as a film, great art it is not.

After the death of his father King George V (Michael Gambon) and the scandalous abdication of King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce), Bertie (Colin Firth) who has suffered from a debilitating speech impediment all his life, is suddenly crowned King George VI of England. With his country on the brink of war and in desperate need of a leader, his wife, Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter), the future Queen Mother, arranges for her husband to see an eccentric speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). After a rough start, the two delve into an unorthodox course of treatment and eventually form an unbreakable bond. With the support of Logue, his family, his government and Winston Churchill (Timothy Spall), the King will overcome his stammer and deliver a radio-address that inspires his people and unites them in battle. Based on the true story of King George VI, THE KING'S SPEECH follows the Royal Monarch's quest to find his voice.

I'm generally okay with movies taking artistic liberties for dramatic and emotional purposes, yet it bothers me here since the film does a good job of capturing the time period so accurately. It does that, but nicks its own consistency by playing up certain things over others in such a way that is becomes rather narrow minded in its focus.

Basically what I'm saying is that the film is heavy handedly exaggerating the king's stammer to get him more sympathy, but it's unnecessary because the audience has no trouble feeling for him to begin with. Last year's Firth vehicle "A Single Man", both stylish and silly, looked like a dress rehearsal for major prizes. This could well be his accession: a sustained piece of precision technical acting that allows us to feel every word catching in the King's throat like a rogue herringbone. Yet just as Eliza Doolittle needed her Henry Higgins, so too the King must have his joker, and Firth's wouldn't be the performance it is without Rush on hand and poke and provoke him into better expressing himself. Logan is not the most fragrant character ever to appear in an Oscar-friendly period piece - he first emerges to the sound of a flushing toilet, and there are no obvious signs he's washed his hands - but his role and purpose is pristinely clear: to relieve the emotional constipation that has been the hallmark of so many Firth performances over the years. It works, too: clock the litany of curse words - real potty language - the unstoppered King comes out with around the film's halfway point... What Hooper's film shares with "The Queen" is a way of getting us to think about the Royals less as an institution than as individuals weighed down by pomp and circumstance. George struggles with his words, Edward with his deeds, and both realise they must embrace New World forms of modernity - whether American or Antipodean, radio or therapy - if they are going to survive. Princesses Elizabeth and Margaret, pretty in pink by the fire with their corgis, are on hand to assure us there will be some kind of happy ending, yet this incisive and quietly subversive filmed history more generally approaches royalty with something altogether more probing and critical than outright deference: for once, they become very much the subjects.

The King's Speech is a remarkable movie in that it perfectly executes the tying together of everything you want in a film: strong acting from every character; a well defined plot based on an interesting premise; a wonderful score; emotionally satisfying.

With WWII looming ever closer and his brother having just abdicated his seat on the throne so that he could marry a twice divorced American woman, Albert (Colin Firth) is thrust into a position he never anticipated. Taking the name King George VI he is to rule the monarchy as it enters war and he knows he must emote a strong and confident demeanor. There is one problem - he has a severe and persistent stutter. The film opens with an emotionally charged scene of Albert in 1925 as he addresses a crowd at the closing ceremonies of the British Empire Exposition at Wembley Stadium. Stepping to the microphone all goes wrong as he completely freezes. With his wife's (Helena Bonham Carter - the future Queen Elizabeth) ongoing support Bertie (his nickname to only his closest family and friends) goes through a multitude of speech therapists in pursuit of solving his problem. It is the eventual meeting with Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) that will forever change his life. Working together closely and running the gauntlet of highs and lows, Logue works feverishly to help the, first future king, and later king as the film leads up to its most pivotal scene - the 9 minute war time declaration speech to broadcast around the world.

At the heart of the film is the relationship between Bertie and Lionel. It is such an unlikely friendship between two very big personalities that it effortlessly leads to high emotional points but surprisingly also lends itself to some very funny scenes and comments, something you may not see coming in this type of film. Firth, Rush and Bonham Carter are all excellent in their roles and it would be no surprise to me to see any of them nominated for multiple awards (though the queen's role may be too limited to be considered.)

George, or Bertie (as he is called by his family), has a problem: he stammers when he speaks. VISO Snapshot: The King's Speech is destined for several award nominations and will probably even walk away with a few statues... BUT it still feels like your father's Best Picture.

Festivals are truly the most interesting part of the film industry. A week before The Toronto International Film Festival we had barely even heard of Tom Hooper's feature film, The King's Speech, and now it has all but secured it's spot in the running for Best Picture and perhaps the first win for the lead actor Colin Firth. As far as the Oscar checklist goes: Period Piece... check. True Story... check. British... check. Yep, this one has a serious shot. But what of the actual film?

The King's Speech tells the story of  King George VI (Colin Firth), who, after his brother abdicates, reluctantly assumes the throne. Plagued by a dreaded stutter and considered unfit to be king, George or 'Bertie' engages the help of an unorthodox Aussie speech therapist named Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). Through a set of unexpected techniques, and as a result of an unlikely friendship, Bertie is able to find his voice and boldly lead the country into war by delivering a rousing... speech. You know, the King's Speech.

The film marks the feature return of Tom Hooper, the Emmy award winning director behind John Adams, and features an all star cast that includes Firth, Rush, Helena Bonham Carter and Guy Pierce. Speaking of an 'all-star' cast, they are truly the best thing about this royal bio-pic and the leading trio each deserves Academy Award nominations (which are all but assured for the first two... HBC has some stronger competition in the Best Actress race).

Colin Firth is absolutely genius in his portrayal of the stammering monarch King George VI... we mean, Bertie, and this may finally be the role that sees Firth walk away with Oscar gold (and he would be deserving of all accolades as he delivers a performance as memorable and demanding as James Franco in 127 Hours or Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network). Rush won't win but he also will probably sneak away with an Oscar nom in the Best Supporting male category.

The writing was as sharp as the acting and there were some breathtakingly beautiful cinematography BUT it also came across as stuffy and antiquated at times. The depth of field is so flat, Hooper seems content to present the story as a series of tableaux-portraits (tableaux vivant) which unfortunately doesn't make the arguably dry subject matter any more dynamic. This is the anti-3D (which is fine since we're not big on 3D anyways).

Like we mentioned before, The King's Speech is destined for several award nominations and probably will walk away with a few statues BUT for our money it's just a little too stale... a little too safe... a little too stiff to truly be the year's best. This is your father's Best Picture.

"The King's Speech" works splendidly on a wide range of levels: as a funny and moving human story; as a document on an important but not widely known piece of history; and as an entertaining character piece with indelible performances. I went into it already aware of its high praise but still found myself responding to it on my own terms. That, I think, is the mark of a truly great film.

It tells the story of King George VI's offhand rise to the English throne and chronicles his inexperience and anxiety leading up to World War II. The title of film is a double entendre, referring not only to the actual speech King George VI gave in 1939 to the British people letting them know their country was at war with Germany, but also to his attempt to overcome his "bloody" stammer. 

After fumbling his speech at the British Empire Exhibition in 1925, the unbeknownst future king, Albert, a.k.a. Bertie (Colin Firth), seeks the help of traditional doctors to correct his impediment. Most of them have antiquated notions for addressing his problem, like telling his majesty to fill his mouth with marbles and enunciating. If such a method worked for the ancient Greeks, who's to say it wouldn't work now? 

Bertie's wife, Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter), seeks a different therapist, an Australian named Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). He's not like the other doctors in that he isn't as hell-bent on paying reverence to Bertie as much as curing him. In a dark, damp and dreary little office, where you have to close two doors to the elevator, Lionel tells Bertie, "My house, my rules." His highness shall not smoke; he shall call Lionel by his first name; and he shall pay Bertie a visit every day, with no ifs, ands or buts about it. 

As Bertie's visits with Lionel proceed, he must also deal with familial issues like his ageing father, King George V (Michael Gambon), who's always put more emphasis on propriety than love; and his irreverently carefree older brother, Edward VIII (Guy Pearce). The film takes us through the history of George V passing away and leaving the throne to Edward, who would subsequently abdicate because he wanted to marry a twice-divorced American woman from Baltimore. With Bertie next in line, Lionel assures him he'd make a great king, but how can Bertie believe him when he can't even speak?

One of the reasons I probably found "The King's Speech" so thoroughly engaging is because I wasn't aware of its history. I actually learned something watching this film. But even if you're familiar with the events, it's still appealing and involving because it puts its characters first. Despite it always relaying the current time and place, it remains a human story instead of just a filmed version of a textbook. David Seidler's screenplay is ingenious the way it's able to weave together the real-life events with the human drama and often laugh-out-loud humor. 

Colin Firth is at the forefront of the picture and he plays stiff and nervous like no other. It helps that Firth already has a boyish face, which matches perfectly with his character's timid disposition. He's sure to receive a (deserved) Best Actor Oscar nomination and may even walk away with a win. But as good as Firth is, he's often upstaged by the magnificent Rush, whose role as Lionel is more juicy and written with more punchy dialogue, or maybe it's that Rush already brings so much to the table he transcends the writing. Either way, he creates a character so cheerful and affable a whole movie could be made about him. In fact, I would have preferred more scenes with Lionel simply reciting Shakespeare. There was just something pleasant about them. 

"The King's Speech" is the type of film where its individual parts--the writing, directing, acting and production values, accented by Eve Stewart's visionary production design, which places us in a distinct 1930s England--come together seamlessly and we realize each artist is at the top of their form. Director Tom Hooper has crafted a picture that's serious and light, deep and funny, and we're able to relax and let it teach and entertain us. As a historical drama, the story's eventual destination is perhaps inevitably preordained, but we're still delighted by how it gets there.

After his disastrous closing speech at the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley, England's Prince Albert is impelled to see Lionel Logue, an Australian speech therapist. Inspiring period film is a stately historical drama about living with a disability, specifically stuttering. Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush are an unlikely duo, engaging as student and teacher respectively. English director Tom Hooper wisely trusts David Seidler's marvelous script to support the film. The words carry the story and empower the actors to give life to the dialogue. They completely inhabit their roles to the point where their verbal exchanges are riveting. A subtle picture that demonstrates the future King George VI was just an ordinary man, a modest man thrust into extraordinary circumstances.  In spite of his wealth and privilege, the audience actually feels pity for a man about to become king.  Similarly unexpected is that something as mundane as a radio-address could hold the comparable excitement of an Olympic athlete striving for the gold medal. Yes, This is one of those distinguished dramas they'll watch in school. It has the respectable feel of a history lesson. The difference here is the entertainment value, genuinely touching and surprisingly funny.  An uplifting tale.

Captivating and magnificent. Those are the words I use to describe this film. It's brilliantly crafted and well written.

For me, the film hits a deeper note. I can sympathize with the Duke of York, as I had a fear if public speaking. Everyone has to do it sometime in their life, and some are better at it than others.

By taking such an epic scope of the film and narrowing it down to the perspective of one man, it makes the film more manageable when it comes to audience participation. We are seeing a Royal family struggle, but from the underdog.

As for the acting, masterful. Colin Firth is at his A game right now, giving King George VI the stammer and a little lisp when he improves. We feel his tumultuous affairs and the weight on his shoulders. Geoffrey Rush plays the everyman, a mentor to the main character with his own goals and motivations.

Also excellent are Helena Bonham Carter, in a movie not directed by Tim Burton. She plays a mix of supportive and homeliness that is not too sappy. And Guy Pearce, he was so good I thought he was British actor Toby Stephens the entire movie, until the ending credits told me otherwise.

The film is well written. The only complaint is the transition between large periods of time, it simply cuts to a new location with a title and new year. They could have done this a bitter better since the movie says it takes place over many years, but it doesn't seem like it.

As for the pacing itself, amazing. Never a dull scene and the dialogue is exemplary. The character development is through the roof, giving humanness to a person of the past I've never even considered reading about in my spare time. It paints a nice portrait of a held back dysfunctional family in disarray over important matters.

The cinematography lends a hand into how it all plays out. There are few locations, but the camera floats in front of King George for some scenes, making it a sort of build up to the next scene. They also play around with angles a lot, giving variety to the scenes with sitting and conversation.

There is a very harmonious usage of Symphony No. 7 in A major, Op. 92, II. Allegretto by Beethoven with the climax. King George must address the nation (therefore the title) and it is used as he speaks. I've seen this done a few times before (Tarsem Singh's The Fall, Knowing) and this tops them both.

Firth takes on the role of King George VI of England, also known to his family as "Bertie", who carries a speech impediment, causing him to constantly stammer. Acting as a voice for an empire which is seemingly on the brink of war, the King must be a voice for a nation and a people in order to achieve unity and strength to fight The Third Reich.

Avoiding details and getting straight to the point, Firth's representation of a troubled Bertie is phenomenal. Ah, yes.  Prestige Season.  The special time of year when the air turns crisper, the season turns jolly and the thoughts of film executives turn fondly to awards season.  Blockbusters may bring in the bucks but awards bring in the margins and if a studio's three million dollar pet project can get some Oscar buzz, it's all profit for Mama Hollywood.  Even better, now is the time when us film geeks get to see the good stuff, the stuff that allows us to wax poetic over pints about films nobody else in the bar will ever leave their homes to watch.  While this can be seen as putting on airs of snobbery to the Transformers crowd, to us film lovers this is our time of year to gloat about our hobby and revel in the cream of the cinematic crop.  And with a ballot leading seven Golden Globe nominations, The King's Speech is definitely on the tip of film foodies' lips this December, and for very good reason.

Providing a bare synopsis of this movie fails in two ways.  One, it makes the film sound haughty and overly high-minded and two, it makes the thing sound unbearably boring.  Allow me to demonstrate:

"The Kings Speech is the true story of the Duke of York, who, after the sudden abdication of his brother, King Edward VIII, has to deal with the political realities of a lifelong speech impediment.  With the help of his wife and an unorthodox speech therapist, the newly crowned king must overcome this obstacle and make an important speech to a country on the brink of war". 

Christ, I put myself to sleep while typing that!  I think the name Edward, all by itself, has the same effect on me as Ambien.

As you can see, nothing brings me down more than a standard biopic and thank the heavens, The King's Speech is anything but.  In fact, director Tom Hooper does an outstanding job of balancing historic accuracy, real human drama and an uncanny knack for humor in his latest film.  While the movie is shot, at times, in a very standard biopic way, Hooper treats the film like a stage performance, giving the characters room to breathe, interact and co-exist.  Also, it's worth noting again how damn funny this film is without ever getting silly, saccharine or overly light.  What results is a well balanced character study of a visionary doctor and a tortured monarch.

Like most films of this type, the setting and dressing would be nothing without some fine performances and this is where The Kings Speech shines brightest.  Colin Firth plays the speech addled duke and does so with a conviction, honesty and integrity that is marvelous to watch.  Unlike the disappointing A Single Man, Firth is unencumbered by high minded photography and is instead allowed to encompass the spirit of King George VI without the overly directed meddling of Firth's last effort.  Brimming with subtlety, humor and raw emotion, Firth's performance just might win him the Best Actor Oscar he missed out on last year.

That being said, if the Academy glosses over Firth, then they better hand over the trophy to the man who plays the good doctor, Geoffrey Rush.  In playing the politically irreverent doctor, Rush also does a great job in balancing humor, empathy and an unwavering knowledge in the human condition.  Firth and Rush complement each other wonderfully and every minute they are on screen together is a joy to watch.  Helena Bonham Carter also does a fine job as Firth's patient wife and the underrated Guy Pearce is well cast as the bad boy King Edward VIII, rounding out one of the best casts of the year.

All told, The Kings Speech is on the short list for winning Best Picture this year and for very good reason.  One of the trickiest things to achieve in any artistic endeavor is balance.  Lean too much to one side of the emotional spectrum, be it too dramatic, too funny or too sappy and you lose a portion of the audience.  What The King's Speech achieves better than any Oscar season film I've seen this year is reach a point where literally anybody could watch this film and enjoy it.  Hopefully the Oscar buzz surrounding this movie is enough to propel it to wide screening status as I truly feel anybody and everybody will find something to love from this movie.  A sublimely made film in almost every aspect, The King's Speech is one of the easiest film going recommendations I've made this year and is a slam dunk nominee for Best Picture.  While I would have whistled a different tune after seeing 127 Hours a month before, the accessibility, charm and stunning acting all make this my current pick for film's highest honor.
