Although it is now emerging as the front runner for the Best Picture Oscar, don't think of "The King's Speech" as a boring, stuffy, Oscar-bait piece of dull safeness. It's not any of that at all- and perhaps more surprising, it may be one of those few critically raved movies that is actually worth all of the raves and accolades that it has received thus far. I don't know if it's worthy of a Best Picture Oscar or not (my own choice would be "Black Swan," which is far too weird for the Academy's tastes), but I won't be pissed off if it wins. This is a beautifully acted film that manages to tell a simple story amazingly well, and I enjoyed every moment of its stately but giggly style. It's funny without being cute, emotional without being sappy, smart without being condescending, mainstream without being bland. This is what a nice night at to the movies is all about. 

What I liked most about "The Kingâ(TM)s Speech" was its simplicity. The movie is really just about two guys who become friends. This is actually, when you get down to the basic definition, a buddy movie- two different guys are teamed together when they don't want to be, and gradually become best friends, helping each other out through a crisis. That is what the "King's Speech" is about at its basic core: friendship, and the strength that comes from that. Even though it is set in a pre-WWII Great Britain and focuses on the Royal Family, that's really what the movie is all about, just these two guys who buddy up. The fact that it is so long ago and involves very famous people only strengthens that underlying point. 

I'm interested in anything with a WWII setting, and that time in history is ripe for filmmaking as there was a colorful cast of political characters involved in various governments. With real life people like Winston Churchill, FDR, and Adolf Hitler, who needs fictional movie characters? "The King's Speech" is all about King George VI, although the film begins prior to his crowning, when he was still the Duke of York. Beginning in 1925, the film spends a lot of time covering how the Duke became the King over the scandal involving his older brother, Edward, taking his crown while romancing a married woman, but the movie really focuses on a more private matter. The Duke was a stutterer, and taking the crown means he will have to do a fair share of public speaking, something the understandably shy and frustrated Duke fears doing with all his heart. 

Colin Firth plays George VI as a man who uses an incredibly amount of bravery and control to get by day to day. He is quick tempered and standoffish, but all of that is understandable thanks to his stutter. The first scene in the movie shows him struggling to spit out words in a speech to a crowd of glaring faces, and it's impossible not to feel sympathy for this man. Firth is brilliant in the part, using body language and facial expressions as much as he does dialogue. He melts into the character and we are never looking at Firth up there; we are looking at King George VI, by God. There is a lot of vulnerability in his performance, but I responded to the struggling strength in this man. Firth's stuttering in the film is also amazingly well done. The stuttering seems believable, and often times can be annoying in films, but here, it is done with so much heart and patience that the viewer never gets annoyed or amused at it. We sit and wait and hope for Firth to finish a sentence, as we would with a stutterer in real life. This year, Firth is tipped to win the Best Actor Oscar, and I would say that is deserved. This is a wonderful, career defining performance from Firth. 

The other lead character in the film is Lionel Logue, played by Geoffrey Rush. Logue is an Australian, highly unorthodox speech therapist/struggling actor, who is reluctantly hired to coach King George by the King's wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter). King George isn't crazy about the idea at first, and Logue seems to have little regard for royalty, so many of their early encounters are awkward and strained. But as film progresses, they put aside their differences and come to understand one another. When George officially becomes King, he finds that he must rally the nation together to make a radio broadcast announcing war with Germany. He is terrified to do so, but knows it will be an important and valued moment. Much of the last half of the film is the preparation and build up to that speech, and when it is delivered, it is a truly crowd pleasing moment. 

Rush is so good in the movie it is unreal. I've seen plenty of great performances of his (and have indeed seen him on stage in New York, where he was impressive when the play was not), but this may be up there with the best of his career, right next to "Shine." He plays the role of Logue with so much good humor and heart that he is also instantly likable, and perhaps more of a connection to the audience, as King George is a bit closed off with his stutter. Logue is the opposite of King George in every way; he is casual, funny, and incredibly articulate. The two lead characters could not be more different, but that is, of course, part of the movie's magic, and the chemistry between the two actors makes it all believable and at times overwhelmingly powerful. Rush gets perhaps the easier of the roles, but he knocks it out of the park here. If it weren't for Christian Bale's work in "The Fighter," Rush would also be a definite winner for Best Supporting Actor here. Rush and Firth equally give two of the best performances I've seen in a film together in a long, long time. 

Tom Hooper directs the film competently; he doesn't show off any kind of wild crazy camerawork, but he doesn't let this become a filmed play either. A lot of the film is just between Firth and Rush in a room talking, and he never lets it become boring or repetitive. He finds a lot of wide angles that are wonderfully framed, and highlights the period surroundings to a believable degree. The movie looks good, but it never distracts you from the story. This is very strong old fashioned filmmaking, and it works. Hooper is making a movie about characters, and he keeps his direction attuned to that. Part of the success of this film is letting the actors and story speak out more than the visuals, and he lets that happen without letting the visuals become dull. 

The supporting cast doesn't get to show off like Rush or Firth, but everyone in the movie still does a wonderful job. It's always nice to see Helena Bonham Carter, especially in a role where she doesn't act crazy like she does in all of her husband's movies (for example, watch every Tim Burton movie from the last 10 years, literally). Carter plays the typical supportive wife role, and although there isn't any variation on it, she does a damn good job, providing a warm and charming presence on screen. I'm not sure her work is Oscar worthy, but it is still very notable. Her screen time is important and enjoyable, and another actress could've been dull in this part. Carter is pretty excellent here. Guy Pearce shows up for a few scenes as the somewhat negatively portrayed older brother Edward, and he does a good job as well, picking at Firth and being the more emotional of the two. Michael Gambon has a nice cameo as King George V, and fellow "Harry Potter" cast member Timothy Spall is absolutely outstanding as Winston Churchill. 

"The King's Speech" is a great, wonderful movie, and while it is not my favorite of 2010 it is definitely one of the brightest and most worthwhile films to find release in the last year. It finds a nice, wonderfully balanced approach to its story and features two amazingly well commanded male lead performances. It is heartwarming to see King George conquer his stutter, and even more powerful to know that it is (for the most part) a true story. I have little interest in historical accuracy in a fictional tale, so all that matters here is that this movie feels true and real, which it does. Hooper has made a quietly and smartly intelligent movie, and I hope that in the wild Oscar campaigning it doesn't get a bum rap because it is about a monarch and was produced by a famous Oscar hoarder (Harvey Weinstein, anybody?). What I hope is that people go see the movie with an open mind and let themselves get treated to one of the warmest, funniest, and most entertaining movies currently out in release right now. "The King's Speech" is a great choice for any movie fan.

"The King's Speech" is an intimate (and at times awkward) portrayal of a man's struggle with himself as well as with the world he is forced to inhabit. It is also a comedy about a speech therapist with a difficult patient. And it's a high stakes drama about a nation's leaders during political upheaval and the threat of war. It handles all these aspects extraordinarily well due to the efforts of an exquisite cast, well paced direction, and a witty script.

It's a great film that will be sadly ignored by most moviegoers who would rather see Bonham Carter and Gambon muck about at playing wizard. And who might avoid this for a somewhat undeserved R rating, while they watch trite sexuality in morally bereft PG13 flicks.  It's a great film that peels back a layer of stuffiness from the oft maligned monarchy, portrays charicatures as real people, and let's a real friendship develop between two compelling characters.

Colin Firth gives a remarkably sympathetic performance while also nailing the technicalities of speech impediments and the aristocracy.  Geoffrey Rush provides generous humor with real wit and panache instead of crude jokes.  Helena Bonham Carter carries the audience's sympathies and hopes gloriously throughout, and the rest of the supporting cast is top notch. My only real complaint on that account is Timothy Spall's Winston Churchill who felt a little too much like a charicature.  Otherwise, all Oscar noms in my book.

Art direction and costuming and the like were all spot on for a period piece, and the locations and sets felt very real.  I did find the overexposed backgrounds a little offputting, but I guess they hid modern-day England easier than expensive CGI would.

Most scenes were also played in very tight shots, many of them often from awkward angles or using an unusual "line." this did help the intimacy and the discomfort inherent in the story, but at times it also highlighted technical aspects of the film that were slightly detracting (very tight focal planes, occasional soft focus, sometimes obviously wide lenses, etc).  But I understood why those were attempted, so despite some brief breaks in the illusion the story came through unharmed.

Again, a very good film worth a look if it's in theatres near you.  And if for some bizarre reason you're concerned about the R rating, then FUCK FUCK FUCK FUCK TITS... There. I just did more damage to you than this film ever would. Go see it.

The King's Speech is a true cinematic treat; a delicious dessert to be devoured at twenty four frames per second.  The film's merits are many, with outstanding performances from Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush, but a frustrating narrative flaw disallows the film to ever achieve the greatness these characters deserve.

The first act of the film is wonderfully paced.  Director Tom Hooper introduces his audience to a cast of colorful characters, each with their own set of obstacles to overcome, and places them in an aesthetically unique, quirky historical atmosphere, created by a deliberately uneven cinematographic and editing style, shifting lenses and endlessly mixing high and low angles.  The portion of the film could exist as a purely visual exercise, if it were not for the deliriously compelling antics of the characters in frame.  This portion of the film is really quite special, as the audience gains insight to Bertie, Lionel, and Elizabeth without ever being numbed by exposition.  Act Two follows a similar paradigm, but perhaps to lesser avail.  The triumphs of the film up to now are lessened by a disappointingly conventional cookie cutter of a third act.  Without going into detail, the narrative structure of Act Three is back asswards.  These characters enter the film more dynamic than they leave, making the audience wonder why they were ever so enthralled with the film in the first place.  That is a serious flaw.  But not a deadly one.

As a whole, though, the film deserves applause.  A true crowd pleaser, The King's Speech is better than most of the offerings at the cinema this year...but to award it too many accolades will ruin the film's legacy.  This is a special film, but not a perfect one.  I would hate for it to be shunned in the future for toppling The Social Network, a much better film.   Instead, I would like to remember this as the touching, incredibly well-acted, and visual delight of a little film I so enjoyed viewing.

But you know - it's one thing to theorize an oscar winner it's another to produce one.  But rest assured, Tom Hooper's The King's Speech is quite an elegant product indeed, thanks in very large part to the trifecta of outstanding performances on display.  

Firth plays King George VI, or Bertie to his family, a stumbling stammering monarch in 1930's England.  Bertie-boy enlists help from Lionel Logue - a speech therapist - to improve his neurotic word choking, so he can speak with strength and dignity for his country on the eve of WWII.    

Though he has no credentials or degree, Logue (wonderfully played by Geoffrey Rush) has loads of experience, including helping shell shocked vets regain their speech.  He's a man of austerity and cognizance, but also faith.  He likes to say that he can cure anyone that wants to be cured.  As a theater hobbyist and Shakespeare admirer, Logue understands the beauty of speech and tries to relate to Bertie that he has a voice and he must not be afraid to use it.    

The King's Speech is predictable, but incredibly engaging because it's not a movie that asks what - that's obvious, read a history book - but why?  Why does the King struggle to speak?  Firth is extraordinary as said king.  He inhabits the man and makes it look effortless: the panicked face and nervous ticks, the quiet self-doubt and sudden bursts of aggravation.  He's a sensitive, ambivalent, and anxious fella who trips and stumbles over his words because he's all bottled up.  Bertie contemplates the commoners he knows nothing of and vice-versa, as well as his callous father and brother of which he could say the same.  He is disconnected.  

Rush's Lionel Logue is able to connect because he doesn't treat him like a king, but an equal, insisting on calling him Bertie and not Your-Majesty.  The psycho-analytical swordplay the two men engage in is both riveting and revealing, of both men. 

Helena Bonham Carter as Bertie's wife, the Queen, also deserves props for her charm and gentle understanding.  She demands attention even up against her screen-hogging costars.

Polished and artistically directed by Tom Hooper, The King's Speech is oscar bait of the most scrumptous variety.  It deserves the acting accolades it will surely recieve.  If history is people, places, and events then Speech is cinematic delight because it focuses in on the people: who they really were and what they were able to say - I mean, after finding their voices of course.

A film like this, with a title like The King's Speech is one that may suggest something it isn't.  Due to the awards buzz that a prestige film, such as this, is receiving, it seems like some may just write this film off as another stuffy, period film, which may be very good, but doesn't have much appeal.  I would really like to emphasize that this should not be the case.  The King's Speech is a fantastic film, which features great performances by its lead actors, tells a very good (true) story about a man overcoming adversity, and is also very funny.  Essentially, this is the story of how a stiff Brit with a disability learned how to loosen up and help lead a nation.

Colin Firth stars as Prince Albert, Duke of York.  Over the course of time, Albert will become King George VI, but for the majority of the film he is mostly referred to as "Bertie".  While a noble man and loving husband and father, Bertie has suffered from a debilitating speech impediment for nearly his entire life.  Bertie has a horrible stammer, which makes him dread public speaking.  In an attempt to solve this problem, Bertie's wife Elizabeth (eventually the Queen Mother, played by Helena Bonham Carter) enlists a speech therapist to help her husband.  The therapist is Lionel Logue, played by Geoffrey Rush, who forms an unlikely friendship with Bertie, as he employs a number of unorthodox techniques to help Bertie find his voice.  This will become much more important in the years to come, because after King George V (Michael Gambon) dies and King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce) abdicates the thrown to his brother, it will be up to Bertie to address his people and unite them as their nation enters World War II.

In a year that has already seen many great performances, this is another film that stacks up its actors among those who will remembered by the years' end as the best.  The three leads, Firth, Rush, and Carter, are all fantastic in this film.  Solid supporting work from Guy Pearce as well, along with smaller roles, later in the film, such as Derek Jacobi as Cosmo Lang (Archbishop of Canterbury) and Timothy Spall (completing a Harry Potter trifecta) as Winston Churchill.  As dapper and dry as some of these characters may be, the actors are all very well equipped and ready to deliver fantastic performances.  It only helps that, as I have mentioned, the film is frequently funny and highly entertaining.

The way Colin Firth portrays Bertie is really incredible.  He is not just stuttering out his lines of dialogue to convey the character's problem, it is all in his body language, the movement and tightening of his jaw, and other emotional elements that reveal themselves, as Bertie struggles with basic speech.  I love how Firth has gone from affable love interest to immersive lead actor.  Similar to his performance in A Single Man in 2009, he moves right into this role, hitting every note just as it should, creating a character that suffers from a problem and goes through the proper arc to solve it.  Bertie is sympathetic, but not perfect, as his temper sometimes gets the best of him.  Even with that aspect, however, we soon come to understand many things about how he has come to be the person he is, with the help of his speech therapist, Logue.

As Logue, Geoffrey Rush is perfectly cast as well.  The first actor to have signed up for the film, this is clearly a role that Rush can play properly.  Lionel is an eccentric Australian actor, who has managed to make a small profession out of training individuals to speak.  This basically requires Rush to make pithy remarks at the expense of Bertie, a member of the royal family, not use to such exchanges, which causes him to exclaim and prove that a true voice is present.  The various techniques that Logue employs are all quite ingenious and very humorous, as we see throughout the film.  Along with that, it is the softness that Rush portrays, when dealing with how to reach Bertie, which does well to convey the friendship that emerges over the course of this film.

Finally, you have Helena Bonham Carter, who, after showing us her wild performances this year as the Red Queen in 'Wonderland' and as Bellatrix Lestrange (that's a fun name to type) in Harry Potter, goes to show that much simpler characters come to her just as easily.  A true supporter of her husband, Carter plays Elizabeth as a strong backbone for Bertie, doing everything she can to help.  The role is certainly not one that folds into the background, but one that is made to seem effortless, due to how good Carter is as an actress.

Another interesting aspect about this film is the direction by Tom Hooper.  Hooper, who garnered much praise for his work on the HBO miniseries John Adams, presents the film from within many interiors and always seems to have shots setup from interesting points of view.  It certainly does not feel as if it were shot like any standard-type period film.  It feels more as if Hooper is trying to confine the viewer, just as Bertie is confined in his speaking, only to open up more in key scenes.  Then you have the scenes where Logue helps Bertie to overcome his problems by having him dance, exercise, shout, and curse (which resulted in this film's ridiculous R-rating) are all filmed in a greatly entertaining manner.

Much of the way this film maintains its solid momentum, regardless of how good the actors are, is due to the scripting of the feature.  Screenwriter David Seidler (who I learned was born in England during Bertie's reign as King and also had a terrible stutter, but is now quite the articulate older fellow) does an interesting thing with the structure of this film.  He has essentially made a sports movie.  The film has its audience get behind what could be considered an underdog character, finds that character a coach, and has him go through montage-like training sequences, before reaching the "big game" at the end.  Other drama unfolds during all these moments.  I think it is because of this structure that the film works as well as it does.  It is that kind of formula that can make for a crowd-pleasing feature film.  And it certainly helps that there is such a great amount of talent stacked behind how this film has been plotted out.

There are great things abound throughout this film.  It is greatly acted, which will easily be the most acknowledged aspect of this film.  It looks great, which tends to go without saying when concerning films similar to this, set in a specific time-period.  But most importantly, it is very entertaining.  The film effortlessly blends the real life drama with many witty bits humor, as well as lots of dead pan moments that only seek to keep the audience on board with the terrific characters presented in this film.  Strong buzz does not build around these types of movies for no reason; The King's Speech speaks of terrific delight.

Colin Firth is inspiring not just in character, but also in his own performance of depth and strength.  So well known as the man of influence and grace in Fitzwilliam Darcy or Pemberley, from the great story of Pride & Prejudice, Firth successfully captures a new breed of upper class aristocracy in Albert Windsor, to become George VI. Winner of the People's Choice Award at the Toronto Film Festival, this British historical drama has been getting a lot of award buzz and has lead in nominations at the Golden Globes. Colin Firth leads this star studded cast after receiving his BAFTA for Best Actor and receiving a nomination for an Oscar earlier this year. Geoffrey Rush, winner of a Oscar, Tony, and a Emmy (I am assuming he is working on some type of musical piece to be entered at the Grammy's) accompanies in a supporting role along with Helena Bonham Carter. Emmy winning Tom Hooper directs, who has established his name primarily through television series with "Elizabeth I" and "John Adams".

Albert Fredrick, Duke of York (Colin Firth) is the second son of King George V. This obviously requires him to be a public speaker and be very involved with people. The problem is that the Duke has a speech impediment (Stammering, Stuttering), so he has a very tough time communicating with people verbally. He continuously went around to different speech therapists but never was treated effectively. 
 
With the nation nearing towards crisis because of Hitler's uproar in Europe, his wife arranges a meeting with Lionel Logue a speech therapist that is known for his unorthodox and controversial methods. When his father dies, and after family issues with his older brother (Guy Pearce) who is heir to the throne; Albert is unexpectedly named King. With a Second World War on the verge, the people are looking to the King for hope; and the only way he can give them hope is with his voice.
 
With a first glance, one could wonder how long can a person actually watch this? It would be a tough time just watching a man that has trouble communicating being the star of a film. Hooper impressively weaves light comic relief and a dramatic quest so tightly together that it creates a beautiful blend that makes it vastly original. What this film has received most attention for though is the performances by the acclaimed cast. 

The lead role of Firth is absolutely spectacular by displaying this emotional journey of overcoming his disability. The amount of effort that Firth put into this is uncanny; he is able to absorb the audience ultimately by his charm and connection. Geoffrey Rush, who plays his speech therapist, provides most of the comic relief because as it turns out he primarily is trying to get the King to step outside his boundaries and discover his confidence. 
 
The witty and charming Rush delivers perhaps the best supporting role of this year, and I won't be surprised to see that he wins. Bottom line, all the performances in this film are fantastic. It isn't very often that a crowd pleasing film and a work of art go hand and hand but led by performances that are sure to be nominated for Academy Awards, "The King's Speech" is delightful and is a wonderful film to see for the holidays.

Naming this the best film of 2010 is kind of like naming Alice the best member of "The Brady Bunch": it doesn't really mean much and no one will probably remember who else was up for the title.   But even though 2010 hasn't exactly been a whiz-bang year for stellar cinema, this is one film you owe it to yourself to track down, despite the fact that its subject matter won't be beating anyone over the head with anticipation and interest.  We're in the years leading up to WWII and King George V is on his last legs - the heir to the throne is King Edward VIII but when scandal hits, in steps his brother Bertie to become King George VI and lead England through the upcoming years.  This would already be a lot to take on but then you add in that Bertie has a severe speech impediment and suddenly things get more interesting (albeit awkward).  Fortunately, Bertie's wife Elizabeth arranges for sessions with speech therapist and aspiring actor, Lionel, to get the King's tongue untied.  And that's basically it.  Your big climactic action here is the speech ushering the nation into WWII after Hitler comes to power and you obviously know the King gets it off without a hitch so you just sort of sit there and meander about with the film as it takes you through equal parts drama and a surprising amount of humor.  Colin Firth excels as Bertie, Helena Bonham Carter is quite adept at Elizabeth and Guy Pearce is either outshone by everyone else onscreen or cannot act as Bertie's brother.  But despite how Firth is gunning for Oscar greatness (something he should have easily netted in "A Single Man") and people will be caught up in the historical importance and context of the film, this is Geoffrey Rush's movie.  I'd actually say he does better than anyone else here as Lionel, and that's no small feat.  You know how it ends and you know it won't be a thrill-a-minute but so what?  Given that just about everything else released in 2010 seemed designed to bludgeon audiences with stupidity, this stands out like, well, like Alice on "The Brady Bunch."

Mark my words: Colin Firth is going to win the Academy Award for Best Actor.  After years of incredibly memorable performances in gems like the Brigite Jones films and "Love, Actually" and last year's Oscar-nominated turn in "A Single Man," Firth will get his due in March.

"The King's Speech," which is a terribly simple film with a double-entendre title, is quite simply the story of how King George VI dealt with his speech impediment while ruling over England in the mid 1900s  by panicking over his radio address to the nation as war broke out between Germany and the UK.  After his father passes away and the next in line, King Edward VIII relinquishes the throne, King George VI is faced with needing to be the voice of England...a voice that could not bring peace and confidence to its listeners if it was delivered with a terrible stammer.

Played with exquisite grace by Firth, King George VI is brought to life with such a perfect mix of frustration, fear and perserverance, it is impossible to imagine anyone else beating this career-changing performance in the Oscar race.

The film itself, directed by Tom Hooper, who pretty much owned the Emmy Awards a couple of years back with his HBO mini-series "John Adams," does have a certain knack of presenting history as entertainment.  I am not going to lie and say this film was an incredibly exciting journey, but it was a wonderful slice of historical life made entertaining by the wonderful performances of its actors.  Firth may be getting all the press and accolades, but there is no denying Ms. Bonham-Carter, possible Oscar nominee Mr. Rush nor even Mr. Pearce their due.  With extraordinary casting, Hooper once again conquered the very difficult: a historically accurate film which will not put you to sleep.

Inspiring story well told.  The movie does not open with the Weinsteins saying "we thank the Academy for their consideration" but beyond this omission this film is pure Oscar bait.  And frankly it deserves to garner a number of the naked yellow ditch diggers.  Most assuredly one of these should go to Colin Firth who plays the spineless, stuttering King George VI-one of the more unattractive royal characters in recent memory-with historical accuracy but yet making him a sympathetic character.  A second statue should go Helena Bonham Carter.  Although she has to do little more than be encouraging and sympathetic to her hamster of a husband in this film she turns in yet another great performance and this plus a string of memorable characters in a long career should get her the award.  Geoffrey Rush will also likely win although his character is the unfailing witty, charming hero throughout the 2 hour run time so he really didn't need to work that hard. It should also win a slew of technical awards for cinematography, art direction and costuming - the production is impeccable.  This Best Picture nominee shoe-in and likely favorite to win has only those shortcomings common to large-scale historical costume dramas - the run-time is a little long, some parts slow beyond comfort and it lacks a real personal connection beyond the miniscule portion of the audience that remembers these events.  Also, "The King's Speech" has to be the least compelling title in recent memory - where were the marketing people?  If Hooper's creation doesn't come up big Oscar night part of the reason may somewhat represent fatigue over the sheer number of movies about English royalty of late ("The Queen", "Young Victoria", "Elizabeth" and "Elizabeth 2", "The Duchess", etc.).  Speaking of which, when does Wallis Simpson get her big screen treatment?  The older, twice divorced American born "Bessie" briefly ruled one-fourth of the world through her domination of King Edward VIII and wound up with a Duchy.  Her story cries out for a biopic.

Kicking off the awards season in a regal fashion is The King's Speech, an intelligent introduction to the time of year that features some highly anticipated contenders in the run up to the prestigious ceremonies.
    Set during the wartime era of 1920's Britain, Colin Firth plays George VI; the son of a king who has the royal duties of giving public worldwide speeches whilst suffering from a debilitating stammer, which he hopes to remedy by enlisting the services of Lionel Logue, a failed Australian actor who has uncouth methods of speech therapy. What follows is an engaging, humorous account of this man's struggle to overcome his demons and adhere to his duties, which will hopefully earn Firth the Oscar he unfortunately lost out to for A Single Man. 
       Helena Bonham Carter also gives a charming performance as the Queen mother, a role which is rarely portrayed on screen, Geoffrey Rush is similarly outstanding, as is the able support from Derek Jacobi and Timothy Spall, who gives a pitch perfect impersonation of Winston Churchill.  
Though its accuracy remains to be seen, the film is a heart-warming depiction of the ties that bind us, the importance of family and the endurance of friendship.

Its been raining for about 3 or 4 days here in Los Angeles. We are 5 or 6 days away for the end of the Holiday season(not counting New Years of course). And we are 2 months away for the Oscars. I am getting ready for the Oscars because I have seen most of what will probably be nominated for Best Picture. Today I have witnessed  The King's Speech, and it is a marvelous film.

Plot- In the era before WWII, Prince Albert(played by Colin Firth, but the film names him Bertie because his father and brother uses that name as a nickname)  attempts to deliver a speech, he has a speech impediment that doesn't allow him to pronounce many words. He is married to Elizabeth(future Queen Elizabeth, played by Helena Bonham Carter) convinces her husband to see an intelligent speech therapist named Lionel Logue( Geoffrey Rush). Logue attempts to help the struggling Prince Albert,  but Albert has not yet witnessed any proof that he could over come his speech impediment. Logue places him through a bet, if he could read an entire page from Shakespeare without any problems, Logue gets to ask Albert more questions. Albert accepts, and angrily leaves his office believing there was no point in helping him. After the death of his father, King George V(Michael Gambon) and the leaving of his brother, King Edward VIII( Guy Pearce), Prince Albert takes the thrown as King George VI. He returns to Logue for help with his speech, they continue his training in preparation for King Georges' speech into the entrance of WWII.

Problems- If you have ever taken a History class in High School, you could easily know what would happen in this film, and while I knew a lot of what would happen, there were moments where the film surprised me. But yes, it is a predictable film with a few annoying subplots.

Cinematography- the cinematography was excellent. I loved Danny Cohen's cinematography. What he does is showing the shot of Firth and Rush talking to each other, but Firth is on the right side of the screen, camera changes, and Rush is on the left, and that is how most of the conversations are delivered.

Score- Alexandre Desplat, who has been nominated 3 times for the Oscar in The Queen, Ben Button, and Fantastic Mr. Fox, will probably get another nomination for his score. It is soothing and Marvelous.

Production Design- The sets are beautiful, it looks very real to the actual buildings in which the historical characters were actually in. And the outdoors looked marvelous, it made me feel like moving all the way to Great Britain.

Performances- Flawless. Colin Firth plays Prince Albert with such ferocity, he will easily be nominated for the Oscar, but my vote would still go to Jessie Eisenberg. Helena Bonham Carter earned my respect again after her one dimensional character back in Alice in Wonderland, she will probably receive an Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actress. Geoffrey Rush is the scene stealer of the film, I believe this is his crowning achievement in his career.

Story- This is a biopic, and a well written biopic. It is written by David Seidler, who will be honored in April 11, 2011, for his work on this film because he actually stutters, and he is actually quite the inspiration because I too have a stuttering issue.

Direction- I can see why Tom Hooper is being honored for this film, it is well made, and its pace is beautiful. Besides, he is the filmmaker behind HBO's epic John Adams and the film "The Damned United".

Overall this is a well made Biopic that will certainly win many Oscars, and it is the 4th best film I have seen this year.

I give it 4.5/5 stars.

After two viewings, I have to admit that this really does live up to the enormous hype. Like many of my friends I was sceptical, fearing a glossy glorification of the Royal Family, but this film certainly does not fall into that trap. Indeed, it is easy to see why the Queen Mother did not want this story told in her lifetime. Her young self, as portrayed by Helena Bonham Carter, is snobbishly precious about protocol and insistent on due deference from her 'â~inferiors', albeit also sweetly supportive of her suffering, stammering husband. The Royals as a whole appear deeply dysfunctional; not a family but a firm, as the tongue-tied prince Bertie (Colin Firth) bitterly remarks.

We come to think of the man who would become King George VI as plain Bertie because his therapist Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) insists that they be on first-name terms, an equal and informal relationship being an essential part of his therapeutic method. The strong inference is that what ultimately helps Bertie most is possibly the opportunity to have a relatively normal conversation with another human being, and eventually to unburden himself about a childhood involving outrageous cruelty from nannies and a distant father openly determined to make his children fear him. Michael Gambon's crusty portrayal of King George V makes that unhappy relationship entirely plausible. 

King Edward VIII has often been depicted as a romantic figure, The King Who Gave Up Everything For Love, but here Guy Pearce turns him into a feckless, selfish playboy, bullying his brother and openly contemptuous of commoners. His relationship with Eve Best's vampish Wallis Simpson seems here to be riddled with a queasy mixture of manipulation and mawkishness. When Edward's abdication forces a desperately reluctant Bertie to accept the throne, thereâ(TM)s an unforgettable scene in which even his two young daughters â" the future Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Margaret â" feel obliged to curtsey to their Dad and call him 'Your Majesty'. We do finally see a positive side of the whole Royal show when the titular speech provides a valuable wartime morale-booster, but the private cost of the public spectacle has by then been all too clearly established. 

The cast is mostly terrific. Firth really is fabulous as Bertie, a brilliant portrayal of suppressed rage and genuinely moving determination. Rushâ(TM)s laconic Logue is equally persuasive; you can believe that this dryly witty charmer would have convinced his privileged client to drop his defences. Derek Jacobi does a lovely turn as a manoeuvring, obsequious Archbishop of Canterbury. The one false move in the casting is Timothy Spall as Winston Churchill. His performance seems more caricature than characterisation, so much so that I wondered if it was meant as light relief â" it certainly drew chuckles from audience members when I saw the film. If so, then it sits rather awkwardly next to the more serious depictions of other statesmen, such as Anthony Andrews's dignified Stanley Baldwin. 

However, that is a small blemish on what is a polished but playfully provocative film. It is a delightfully entertaining tale, and it's beautifully photographed. If the expected shower of Oscars arrived, then I hope it includes one for the wonderful cinematography that frames faces and scenes so superbly throughout this film. There is plenty for the eyes to feast on here, and a fair helping of food for thought too.

When it comes to subject choice in movies, one of the most well-explored areas is royalty, which raises the question, do we really need another one? We've been through everything from butlers to monarchs with results varying from good to terrible. However, The King's Speech is not just another royalty flick. It stands tall among the very strongest of its genre through the strength of its script, direction and especially its performers.

The King's Speech is the story of King George VI, Bertie (Firth) to his friends, and his ascension to the throne after the death of his father (Gambon) and his brother's (Pearce) abdication. The only problem is his stammer. Bertie can barely blurt out a sentence without st-stuttering through every word. In order to overcome this impediment, his wife (Carter) enlists the help of a slightly unorthodox speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Rush). This may seem a thin premise to hang a film on, but the themes explored with admirable confidence are more than enough to fill two hours with.

The entire cast, bursting at the seams with talent, put in oscar worthy performances, with the fiery yet burdened Colin Firth incredible as the King, the demure yet commanding Helena Bonham Carter as Queen Elizabeth and the inimitable Geoffery Rush as Lionel Logue. Leading the cast is Firth whose entire career is littered with brilliant performances, and he outdoes himself yet again with a beautifully restrained, utterly human performance which you cannot help but feel for. He also pulls off some welcome flashes of humour and brings on the fire and brimstone with fantastic conviction, all the while maintaining a perfectly imperfect stammer which pervades, but never gets in the way of, his towering performance. And the chemistry which he finds with his co-star Geoffery Rush makes for one of the more believeable and exciting male partnerships in years. Rush's own performance matches Firth's in terms of subtlety and nuance as well as the same level of perfectly judged restraint, yet the two never seem at odds, finding a rhythm with each other in their slowly building friendship which is at times flat out hilarious and at others brilliantly intense. It is an breathtaking display of two top-class actors working seamlessly together. Helena Bonham Carter plays the ever-supporting Queen Elizabeth who, in the hands of a lesser actor, could have turned into a stereotype but is instead a strong, quiet character in her own right. She is able to command a room with a look but also able to guide her husband through some of the hardest days he has had to face, showing a beautiful light and shade in an entirely selfless performance. Guy Pearce, though lacking a lot of the screentime his co-stars are given, makes and incredible impact in every one of his scenes. His slimy Edward is the unofficial villain of the piece and he manages to be spitefully real at every turn. It's one of his finest performances and, in comparison to his co-stars, he barely graces the screen.

The script which all these performances hang off is a thing of beauty. It manages to combine reality and creativity seamlessly with never a moment devoid of the reality it deserves whilst never missing out on an opportunity for the humour and intensity which the film is strewn with. Unexpectedly, the film also quite a bit of abbraisive language, but the context which it's in means that even the most sensitive of viewers won't be turned off. But its greatest achievement is the very real characters it helps create and the relationships it helps to extend.

Tom Hooper nails the direction, despite the tremendous leap forward in terms of content and responsibility. His biggest venture before his latest is 2009's The Damned United, so it's quite a step up in exposure, yet he never seems to show it, taking bold risks with confidence. His use of fisheye lenses is reminiscent of Kubrick and he uses the effect sparingly and effectively. He also pushes the rule of thirds to the extreme, making for some eye-catching shots which are either genius or annoying depending on your point of view. I'm for 'genius' by the way.

But the greatest part of the movie is the tangible connection created between characters and audience and the pounding in your chest when Bertie takes the microphone or Lionel oversteps his bounds on a morning walk as every part of the film works together in a beautifully restrained piece of filmmaking.

Any scene where Colin Firth and Geoffery Rush are onscreen together. But more specifically the ending speech, conducted by Logue.

I don't think many people would argue with me when I say that 2010 has been quite a disappointing year at the movies. Yes, there have been a few exceptions, but for the most part, I can think of only a small handful of films that actually left a lasting impression on me. Maybe I'm getting a bit too cynical and have let my biased education get the best of me, but now that the world of cinema has effectively become nothing more than an obnoxious 3D spectacle, it's gotten to the point where I can't help but feel like Hollywood is letting us down.

"The King's Speech" has been described by many of the industry's top critics as "a World War II-set British royalty drama". Most people typically roll their eyes and dismiss period pieces that involve lots of sophisticated British people walking around and talking until their hearts desire. But, I must admit that they would be making a big mistake this time, for this one happens to be one of the most charming and pleasant cinematic experiences I've had in a long while. Acclaimed director Tom Hooper has crafted both a visually stunning and historically fascinating film that will unquestionably be amongst those crowned on Oscar night.

Set in 1930's Britain, the film tells the inspiring story of how King George VI- superbly portrayed by Colin Firth who gives on Oscar worthy performance here- assumed the throne while dealing with a hindering speech impediment. The scenes in which we watch his attempts to speak publicly are absolutely heartbreaking and Firth sells them perfectly, as he truly becomes a man trapped in the shackles of his own mind without a voice.

Bertie's loving and devoted wife Elizabeth, played by the always incredible Helena Bonham Carter, who after searching high and low for an appropriate source of guidance, seeks after the help of Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), an Australian speech therapist and failed actor who employes strange and rather unorthodox methods. This naturally proves to be quite problematic for the secretive and reserved royal family, but once Logue finally gains their trust, the relationship that forms between them is nothing short of beautiful.

Films like "The King's Speech" are typically made as an excuse to showcase certain actors' abilities, and between all three of the leads giving tremendous performances, each scene flows seamlessly from one to the other, thus always leaving the audience wanting more. Unlike most other period pieces, this is that rare exception that won't have you gauging your eyes out from boredom. It may not be as exciting as "Inception" or as mind-bending as "Black Swan" or as invigorating as "The Social Network", but this is, without a doubt, one of the best films of the year and one that should by no means be missed.

"If I am King, where is my power? Can I declare war? Form a government? Levy a tax? No! And yet I am the seat of all authority because they think that when I speak, I speak for them."

Essentially the Rocky of speech impediment movies, The King's Speech is an engaging, well-made period piece featuring excellent performances, sublime character nuances, a touch of wit and top-notch production design, and it was all stitched together by Tom Hooper's consummate direction. Not to mention, the film delivers solid drama with a rousing climax, and it manages to be a both highly satisfying and uplifting picture which achieves its dramatic potential without sacrificing historical accuracy. In short, it's precisely the kind of Oscar bait that's distributed each December, but it is nonetheless one of the most accessibly entertaining and satisfying films of its kind to be released during 2010.

Faced with the prospect of life in the public eye, the future King George VI (Firth) - a.k.a. Prince Albert or "Bertie" - is plagued by a severe stutter which constantly embarrasses both him and his judgmental family. With his wife Elizabeth (Bonham Carter) by his side, Bertie has endured numerous treatments for his verbal handicap, but to no avail. Until, that is, Elizabeth brings Bertie to see an unorthodox speech expert named Lionel Logue (Rush) who comes from Australia and treats the future king like any other patient. Thus is born an unlikely friendship, the importance of which escalates when circumstances conspire to make him the king of England on the eve of World War II. See, after the death of King George V (Gambon), Bertie's playboy brother (Pearce) abdicates his position as king in order to pursue his own interests, which thrusts Bertie into the role of leadership and public attention he never expected to bear.

Interestingly, the "Speech" of the title bears a double-meaning: it describes both the king's address to the nation which declares war against Hitler's Germany, and Bertie's impeded speech which he's fighting to overcome. Unfortunately, the story of King George VI working to overcome his impediment is intercut with Bertie's interactions with his father and his brother, which slows The King's Speech to a crawl during the midsection and sacrifices the intimacy of the extraordinary early scenes. While it may have been necessary to clarify these events, the refocus disrupts the pace and is not as interesting as Bertie and Logue's story. Luckily, things get back on track for the sublime final act, which pits Bertie against his worst fear: addressing his subjects over the radio.

The finale of The King's Speech not only represents the movie's climax, but also the moment in which all the elements of the motion picture come together: Firth and Rush's acting, Logue and Bertie's friendship, the strains of the classical score, and the stark simplicity of the set design (the room in which the speech is delivered is, after all, unadorned and unspectacular). The microphone is depicted not as a mere aid for voice amplification and recording, but as an implacable, faceless antagonist which Bertie must defeat by exorcising his personal demons. It is, in a word, extraordinary; leaving viewers with smiles on their faces, goosebumps all over their bodies, and lilts in their hearts. Additionally, the emotional power is considerably augmented by the fact that these events actually transpired in real life. This is indeed an amazing story.

While The King's Speech is a positive and life-affirming movie picture, director Tom Hooper (The Damned United, John Adams) and screenwriter David Seidler have crafted a picture which, at its core, is a story more concerned with the unlikely friendship forged between Bertie and Lionel. Quietly respectful of one another yet stubborn and set in their ways, it's undeniable that - because the couple are so distinctly separated by class and profession - they would never have grown such a bond were it not for Bertie's speech impediment. Added to this - although The King's Speech is a historical drama, an underdog story and a buddy movie rolled into one - there are plenty of humorous moments throughout which are never overdone or out-of-place. Every single frame of The King's Speech evinces a refined maturity as well as a professionalism rarely witnessed in this contemporary cinematic climate.

In their infinite wisdom, the MPAA chose to give The King's Speech an R rating, believing that the picture contains too many uses of the word "fuck". Admittedly, there are several profanities, but they are anything but gratuitous - they serve a very specific purpose within the context of speech therapy. This decision once again displays the MPAA's narrow-mindedness, since these profanities are the only reason the film is R-rated (there is no sex or violence). Heck, in England the film's rating was downgraded from a '15' to a '12A', as the BBFC were able to recognise that the inclusion of profanities was essential for the story.

As exceptional as the writing and directing is, The King's Speech is ultimately a performance piece which lives and dies by its cast. Luckily, all of the stars were up to the task. Leading the pack is the phenomenal Colin Firth, who rightfully deserves the highest praise of all the actors. It would seem Firth literally shed his skin and crawled into the skin of Bertie - we believe he is the role. Most impressively, the stutter was not overdone - it feels natural and real as opposed to faux and contrived. Alongside him, Geoffrey Rush is the perfect complement for Firth; his performance is effortlessly energetic, focused and charismatic. The chemistry between the stars is triumphant as well; essaying a stiff-upper-lip standoff between teacher and student which ultimately melts into an alliance. There's also no shortage of chemistry between Firth and Helena Bonham Carter, who is a delight as Queen Elizabeth. Bonham Carter is sharp-witted and whip-smart, but able to express great caring and humanity. Meanwhile, the secondary cast is populated by notable names, all of whom delivered sterling performances. Most notable is Timothy Spall, whose portrayal of Winston Churchill is more than a mere exercise in mimicry. Also of note are Michael Gambon and Guy Pearce as King George V and King Edward VIII, respectively.

With all of the film's superlative elements combined, The King's Speech illustrates by example how disappointingly lacking so many would-be dramas and Oscar contenders have been (Winter's Bone, anyone?). For the picky crowd, the film may play out a tad too simply, but this does not even slightly matter, nor does it dilute the thematic resonance. This is simply a magnificent motion picture; one of the very best films of 2010, and one that's so engaging and uplifting that it deservedly became a box office smash once word of mouth hit the streets.

Every year there's a movie that critics alike deem the awards season frontrunner. This year, it's The King's Speech. Director Tom Hooper's incredible depiction of the events leading up to the reign of King George VI garnered the most Golden Globe nominations, and many speculate it will head the Oscar nominations as well. The King's Speech was out in limited release as early as November 26th. In its first weekend, having only been released at 4 theatres nationwide, the film grossed about $350,000 (an astounding $88,000 per theatre). In addition to its financial recognition, The King's Speech was also an early festival favorite throughout the world. After winning numerous awards, it was clear that this film would be difficult to dethrone.

Prior to becoming King George VI (played by Colin Firth), he was known as the Duke of York. Being the second eldest son of King George V, the Duke was sure to never see the throne. His eldest brother David (played by Guy Pearce), was the next in line. Deep down, the Duke, also known as Bertie to his close friends and family, was quite conflicted. After the passing of his sick father, Bertie believed himself to be the most qualified to hold the throne. However, with the invention of wireless broadcasting, Bertie's speech impediment (he stammers) inhibited him from being a strong public speaker. Through a sequence of uncontrollable events, Bertie's wife Elizabeth (played by Helena Bonham Carter) and a local Speech expert, Lionel (played by Geoffrey Rush), helped him overcome incredible odds on his way to becoming King George VI during World War II.

The King's Speech is a well crafted, beautifully acted film. Tom Hooper constructs a witty masterpiece that's extremely easy to watch. Fresh off a difficult Oscars loss, it will be interesting to see if the hangover sways voters to cast their ballots for Colin Firth. His performance was brilliant, but he's up against some stiff competition this year. It's a similar story for supporting actor Geoffrey Rush. He's absolutely charming as the profound Speech coach, Lionel Logue. Yet, Rush finds himself as a suitable number two behind Christian Bale (The Fighter). Despite the fantastic performances by Firth and Rush, perhaps it's Helena Bonham Carter who delivers best. Queen Elizabeth is such a wonderful character, and Bonham Carter brings her to life. "Now all I have to teach you is one word - everything."

Those lines come from Annie Sullivan, who said this with a grunt in the 1962 Miracle Worker. Now, The King's Speech is a reverberation of The Miracle Worker, in twentieth century Britain, under an aspiring monarch whose speech is 'everything'. Like any competent king, his confident voice is his projection, charisma, and wisdom to satiate the public. The Duke of York - Prince Albert - (Colin Firth, electric - topping his role in A Single Man) is the timid and sullen son of King George V (Michael Gambdon).

His entire life Prince Albert has been punished for his incessant stammering and awkward cessations. His lack of delivery makes him an ignominious discharge to the royal family, a bastard to all good examples of leaders, and a frivolous person in general. He can barely control himself: he has abrupt outbursts of rage, can barely finish a sentence, and is too modest to rule sternly. His brother, King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce) is to become king, but is enamoured with Wallis Simpson (Eve Best), who later was recognized as the Duchess of Windsor - she's barely given any time here. 

The King's Speech is centred more on Prince Albert. Good choice. Even his wife, Queen Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) is only the support and is not given much of a character arc or true personality as a woman of royalty. She's Helena Bonham Carter, and she has enough talent to make Queen Elizabeth clever, comical, and shrewd. 

The film opens to an excruciating situation where Prince Albert tries to deliver a speech to a vast audience at Wembley Stadium. His stage presence is far from apt; he looks like a young boy with his pants down, shivering in fear as if it is the bitter winter. The British spectators stare in dismay, shrugging more and more disappointingly as Prince Albert trips over each word. Tough scene to watch.

Which is necessary if we are to care about what is to come and conclude in this film. The King's Speech is thematically laden with austere settings and a simple storyline. Nevertheless, director Tom Hooper (The Damned United) is an artist with a vibrant originality who shoots the king's speech and his journeys to the microphone with surprising kinetics. Point of view shots of Prince Albert's mouth wavering around the microphone and jump cutting to make the camera just as guilty for stammering.

When Prince Albert is introduced to the speech therapist and Shakespeare fanatic Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush, equally up to snuff with Firth) their erratic relationship is a delightful comedy of errors (if you get my glaring pun). Geoffrey Rush plays Logue like a real thespian: calm, collected, sly, and bourgeois. He is the perfect teacher for Prince Albert because their political status are polar opposites. Prince Albert is showered in a life of indulgence and luxury, whereas Logue is self-taught and lives a life of scarcity. Logue uses this difference to his avail, betting Prince Albert one shilling he could read perfectly fine. We predict quickly how that will turn out.

The King's Speech, respectfully so, is a predictable movie. All historical films are, in that they dramatize events that have already taken place (but not necessarily concluded). That is not where The King's Speech falls short. It plots in the direction of standard drama, in that most scenes that occur are set up to explicitly explain what will follow next. When there is a falling out between the characters, it does not require historical fact to predict they will make amends. It is just film convention - they can irk us all.

But The King's Speech is still one of the most rich and decadent films of the year. It is full of characters, who evoke an opinion from us and have a say around the whole king's speech. Neville Chamberlain (Roger Parrott) has a resonance on the insidious rise of the Second World War. And in particular, Winston Churchill (Timothy Spall) plays the classic Churchill: rotund, affluent, respectful, and succinct. 

Colin Firth too is assured an Oscar nomination (the film itself is too). He plays Prince Albert as an inferior living in a superior world. His presence conquers him and he is ashamed not because he believes he is unworthy but because he cannot meet his obligations. Firth evokes pity, contempt, and admiration towards Prince Albert, which alleviates the prejudice depictions of the British monarch: aristocratic and snide. Firth demands true sympathy here.

The best moment in The King's Speech (subsidiary to the Firth-Rush bromance) occur at the end - the big finale, where the king's speech in 1939 is another form of the 'big game' in typical sports movies. When Prince Albert and his family must watch a short film on the process of crowning the king (since King Edward VIII abdicated the throne), the projector cuts to footage of Hitler and the Nazis. We stare at horror, the brutal juxtaposing divide of Axis/Ally, but Prince Albert stares in amazement: "[Hitler] is a great speaker." Great scene, fierce irony. 

When Prince Albert delivers that final speech (at least in the movie) we seriously feel his pressure and anxiety. The whole nation gazes at him through a microphone; his words are his persona. What is fascinating is that this was a speech, explaining that war was imminent and courage was now a top priority. It's a strong parallel to Prince Albert's life: one that requires vigorous bravery to endure personal hardship and create a greater good. Because without a king with vocal power, his nation is just as downtrodden. 

In this scene however, our focus is not on the poignancy of war, but our high hopes are that Prince Albert, now King George VI, will overcome his fears and stammering utterances. The war itself becomes secondary, which is genius in that The King's Speech becomes apolitical and a personal journey for King George VI, not Britain. It is clear that The King's Speech does not attempt the epic.

If I can digress for a moment, I want to use this film as a prime example why Hooper's The King's Speech tells the right story and how David O'Russell's The Fighter did not. I was in the minority on O'Russell's film, which dealt with similar concerns and emotions as Hooper's film. The Fighter overstuffed itself with other characters all having to project their problems onto 'the fighter' - Micky. By the end, it became more about a family than a fighter, which missed the point of emphasis. The King's Speech, despite its wide range of characters, effortlessly proves that this story is about Prince Albert and his struggle. The others are just watching the show - after all, they are his audience.

The King's Speech, therefore, can be taken in two tones: this is about a finale, a speech that tests a man's inner power rather than his obliged one and the second way to read the title is that this is just about a king, his way of speaking, and how his stutters are just a subtle metaphor for the stumbling dissension of that time.

One of the year's finest films boasting stunning cinematography, deft performances, and an untold though predictable storyline, "The King's Speech" shines in its structure and sophistication. Colin Firth fits the part of the stammering King George VI remarkably well, relaying what is quite possibly the year's greatest acting performance (I'm still torn between this and James Franco for "127 Hours"), and Geoffrey Rush gives the performance of his career with understated wit and eccentric presence -- both characters enabling the audience to feel for their individual predicaments and root for their ultimate successes. Even Helena Bonham Carter and Timothy Spall, in their brief and understated roles, manage to pull off important background characteristics with surprising dexterity. This story is expectedly predictable, relying on a lot of the formulaic events that most sentimental historical films utilize, focusing with a most-likely-exaggerated lens upon the friendship between the famous King and his speech-therapist. Nonetheless, the script succeeds because of its n'er-before-told nature, as well as a constant and omnipresent sense of love that the screenwriter clearly has for these two kind and delicately tragic figures. Last but not least, the cinematography...Oh! the cinematography is incredible in this film. If it weren't for the dazzling camerawork in "Black Swan" and the impeccable use of state-of-the-art camera technology in "The Social Network," I would declare "The King's Speech" wholly worthy of the award for best cinematography in 2010. From austere foggy English days to towering Cathedral domes to poverty-ridden drywall rooms to lavish royal estates, the cinematography never fails to take the simple, would-be forgotten, details of British living and transform it all into breathtaking and sophisticated images. Absolutely wonderful. In the end, if you like history, visually artistic movies, superb acting, or just plain sentimental stories about good friends, "The King's Speech" is for you. Without a doubt one of the year's most simply, structurally, and beautifully satisfying films.

There's not a doubt in my mind that "The King's Speech" was conceived to be a prestigious period-piece aimed at the often excruciatingly closed-minded Academy voters for that Oscar nod. Every bell and whistle attached to "The King's Speech" chimes out its rebellious spirit towards the modern blockbuster medium of Hollywood entertainment. It shoots, left and right,  nasty glares at the neon-lit fantastical atmospheres of the recent follow-up to "Tron", mostly because that atmospheric visual flare was the film's only purpose. Instead of trying to satisfy our visual appetite with state-of-the-art 3D and a big-budget, Tom Hooper directs the movie with a supreme sense of directorial awareness. Instead of trying to hide that it's a movie we're watching, he does some incredible things with the camera and how it navigates each scene. It's a pleasurable experience to look at. You wouldn't expect something so visually delightful from a project of this nature but it's delivered. 

All of the critical buzz has been floating around that this is a shoe-in to take home the Best Picture award if "The Social Network" doesn't have anything to say about it. I agree. I already have explained why this is the typical Oscar-bait. The Academy won't ignore any film released containing facts of  historical importance, a relatively decent script and some passable performances. On most occasions, like several in the past, these types of movies succeed in pissing me off upon other things. However, "The King's Speech" is the exception. It does contain some historically important and accurate information, but it has a witty, wonderfully intelligent script that is versatile in content and has a distinctive flow and self-composure. On top of that, the screen is graced with a phenomenal performance from Collin Firth, as well as Geoffry Rush as Lionel Logue who is just the icing on the acting cake. 

"The King's Speech" also accomplishes something to an extreme extent: it's a period-piece that never feels like a run-of-the-mill period piece. No one of the actors feels the need to play up his or her already-developed accents in order to seem more formal or intelligent. All of the characters seem like real living human beings. Basically, none of it feels staged. It's a feat that is rarely accomplished in cinema, but like 2009's "An Education", it works. 

Becoming a modern masterpiece that will be remembered for years is a difficult task, one that "The King's Speech" also tries to attain in its roughly 2 hour run time. Sadly, it can't quite meet the standards of 'masterpiece'. It comes shockingly close, but the emotional boundaries are never pushed far enough nor are the stakes high enough to warrant such praise. It suffers from being a little too predictable, but only the slightest bit. The sheer brilliance of the directing, acting, and script washes away all of that. 

The movie circles around the eventually crowned King George VI, a political leader with a stammering issue. Collin Firth plays King George VI before and after he was crowned King George VI. Known in his family as Bertie, he and his wife seek treatment from a doctor dealing in speech and fluency where they meet Geoffry Rush's character, Lionel. He has unorthodox methods of helping with the speech impediment, but throughout the film, the methods do prove to be successful. We get many scenes in which Lionel helps Bertie overcome his speaking issues, many of them deliver some great witty banter between Firth and Rush. There's also a priceless moment where, and skip down a few lines if you don't want it spoiled, Lionel is training Bertie to let go and speak his mind fluently, so he instructs him to swear and yell out what's in his head. With a little convincing from Lionel, Bertie surely lets go and sounds totally fluent as his vulgar screams fill the room, Lionel's children sitting right outside the door. At this scene we begin to see the friendship between the two leads develop. Their relationship is believable and charismatic as the film continues. 

Then we do really get into it... the speeches. The anxiety and inner turmoil within Bertie during his messily delivered public speeches can be so easily seen on his face due to the excellent execution of the character by Collin Firth. As Bertie's lips quiver, and as his whole bodily system goes numb, we as the audience feel as though we have become King George VI, and for a brief second, we become the movie and feel it all around. I guess you could argue that the lengthy speeches are only there to show that Collin Firth is really good at not talking right, but hey, it's really interesting to watch so it's fine by me.

This one is a weird one.  I mean that in the way that it is a spectacular movie.  It is very well done, very well acted, very well written, very well everything but it just touches a bit of a sensitive spot with me.  Spots that I had actually almost forgotten about.  I'm lucky in that my own stutter is unnoticeable now (it only appears when I'm in an extreme emotion wise - pissed off, angry, sad, nervous, happy, you get the idea) and I did just sort of eventually get better (I had a speech therapist but not one like Lionel) but I've been lucky in that I've never been so crippled in my adult life.  It happens once in awhile, especially when speaking publicly, but it's really something only I notice now.

It hit nerves without being insensitive.  That is fantastic.  There were so many ways that Colin Firth could have messed this up.  He could have turned it into a gag, however unintentionally, or else totally ignored it and trivialized it.  This was perfect.  A spectacular job on his part.  Sensitive, determined, proud, all those wonderful things that make a stutterer as much as a King.  Bloody fantastic.  The Oscar should have his name on it this year.

Geoffrey Rush and Helena Bonham Carter also should be on the list (and win) this year.  Rush's performance is understated, which fits in so well with Lionel's character in the film.  He's a man of experience with no credentials who is quite ordinary and stands back whenever he needs to.  Carter is fabulous in that we see here that she can play a dramatic role in a period piece instead of a witch or a drama a la her husband Tim Burton.  

Timothy Spall, Derek Jacobi, and Michael Gambon also stand out in their bit parts.  I balked at the idea of Wormtail playing Churchill but he pulled it off and I loved the little touch of Churchill and George VI talking speech issues at the end there.  I always held up Churchill as an example whenever I had issues in middle school and high school.

Another strong suit of this film is that it is hilarious at points.  Really god damned funny and funny without being awful.  I thought that needing to curse to help words flow was my own special quirk and I was pleasantly surprised and delighted to find Bertie doing it too.  There are so  many great one liners in the film that it's impossible to list them all.

Another reviewer made the point that this is structured very much like a sports film (underdog player + coach brings montage sequences before the Big Game).  An interesting and a great way to take it if it was deliberate, even if it's not.

It's understated.  It doesn't proclaim itself as loud as Bertie's curses or shouts of vowels out of open windows but it is oh so effective.  I've seen stuttering characters in film before and this is the first one where I've seen too much of my own situation for comfort.  That is a great achievement.

A biopic set in pre-WWII England. A pedigreed cast. Rich, regal sets. And, it's about the royals, who, thanks to Wills and Kate Middleton, are hotter than ever. Even if it were a snoozer, this flick would have Oscar written all over it. 

But, a movie about an accidental king with a life-long stutter turns out to be anything but dull. It's absolutely engrossing. And, so dear.

Here's the setting: King George V (Michael Gambon) is in declining health. His eldest son and heir to the throne (Guy Pearce) has embarked on an ill-advised love affair with a twice-divorced American. His second son, known as "Bertie" (Colin Firth) may well be called on to lead the kingdom, but Bertie has never been prepared for the duty. Even the nanny regarded him with little respect when he and his brothers were young. 

As England will eventually be pulled into war with Germany, the kingdom needs a skilled orator to reassure an anxious public. A reluctant Bertie is hardly suited to the challenge.

But, he has a sweetheart of a wife (Helena Bonham Carter) who is willing to try an unorthodox therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), since all the other approved doctors and methods have failed. 

Logue's approach is so unorthodox, in fact, that he insists on Bertie treated him as an equal. This doesn't set well with a monarch -- even a reluctant one. But, after initial reservations, Bertie is willing to go along with the treatment because it is, surprisingly, effective. 

What happens next could be called a royal bromance, as the king and his speech therapist spar, needle each other, share childhood hurts and grow genuinely fond of each other. Firth will surely be nominated for an Oscar and is likely to give a big speech of his own at the ceremony in 2011. He'll deserve to. See it!

A good, if straightforward, biopic about King George VI (aka Prince Albert), who took to the throne after his brother, Edward, abdicated to marry a divorcee. "Bertie", as friends and family called him, suffered from a debilitating stammer which seriously impaired his ability to command power and respect as a leader, especially in the age of radio. Bertie goes to see Dr. Lionel Logue, an unsuccessful actor and speech therapist whose unconventional methods (including, notably, delving into the psychological reasons one might have a speech impediment) threaten to turn the deadly serious Bertie away from treatment. By the end of the film, however, a deep friendship between the two men blossoms and the king is able to deliver his titular speech on the eve of WWII.

Colin Firth, playing Bertie, is excellent and heartbreaking as a man who, in theory, has everything: riches, power, a loving wife, etc...yet who, behind closed doors, has been tormented by his family to the point where he can barely look his brother and domineering father in the eye. Firth, who was nominated for best actor last year for his portrayal of a grieving, closeted gay man in A Single Man, will surely be nominated again this year--and it may finally be his year to win.

The supporting cast, specifically Geoffrey Rush as Logue, is incredibly strong. Rush provides a bit of comic relief in an otherwise straightlaced period movie and gives his character an lighthearted, laid back vibe that contrasts nicely the other, more dour and traditional characters.

Just as in any other good presentation, "The King's Speech" uses multiple strategies to win over its audience. The first ploy is an appeal to patriotism: You don't have to be a British subject to choose sides in a film about World War II. The second strategy is to charm the pants off of you. In this regard, the movie has an unbeatable combo in odd couple Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush. Firth stars as (the eventual) King George VI, a decent man suffering from a debilitating speech disorder. He stutters. Through his wife (Helena Bonham Carter), George engages Lionel Logue (Rush), an eccentric Aussie with peculiar - though possibly effective - vocal techniques. "The King's Speech" is an actors' showcase. The verbal and social jousting between Firth and Rush is at the heart of the film, and when the two of them are sequestered in an office, experimenting with everything from recorded music to profanity-laced tirades, the movie is at its best. It is "Pygmalion" in reverse, with commoner Lionel wielding power over blue-blooded George. Looming in the background is all manner of social turmoil: World War II, the abdication of George's brother, the feckless Edward VIII, and the Great Depression. Director Tom Hooper and screenwriter David Seidler try their damndest to link these monumental events to George's personal struggle, but no matter how hard you try - and the filmmakers certainly do - you can't gussy up a five-minute radio address to the same dramatic effect as an invasion of Omaha Beach. "The King's Speech" is a small movie, often amusing but not very profound. Despite Hooper's attempts to make us sweat the fate of England, the overriding impression is that there is just one thing at stake: George's self-esteem. Expanded Review At: Grouchyeditor.com
