In the modern Western cinema landscape, commercial awareness is everything. As a consequence, ninety five percent of all films these days over-promote themselves with marketing strategies which boost audience anticipation to the point of bursting only to finally reveal the finished product as a monumental let down because all the best footage has been used in the trailer. Thank goodness therefore, that the Oscar nominated The King's Speech is one of those rare treasures which not only lives up to it's lofty, borderline elitist prestige but transcends it to become a truly inspirational story of one man's triumph over personal and political adversity.    

Considering all the hype which went into The King's Speech by trying to create its upper crust veneer, what makes it work is that it feels so down to Earth. At its simplest level, the film is not the story of a monarch striving to lead a nation but simply of a man trying to do right by his family whilst struggling to overcome his own debilitating personal demons. It is also pleasing to see how director Tom Hooper makes no qualms in his desire to show the degree of hard work, dedication and personal toil which an actor must go through in order to streamline and refine his craft. The coaching sessions between Colin Firth's King George and Geoffrey Rush's Lionel frequently carry the audience through the whole cacophony of human emotions and these remain the film's most defining scenes. Whether it be the hilarity Rush is encouraging Firth to swear out loud or the sorrow of recalling George's loveless childhood, the sentimental theatricality of the character's sessions is engaging throughout and never slips into cheese or shmultz. 

This is of course complemented by the ensemble supporting cast. Michael Gambon is every bit the cruel Victorian parent as the ailing King George V; Timothy Spall proves a wise though unconventional choice for Winston Churchill and Derek Jacobi gives Christopher Plumber's 'evil church guy' routine a good run for its money as the Archbishop of Canterbury. 

The only real criticism with the film is that it could easily have been a three hour epic had the writing in some areas been more extensive. This is particularly true of Guy Pierce as bullying older brother and party boy monarch Edward VIII. The always excellent Guy Pearce gives an honorable turn in the role but would have been given more room to grow if the writers had expanded on the troubles of his marriage to Mrs. Simpson or put aside the film's strict royalist leanings and explored Edward's indulgence in pro-Socialist philanthropy (totally unheard of in the pre-Princess Diana era). 

Nit-picking aside, The King's speech is still another Stellar piece of British cinema. A rare gem of deep, sentimental, meaningful storytelling among a black sea of stinkers.  As right-wing and nationalistic as it is, cast and crew should all still be very proud.

This is a powerful, hilarious and deeply moving story, told against the backdrop of a critical juncture in modern history, of the emergence of a deep friendship out of a professional relationship between two men who would otherwise never have socially interacted. The screenplay, written by David Seidler is excellent. The dry British wit is hilarious. I was literally slapping my knee during some of the scenes. Tom Hooper does a superb job directing this movie. The buildup to the climactic finale is skillfully executed and prompted the audience to erupt into spontaneous applause. Geoffrey Rush does a fantastic job as Lionel Logue and Colin Firth is excellent as King George VI.

It turns out that David Seidler also had a stuttering problem as a child and drew inspiration from the king's struggle. Early in his career he wanted to write a screenplay about it. He dutifully asked the Queen Mother for permission. She agreed but told him "not in my lifetime". Little did he know she would live to be 101 and he would have to wait another 30 years.

Another interesting tidbit we learned was that near the end of the shoot, the crew finally located one of Lionel Logue's grandsons, who just so happened to live about 10 minutes away from the director. They got access to Lionel's diaries and correspondence and managed to incorporate some of it into the script.

This movie is an unqualified must see.

This is a an important history lesson, as well as an uplifting story of a shy, reluctant king who struggled to over come a physical hindrance to become a symbol of national and international pride and unity.

Albert Frederick Arthur George, was fourth in line for the British throne when he was born in 1895, behind his grandfather, father, and older brother Edward.  Albert, or Bertie to family, was always in the shadow of his brother, who barring death, was destined to eventually be King of the British Empire.  Bertie was a shy kid, raised by sadistic nannies who favored Edward.  He was prone to crying, had knock knees which required him to wear painful metal leg braces,  and he had a bitch of a stammer.  Never outgoing, Bertie accepted his fate and was content, even preferred, to stay in the background and let his more dynamic family members perform the royal duties.

As Duke of York, though, Bertie was required on rare occasions to speak in public, a task that he dreaded.  He and his wife, Duchess Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon exhaustively sought out therapists to help the Duke shed his impediment.  To no avail.  That is. . . until they found "Dr." Lionel Logue, a quirky, unconventional occasional actor who promise the Duke and Duchess that he would absolutely be able to cure Bertie if and only if they put their complete trust in him and his sometimes outlandish methods.

Here began a wonderful journey and a friendship unlike Bertie had ever known.  There were the expected ups and downs of the relationship, but the understanding and rapport they had with one another was too great, and eventually became immune to collapse.

Along the way, Bertie's father, King George V died, and his brother, Edward ascended to the throne.  But ahh. . . .   there's a big problem here. . . .   Edward had fallen in love with a "commoner" and, if he was to marry her, as was his plan, he would have to abdicate the throne, making Bertie king.   That is the LAST thing Bertie ever expected or wanted.  But that was his fate, and like it or not, that's how it was going to be.  Oh well, at least the Coronation Rite required him to speak only three lines.  Easy Peasy Japanesey.  Right?  Wrong!  

World War II was moving into full swing, Britain and Germany had declared war on each other, and the British countrymen were looking toward their new king for comfort and guidance.  At this point, Albert (Bertie) took the name George VI because Albert was too "German."

Oh no!  George had to address his loyal subjects LIVE on that new-fangled thing called radio.  A full scale nine-minute address.  This, his first time addressing his public, would set the stage for how he would be permanently perceived.  His first impression.  He HAD to get it all out and get it out with the confidence his country needed at this troubled time.

This is one of those movies that is almost flawless.  Beautiful to look at, a period piece that kept moving at a brisk and always interesting pace.  Great direction and editing.  The cast were all perfect and totally believable.

Just saw The King's Speech. A tremendous film. Terrific performances by Colin Firth, Geoffrey Rush & Helena Bonham Carter. It's a tremendously unlikely subject for a two hour movie. It's about a man with a speech impediment. Not too exciting. But the man's job puts him in the public eye constantly so something that most of us would find tense but not difficult, for him - it's excruciating. And then he winds up as King of England and then WWII happens and he has to get his act together in a hurry. So a very common little problem is elevated to the level of international politics. A wonderful story and the film makes you identify completely with Albert's problem. It'll have you squirming!

This is a straight-up great movie, one that virtually everyone will like. It's the sort of movie that if you don't like it, there might be something wrong with you. You could call it a "crowd pleaser," and indeed it will please the crowd, but the movie is not as facile as that term implies. Its inspirational qualities feel genuine and well-earned.

It is above all else an actor's picture, and boy is there some great acting here. The movie largely hinges on Colin Firth's performance, which is truly Oscar-worthy. He completely inhabits the role, making the king's ever-present stammer seem utterly real. If you showed this movie to someone who had never heard of Colin Firth, they might well think he actually stammers. He is absolutely brilliant in the way he twists and contorts his speaking voice beyond recognition. His character, Albert, is a good man who never asked to be king. He is not made to seem unduly pathetic; he is a generally competent man, capable of being a good husband and father, who just so happens to be obligated to do the one thing in the world he cannot: speak publicly. The degree of pride that he does indeed have (he is a prince and later a king, after all) does not blind him to his own weaknesses, and he works hard to overcome them. Firth is also extremely funny in certain scenes; one particular outburst of naughty words is one of the funniest scenes I've seen all year. It's a shame they can only give out one Oscar per year; between Firth's excellence here and James Franco's performance in 127 Hours, I wish they could both win.

The supporting cast is also excellent. Geoffrey Rush, who might well earn a supporting actor Oscar nomination, plays the speech therapist as a man of warmth, patience, and wisdom, but who nevertheless has a bit of an insubordinate side. Helena Bonham Carter might also be due an Oscar nod; known for going wildly over the top in films like the Harry Potter series and Alice in Wonderland, is here the very model of acting restraint. She plays the king's wife as understanding and genuinely loving of her troubled husband, but she is also not overly sentimental, and she is realistic about her husband. There are some good actors in smaller parts, as well: Timothy Spall (Peter Pettigrew in the Harry Potter movies) does a very good Winston Churchill impression, Guy Pearce is fine as Albert's brother, and Michael Gambon (Dumbledore in the Harry Potter movies) has a couple of good scenes as the imperious and old-fashioned King George V. 

Stylistically, the movie is well-crafted in a straightforward, traditional way. Tom Hooper's direction exhibits no unnecessary flourishes or directorial funny business. When you have material this strong, I think that's the best approach: just get out of the way and let the story tell itself. In many ways, the movie is as old-fashioned and proper as the people it depicts; but that is not to say that it is stodgy or boring. Far from it: the movie makes a scene of a man speaking alone into a microphone much more thrilling than all of the action in the Prince of Persia movie combined. With a story this good and a cast this superb, it's really no surprise that this is a great movie; it feels like it was destined to be great from its conception. Watching this movie be excellent is like watching pre-scandal Tiger Woods win a golf tournament: one the one hand it was obvious that you would witness greatness, but on the other hand it does not make that greatness any less impressive. As far as old-school storytelling goes, this is one of the very best movies of 2010.

I'll admit this film is by the numbers Oscar bait. Yes, I hear the groans that wonder why we need another movie about British Monarchs. Here's the thing, The Kings Speech could be called an auto-pilot Oscar film but that dismissal ignores first rate acting, Colin Firth is superb, universal and relevant themes, and a sense of simplicity that fuels a film that is serious but never takes itself too seriously. Call it what you will but do yourself a favor and judge The Kings Speech after you see it.

The King's Speech is not a bad movie, and it is certainly a tour-de-force in terms of performances, but it is far from being a masterpiece. In fact, it is far from being the best film of the year (my favourite this far is the Social Network), or even the month (the much more subtle Blue Valentine beats it on almost every front, even matching its great acting turns). 

What particularly bothered me was that the filmmakers seemed to be unsure what angle to take in building up to the film's denoument. The half hearted approach meant that we got a little bit of two stories. The first is that of a human being who grew up in the heartless and pathological environment of the royal family and is searching acceptance. 

The second is that of a flawed and unwilling leader on whose overcoming of his not-so-inner weakness lies the fate of a whole nation. In my mind, neither of these stories was developed enough to make me care for how the final 'King's Speech' will actually sound like. I believe that Tom Hooper especially wasted the film's potential in this second aspect. We see Albert very early on presciently raising the question of German aggression before the invasion of the Sudetenland. When his brother waves off his warning, the next time we are instructed to focus on political questions, the new King is already heroically rallying his people to the battle against fascism. The film leaves out what happened in the intervening period. Where is the building sense of peril? Where is the looming danger? Where is the suspense and the reason for which I should actually care for the stutterer to beat his affliction?

For a movie that hinges on a remarkable true story, its substantial amount of historical innacuracy made me cringe a little as well. First of all, Albert's stutter was in real life nowhere close as bad as that Colin Firth (brilliantly) endowes his character with. However, this was a minor flaw and could be explained by reasons of plot integrity. What I can't understand is why Churchill was presented as supportive of the abdication of King Edward VIII, while in reality he violently opposed it. Minor, but annoying fallacies include the very end of the movie, when Churchill, , along with the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain turn up to Buckingham Palace to witness the King's broadcast on the day war broke out in September 1939, as though they didn't have better things to do. The same applies to the huge crowd waiting to cheer for the King while he finishes his broadcast. 

However, with me rumbling about the finer points of the story, the fact is that I failed probably  to engage with this film that talked about the problems of someone who was born priviliged and never had to worry about the down-to-earth problems in life. The King's struggle simply failed to move the feeling of empathy in me. I would much rather watch the story of another stammerer, Aneurin Bevan, the Welsh miner who grew up in poverty, victoriously battled his stutter without the aid of the best speech therapists money could buy, was elected head of his mining lodge at the age of 19, became well known as an incredible orator, and led the creation of the National Health Service. Now, that is a story worth telling!

Movies about overcoming obstacles are usually pretty good.  Granted, they are fairly predictable and tend to have a sense of self-satisfaction or agenda.  Add to that a general tone that makes the main character a victim rather someone who's got determination, and most of these films generally fade into oblivion.  However, every now and then, a movie comes along that defies the odds set before it.  This is that film.  This isn't one of those solemn films featuring an overacting thespian vying for Oscar glory, but rather a fairly light-hearted film with Oscar-caliper performances of their own right.
Alfred, the Duke of York (Colin Firth - 'Easy Virtue'), has speech problems.  He stammers and gets so overly anxious when asked to give public statements on behalf of his father, King George V (Michael Gambon - 'The Book of Eli'), that he often can't spit a word out.  He and his wife, Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter - 'Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part I'), have tried everything.  Speech therapists don't appear to be working.  In a last-ditch effort, Elizabeth decides to seek the services of Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush - 'Shakespeare in Love'), an Australian speech therapist and amateur actor.  His methods seem strange to Alfred, but he soon begins therapy with Lionel, and makes some progress.  Meanwhile, King George V, falls ill and dies, leaving the throne to Alfred's ungrounded brother, Edward (Guy Pearce - 'The Road').  On the brink of World War II and his blossoming affair with a divorcee, Edward abdicates the throne to Alfred.  Alfred is terrified at the thought of having to be the voice of a nation, but with Lionel's help, he might be able to make it - without resorting to coarse language when frustrated.
Colin Firth might just walk away with an Oscar this year.  I can't vouch for his performance in 'A Single Man' because it just didn't appeal to me, but he's obviously an accomplished actor who's work in this film should be awarded.  The beauty of his performance is that he shows that this is Alfred's burden to bear, and not someone's fault or something that can be fixed by flipping an unseen switch.  Geoffrey Rush is fantastic.  He brings a much needed humor - though, it's quite dry - to a fairly serious film.  The caustic wit and strange methods of his character give the movie such a light-hearted nature that it needs.  
The film is guided by the steady hands of Tom Hooper ("John Adams") and it's delightfully handled.  There's some serious tones, but he gives the film the lighthearted edge above the dreary films that generally populate the Oscar ballots.  Along with Firth and Rush, Helena Bonham Carter is a delight.  She doesn't have much screen time, but it's very nice to see her outside her generally unusual roles.  Guy Pearce and Michael Gambon both turn in their usually good performances, and Timothy Spall (Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part I) really shines in his brief appearances as Winston Churchill.  Composer Alexandre Despalt (Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part I) continues to show his talent with the beautiful score, and cinematographer Danny Cohen ("John Adams") gives the film a beautiful touch.
This film is one of the best films of the year, even though it's not getting the business that such a film warrants.  Sure, it may not have the mass appeal of, say, 'True Grit' or 'The Social Network', it's still a cut above most Oscar bait.  If for nothing else, it's worth seeing for Firth and Rush's performances.  It's true, playing someone with a disability is risky, but the payoff for Firth here is worth it.  Rush is the right amount of comic relief.  It may not be to everyone's taste, but for those looking for story about overcoming obstacles without the preachy message, then this is the movie for you.

Absolutely: "The King's Speech" is a visual wonder; the harsh compositions weave tension into the very texture of the film.  It's supremely well-written; the dialogue alone creates a fascinating war between social classes.  The performances are uniformly superb; not a single character is miscast.  There's so much to say about the film's technical achievements - it's sound design, production design, costumes.  It's an empathetic historical drama, masterfully placing us on the fringes of world wars.  But: The great value of "The King's Speech" is its portrayal of friendship and the merging of these classes.  Colin Firth's Bertie is a man plagued with fear, and there are a handful of extraordinary scenes in which the sources of his fear are slowly drawn out by Geoffery Rush's Lionel.  Here, in the divulging of his past hurts, we the "common man" begin to understand and relate to this soon-to-be king.  This is a uniquely funny and very moving portrait of human weakness directed by the gifted Tom Hooper.  After this and his first film, "The Damned United", let's hope for a long career from this young auteur.

A charming and joyous film about the power of speech. Tom Hooper's film about the reluctant monarch King George VI is a beautiful, simple film about a man trying to overcome his personal issues to instil faith in his leadership.

Colin Firth is superb as George (Bertie) - anguished by his stammer, yet proud and easily angered at suggestions of weakness. Firth does well not to let the characteristic stammer take over the role, always revealing the strength and intelligence of the man behind the fear of ridicule. The final titular speech is so uplifting because we have overcome the impediment with him, and with happy dramatic irony we know his rallying cry will help win the war.

Geoffrey Rush is also excellent as unconventional speech therapist, Lionel Logue, whose over-familiar demeanour and eccentric working methods seem completely improper for the staid George. It feels less of a focused performance than Firth's (you almost suspect that he's playing himself) but, even so, he's perfectly cast in the role, and so determined and canny that you want him to succeed. His bouts of Shakespearean humour he enacts mostly for his family offer welcome relief from the scenes of royal fustiness.

Helena Bonham Carter plays Bertie's wife, Elizabeth (the Queen Mother), and it is doubtful whether a lesser actress would be able to convey her wit, warmth and all-encompassing strength. Timothy Spall does an accurate Churchill without becoming too much of a caricature and Guy Pearce rounds out a stellar cast as George's playboy Brother Edward VIII, whose scandalous relationship with Wallis Simpson forces him to abdicate so passing George the crown.

David Seidler's screenplay is tight and snaps with wit and neatly-cued character drama. Tom Hooper's direction is sublime, mostly filming indoors; he initially keeps George in backgrounds in royal scenes and then brings him to the front where he is dwarfed with courtiers and royal occasion. Lionel, conversely, is always presented in simple surroundings, his family life having no fanfare, and no need of it. His presentation of the royal family as a family, viewed without the aloof trappings, makes them palpably real people rather than untouchable dignitaries. 

It may not be deeply profound but it's a wonderful piece of history, and a charming treatise on the power of the spoken word.

The King's Speech. What is it about? Well, the "King's" Speech. One might suggest the title to be a tad pretentious but it's actually befittingly christened. It's almost like everything leading UP TO the king's speech, and we focus on a man (King George VI played magnetically by Colin Firth) who not only suffers from a stammering speech impediment, but is cast into a conflict: To answer Germany's war threat, uphold the values of his country, and, most importantly, speak for the people. Given the recalcitrant nature of King George's--Bertie as his family calls him--refusal to adhere to monarchal reponsibilities, one might imagine how this conflict is a tad bit difficult--especially that last part. 

Stammering is a lifelong curse Bertie has carried for as long as he can remember. Through thick and thin, his wife, Elizabeth, stays by his side. She seeks the aid of a speech therapist named Lionel Logue (played by Geoffrey Rush who almost outperforms the film's lead). Unlike the highly esteemed therapists, Lionel's methods are more down to earth. From here, the film gets the ball rolling. Although there is the ubiquitous malaise of a second World War eroding through the more sublime moments of this film, it is always the conversational, therapeutic scenes between Firth and Rush which really captures our attention. The two are brilliant actors, playing off of one another. I applaud both of them. On the one hand there's Rush, who gets to flaunt his Australian background in a mixture of comically timed one-liners. And on the other hand, Colin Firth holds the film's foundations securely. He captures the anxiety a stammerer must feel, from the mumbling reluctance to speak to the explosive, vehement tantrums. Firth's performance is impressive; I felt anxious, anticipated, and even frustrated having to watch his character try to strike up a decent conversation with any other character in the movie. And for that matter, the film addresses these emotions properly. We have Bertie's wife Elizabeth who sympathizes with him; his brother David (Guy Pearce) who ridicules him; his own father (Michael Gambon) who explodes impatiently at his ineptitude to speak; and of course, Lionel, who knows that the only true way to help Bertie is through friendship. 

The King's Speech is certainly a great drama with perhaps a dilemma even stronger than its story. It reminded me of other great dramas like Scent of a Woman and Good Will Hunting. Considering the outcome of Britain during WWII, the optimistic ending of this movie is almost ironic. But we are not concerned with Hitler's agenda, we are concerned with King George's. And his is a dilemma so relatable, and adapted here so well, that the story--regardless of it's 1930's time frame--feels very real. 

I'm sure it will win a few Oscars, granted it has competition in the best picture category, but as for Firth's pathway, I believe it will be a golden statue long and well deserved.

EDIT: 

Having just reviewed the film, I declare Tom Hooper's direction commendable. There are numerous tight-spaced, claustrophobic shots to enhance Bertie's discomfort; on the contrary, Hooper also utilizes cameras with extra-wide lenses (the type seen in Stanley Kubrick's A Clockwork Orange) to illustrate Bertie's alienation and giving the film a distorted feel.

Ted Williams got famous in less than a week because he sounds just like John Tesh and has the charm of Jesus. I'd consider myself somewhat of an ignorant American when it comes to history (foreign history especially), so I knew very little to nothing about the events portrayed in 'The King's Speech'. One could say that the film is predictable, which I would hope to be the case if it's based on a true story, but with little knowledge of King George VI's speech impediment being elaborated on in any other film (that I'm aware of), it makes this film less predictable for viewers, like myself, who aren't aware of this story.

The story is simple. The British King George V is dying, and he asks for his son George VI (they refer to him as Bertie actually) to deliver a speech to a massive crowd. The only thing is that his stammer makes the entire occasion an embarrassment for everyone. Good thing he's second in line to inherit the throne. Regardless, his wife (Helena Bonham Carter) enlists the help of a lower-classed speech therapist Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), whom Bertie does not get along with at first. When his father dies and his brother Edward VIII (Guy Pearce) takes over as King, the Shakespeare allusions (mostly to Richard III) soar left and right, but you'll have to watch and listen closely to catch all of them. Since Edward lives the partying lifestyle, his "highness" becomes too much for him to handle and he eventually passes the throne to his little brother. It is then that the show begins to intensify.

See, at the time World War II was just beginning, and there was no time for Bertie to pussyfoot around and make Britain look bad. With the help of Lionel, he learns more than just how to talk properly, but also about the value of respect, power, and most importantly, friendship. As the two work together we get to see Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush in what may be both of the actor's best performances, although I have seen many other amazing roles from the two.

Some may complain about what may seem like dragging scenes in some spots, and if so, then I assure you, Yogi Bear is the perfect film for you. The film is all about the patience required to achieve greatness, and it's all worth it in the end. Honestly, I don't know anyone I wouldn't recommend this to. The R rating is all for a few incidents where Bertie drops the F-bomb a good number of times, but in a very humorous manner, so don't worry about anything else unexpectedly R-worthy. 'The King's Speech' is incredibly educational, surprisingly intelligent, beautifully shot and scored, wonderfully directed, and perfectly casted. I can't say anything bad about it. It deserves anything it wins this awards season, and I'll say it loud if I have to.

A by-the-numbers, join-the-dots, predictable biopic raised above the norm by two superb performances from Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush.  It's thoroughly entertaining with great production values but there are many flaws.  Historically speaking, it's utter bobbins.  Condensing the timeframe is fairly understandable in dramatic terms, along with the invention of Logue's lack of deference to the King (oh how the middle-class audience laughed at a posh man swearing!).  
In its treatment of the wider historical context, however, it is misleading and fundamentally dishonest.  Given that the filmmakers consistently trumpeted their adherence to historical accuracy, you would have thought it would have been easy for them to find out that Baldwin did not resign because of the failure of appeasement, and that Churchill (an uncharacteristically appalling performance from Timothy Spall) was not George VI's strong supporter during the abdication crisis.  
The Chamberlain years are largely airbrushed from the movie, and an unknowing audience might wonder why there was such resentment towards the 'Guilty Men' throughout the war.  Ultimately the film moves towards the conclusion that the King needed to find his voice to lead the British people through the dark days of World War Two.  To emphasise this we have a Boat that Rocked-like scene of glum working class faces suddenly inspired by the King's voice on the radio, which does a disservice to the ordinary British people who really pulled the country through the war.
Overall, this is skilfully-made A-grade entertainment with two great actors on fine form.  I found it very enjoyable, but its depiction of Britain's approach to the war left a nasty taste in the mouth.  I realise that films do not need to be 100% historically accurate, but I do question the agenda behind some of the historical liberties taken here.

Cracking stuff, and well deserving of all the praise and critical plaudits that have been heaped on this film! British cinema needs a shot in the arm like this, if only to keep Hollywood at bay that little bit longer. Colin Firth, an actor I hadn't really been all that privy to, gives what is arguably the performance of his life as King George VI, he of the wartime speeches, the marriage to the future Queen Mother, and of course father to both Margaret and our present monarch, old Liz II. Playing a Royal is not only a tough gig, but also a role that pretty much makes you a favourite for all sorts of awards (Judi Dench was nominated for playing Victoria in Mrs Brown, but won for Elizabeth I, and Helen Mirren won the Oscar for playing the Queen in...The Queen). So, it comes as no surprise that Firth has just won a justly awarded Golden Globe, will probably bag a BAFTA, is a certainty for the Oscar next month, and will probably pick up a Pulitzer, a Booker Prize, and a Blue Peter badge. Yes, I'm kidding, of course, but the point is made. If you want an Oscar, play a Royal. Better yet, play a Royal with a stammer.
George VI was cursed with a stammer, and because such a public figure has to....you know....hobnob with the general public, clear oration is essential. In steps linguist Lionel Logue (played with gusto by Geoffrey Rush), who proceeds to teach him how to pronounce his P's and so on. As the years progress, and war looms, Logue and the King (referred to as Bertie) become inseparable, and important friends during a time of great hardship. 
Let's get this straight; in spite of my jocular review, this film is very, very good, with not a performance out of key, and the time and place, and sense of history are all spot on. I'm guessing the Weinstein's exercised alot of cash to give this film some polish; unlike staged films like The Queen and Mrs Brown, this is purely cinematic stuff, with weird framing and some odd wide-angled vistas that helps to take this story out of its stuffy origins (this thing started out as a radio 4 play), and give it some cinematic gold. The ruse pays off, because you are instantly swept into the story. Also, although the story is basically about a monarch struggling to be King to a people under oppression, there are moments of light comedy to savour. The first shot in the film is of a man gargling water, clearly a portent for the vocal difficulties endured by the King, and moments later dear old Derek Jacobi pops up playing Archbishop Lang, the codger who eventually placed the crown on George's head in 1937. Jacobi, of course is famous for, among other things, playing the Emperor Claudius in BBC's classic mini series, I, Claudius in the 1970's. Claudius was famous for being a stammerer, and Jacobi pulled it off masterfully. Needless to say, I spotted the connection immediately, and found it amusing. Yet, even if the intent wasn't there, I certainly found it a nice touch. Luckily, Firth is also a dab hand at stammering, his muddled King providing the film with true heart. The Royals are, to be fair, a bunch of stuffy old rich buggers (even the present lot are not to trusted either), and yet Firth manages to makes us care. He clearly knows he is giving his defining screen performance and doesn't put a foot wrong. The rest of the distinguished cast follow suit; Rush is always reliable, as is Helena Bonham Carter as the stuffy Queen Mum-to-be. Further down the cast list is Michael Gambon in a small role as George V, Guy Pearce as Edward (he of the Wallace Simpson shenanigans), and even good old Timothy Spall as Churchill. But the film belongs to Firth. He inhabits the role completely, giving his all to a difficult part, and not overplaying it to reach for pathos in the audience. In fact, so good is he in the part that you forget the actor and accept the artifice. In short, he becomes the King. When the cathartic climax comes, you are so caught up in the story and the performance that you will find yourself quietly cheering. If you've seen the film, I'm sure you will agree with me that the actual speech itself, delivered at the very end of the film, to the strains of Beethoven's 7th Symphony and the Emperor's Concerto, is an inspired touch. I, for one, was swept along with the whole thing, and not for a second did I miss all that flashy, false Hollywood glitz. Not only that, but at the very end of the film, we have what can be best described as 'a happy, feelgood ending,' and yet, without giving anything away, this 'happy ending' hinges on the terrible news that the World will be at war for six punishing years!! That's crazy enough, but the truly crazy thing about the ending of this film is that you come away feeling amazingly patriotic about this country. I never thought a film dealing with those 'stuffy old buggers' could not only be grand entertainment, but also good enough to make you want to remember all the words to God Save The Queen again!  It just goes to show that, with the right script, the perfect cast and somebody behind the camera with vision and brains, we can deliver the goods just as easily as our cousin's across the pond. 
Yes, it's bloody good to have an excellent true-blue British film again, and The King's Speech is definitely that film.
Firth has by now placed his Golden Globe award at one end of his mantelpiece; my money is now on the other end of his mantelpiece being occupied by an Academy Award come February.

With movies like this, there are a few things you can take for granted. Yes, the costumes and set dressings are rather extensive. Yes, the script has that oft-irkful air of pompousness. Yes, the acting from the leads is terrific. What isn't always guaranteed is just how entertaining the film may be. While theres a lot of interesting history and monarchal drama, The Kings Speech greatest success is perhaps giving a feel similar to very good sports movie in a strange way rather than a slow-moving period piece, something refreshing to both genres. While fans of period pieces will enjoy it either way, fans of general dramas or even the odd buddy comedy may find themselves surprised by one of the best story-telling films of the year.

The Kings Speech documents the rise of King George VI in the late 1930s. While not the focus of the film, it covers a great deal of incredibly interesting history. Perhaps the single most interesting piece of royal history  is the abdication of King George's brother King Edward VIII, covered in detail yet not laboured upon. Of course, the events are also all building around the threat from Nazi Germany. While not a WWII movie, war buffs will indeed get something out of the film from a more political angle.

While the history is actually incredibly interesting, the film is about King George VI himself, or Bertie as he is called by his family. Despite being expected to help lead the nation, Bertie is crippled by a stammer, making him incredibly socially awkward. After trying numerous doctors, an unconventional method is attempted with speech therapist Lionel Logue, who uses bits of psychology to attempt to find the roots of the problem. Theres an excellent scene where Bertie and Lionel discuss his relationship with his near-tyrannical father and bullish older brother.

A film about a stammer doesn't seem that interesting though, so thankfully there is another level to it. The stammer is a representation of Bertie's nervousness toward responsibility, progressively improving in time with his acceptance of his position. Its not pure coincidence, as much of it is due to Lionel, who acheives an excellent rapport with Bertie. This is where the film begins to feel like a sports drama or buddy comedy: montages of vocal exercises and light jabs (at a Prince, getting points for guts) produce more laughs than expected and the relationship between teacher and student is written extrordinarily well. The final speech has a similar vibe to the final football game in ye standard sports flick.

Most of the weight lies on the cast in this film, and they deliver in spades. Colin Firth gets the most attention, and does indeed deliver his lines incredibly convincingly with the stammer and adds numerous subtle layers to his character. It should not be understated how great he is, but he gets all the attention, so lets shift to perhaps the real star of the show: Geoffrey Rush. While Firth is the emotional center, Rush is the reason to rewatch the film. His performance as Lionel is believable, entertaining and animated, yet never feels like acting. 

Helena Bonham Carter goes decidedly non-crazy as she who became The Queen Mother Elizabeth, portraying a much warmer character than I thought she could. Guy Pearce does very well with a smaller role as King Edward VIII, as somewhat of a spoiled brat who somehow maintains sympathy even as he shirks responsibility. The only misfire in the cast is Timothy Spall as Winston Churchill. Perhaps I have trouble dissociating him from Wormtail, but he seems to try to steal every scene he appears in and gets tiring quickly.

While it starts off slow and will definitely bore some, for those who appreciate dramas of any kind, The Kings Speech is a great film. Well acted, well scripted and surprisingly funny, as well as seemingly quite the crowdpleaser, The Kings Speech is the best awards bait in some time.

I freely admit that I'm love British culture and history. This was a time period in England that I knew next to nothing about, so I was very intrigued by this film going in. I also love Colin Firth, especially after last year's Single Man (which I would have said was the best performance of 2009).

At the forefront of the movie is the fact that we are headed to war against the most evil man who ever lived. You even get a look from Lionel that knowingly shows his son is headed to war. I left the film not thoughtful, not inspired, I would say. The King's Speech is a stunning piece of Oscar bait.  Every element of the film is masterfully, meticulously handled.  Tom Hooper, who directed the amazing and under-appreciated The Damned United, brings the story of the stammering King George VI to brilliant life, working from a well-written screenplay by David Seidler, himself a stutterer in his youth.  

Of course, most of the film's praise has been rightfully directed at the amazing cast.  Colin Firth delivers perhaps his most impressive performance to date; it's unfathomable to imagine the time and effort that went into creating his portrayal.  The tics and hesitations sound perfectly natural, and Firth handles each scene with seeming ease.  He's especially great in the scene that earned the film its R-rating and during the final, climactic speech.

Just as worthy of praise is Geoffrey Rush, who plays the speech therapist to the king (sing with me: It's a difficult responsibility....).  Rush brings some of the boyish energy he displayed in Pirates of the Caribbean to the role, and the way he pokes and prods His Royal Highness is sublimely entertaining.  Together, Rush and Firth make an unforgettable pair.

Sadly, Helena Bonham Carter gets the shaft regarding screentime and things to do.  She is perfectly fine in her role, but there's nothing at all showy or particularly impressive about it.  It's strange to me that she's garnered awards attention for such a slight part, but there you are.

It's hard to find any fault in The King's Speech, but that in itself almost becomes a problem.  It's a film that was is so obviously an Oscar contender that it's almost obnoxious in its quality.  It's an odd complaint, but it's almost too typical a story to garner much passion beyond the acute admiration it so easily deserves.

The chemistry between Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush is what makes "The King's Speech" the masterpiece that it is. The comedy within this drama will have you cracking up, as well as the many charming performances like Guy Pierce playing the bully brother to Firth's King Geroge, and Timothy Spall as Winston Churchill. The camera work is brilliant such as the fish head, hand held closeups on the King as the weight of the world is on him. The pacing can be a bit slow at times, but whenever Rush and Firth are on the screen, you will be mesmerized.

It's easy to shrug off awards films when the season rolls around, and on the surface, "The King's Speech" shows all the symptoms of shameless Oscar bait. It's a period drama loaded with stiff English accents, led by a cast of previous Academy Award winners and nominees. In all honesty, the average moviegoer doesn't have a whole lot to be excited about in Tom Hooper's new film, but those compelled by the idea of a character study detailing the relationship between King George VI (Colin Firth) and his impertinent speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) will find this an often lively and effective drama.

The speech angle is an interesting distinguishment. Unlike many of the films that helped lend the genre its dry reputation, authentic atmosphere doesn't substitute for drama here. "The King's Speech" works not because we watch a historical personage overcome a debilitating verbal ailment, but because we watch a human being do so. Colin Firth has received much kudos for his performance, but it's likely many honored him for the wrong reasons. Firth is excellent because he humanizes George VI--making him rounder than some haughty profile--not because he can act with a stammer.

Rush plays his counterpart with absolute authority. We get a sense of the coddled life George leads as a prince, and the implicit respect he garners from the countless instructors he's worked with before. Logue, who operates out of the basement of his shabby apartment building, is the first to deny George (or Bernie, as he presumes to call the future king) special treatment. His cheeky remarks and irreverent lessons occasionally offend, and the nature of their relationship is often antagonistic. The one thing His Royal Highness can't argue with, however, is the results.

The greatest filmmaking fault then, out of necessity, is that "The King's Speech" must divide its time between these enlightening lessons and more typical period drama affair. The impending death of King George V and a scandal between Prince Edward and an American divorcee play major roles in shaping the narrative arc, though are significantly less interesting to watch. In merely retelling history, Hooper loses the character-driven force that makes the one-on-one therapy segments so special. Outside of Logue's office, "The King's Speech" becomes just another stylistically restrained biopic.

The speech lessons, by comparison, free the director up. Probably there is no official record of what was said between George VI and Logue, and the scenes are infinitely better for it. "The King's Speech" is almost a different film when released from the short reigns of history. The two characters come alive, as does the camerawork, exclusively in these instances. The difference isn't jarring enough to make the film feel disjointed, but there is scarcely a memorable moment that doesn't involve Logue.

On the whole, "The King's Speech" goes above and beyond most uninteresting but extravagantly decorated period films. The performances elevate the material beyond biography regurgitation, and by focusing on his characters above the historical events they instigated, Hooper avoids the most popular pitfalls of the genre. Ultimately, his film is still one caught between two worlds, and the balance struck between them isn't always perfect. The great atmosphere he creates within the context of the speech lessons is his own antagonist--he can't match that energy elsewhere.

But even being intermittently captivating, "The King's Speech" is absolutely worth seeing. It's not exactly what I would consider award-worthy, but that seems to be the only context in which such a film will be seen by most. In all honesty, you'll be better off ignoring the hype and seeing the movie simply because it features an unusually intimate portrait of a king, and a compelling story of personal triumph. Oscar who?

JOE'S REVIEW - Fans of both historical docudramas and good acting will like this story of England's King George VI, (Colin Firth) who ascends to the throne right before WWII. There is a problem however; he can't deliver a speech w/out stuttering, A stuttering king would not instill confidence in a nation about to go to war. So his wife (Helena Bonham Carter) enlists the help of an unconventional "speech defects" (the pre- PC days) expert Lionel Logue, (Geoffrey Rush) whose weird methods actually help the new king to make his speech on the eve of declaring war on Germany w/out stuttering, and many more after that.
This sounds like it may be a stuffy, boring historical drama, but it is often quite funny, and very touching, and it is essentially a buddy flick between Firth and Rush, not unlike, say, The Odd Couple or 24 Hours. Both men give top-notch performances, and their scenes together are great, and both may see Oscar nominations from their roles in this thoroughly enjoyable movie.

With the help of his wife Elizabeth (Helen Bonham Carter) he reluctantly begins working with an eccentric speech therapist Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) to help with his problem.

 Firth is simply fantastic and automatic favorite for the  Best Actor Oscar. Carter and Rush have also recieved well deserved Oscar nominations. It is a very rare occasion when a film comes along which can be described as near flawless, but when it does, it is a film and time to be cherished. "The King's Speech" is an extremely powerful and awe inspiring film. It does not have visual effects or crazy CGI images in which many films are these days measured by, it relies purely on the amazing performances by Colin Firth, Geoffrey Rush and Helena Bonham Carter and a brilliantly written screenplay to create an emotionally charged film which is almost completely character driven. The film opens with the Duke Of York (Colin Firth), affectionately known as Bertie by his family, giving a speech at Wimbeldon. As soon as he opens his mouth, realisation sets in that he has a bad stammer and is incapable of speaking in the same manner as others because of it. His wife, Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) seeks out the help of Ausralian speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) to help with her husbands problem after a series of failed attempts by advised psychiatrists. Although Bertie is cynical at first of Logue's methods, the most unlikely of friendships starts to form and Logue becomes an even more crucial part of his life when he becomes crowned King George VI.

This movie is an amazing story of real human emotion which can be felt by anyone, not just the King of England. There are millions of people out there who have problems with public speaking or have low self esteem because of one reason or another. This movie reaches out to those people and pulls on their emotional strings. It is extremely rare for a film which is based on a powerful and historical figure to become one which everyday people can relate to. This film would not be what it is without the amazing acting by the three lead's. This is very much a character driven film, which means that the acting had to be superb in order for it to be any sort of success. Tom Hooper certainly knew what he was doing when casting this film. Colin Firth is absolutely incredible as Bertie. He well and truly becomes the character and the audience becomes completely lost in the character to the point that you completely forget that this is Colin Firth you are watching. Gone is Mr Darcy and every speck of "Pride And Prejudice" and "Bridget Jones' Diary" which Firth used to project when he appeared on the screen, this man is the real deal. He shows the pain and embarassment he feels over his stammer right from the first sight of him on the big screen. He truly becomes the character right down to the smallest detail. Firth carries himself like royalty and his stammer brings tears to your eyes.  He has indeed reached he pinnacle of his career, and there seems to be no real threat in sight for the Best Actor Oscar.

Geoffrey Rush is great as Logue. Unlike Firth, it is not the hardest role he has ever done, but he nevertheless is brilliant and extremely likable. Like Bertie, the audience feels pity for Logue. His character is extremely witty and funny. Helena Bonhom Carter is also brilliant as the future Queen mother. In this role which see's, for the first time in a long time, take on a film role which is not a quirky Tim Burton or Harry Potter role. It is not the first time she has played royalty ( as she was cast as Anne Boleyn in the TV movie "Henry VIII" in 2003), but it is defiantely her finest. She is sublime as Elizabeth and you can see the love she has for her husband and the pain she feels for him in his eyes. Timothy Spall was also brilliant as Winston Churchill, taking on the persona ansd mannerisms of the man to perfection. 

The screenplay is brilliantly written. The reference for this film was the diaries which Lionel Logue left behind and these diaries were available to Hooper and and writer, David Seidler when putting together this film. The research which has gone into this film is just incredible. It is also quite funny in parts, such as when Bertie is learning how to swear, which is quite unusual for such an emotional drama film. The cinematography and musical score enhance every emotion throughout the film and create suspense and intrigue. The monologue of Bertie and Logue's therapy sessions is very clever and highly enjoyable. 

In colnclusion only one thing can be said to sum up everything which "The King's Speech" is. The future best film of the 2011 Academy Awards, and that is no light statement.

First of all, if Colin Firth doesn't win all of the major awards for best actor this season something is wrong with the world. He can be known for phoning in a standard Mr Darcy performance but this role is so well played that you feel so many different emotions for Bertie, it is poignant and beautiful.

I must also mention Helena, always one of my favourite actresses (as much for her taste in scripts as her performance) she delivers another fabulous character.

Geoffrey Rush is also getting overlooked in such a superb cast, his character is very likeable but also has a lovely depth for a supporting cast member.

The story itself is simple but effective. The pace is slower than your usual blockbuster film which can take a little adjusting too, however it is perfect for the subject, era and story.

It's final compliment is it's patriotism. It is not overt patriotism as with American films but you do leave the film feeling very proud to be British.

The King's Speech focuses on King George VI (Colin Firth) and before he became the head of the monarchy, he was the Duke OF York when Edward VII (Guy Pearce) decided to marry an American divorcee and given that the regulations is that he's the Head Of the Church, the Church cannot take the Duke's wish of marrying a woman who's twice married and so Edward abandoned his place to the Royal throne to George. The man who wouldn't be called King by the whole public never wished to be King because it involves public speaking or making speeches which he truly dreaded. George has a speech impediment that not only disallows him to make a speech, he constantly stutter when having a conversation or when he tells a bedtime story to his daughters Elizabeth (our Queen today) and Margeret.

Having no hope to treat this impediment his wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) went to Australian speech therapist Lionel Logue (Geoffery Rush) where his unorthodox methods not only treated Bertie's (his family usually calls him that) weakness but grow a special relationship between the two during times of war and post war

The only thing I heard about The King's Speech is that like The Social Network it is one of the best films of 2010. I went into the film with no expectations because the Royal Family never had me interested. And also anyone under the age of say 50 wouldn't be interested about the film's premise. But then when I came out of the movie once it was finished I was really astonished and impressed with this film and knew why it had to be the year's best.

The plot was really fascinating in many levels as it's about the biggest weakness of a King who's an icon for National Resistance during World War II that's supposed to be the King's duties. It's also fascinating of how Bertie has to become King because his brother Edward marries someone who is not the Church's type.

It is also unintentionally hilarious as the humour for the film comes quick and fast. Not to mention it is filled with a lot of wit. But the problem with this movie's humor is when to laugh. Most of the audience had laughed between scenes and it's great that they're enjoying themselves.

Colin Firth should receive an Oscar for Best Actor because he portrayed a famous King as we never had learnt before. Bertie's emotions have me sympasise for him because he's kinda feels like he's autistic. He's not confident and has a lack of communictation with the public because of his handicap and he'd get picked on by his father for not speaking perfectly. However Firth makes his character really inspirational and motivating as whenever words come out of his mouth at any stop it's exciting that he had overcome his weaknesses. Geoffery Rush is hilarious and fun to be with as an Australian speech therapist who's character is very riveting as he helps Bertie to be a King along wars and troubles and has a play-by-my-rules stance.

Even Helena Bonham Carter is splendid as Bertie's wife as this is a departure from her usual character as a melodramatic psycho. She also supports Bertie with seldom where she's the only person in his family who does that since none of his family never cared if he had trouble speaking.

But apparently The King's Speech is not perfect. What would've made it perfect is that many historical dramas have this particular formula that I have trouble with. I mean we know the main character has something bad that restricts his duties as the head of a powerful monarchy but then it's when he's starting to take over and it's make it so predictable at the end of the film and once you get to the ending it's just that is that.

In the wake of its Oscar success - Best Picture, Actor, Director, Screenplay - The King's Speech needs little introduction. However, it is worth remembering that the film has become so highly decorated for a reason. So, while some have delighted in pointing out its historical inaccuracies, and others that it glosses over King George VI's alleged Nazi sympathies, these issues don't impinge upon what is clearly a beautifully made movie. As George, Colin Firth is equal parts wounded and defiant, a man whose rapid ascension to the throne is tainted by a speech impediment that renders him impotent when, with war approaching, his country needs him most. As Lionel Logue, the Australian speech therapist who helped the King, Geoffrey Rush could consider himself unlucky not to have snagged another golden statue. This biography film boasts an exceptional British cast, which includes Helena Bonham Carter, Timothy Spall, Michael Gambon, Derek Jacobi, Claire Bloom and Aussie Guy Pearce, all of whom help contribute to the picture with the smallest amount of screen time.

An excellent film about a little-known period of drama between the two world wars. The casting is perfect with Colin Firth as the stuttering Prince Albert/ King George VI ,Helen Bonham Carter as his wife (proving she can do more than act crazy), Timothy Spall as Churchill, Micheal Gambon plays all-too-short role as King Edward and Geoffry Rush who steals every scene as Lionel Laude, the speech therapist. 

The best thing about this film is the back and forth between Firth and Rush, giving the film much needed conflict and comedy, while the threat of German invasion grows. The king after Edward's death, David (Guy Pearce being perfectly arrogant and nasty) chooses to abdicate for personal reasons leaving 'Bertie', who is inflicted with a terrible stutter he's had since childhood, to assume the throne.

The second best thing about the film is that there is no simple cheesy montage of Firth's character going from stutterer to being able to articulate every word perfectly, as there would be if this was an American film. It's a personal journey for the King, and while the film could've gone deeper into the emotional reasons for his impediment it's brilliantly scripted and well paced.

King's Speech will also strike a personal chord for people like myself who have or used to have speech problems as it effectively communicates the frustration and self-doubt that comes with conditions such as stuttering.
Go and see this film.

From start to finish, Colin Firth gives the best performance of his career as the stammering King George "Berty" VI, effectively carrying one of the best historical dramas in the last decade, if not in history. The film tells of the story of the Duke of York, who, at the beginning of World War II, is tasked with becoming king and uniting his country in a dire hour after his arrogant, cruel brother shirks his responsibilities as king and runs off with an American divorcee. Berty fears the position as king because of its requirement to make speeches, something his impediment largely prevents from happening. Firth is absolutely brilliant as the King, putting on the outside an aura of strength and bravery, and yet also concealing inner fear and disgust at the sound of his own voice. In one of the films most powerful scenes, Berty tells his children a story at their request, and rushes through it as their expecting, eager eyes stare back at him. He does not wish to let them down, but wishes also not to embarrass them with his frequent stammer. 
 After seeing a number of doctors about his impediment, Berty's tender, loving, and endearing wife-an exceptional Helena Bonham Carter in her best, least freaky role to date-eventually resorts to an unconventional doctor with little to no credentials who's unorthodox methods and quirky personality eventually aid Berty in building the persona and speech fit for a king. Geoffrey Rush plays the unconventional doctor and often steals the scene from the equally brilliant Firth. The two are a joy to watch together, and form one of the most dynamic acting duos ever to grace the silver screen. 
 Other awe-inspiring performances in the film include Guy Pearce as the irresponsible brother, Michael Gambon as Firth's father, and Timothy Spall (in a stroke of casting genius) as Winston Churchill. 
 Overall, King's Speech is a must-see and a surefire Oscar winner. firth is a shoe-in for best actor as he was also nominated last year, and both Carter and Rush are guaranteed supporting nominations. In fact, this spectacular film may even steal the top prize from the Social Network.

Firth deserves the Oscar 100% - I'm as surprised as anyone at just how, after his modest English gent act of previous years, he has emerged not only a dark horse movie star, but a proper actor of competitive calibre. Rush's unique screen presence alone should net him some deserved recognition - I could only see Barbossa at first, but this disappeared almost immediately (a similar reaction to Timothy Spall as Churchill). Helena BC, meanwhile, plays the future Queen Mother with the same offputting aloofness she became known for - but here it doesn't take long to notice the twinkle in her eye. It's also great to see Guy Pearce in something good again, and while his accent may be a touch too much, he fits the arrogant scoundrel role ideally. Final props should undoubtedly go to Hooper, who directs with an artist's eye but never once intrudes on the story or his dedicated cast - following The Damned United with clinching proof that he is a modern maestro in strong character drama.

Not really my kind of film at all, but was very good. You'd expect this to be well acted, well scripted and well made, but what I didn't expect was that it wouldn't take itself (or the royals) too seriously, and overall that'd what made it an enjoyable film.

I'd heard 'even Marxists will come out liking the royals' so was a bit worried this would be an upper class toff-fest, which largely it was, but it wasn't overly reverent of the royals, painting them as fearful people living in their own little world yet affected with the same personal problems as the rest of us. I thought and the humour worked well in making sure this film didn't celebrate them as some films do and as a social-liberal republican I thought there was a good balance between the nonsense pomp of royalty and the fact that even royalty think its all a laborious waste of time. I'm not quite sure how accurate Geoffrey Rush's character's near-treasonous humour in the King's presence was, I'm hoping it was accurate as at least then the royals have a sense of humour about themselves, but somehow I imagine it was played up a bit. There was always the lingering 'nice speech Bertie, but the people you've just made it to are going to spend the next few years in the trenches while you swan around worring about a weekly radio broadcast' feel, but as a film the speech worked as a symbolic representation of perseverence against odds, just what the 'common' people would show in the war years to come. Looking at it in reality though; making a speech vs fighting a war... impedement or not, there's no genuine comparison really is there? 

At least royals do get out there and fight wars a bit so that's something, but let's be clear to the non-British watchers that the people prop up the monarchy because they trust them more than they trust the politicians who get in. If the British electoral system was more equal, the monarchy would likely be made a tourist attraction only or gradually phased out altogether. Great for historical movies; a waste of the tax payers money in real terms. Though there seem to be a large amount of royalists left in the UK so I don't speak for everyone. Then again we don't like our politicians much at the moment so I imagine that has something to do with it.

That's all beside the point of the film though, which is well written, well executed and well thought out- you don't have to be a toff to like it, and in lots of ways it wouldn't help because laughing at toffs is one of the main requirements of enjoying this film. Colin Firth is bound to get the Oscar for this, which you have to say is well deserved because it is a very convincing and difficult performance. Helena Bonham Carter and Geoffrey Rush are very good to and this is definately an 'actors' film. Timothy Spall's Churchill though... let's just hope they don't make a film about that.

The film is based on the story of King George the VI's (played by Colin Firth) ascension to the throne, due to the abdication of his predecessor (his brother, Edward), and subsequently hiring speech therapist, Lionel Logue (played by an amazing Geoffrey Rush) to help him overcome his stammer.

The film moves at a relatively fast paced, considering the type of film that it is. The speech therapy sessions wiz on by with the brilliance of Colin Firth, who manages to communicate fluidly with the audience, without even uttering a syllable; and Geoffrey Rush's wit and charm also shine. The film is also very funny, which more than just surprised me. It's Rush who cracks most of the jokes, but Firth also gets in on the act later on (his incoherent swearing is hilarious).

Once George is given the reigns as king, after his brother abdicating it due to his urge to marry an already divorced woman, the film accelerates in to a modern classic. The scene in which George has to give his first wartime speech is, not only the culmination of everything he and Lionel have been working on, its a real heart warmer.

The performances are right out of the top draw. Colin Firths King George (or Bertie, as he is known by for most of the film) is stunningly portrayed. Firth just missed out on the Academy Award last year for A Single Man (also a terrific film), but there is no real justification for him not to get it this year. He delivers his lines (when he actually has any) to perfection, but he also adds such a depth too the character. Do not be surprised if Mr. Firth is on stage next month collecting his Best Actor award. It would also come as no shock to see Geoffrey Rush claiming the Best Supporting Actor award. An utterly brilliant performance. Such elegance, but also such an unmitigated charm is given to his character that, even Garfields performance in The Social Network may struggle to hold on to an award that, prior to this, was almost (in my eyes) certainly his. Helena Bonham Carter also puts in a good turn as Georges wife, Queen Elizabeth, her first in quite a long time. It was also nice to see Guy Pearce crop up in a film. He puts in a stellar turn as King Edward, Georges brother.

The cinematography is fantastic, too. Luscious shots of rooms (Lionels therapy room is of a very bland color palette, but is captured perfectly), the actors, and the outdoors. Slick editing, and a nice period score make all the technical aspects up to standard.

Verdict:

A tremendous feel good movie, that also packs an emotional punch. Great performances all round, especially from Rush. Pure 'Oscar' bait, and do not be suprised if this sweeps the board, come February.

Upon the arrangement of Queen Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter), The King's Speech center's around Bertie (Colin Firth) and the unlikely friendship he forms with his speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) as together the two mechanically try to rid-through an unorthodox course of treatment and various exercises-Bertie of a stammer in which he has been acquainted with all his life. It is not until the death of King George V (Michael Gambon), his father, the abdication of the scandalous King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce), his brother, that Bertie is crowned King George VI of Britian in a time when a nation is desperate for a leader.

As Germany's troops failed to abandon Poland, it is such that Great Britain declared war upon Hitler's regieme. Now, Bertie is to recollect all his sessions of therapy and deliver a war-time speech to inspire his great nation and unite them for the potential darkness that await in the shadows of the days ahead.

Colin Firth's quintessential performance as King George VI is undoubtedly the performance of his career. His poignant reenactment of King George's stammer adorns the film and intelligibly captures, with high proficiency, the agony and terror of a man afraid of his own voice. Admittedly, the entire supporting ensemble is splendid. Though of them, it is Geoffrey Rush who truly is remarkable as the unorthodox, quick-witted, Lionel Logue.

Danny Cohen's cinematography breathes divinity, class, and under the masterful direction of Tom Hooper, the whole of The King's Speech is seen through a stylish eye in which enriches the film's eloquence to an articulate grandeur. Not a instant is idly wasted here from actor or environment as even each set piece, in itself, delivers a performance of unimaginable heart.

At last, Alexandre Desplat's original minimalistic score plays expertly against Ludwig van Beethoven's finest symphony and concerto setting a most unnerving melancholy to the scene in which it tolls.

With its stylistic direction, haunting score, and enthralling performances, The King's Speech is a tremendously developed piece of cinema which remains consistently gripping from its opening scene where one's attention is first captured.

âThe Kingâ(TM)s Speechâ opens in 1925 as Prince Albert (Colin Firth,) son of King George V, is preparing to give a speech to thousands of eager listeners at Wembley Stadium in England. His dearly supportive wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) stands close by, gazing over at her husband, hoping for success. Alas, Albertâ(TM)s voice refuses to cooperate, and his stammering speech gets the best of him. 

Because Albert is in such a prominent sociopolitical position, he dreads the frequent speeches that he must give to his country through the radio. He hires many different speech therapists, all knighted and credentialed, but no techniques they offer can cure his stammerâ"not even a mouth full of marbles does the trick. His wife therefore decides to seek out a lesser-known speech therapist, and we finally meet Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush.) Logue is known largely for his relatively unorthodox methods, and when Elizabeth first meets him and asks him to help her husband, it is clear that he knows he is damn good at what he does.

So begins Albertâ(TM)s struggle to conquer his stammer with daily lessons from Logue, who insists that they communicate on a familiar, first name basis, despite Albertâ(TM)s objections concerning their differing social statuses. These are some of the most wonderfully written scenes I have seen in film, as Logue manages to peel away the layers and reveal the roots of Albertâ(TM)s stammer. As Humphrey Bogart once said, this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship.

Through these scenes, we actually get to witness the birth and growth of a true friendship, one that is built on trust, courage and the need to overcome the challenge of being unable to speak publicly in a job that demands it. After his father dies, Albertâ(TM)s brother David (Guy Pierce) briefly takes over, but due to his plans to marry a divorced American woman, he quickly steps down and Albert inherits the throne as King George VI. 

Firth has already won the Golden Globe for Best Actor for this performance, and he will no doubt win once again at the Oscars. It is a tremendous performance that resonates strongly with anyone who has ever felt insecure or had stage fright.  Being put on the spot is never a fun experience, especially when you are addressing a nation that is relying on you for guidance at the onset of WWII. 

Rush is equally brilliant in this film. He is an actor who can blend seamlessly into any roll he is asked to perform, from the Marquise de Sade to Peter Sellers, and Lionel Logue is a perfect fit. Rushâ(TM)s tone and delivery in every scene are marvelous. As Logueâ(TM)s confidence in his work and in Albert remains intact throughout the toughest of times, we see their relationship become deeper and more genuine each time they meet. 

Pierce and Gambon are terrific as Albertâ(TM)s brother and father, respectively. Pierce brings an authentic nuance to David and Albertâ(TM)s relationship, suggesting that he has forced his own insecurities upon Albert, including in one particular scene when he reminds his stammering brother of a cruel childhood taunt, calling him âB-B-Bertie.â Gambon is very good as a father who couldnâ(TM)t understand his son, and wouldnâ(TM)t try to. In one scene, he commands Albert to just spit it out for the sake of not sounding like a fool, and thus tarnishing the royal name. Itâ(TM)s a cruel world that Albert lives in, and Logue is his guardian. 

âThe Kingâ(TM)s Speechâ is a beautifully universal film about the expectations and obstacles that are passed down to us, and the means by which we can all manage to overcome them. With some terrific performances and superb work by director Tom Hopper, the film also carries with it some important and inspiring messages. It is rated-R for the use of one or two naughty wordsâ"an unfortunate truth. It is a wonderful film that is more than suitable for a wider age group than its rating permits, and it is certainly one of the best films of 2010.

When it comes to films such as "The King's Speech" it is hard to ignore the fact that these are the types of films the Oscar voters will look at. It brings a completely different kind of aspect to the viewing role if you have any interest in film or the awards shows. And while I enjoyed this film very much, I wouldn't put it at the top of my favorites. While it is a beautifully made film, it isn't the most beautiful film I've seen in recent memory. 

What I am trying to say is that there is no doubt the two lead actors here, Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush, will garner Oscar noms and at least one of them will probably win. Deservedly so, but what is there of this film after all the awards talk is wiped away? After we take away the pre-conceived thoughts the rave reviews have planted in your head and simply go into this with a clear mind. What would you think had you heard nothing of this film prior? That is what I went in trying to answer and I am happy to say that even without the positive hype I still found myself loving much of this film. It is a movie of moments, both touching and humorous. It opens up a fascinating world and while it is clearly a slower paced, artistic movie, it is never not entertaining and in that was where the victory was won. 

In 1936 Firth's Bertie must take over the role of king after his father dies and his brother abdicates the throne. It is all completely true and completely fascinating. The catch here is that Bertie has battled with a stutter most of his life and when it comes to public speaking he is overcome and ultimately defeated by it every time. Enter Lionel Logue (Rush) the unorthodox speech coach that will overcome the King's handicap and lead him to a victory during the point in his life when he needs it most. 

The acting here is fantastic. As Bertie Firth is nothing less than brilliant, truly, he inherits the character and leads the movie with a fearless quality that makes us wonder how he will cope with the predictable structure of the film. Though we know how everything will play out, it is the interaction between Firth and the wonderfully awkward Rush that make this film feel special. It is beautifully designed and shot. Its angles possess an in-your-face feeling. Putting you right behind the microphone or right in front of the audience that seem to be towering over you. It is almost nauseating at points and we see why Bertie is as nervous as he is. The style sometimes disrupts the uptight nature of the films subject but it does nothing short of aiding the storytelling. 

As Lionel, Rush is not the high brow academic he portrays himself to be in the presence of his patients. He is simply a struggling actor who finds he has a talent for aiding those with speech impediments. Thus meaning his character isn't the usual quirky oddball, but he is a kind of deceiver, but in the terms least harsh of meanings. Lionel does what he does because he truly means to help his patients. As the time and lessons continue between he and the king, they naturally become good friends who by the end are much more than student and teacher. We see it coming, but this is the finest example of a buddy film ever made. And as exuberant as Rush is in his role, it is good to see such amazing support by such amazing and invested actors like Helena Bonham Carter's Elizabeth, who is always there for her husband, always supportive, always striving to help. Bonham Carter makes a turn here for the best, creating a calm and natural role from an actress that is known for her eccentric characters. Guy Pearce shows up shortly as the slimy King Edward VIII and Timothy Spall and Michael Gambon portray more famous historical figures that are filled out just fine. 

What amazes me most about the film is the simplicity of its story. There is no rising action, no big climax we are really building to here. And what tension there might be is easily relieved by the fact we know what to expect or what is going to happen, if you know even a little bit of history. The pacing, acting and beautifully graceful musical score all help this move along in a way that doesn't necessarily require our short attention spans to be looking for that familiar conclusion. Instead we have become so invested in this character that Firth is playing so wonderfully that we only hop he can overcome his fear and lead his country at a time when a strong leader is most needed. 

"The King's Speech" is not a large drama that has gained its status as serious Oscar contender because of its original story or its groundbreaking storytelling, special effects or even its sense of prestige. Instead it is just a character-driven story that relates a universal theme through an individual we would expect to have everything figured out. To see that even the most privileged of us all still have their issues is not just refreshing but it offers opportunity galore for a character actor to spread his wings and suggest the idea of what it was like to be that person they are portraying. All the actors here did that well, but Firth did it perfectly and as much as I tried to keep the awards chatter out of my brain, I could not escape the thought that Firth will no doubt be holding a golden statue come February.
