Upon the arrangement of Queen Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter), The King's Speech center's around Bertie (Colin Firth) and the unlikely friendship he forms with his speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) as together the two mechanically try to rid-through an unorthodox course of treatment and various exercises-Bertie of a stammer in which he has been acquainted with all his life. It is not until the death of King George V (Michael Gambon), his father, the abdication of the scandalous King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce), his brother, that Bertie is crowned King George VI of Britian in a time when a nation is desperate for a leader.

As Germany's troops failed to abandon Poland, it is such that Great Britain declared war upon Hitler's regieme. Now, Bertie is to recollect all his sessions of therapy and deliver a war-time speech to inspire his great nation and unite them for the potential darkness that await in the shadows of the days ahead.

Colin Firth's quintessential performance as King George VI is undoubtedly the performance of his career. His poignant reenactment of King George's stammer adorns the film and intelligibly captures, with high proficiency, the agony and terror of a man afraid of his own voice. Admittedly, the entire supporting ensemble is splendid. Though of them, it is Geoffrey Rush who truly is remarkable as the unorthodox, quick-witted, Lionel Logue.

Danny Cohen's cinematography breathes divinity, class, and under the masterful direction of Tom Hooper, the whole of The King's Speech is seen through a stylish eye in which enriches the film's eloquence to an articulate grandeur. Not a instant is idly wasted here from actor or environment as even each set piece, in itself, delivers a performance of unimaginable heart.

At last, Alexandre Desplat's original minimalistic score plays expertly against Ludwig van Beethoven's finest symphony and concerto setting a most unnerving melancholy to the scene in which it tolls.

With its stylistic direction, haunting score, and enthralling performances, The King's Speech is a tremendously developed piece of cinema which remains consistently gripping from its opening scene where one's attention is first captured.

In what could have been another formulaic addition to the tome of films chronicling a member of the British monarchy, director Tom Hooper instead crafts a thoughtful film about the creation of a king through his ability to overcome disability.  What was most striking about this movie was its ability to take a subject like King George VI's speech impediment and make it into compelling storytelling.  As an audience member, I cringed right along with British citizens as "Bertie" attempted to make speech after speech and fail.  I was also on the edge of my seat as he was finally able to conquer his impediment and deliver his wartime speech.

While Hooper masterfully wove together a clever and oftentimes humorous screenplay by David Seidler, I cannot imagine anyone else tackling this role other than Firth.  As the king, Firth was fantastic and a sure frontrunner for the Oscar this year.  From small facial movements to his emphatic swearing, Firth was able to manifest the the frustration of a man whose job was to be stately and eloquent, but whose body refused to cooperate.  Almost equally compelling was the supporting cast, led by Rush's turn as the royal speech therapist whose self-described unconventional methods ultimately prove to be effective. This film tells an unfamiliar story in an entirely familiar setting. We all know the story of the abdication, of Edward and Mrs Simpson, of David and Wallis. Most of us will also know of the stammering and reluctant prince that had the crown thrust upon him.

This film tells the story of Bertie (latterly King George VI) and his battle to overcome his speech defects.

And it's a wonderful film: a tremendous story portrayed through three superb central performances.

First up we have Colin Firth as the faltering Duke of York. Firth is entirely credible as a member of the royal family and his performance demands the compassion from the audience essential for the development of the plot. From the earliest scenes of the movie where Bertie must address the closing ceremony of the Empire Exhibition at Wembley, director Tom Hooper takes us with him - forcing us to share in the frustration and helplessness.

Helena Bonham-Carter was, of course, born to play the late Queen Mother (Gawd bless 'er).

Speech therapist Lionel Logue is portrayed by Geoffrey Rush at his absolute best. How can this be the same actor that pitched up in the recent Warrior's Way? I confess to have rather been a bit if an agnostic when it came to Rush - rather too much Pirates of the Caribbean for my taste - but with this performance I am a convert.  

What could be such a small story is played as great drama. We understand the importance, and the impossibility, of the task ahead and are willing them to succeed. Don't go thinking that this is simply a dramatic piece, though. There are numerous laugh out loud moments, played with perfect timing.

Special mention must go to the set dressers and the director of lighting. They both set the scenes admirably.

Perhaps the only criticism of the film us that a few subsidiary characters are a little flat. David and Wallis, in particular, are a tad one-dimensional but maybe they must be for the story to work.

And work it does.

Finally, is it wrong to quite fancy the Queen Mother when she's being played by Helena Bonham-Carter?

Along with "127 Hours," "The King's Speech" is definitively one of the most hopeful, illuminating, and uplifting films this year. Director Tom Hooper and Oscar-nominees Colin Firth, Helena Bonham Carter, and Geoffrey Rush lead this wonderful World War II-era tale of King George VI and his battle to overcome his speech impediment. This film is built on solid performances, and Firth, Bonham Carter, and Rush go above and beyond the call of duty and really propel this film forward. The performances are easily the best part of this film. You are intrigued and invested in George, his wife, and his speech therapist. You never want to look away. With every long pause and stutter given by Firth makes you want to stand up and help him. He plays George's impediment beautifully, making the audience feel sorry and almost hopeless. Bonham Carter, as Queen Elizabeth, is exquisite. She balances her husband with lots of love, hope, and respect, and Bonham Carter does an incredible job playing those strengths. The chemistry between Firth and Bonham Carter as so genuine, you forget that they are actor and actress and believe they are indeed husband and wife. Their chemistry is so natural, it adds even more to the film. And Rush is unbelievable as Lionel Logue, George's speech therapist. I seriously believe that if there was an upset at the 83rd Oscars, this would be it. Rush's performance is simply extraordinary. I can't even begin to describe how wonderful he was. Then Tom Hooper's incredible Oscar-nominated direction brings this broad topic right down to its core: the relationship between George, Lionel, and Elizabeth and the implications if Lionel fails in his job. There's a lot of pressure on these three characters, as the nation prepares for war against Germany. But Hooper downplays the war to a point where the characters in the film and the audience members feel that looming threat of war, yet feel hopeful to see whether George can overcome his impediment to unite his countrymen. Hooper has an incredible crew helping him tell this optimistic tale. Production Designer Eve Stewart and Costume Designer Jenny Beavan beautifully and accurately recreate the look of World War II England. You can tell they took their time with every intricate little details, from the cracks in the walls of Lionel's office to the suits and gowns each character wears. The cinematography by Danny Cohen further enhances this gritty, realistic era. It's simple, restrained, naturalistic, and almost unorthodox, as most shots include the characters restrained in a small part of the screen, surrounded by lots of negative space. And composer Alexandre Desplat brings the hopeful side of this tale to new heights, as his music beautifully portrays the struggles and triumphs of George and company. Overall, this is easily one of the best films of the year. If there's one thing this film brings up the best, it's that no matter how tough things can get, you can triumph if you try.

The King's Speech is the true life story of King George VI (or more affectionatly knonw as 'Bertie), and how he battled to overcome his crippling stammer, both before and after becoming king of Great Britain, with the help of a rather unorthadox speech Therapist, Lionel Logue.

I have to begin by praising Cling Firth, first and foremost, who, undeniably makes the film what it is, and without his presence, would be a much lesser film. Firth Plays George with a loveable amount of stiff-upper-lipness and regal restraint, showing him as a private man, who struggled to let himself go, accept with his wife and children. This aspect that Firth portrays only makes the scenes between he and Geoffrey Rush's Louge, to be all the more amusing and heart-warming, as Logue works to cut beneath George's rigid, but brave outer shell. Firth is both humerous, and refined, loveable and noble, and paints the perfect picture of a troubled man, who never wanted to be king.

Firth may be the brightest gem in the crown, but there are plenty more to admire. Helena Bonham-Carter's, Elizabeth, is supportive and kind, but also determined and noble, and the chemistry she shares with Firth is genuinely moving and a pleasure to watch.

Geoffrey Rush also gives a performances to be reckoned with, as the unflichingly honest, and understanding Logue, who is humorously shameless and confident in his mission to cure George.

The King's Speech, however, holds up as agreat film, not just by it's performances, but by it's sheer magnetism, and moving, story-telling. This true story, with many aspects of which most are familiar with, is handled in such an intriguing and personal way, that the tale feels more human than it might have, and less copied clinically out of the pages of a history book. It's finely crafted, with an ecclectic mix of highs and lows, laughs and tears, but never becoming melodramatic.

One criticsim might be the predicatblity ofthe story, but with historical adaptations, that tends ot be the norm. And bsides, it's less about what happens in the story, but how it unfolds is what makes this a truly magical experence.

Summary - a finely crafted, moving drama, strung together by generous a handful of astounding performances, and rich chemisrty, that forms to make a regal but involving peice of cinema.

A historical drama depicting the overcoming of adversity and the unorthodox friendship between a royal and a commoner, as presented by the Weinsteins, The King's Speech practically screams "Oscar Bait!!!", but such a cynical viewpoint is ultimately irrelevant, as this is simply a great film.

Colin Firth gives a standout performance as "Bertie," otherwise known as the man who would be King George VI, who must overcome a crippling stammer that has been a source of embarrassment and derision since his early childhood; thanks to the new invention of the radio, a king has to do more than pose for photographs and not fall down in public to impress the people.  After dealing with quack doctors (Smoke more! Put these marbles in your mouth and enunciate, damn it!), Bertie is referred to speech therapist Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush, also excellent), and the movie follows the men's growing relationship against the backdrop of Bertie's reluctant rise to power.  The development of their friendship, and of Bertie's therapy, can be rightfully criticized as somewhat predictable and sentimentalized for the sake of entertainment, but it hardly matters when the performances are so good and the movie is so genuinely entertaining.  The two men are ably supported by a strong cast, led by Helena Bonham Carter as Bertie's loving wife, perhaps the only family member (along with his doting daughters) who has never ridiculed "B-B-Bertie" for his defect.  Characters such as Bertie's brother (Guy Pearce) are not depicted with much dimension, but the multifaceted portrayals of the lead characters more than compensate.

If you're looking for a film in tone and feel of The Young Victoria, then this is for you.

Colin Firth is excellent in his performance as Bertie, from his role as second in line to the British throne through to his first wartime speech as George VI, and it is performance which will keep you transfixed throughout.  His portrayal of a person with a stammer is sympathetic but never "weak".  Indeed, through the script he is able to inject the character with humour, such as in his early exchange with his speech therapist, Lionel Logue, by saying that he is unable to tell jokes as he's not good at timing.

Geoffrey Rush, who is also one of the Executive Producers, provides an effective counterbalance in the role of Logue.  The character is respectful of Bertie's position as Duke of York and King, but there is also a playful sparring and a levelling of the playing field right from the outset of the film.  As he explains to Bertie when he visits for an initial consultation, "My castle, my rules".

Helena Bonham-Carter also excels as Elizabeth, the future Queen Mother.  Her portrayal of the role is sensitive, yet strong.  From the outset, she is the one who sets the ground rules for Bertie's treatment and she is the one who is very much portrayed is the central structure that Bertie gains strength from.

As this is a film that is based on real events, there is no villain, as such.  However, there needed to be a focus for the reason behind Bertie's speech impediment and this is shown in three different ways - Bertie's preparation as a potential future heir to the throne by his father, George V, brilliantly portrayed Michael Gambon; his relationship with brother David, the future Edward VIII, portrayed by Guy Pearce, who although not an out-and-out bully, mimics his brother's afflication and intimidates him when; and, finally, through the events that take place at home, with his brother's relationship with Wallace Simpson, and internationally, in the run up to the Second World War.

Rounding out the supporting cast, there is the cream of the acting profession including the likes of Derek Jacobi as the Archbishop of Canterbury, Timothy Spall as Winston Churchill and Anthony Andrews as Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin.

The direction by Tom Hooper and the script by David Seidler is perfectly pitched for the aim of the film - which is to show how two men of different social rank are thrown together by circumstance and how they develop a bond, even a friendship, to overcome adversity and in so doing releases an individual's potential.

This film was well worth my admission fee, satisfying enough that it didn't feel like a waste of time or money, yet not too long that it didn't drag on.

This is the story of a man named Albert or "Bertie" (Colin Firth) who was eventually to become King George VI. His brother King Edward VIII was next in line to take the throne, but due to personal matters he steps down, and Bertie must become King. England is on the brink of war, so Bertie's wife Elizabeth (Helen Bonham Carter) goes to find a speech therapist named Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). The sessions do not start very well, however, after time and much improvement on Bertie's speech, Lionel and Bertie become very good friends helping the King in his speech that will take them into war.


In making this film, Tom Hooper has created an absolute masterpiece. He has not done very much in his career, seeing as he has only made a few movies. But in making The King's Speech he has moved many people across the world. Considering that this film is nothing but dialogue, a lot of people will probably walk out of the theater either just waking up from a long nap, or talking about how much they wanted to nap through the film. But, that is for people who do not enjoy films as much as some do. The writing was superb. Some of the most well written dialogue I have heard in a long time, at least in theaters that is. I have heard some people complain that the film was too "predictable" but, I am not really sure how you can complain over such a thing since the movie is a true story. David Seidler did a really good job writing this movie. The character development was perfect. We start the film off knowing Bertie as the Duke of York, and slowly through many sessions with the speech therapist we begin to learn more and more about the lives of both Bertie and Lionel. And considering that I am a firm believer that a film requires great character development in order to be great, The King's Speech really nailed that spot.


However, it takes much more than just a director and a good screenwriter to make a movie as good as this one. At the beginning of the year I thought Leonardo DiCaprio should be getting best actor for his performance in Inception, then later Jeff Bridges came into the picture after True Grit. But neither performance compared to Colin Firth in my opinion. Now Colin Firth has had a very succesful career as an actor. He may have played in his share of terrible films, but so has every actor. He has also played in many good films, and has given many good performances. But in my opinion his performance in The King's Speech is no doubt the best of his career. I fully believed wile I was watching this film that I was watching King George VI stammer as he tries to give a speech. It is rare that I find a film that I care so much about the characters in the story that i'm sitting on the edge of my seat waiting to see if anything is going to happen when nothing at all is going on in the film. That takes character development and how believable the actors can be. Colin Firth was in every way possible believable. But, he was not the only good acting performance in the film. Helen Bonham Carter was as convincing as anyone can be. Now she is also someone who has played in some great films, Sweeney Todd being one of them, but her performance in this film is about as good as they will come, and it was not as easy one at that. And then comes the great Geoffrey Rush playing the part of the speech therapist, Lionel. He was actually very funny in this film, nearly the entire theater roared in laughter at certain times of the film. And even if I had my pick, I would not want a different actor playing in this movie, because he was absolutely brilliant. These three actors all deserve to be nominated for an acting award at the Oscars, and I have no doubt in my mind that they will be.


Also, the musical score in this film was beautiful. There were times that not only me, but many people in the theater were nearly brought to tears, and the music as partly to thank for that. It at least deserves a best music nomination, because I thought it was fantastic. Just the overall feeling to this film was great. There are certain films that everyone seems to love that are just your basic shoot 'em up, and that is the entire movie. But for me this is my favorite kind of film. It may not have the most interesting topic, and the most interesting things may not happen, but with some great acting and directing we actually learn a little bit about our lives, and other people's lives while watching this film.


Overall, The King's Speech was a moving film that nearly made me cry in several parts. Colin Firth, Helen Bonham Crter, and Geoffrey Rush together in this period drama is about as fine of acting as you will ever seen in any movie, and that is coming from a true fan of movies. As I already mentioned, the screenplay was perfect and the direction was great, along with a moving musical score. This is one of the best movies I have seen in a very long time in theaters. The King's Speech has my pick for best picture.

Isn't it peculiar when a film comes seemingly out of nowhere, and produces such an unstoppable surge of interest and acclaim that after only a few days it seems like it has been around forever. The King's Speech is just such a film, and by the looks of it it is in no mood to surrender it's grip on the nation's (not to mention the various awards panels) heart strings. In essence it is a very simple and straight forward story of a man over coming a speech impediment. But, life being what it is, this is not an ordinary man and those were most certainly far from ordinary times. The film starts off with us all being very able to recognise when and where we are, and what is over the horizon for all on screen. The film is rich in detail, unafraid of using large set pieces to get points across, and the camera work is done expertly to make you feel both inside someones personal relationship and entirely isolated and alone amongst 100,000 people. Where the film truly takes off though, is in it's central relationship between Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush, who both turn in excellent performances. It is in this relationship that we get glimpses into the minds of the two men, particularly the King, and see what personal demons are haunting him besides his obvious affliction. The film takes you on the journey with him and in the cinemas you can see those around you wince at him when he is in trouble, but equally laugh, smile and even clap when he succeeds. It is a joyous journey, and even the most cold hearted republican will betray a smile come the final few scenes. The hype surrounding is has been, to mind mine, entirely justified, and I truly believe you will not find as many as a handful of people who will come away from it feeling that it was not money well spent. 
That being said however, it is not a perfect film. In it's necessary focus on the central relationship it leaves a lot of the history stuff to be almost crowbarred in here and there, and at times it does feel like box ticking rather than a necessary diversion to help continue the narrative, but this is a small trifling matter that will not detract from anyones enjoyment. 
The King's Speech is the definition of a heart warming film, and will entertain young and old in equal measure. It is a wonderful story, wonderfully told, and if you haven't seen it yet, then you must go as soon as possible, or risk missing out on sharing something truly lovely with your fellow cinema goers.

When British cinema gets it wrong, we get it spectacularly wrong but when we get it right, we can produce some of the finest movies around. I'm glad to say that The King's Speech definitely falls into the latter. This is a triumph.

The second son of King George V has a problem; he stammers, especially when forced to make public speeches. Having seen doctors who claim they can cure him, his wife, Elizabeth, is desperate to find someway of getting him over it and so heads to a small street in London where she meets speech therapist Lionel Logue, an Australian failed actor who doesn't bow down to ceremony. Reluctantly Bertie, the nickname for the royal, meets Mr Logue and so begins an awkward working friendship while Bertie has to deal with the death of his father, his brother's relationship with Wallis Simpson and his eventual crowning just before war breaks out.

A lot has already been written about Colin Firth's extraordinary performance but it is incredible. Tipped to win this year's Oscar, here is a man who cannot control his speech problems and so is equally frustrated, angry and slowly losing any will to correct it until he is forced to. You genuinely feel his pain and it is, without a doubt, Firth's performance of a lifetime.

Geoffrey Rush is perfectly cheeky as Logue, a man who is unfazed by his student's status and he delivers another pitch perfect performance. As does Helena Bonham Carter as the future Queen Mother. With a sparkle in her eye, she brings a human touch to her persona.

That's one of the things that works so well. You get a feeling that these are more than Royal, they are human, they are just like everyone who views them. They are all played with affection and never with any malice.

Tom Hooper's direction is also interesting. He could have quite easily pointed the camera at his actors and let them do the work, but his framing makes it even more fascinating to watch. 

One word of warning, however, is the language.  This is a 12A in the UK, and yet there are a few scenes in which the F word is uttered, nah, shouted more often that Hugh Grant's opening gambit in Four Weddings and a Funeral. Amazing how times have changed.

Along side a historical story that very few would actually know about, this is an incredibly uplifting tale of an underdog fighting against the odds. Tom Hooper has created a cinematic masterpiece.

Tom Hooper's follow up to 2009's The Damned United has been lauded as a potential Oscar contender ever since it first appeared at the London Film Festival in October.  It ticks the Academy's boxes of what it likes; a regal subject matter, a British actor at the top of his game and a former Best Actor winner.  The film tells the story of King George V's son Albert, the Duke of York, played by Colin Firth and his rise to the throne after his father's death and his brother's abdication to marry Wallis Simpson.  That element of the story has been the subject of many books and a film (Edward and Mrs Simpson) but this time the story centres on Bertie's stutter and his attempt to curb it.  His wife who was to become known as the Queen Mother played by Helena Bonham-Carter employs approaches Lionel Logue as Bertie's therapist, mainly due to his 'controversial methods'.  What follows is Lionel and Bertie's burgeoning relationship and Logue's refusal to enter into any regal social conventions that Bertie initially wants him to adhere to.  It is this relationship that makes the film and the two actors will get Oscar nods and surely Firth will win but the supporting performances of Bonham-Carter and the hammy Guy Pierce and Timothy Spall act as complementing textures in a film that mixes its tragedy and comedy to great effect.  Make no mistake however, this is no TV Movie beamed onto the big screen, Hooper chooses his locations beautifully and another superb supporting character are London and Sandringham, evoking the loneliness of Bertie and Edward's public privacy.  A solid film which will perhaps sweep up in Hollywood in February.

A return to the British heritage film; although not quite the heritage films we may remember. The King's Speech isn't as interested in showing us opulent drawing rooms and pagentry as it is the close ups of characters faces as they either process bad news or try to speak without stuttering.

Usually the return of the heritage film means a production which smells eerily of awards bait. There are certainly shades of that here; but it is a fine movie by itself to boot. The character of George VI, for example, is given all the vocal ticks and journey to self enlightenment that we would expect. But Colin Firth is unable to play things so simply and often works to make the character *more* strange and alienating so that his victories feel earned.

Similarly, Helena Bonham Carter is a welcome returnee to this sort of film but I really like what she's allowed to do with her Dutchess of York. Clearly playing a normal woman who deftly wears her royal persona but who is able to strip it back when necessary for her husband and family's benefit.

It becomes slightly more ham fisted in the final act as the heritage film tropes rear their ugly heads. In wanders Derek Jacobi to become the villainous face of "the establishment" and there's all that Rocky style buildup to 'the most important speech ever.' But that speech itself is filmed remarkably. Again; in closeup and in the detail of the reactions of those listening to it. 

Like a stuttering king; the movie occassionally looks like it's about to stutter over its heritage cliches and become disposable. But then overcomes them with both unexpected visual and scripted delights before finally landing as a triumph.

The King's Speech is a wonderful historical drama surrounding the stutter of King George VI that is both engaging and pleasurable. For a director that has recently come into the major motion picture scene, it must not have been an easy transition. The script only added enhancement to the experience of the viewer. Combined with great direction, a historically accurate script, and brilliant acting the film creates a real treat for the audience.
	The direction by Tom Hooper (Longford) was great. Though the jump from television to film is a difficult task it is being seen more and more, though many directors stumble and fall. Hooper, however, does the exact opposite creating a brilliant image for the viewer. Though he appears to only have unheard accolades, he takes a script that was originally thought only well enough for stage and turns it into a breathtaking film. He was able to get the most out of his actors, though this could not have been hard given their professionalism, and in return receiving something truly extraordinary and brilliant.
	The script by David Seidler (Son of the Dragon) of the film was incredible. Depicting a subject that could have been rather boring and historically inaccurate turned into a great work of art that had both the ability to engage the viewer and almost give the feeling of placing them in history. While a little slow, the only real mark against the script is that it jumps in leaps and bounds through the years of struggles of King George VI's stutter, though this was a possible angle for increased dramatic effect. The main argument for historical inaccuracy was that of Winston Churchill's role during the abdication of King Edward VIII, where he was opposed to Edward leaving the throne. While this is a glitch in the script, it is not a major one as one hundred percent historical accuracy in any film is almost impossible. With a film this powerful, it is something that can be overlooked as the rest of the script overshadows it with excellence.
	The acting as a whole was flirting with genius. Colin Firth (A Single Man) was beyond brilliant as he played King George VI. His portrayal of this character was incredible as he was able to capture the audience with every emotion he was attempting to get across, drawing the audience into the scene with him. The stutter he brought to the screen appeared to be both realistic and gave the feeling that it was in fact his own. While I cannot say for certain, I do believe this to be one of the best performances of his career and most definitely of the year. Geoffrey Rush (Pirates of the Caribbean: Curse of the Black Pearl) was good. His portrayal of the strong and honest character of Lionel Logue was great. Rush continues to amaze with his range of acting ability, showing true charisma in the character of Logue as he continually battled the King with his disability of language along with the King's anger and frustration with it. Helena Bonham Carter (Alice in Wonderland) did very well as the King's supportive, yet commanding wife. Though the part did not require much depth, Carter fit the role well creating a demanding but loving character. The rest of the supporting cast was good, holding up their roles with great stability. Guy Pearce (The Hurt Locker) was good as King George VI's brother Edward as was Michael Gamdon (The Book of Eli) as his father King George V, both creating different kinds of pressure for George about his disability. The overall chemistry of the cast was great. The ability to support each other on the screen and getting the audience to believe what is being portrayed seemed to come with ease amongst this crew and brought forth a more enjoyable film for the audience. 
	When the script is a shining star, it is up to the director and cast to give it life and that is exactly what the entire crew is able to achieve with this film. The real standout is Colin Firth as his brilliance radiates throughout the entire picture. Only enhanced by his surrounding cast is he able to achieve this level of acting. He truly brought this script to life with the help of Tom Hooper, who was able to pull one of Firth's best performances ever. As one who is slow to be impressed by biographical films (and even this one has the damnable final notes before the end credits), I was impressed, even delighted, by THE KING'S SPEECH. The two lead actors helped with this a great deal: Colin Firth, while not as transcendent as he was in A SINGLE MAN, is wonderful here, taking what could have been a gimmick--George's stammer--and making it utterly believable. He disappears totally into the role, embracing George's (or Bertie, if you prefer) stubborness, love for his family, and love for his country. Geoffrey Rush is every bit his equal as his therapist, Lionel Logue--appropriate, given Logue's insistence on treating the King-to-be as an equal. His hangdog face and Australian drawl provide a sort of entertainment all their own, yet as with Firth, Rush is entirely convincing, and he and Firth have a fine interplay. Helena Bonham Carter gives a fine, unaffected performance as Mary, the Queen-to-be, one her best performances in years; Guy Pearce has a nicely slimy edge as George's brother Edward VIII. The rest of the cast is generally excellent, although Timothy Spall's Winston Churchill seems just a touch off; he's not bad, but he doesn't bear a strong resemblance to Churchill (less than, say, Rod Taylor in INGLOURIOUS BASTERDS).

David Seidler's script is intelligent, warm, and often quite funny; one scene where George is encouraged to overcome his fears by indulging in a stream of profanity in particular is funny in the way real life can be. Tom Hooper's direction is crisp, with some delightful touches, especially the grotesquerie of Dr. Blandine Bentham (Roger Hammond), who tries to cure George by making him speak with a mouthful of glass marbles, and the absurdly detailed preparations a BBC announcer (Adrian Scarborough) makes before a broadcast: gargling with mouthwash, spraying his throat, measuring his mouth's distance from the microphone, etc. Hooper also displays virtuosity in the climactic speech, which intercuts George's speech with shots of his subjects across the world, and combines Firth's tense but determined delivery with Beethoven's Symphony no. 7 in A Minor; it's a remarkably powerful sequence.

Danny Cohen's sharp, clear photography evokes the era beautifully, as does Eve Stewart's production design, which triumphs best with Logue's delightfully decrepit study (with a wonderful decaying wall which has the quality of a mural). Alexandre Desplat's music tops off the package perfectly, a lovely combination of original and classical pieces. Anyone with an interest in British history will automatically take to this film--but I can't think of anyone who wouldn't be won over by it. It's one of the best films of 2010.

I'm always a little wary of movie posters and reviews which scream "Oscar contender"; often it can be a studio marketing trick to make us look at the film differently than we might normally, or even just to drag in more viewers ... however on this occasion I am delighted to concur most heartily. This is an absolute gem of a movie.

With Colin Firth brilliantlyy cast in the lead role, the film describes the true story of Prince Albert, Duke of York (the future King George VI), his crippling stammer, and his 20 year relationship with a maverick Australian speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). As the film opens, we see Albert about to make his first public broadcast via the new medium of wireless, to close the 1925 Commonwealth exhibition. It's an unmitigated disaster, which gives the young Prince crippling mental scars. To make matters worse, his father George V and elder brother David (future king Edward VIII) bully him about his condition whilst speaking publicly with ease and panache.

The future Queen Mother (Helena Bonham Carter), takes her husband to all manner of doctors, with no success, before finally she pays a visit to Lionel Logue on a personal recommendation. Irreverent and unconventional, Logue demands that the Duke visit him in his own offices, and insists on referring to him as "Bertie", an affectation only previously allowed to Albert's own family. The relationship is initially strained, but as time passes, the Prince gradually accepts Logue's strange ways and a friendship develops.

As time passes, George V dies, placing the crown in the hands of David, now Edward VIII. Of course, his relationship with the wayward American divorcee Wallis Simpson is soon to force him off the throne, and put Albert into the position of British Head of State. With war with Germany also imminent, it's time for Logue to step up and transform the stumbling George VI into a speaker worthy of inspiring his nation.

The film makes for uncomfortable viewing at times. Speech defects are of course horrid to behold, except of course that time when Gareth Gates launched his new website (www.wwwwwwwwwwwwwwww........), and Firth conveys the King's stammer in a tremendously convincing manner. He is a tragic figure, torn between his desire to please his wife, gain confidence, lead his nation, yet crippled with self doubt and strain over hsi inability to communicate publicly.

Firth and Rush are awesome in their roles. Oscar nominatiosn are a certainty, and there may also be a nod for Bonham Carter, who looks and sounds the part too (though far less sexy than her demented portrayal of Bellatrix in the Potter flicks). Guy Pearce, too, shines as the roguish Edward VIII, clearly revelling in his wayward lifestyle and flirtation with Wallis. He's come a hell of a long way from Ramsay Street.

The movie belongs to the two central protagonists, and their moving relationship is a joy to behold. There are even moments of great levity (Firth screaming "tits" out of an open window in an exercise to loosen up is fabulous). Of course, the true nature of the story adds to the drama, and research confirms that this is pretty close to the real events. 

An Oscar cert, go see the King's Speech if you want to see two heavyweight actors giving it their all. It's a classy film, and the hype is definitely not greater than the film itself. The first 5 star film of 2011.

Colin Firth plays King George VI, who reluctantly assumes the throne when his older brother Edward abdicates after one year as King.   The film starts however with him years before as Albert, Duke of York, making the closing speech at the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley in 1925.  This speech proves such an ordeal because of the Dukes pronounced stammer that his wife seeks out the services of an unorthodox Australian-born speech therapist called Lionel Logue, played by Geoffrey Rush.  The film then follows their by turns turbulent and touching relationship, culminating in The Kings Speech of the title, which is his rallying call to the nation following the announcement of war with Germany.    

There is an affecting central performance by Colin Firth and an equally engaging one by Geoffrey Rush.  You wonder at the patience it must have taken Firth to create such an authentic stammer.  It is also filled out with fine supporting performances from a restrained Helena Bonham Carter as the Duchess of York (after playing a series of grotesques in Tim Burton films) and Guy Pearce as Edward VIII.

Most of the action takes place in close up and in confined spaces and so it is not a film that has to be seen on the big screen.  In fact the project started out as a play, before they decided to make it into a film instead and its theatrical beginnings are evident from the number of scenes just between the two leads.  It also contains a lot of humour, much of which derives from Logues unconventional techniques that involve singing, swearing, and repeating tongue twisters during therapy!  

The Kings Speech is bound to give Firth his, wholly deserved, second successive Oscar nomination and you would fancy him to be a strong contender to win it, just as long as he is not unlucky enough to be up against someone for whom it is their turn!

This is a great film. It should not, however, have won Best Picture. Whereas The Social Network presented a new, important look at the world today, and was filled with great acting, had a great screenplay, and is the masterwork of one of today's greatest directors, The King's Speech is a conservative film featuring only three truly great elements: Colin Firth, Geoffrey Rush, and David Seidler's screenplay. It should not have won Best Director, for example; David Fincher rightly deserved that. Just because its success went further than I think it deserves, however, does not discount this film in the least. It is still a very strong, if somewhat conservative, period piece with great acting and a great screenplay.

There is no limit to the number of superlatives that Colin Firth's performance has received, and each is rightly deserved. His performance as the stuttering, stammering Prince Albert, later King George VI of England, was remarkable, exceptional, extraordinary. I could go on all day with superlatives about his performance, but that's what everyone else has already done, so I'll leave it be. After all, winning the Oscar generally certifies the fact that you're an exceptional actor, unless your name is Nicolas Cage. Colin Firth deserves all the recognition he has received, and will receive, for his performance, which was vital to the success of this film.

A great surprise in this movie was Geoffrey Rush, who portrayed the speech therapist Lionel Logue with great enthusiasm and talent. His portrayal served as a great way to ground the film and the audience's view of the main character, as well as providing a bit of comic relief at points and generally making the film more enjoyable. Until I saw The Fighter, I was sure that he deserved the Oscar. However, Christian Bale's performance also deserved praise, so Geoffrey Rush should be contented with the fact that his performance can also have a plethora of superlatives attached to it.

The true core of this movie wasn't the King overcoming his stammer, which he didn't fully do anyway; it was the relationship between the King and Lionel. There are three people who deserve credit for that, and they aren't the triangle of man-love (Firth, Rush, and Hooper). They are Firth, Rush, and screenwriter David Seidler. Seidler's script was full of witty dialogue for Logue, plenty of room for Colin Firth to get emotional and stutter in, and focused in on the relationship between Logue and the King. It is that relationship which drives the movie forward, and makes the King much more relatable, personable, and pitiful at the same time. Without this screenplay, this film wouldn't have even remotely close to the film it is. It also wouldn't have been rated R, but that scene was definitely worth it.

There are other notes of merit for this film, of course. While I don't believe that Tom Hooper should have won the Oscar for Best Director, he was very capable in his role for this film. While I would've liked him to try to lower the conservative tone of this film (even with the swearing), he is obviously very capable of taking a film like this and making it the best he can, and for that, he deserves praise. I also thought that the costumes and production were very nice; while the cinematography was lacking a bit, this film still looked the part nicely. I also enjoyed Alexandre Desplat's score, which was both pleasing to the ear and fitting to the film. Finally, I enjoyed Guy Pearce's small role as Edward VII, even if his character was rather despisable.

All in all, The King's Speech is a great film, even though I believe its praise has gone too far. Combining superb lead acting, great supporting acting, and a wonderful screenplay, this film is a near-perfect historical drama.

The ending of The King's Speech was completely over the top. There was the king, George VI, played by Colin Firth, delivering the most important broadcast of his life to the nation and the empire beyond. It's Sunday, 3 September, 1939; it's the day Britain declared war on Germany; it's the day the king walked with destiny. The nation needed to hear the voice of the king, needed comfort and reassurance. George, who suffered from a debilitating speech defect from early childhood, begins hesitantly, but conducted - literally - by Philip Logue, a speech therapist played by Geoffrey Rush, he makes his way steadily towards the end, all against a background of Beethoven. Among the palace audience, Elizabeth, the queen consort, played by Helena Bonham-Carter, was in tears, a moment of shared emotion, for I, too, was in tears! It was beautifully over the top. The King's Speech, directed by Tom Hooper, is the kind of historical and personal drama that I love, full of nicely observed details. There are really two stories at work; one telling of the relationship between George and Logue, the other that of the relationship between the stuttering prince and the rest of the royal family, the firm, where he is known as Bertie. There are some superb supporting roles. Michael Gambon is first class as George V, Bertie's father, a bullying martinet, and Guy Pearce as David, the future King Edward VIII, a contrast in every way to his shy and diffident brother. Derek Jacobi gives good value as Cosmo Gordon Lang, the archbishop of Canterbury, at once imperious and subservient, and Timothy Spall does his best as Winston Churchill. Spall is a good performer but I seriously doubt that any actor, even the best, can depict Churchill without descending into caricature, amusing and absurd at one and the same time. If you care about this sort of thing there are some serious historical inaccuracies in the movie, the most obvious of which is the depiction of Churchill as a confidant of Bertie's during the Abdication Crisis, when Edward, who had since succeeded his father, is obliged to give up the throne because of his insistence on marrying Wallis Simpson, an American divorcee, played here by Eve Best. In fact Churchill was one of the most prominent members of the 'King's Party', Wallis or not, in what must count as arguably the greatest political error of his career. Still, don't let this quibble detract from a hugely enjoyable film, a hugely impressive performance by Colin Firth, masterful as always, an utterly convincing stammerer. He shows Bertie as a vulnerable human being, painfully aware of his disability and yet immersed in notions of etiquette and the stiffest forms of protocol that only served to compound the problem. The thing is, you see, Bertie is a product, a product of his upbringing. Though born left-handed he was made to use his right, one of the causes, supposedly, of childhood stutters. Overawed by his formidable father and mocked by his rather obnoxious brother, his verbal constipation is an expression of the constipation of his personality. It might not have mattered - after all he was only the spare, not the heir - but, as daddy says, the days when all a royal had to do was look good on a horse are over; now they have to speak to the masses. The movie opens with Bertie, then duke of York, giving a speech, sorry, that should be not giving a speech, on behalf of the king at the close of the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley in 1925, clearly an occasion of deep humiliation for him and acute embarrassment for the audience. Something has to be done, but what? Various methods are tried, including stuffing the poor chap's mouth with marbles then asking him to read, or the king shouting at him "Get it out, boy!" As a last resort the duchess of York learns of a specialist based in Harley Street who comes recommended. I loved Helena Bonham-Carter in the part, at once puckish and condescendingly snobbish. But Logue - a super performance by Geoffrey Rush - is having none of it. A blunt Ozzie and something of a performer - as it turns out he is a failed actor - he won't go to the mountain; the mountain must come to him. Bertie, with some reluctance, leaves the cocoon of the palace and comes to Logue's shabby office. After a start as hesitant as his speech the two men strike up a rapport. This is not the end; it's not the beginning of the end, but it is the end of the beginning. Logue achieves two things; he begins to break the duke's verbal logjam by breaking the logjam of his personality. Cutting through all protocol, he insists on calling Bertie Bertie, though nobody outside the firm has ever dared address him in such informal terms. As the therapy proceeds the two men strike up a kind of friendship, the first the duke has ever had, certainly with a commoner. As he relaxes his speech also relaxes. But then the real crisis comes: Mrs Simpson comes. Edward, now on the throne, and frustrated in his desire to marry his American mistress, intends to abdicate. Bertie is no longer the spare; he is the man who will be king, like it or not; he will be George VI. He doesn't like it; he panics, fearful that he will go down in history as Mad King George the Stammerer, an echo of his ancestor Mad King George the Third. But Logue, rejected at one point for his personal and political importunities, continues to be on hand, seeing his friend through the coronation, despite the resentment of the establishment, most established in Archbishop Lang, and beyond, to that final moment of destiny on the first day of war. This movie will last, well placed in the stable of royal thoroughbreds along with Mrs Brown, Young Victoria, The Madness of King George and The Queen. It's a good story well told, well directed and superbly acted. It's also a movie for the modern age, an age which does not really approve of stuffy royals and court protocol (the relationship with the real Logue was much more formal than the movie suggests). It's a movie that humanises royalty, one that makes George just another chap, worthy of majesty once he is worthy to be a man. What infinite heart's-ease Must kings neglect, that private men enjoy! And what have kings, that privates have not too, Save ceremony, save general ceremony? And what art thou, thou idle ceremony? What kind of god art thou, that suffer'st more Of mortal griefs than do thy worshippers? What are thy rents? what are thy comings in? O ceremony, show me but thy worth! What is thy soul of adoration? Art thou aught else but place, degree and form, Creating awe and fear in other men? Wherein thou art less happy being fear'd Than they in fearing. What drink'st thou oft, instead of homage sweet, But poison'd flattery? O, be sick, great greatness, And bid thy ceremony give thee cure!

Geoffrey Rush gives his best performance since his brilliant portrayal of Peter Sellers several years ago. He always knows how to act with such power over everybody else in his films, and he definitely demonstrates it in this film. Last but not least, Helena Bonham Carter is fantastic as the King's wife who none the least wants to help her husband with his speech impediment. She also plays her role with a "no-nonsense" logic and never ceases to amaze me. Also, it's nice to see her in a role where she is not a villainous witch and a role directed by Tim Burton. It's a lighter but forceful side of her I have never seen. This is a film for critics and film lovers, not today's people who want to see explosions and sex scenes (go see a Michael Bay film). It's just a great period drama.

"The King's Speech" is the true story of George VI (Colin Firth), who was King of the United Kingdom starting in 1936. The title refers to a radio speech which George made in 1939 to announce the British declaration of war against Germany at the start of World War II. 

When the film begins, George is still named Albert (he goes by "Bertie") and he's only the Duke of York. His mean old father George V is the current king and his older brother Edward (Guy Pearce) is next in line to the throne. (I thought Bertie looked much older than Edward. No wonder; turns out Firth actually is seven years older than Pearce.)

Albert has a stuttering problem. The film opens with Bertie making a painfully bad speech to a stadium full of people, after which his wife (Helena Bonham Carter) takes it upon herself to find him a speech therapist. After first seeing a quack who has him stuffing marbles in his mouth, Bertie eventually winds up in the run-down office of Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), who insists that during their sessions, the two men must treat each other as equals. 

Lionel uses some rather unorthodox treatment methods and Bertie is skeptical at first, but as desperation sets in, he starts to cooperate. Meanwhile, Bertie's brother Edward is becoming serious about his twice-divorced girlfriend Wallis (Wallis??), which throws the other royals into a bit of a tizzy because apparently marrying divorcees is a big no-no in the royal family. This ups the pressure on Bertie to learn to speak mellifluously because if big bro doesn't come to his senses before their father dies, Bertie fears he'll end up leapfrogging over him to become king. 

"The King's Speech" is as much about the friendship that develops between Lionel and Bertie as it is about Bertie's stuttering problem. There's also a smattering of pre-WWII history with Hitler on the newsreels and actors playing Winston Churchill and Neville Chamberlain. And, of course, there's the whole period-piece atmosphere you'd expect in a movie about the Royals of this era: fancy costumes, yapping Corgis, formal parties, manicured lawns, and the like.

One thing I found striking in comparing the period depicted in the film with modern times is the relative anonymity of the royals' lives back then, before TV and the internet. While he's the Duke of York, Bertie and his wife are able to travel all around town seemingly unrecognized. Compare that to Prince William and Kate Whats-her-name, whose pictures are regularly splashed all over the tabloids and celebrity gossip magazines. Even the Amish must know what they look like, assuming they end up waiting in line at the supermarket once in a while.

When the movie ended, I overheard the woman behind me tell her friend that "this was the best movie I've ever seen in my life...ever!" I agree that it's well-made, well-acted, interesting, enjoyable, inspirational, and suitable for people of all ages (despite its ridiculous R rating for a few therapeutic swear words). It's filmmaking at its finest. And yet... 

And yet, it really didn't do much for me. If you developed software to analyze the components of all past Oscar winners to determine the formula for the Best Picture, this movie would be the result. The story, the acting, the costumes, are perfect. It's the ideal movie for those people who only see one movie a year and want to feel like they got their money's worth. The thing is, I'm not one of those people.

There are few subjects which interest me less than the British royal family, nor am I a big fan of costume dramas. I can relate more to films about the everyman - maybe a stuttering butcher in a blood-stained apron struggling to ask his customers how thinly they'd like their cold cuts sliced. It's not that I wasn't rooting for Bertie - I was, despite being all but guaranteed of a happy ending - it's that I was always aware that he was just a character in a high-quality historical docudrama. 

If you haven't yet seen this movie, I'd definitely recommend it. Invite your parents and your grandparents - it's a perfect senior citizen film. I'm giving it an 8 because it deserves an 8. But deep in my heart, it only feels like a 7.

Despite a slow start, The King's Speech builds gloriously into a captivating and emotionally rich drama featuring incredible performances and an inspirational conclusion.

Expectations are undoubtedly high for The King's Speech as it's been dubbed the most likely candidate to dethrone The Social Network as the favourite for this year's Best Picture Oscar. And with good reason, for The King's Speech is a film of great integrity, telling a wonderful tale of overcoming adversity that many can relate to. Director Tom Hooper may not be a visionary like Fincher, Nolan or Aronofsky, but his work here is of an equally high quality. He prevented this film from treading the standard Merchant-Ivory period path, and instead created a gripping drama that is beautifully styled and laced with lighter moments.

Screenwriter David Seidler has done a fantastic job of recreating the stuffy world of the British monarchy. His script cleverly blends the human aspect of Bertie's handicap with the businesslike royal issues, as Bertie's brother Edward abdicates the throne and the stammering prince is crowned king amidst the onset of World War 2. Also testament to the film's success is how its ordinarily depressing ending with the announcement of war is actually very uplifting; this goes to show how much the audience is behind Bertie, and that is undoubtedly because of Colin Firth.

There have been murmurs of Firth being the frontrunner in the Best Actor race solely to make up for his snub in A Single Man last year. This is totally unfair. Firth's performance here is the most impressive of his career, creating in Bertie a hero that anyone who has had to overcome their fears in the face of adversity can relate to. He is so convincing in his stuttering that it feels incredibly natural for the viewer to will him along in his efforts. On top of this he provides great complexity to the emotional side of the character, which is expertly hidden behind that royal reserve. Opposite him Geoffrey Rush plays Lionel Logue, the unorthodox Australian speech therapist charged with treating the King. Once again his performance is of the highest caliber, bringing some honest humour to proceedings but much more importantly acting as the friend Bertie never had. 

It is in the exchanges between these two characters that the film really triumphs, and I must admit that it wasn't until these scenes found their rhythm that I found myself truly gripped by the film. However from the moment their apparent 'bromance' begins, the screen is lit by some of the finest chemistry of the year, with the earnest commoner and the uptight king sparring off each other in the most joyful of ways.

Let us not forget the supporting players led by Helena Bonham Carter as Bertie's wife, more commonly known today as The Queen Mother. She proves that the many years of great but overwhelmingly dark roles have not diminished that delightful young lady who began her career in the likes of Howards End and A Room With A View. She brings great warmth to the film and is more than deserving of some awards recognition for her work here. Also worth noting are Guy Pearce as the irresponsible older brother, Michael Gambon playing Bertie's father, and Timothy Spall  as a slightly hammy Winston Churchill; rounding out what is a quality cast list.

In regards to claims of the story being better suited to a TV movie, during the first twenty minutes I was inclined to agree. However it did not take long to realise that this film is of a much higher standard, on every level, than what constitutes television drama. Most notably those performances are more than enough to ensure that viewers remain at the very least interested in the story, but will surely have most truly gripped. 

Therefore The King's Speech is a magnificent film, that serves as both historical epic and on a much more human level as an inspirational tale, portraying a true story that deserves to be heard.

In the run-up to the release of The King's Speech, there had been a great deal of public build up. Everyone was talking about how good they were expecting the film to be, this is usually a film's downfall. A film that isn't solid enough to withstand being hyped up immensely, may be a good film, but not a great film. However, The King's Speech far surpassed anything the media could throw at it.

The film begins with a horrifically tense scene where the Duke of York or 'Bertie' (Colin Firth) attempts to give a speech at Wembley. As he rises to the top of the stairs and approaches the microphone, all eyes turn to him. Silence. He attempts to talk, but he stammers uncontrollably. Understandably, he attempts to get help, but after trying a number of therapists, he gives up. However, on a recommendation from a friend, Princess Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) goes to visit a new therapist (Geoffrey Rush). Bertie obliges his wife's request that he at least attends a session with Logue. He begins to attend the sessions regularly, and he sees a small improvement. Soon after Bertie's sessions with Logue, his father dies, leaving his brother to take the throne. However, his brother is attempting to marry a divorcee, and is forced to abdicate, leaving Bertie the King of England just as the war with Germany is about to erupt.

Right from the word go we feel a great sense of pathos for Bertie, he has been stricken with a terrible impediment and particularly the first scene shows the predicament he is in, to great emotional effect. In this sense the plot is brilliant. I was completely and utterly enthralled by the plot, no matter how linear it was. But it was linear, in retrospect; this is the only fault with The King's Speech. However, its predictability is no hindrance as the film's superb acting carries us through beautifully. 

With Colin Firth having won Best Leading Role at the golden globes, I should think he will be hotly tipped for the same award at the Oscars and Bafta's. He is simply superb, showing an emotional and compelling side that we saw in A Single Man. Although Firth is great, the supporting ensemble is truly brilliant as well. Geoffrey Rush is sublime, filling the film with some brilliant comedy moments and being the catalyst in releasing Bertie's voice.
 
As well as sporting a great, although somewhat linear plot and sublime acting, The King's Speech has some very subtle and affecting cinematography. Some of the shots used by Tom Hooper are great, particularly the still shot of Bertie giving his war speech showed the emotion and capture the event perfectly, nothing too opulent, no self-indulgence, and just great camerawork. 

Overall, The King's Speech is practically fault-less, providing an emotionally affecting film for the more mature film going public. With compelling acting, great cinematography, a great score and a sharp script, there is nothing that could knock The King's Speech down from a 10.

Whenever one watches a feel-good Hollywood film, one expects certain ingredients and standards, if not all. Some of these are cheesy romance, moral comedy or a good old, worn out educational message. So in a way they usually lack true substance or an interesting story or character development. (Although I won't say Hollywood doesn't have a few good ones, like Remember the Titans and The Notebook) British feel-good movies, however, are the opposite of that, they often don't end on a good note, but they do carry on with a wonderful message that will cover a bigger audience range. King's Speech is a perfect example of that.

When I went to see this film, I went into it blindly, without any prior knowledge of the ratings or a slight hint of what the story is. The only reason that merits my decision is that any film that has Colin Firth, Geoffrey Rush and Helena Bonham Carter all in one cast is a must-see film, no matter how bad or good it might be. But in this case the film was great.

The story revolves around the Duke of York (Colin Firth) in the 1930's (Also known as Prince Albert and the future King George VI) who suffered from a serious stammer and fear of public speaking. In order to remedy this long lasting speech impediment his wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) tries a few, some uncanny, solutions for this problem. They were all futile and unsuccessful, which forced her to hire a secret speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) to help them pass this ugly predicament. The help he managed to give the prince was beyond anyone's expectations and resulted in revolving Prince Albert's life 360 degrees.

Now, I'm not sure how accurate the story is compared to the one in real life, but from whatever research I made (mostly on Wikipedia and then the rest of the internet), it seems that they stayed quite close to the truth. Although I am quite sure some of interactions were invented to egg on a heartwarming or a comedic moment. 

This film is heavily dependent on its actors, since the story was very much carried through with the help of dialogue and character development, and what better cast to do the job. Colin Firth was once again flawless in his impersonation of the weak and stammering Prince Albert, with his painful hiccups and heartbreaking self-consciousness. As for Geoffrey Rush, his work is always effortless no matter what character he takes on. Helena Bonham Carter, it is so odd to see her play a wonderful warm character, let alone a happily married loving wife, extremely unlike her usual roles of a mad woman in varying degrees. Yet the confidence she usually exudes through her characters was still apparent, which works superbly as the bases of her character's successful and trustworthy relationship with her husband. 

The best part of the film is the relationship between Lionel and the Duke of York or "Berty", as he least liked it. The dialogue between the two characters was both hilarious and heartbreaking and full of real pain. It is not a story about a Prince who finally learns his lessons to become a great king. It is a story about friendship and equality, and how difficult of a road it is, especially when both friends come from two different walks of life--a constant uphill battle.

A stunning display over the determination of the Duke of York and his dedication to his country in 1930's England. 

In 1930s England, King George V (Gambon)  rules over the land as a powerful monarch and a commanding speaker to his country. His son, Duke of York Albert George (Firth), has a stutter and a fear of one day ruling in his father's absence. After seeing the best physicians and doctors in the country, Albert's wife Elizabeth (Bonham Carter) discovers a speech therapist named Lionel Logue with an unconventional style that may cure Albert of his stutter and gain a composure suited for a king. Soon, Albert's brother David (Pearce) has abdicated the throne and now Duke of York Albert has become King George VI of England....

The King's Speech, based on the true relationship between George VI and Lionel Logue, is a riveting drama where the spoken word commands all and the ability to speak one's mind is of the highest importance, whether they be king or commoner. The attention to every word spoken, to the impact of conversation amongst the royal family, is a battle of wills and power that is stagging to behold yet so familiar the audience can relate to Albert's struggle to control his stammer and speak his mind. Speaking of Albert, Colin Firth is staggeringly fantastic as Albert, moving through the room as a royal yet wanting to know the life that an everyday Englishman goes through. There's a striking sadness when Albert pours out his soul to Lionel, such as when the two have a session where Lionel instructs Albert to "sing" everything he wants to say. The rest of the cast is fantastic, from co-star/executive producer Geoffrey Rush, to Timothy Spall doing an amazing performance capturing the nuances of Winston Churchill.

A tale of a man trying to express his presence and authority in times of war, The King's Speech is an amazing story with a stellar cast of British and Australian talent.

Amazing performances from Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush make the story seem fascinatingly fresh and real. Despite it's predictability The King's Speech is still remarkably entertaining an believable, while not losing too much of the actual story in the mess.

The film follows a series of events about Prince Albert, Duke of York and later, King George VI, and his inability to speak in public due to a stammer. After many failed attempts at rehabilitation, Albert (Firth) is introduced to controversial speech therapist Lionel Logue (Rush) by his wife, the Duchess of York (Helena Bonham Carter). Lougue is adamantly opposed to calling Albert the Duke, and instead calls him "Berty" to keep things personal. After the death of Berty's father, King George V, his brother, the Prince of York ascends to the throne as King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce). Soon, however Edward is abdicated from the throne due to an illegal marriage, and Berty ascends, as King George VI. Things between Louge and the King get heated, but ultimately Logue helps the King overcome his stammer, and deliver powerful speeches- most notably his wartime speeches in the late 1930s and early 1940s.

What viewers and critics are certainly to like most about the film is how accurately the characters portray their inspirations, and how accurate the story is. Director Tom Hooper worked tirelessly to make sure the real story of this remarkable man/event came to light. Hooper spent months researching notes and letters from both King George VI and Lionel Logue [1]. While there are sure to be some critics of historical accuracy out there, they will be minor, due to Hooper's extraordinary efforts.

In order to truly appreciate this film, one must listen to the music put together by Alexandre Desplat. Desplat uses a combination of classical works by famous composers such as Beethoven, to really create the sense of royalty throughout the film. The music is absolutely fantastic, and also Oscar-Worthy. 

Both Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush give Oscar-Worthy performances, and some are even saying this film will receive more nominations than any for 2010. It's hard to disagree with that considering The King's Speech has so much going for it. A must see for all, this film is powerful, sensational, and uplifting. Long live the King!

This isn't so much a movie about a king's speech impedement as it is about the life of royalty.  Although it doesn't portray this life nearly as well as 'The Queen' does, Peter Seidler's screenplay is remarkably funny and touching.  Colin Firth, starring as King George VI (or "Bertie" to his family), gives the best leading performance by a male actor I've seen all year.  Although he doesn't nearly match the supernatural talent displayed by Hailee Steinfeld in 'True Grit', the feelings, the triumphs and the shortcomings, the embarassment and the pride, the love and the hate, flow fluently and easily from Firth's mind to our eyes.  Geoffrey Rush earns himself a shoo-in to the Best Supporting Actor category this awards season as Firth's wacky, "unorthodox" speech therapist.  Rush's humour and natural ability to capture characters' personas is remarkable, and this is no exception.  Helena Bonham Carter deserves an awards nomination for Best Supporting Actress, but nothing more.  She nails the character, but she has greater potential than she shows here.  Nonetheless a good performance.  I would've liked to have seen more of Timothy Spall's portrayal of the great Winston Churchill, but from what I saw, he captured Churchill's mannerisms and impression perfectly.  It's too bad we saw him only a handful of times or he would've made a strong candidate for Best Supporting Actor awards.  We witness the frustration of a man who is too often ignored, and pitied.  A great man with such great potential, crippled by his stammer, perseveres to prove himself to his doubtful nation.  With the unflinching loyalty of his supportive wife and the relentless and effective methods of his speech therapist, Firth takes England, and his oppressive family, by honorable surprise when he takes reign of the nation in wartime.  Previously unknown director Tom Hooper makes his mark here, I look forward to seeing his future films. A

Simply said, The King's Speech is somewhat remarkable.  One would think that a story about one man's triumph over a speech impediment is hardly moving stuff.  But it is.  Indeed, the film is about much more than just "Bertie" overcoming his infamous stammer.  As the film powerfully conveys, England and, in some ways, the royal family itself was at a critical crossroads.  Hitler was marching ever more incessantly towards war with Europe.  King George V's death left the British monarchy in the questionable hands of Edward VIII, whose energy was being consumed by his lustful desire for divorcee Wallis Simpson at a time when the need for monarchy appeared to be in its sunset (the Czars of Russia and Kaisers of Germany were now but pages of history).  Enter the reluctant yet proud hero in King George VI (also known as Bertie to family and friends).  Through the help of Lionel Logue and some rather unorthodox techniques, Bertie is able to overcome his lifelong disability and lead England through dark days to perhaps its finest hour.  Firth masterfully balances both the frailties that his character is attempting to overcome and the regal nature needed to play a convincing king.  Rush's quirkiness and Bonham Carter's soft spoken nurturing make the film feel genuine.  Charming and albeit somewhat quirky, the King's Speech seronades us with its tender story.

"The King's Speech" is one fine motion-picture and surprisingly it stands as one of my new favorites of last year. It's wonderful pacing and incredible balance with humour and drama keeps you intrigued all the way to end, plus, it offers the best on-screen chemistry I've seen in such a long time. Being a huge history nut, I was very shocked to learn of this incredible untold story. Walking into "The King's Speech" I knew who the movie was based on, but, I wasn't really too familiar with the plot itself so I was very surprised and incredibly blown away by what I witnessed. This is true cinema and one of the finest films seen about history in a few years. Breathtaking! 

As I already mentioned, the story of "The King's Speech" was a surprise to me entering the theatre yesterday afternoon. Saying that, it was a great surprise for sure. The movie takes a place mostly in the 1930s in Britain and focuses on the incredible untold story of King George VI...I'll call him Bertie, though. Bertie has a horrible problem with speech. He stammers and with his work, it doesn't help. When his wife Elizabeth finds him help from a man named Lionel Logue, who is known for his strange ways in therapy, the two start off rocky but soon form a bond just as amazing to witness as the bond between the two main characters in "Good Will Hunting". After the death of his father, Bertie's brother takes the throne. But when an unexpected calling comes onto Bertie to the throne, and with war on its way soon, his country needs him the most. "The King's Speech" is the most beautiful film I've seen all year and that's putting it little. 

Colin Firth, who just recently won himself a Golden Globe award (and probably the Oscar) gives one hell of a performance as King George IV. His stammers are spot-on, and seemed very real, and his character is certainly very likeable thanks to his hard work in his performance (and rock-solid script). Geoffrey Rush also deserves himself an Oscar-nod for his incredible performance as Lionel Logue. Lionel is best thing about "The King's Speech". His character is a hoot and keeps the film on a humorous path that has the audience loving the chemistry all the more. What a performance! What a performance, indeed. Helena Bonham Carter plays Bertie's wife, Elizabeth. For once, I must say, Carter gives a very fantastic performance. Usually working with eerie stories from her husband, Tim Burton, Carter never really gets the breakthrough chance she deserves to shine in the spotlight. In "The King's Speech", she does! If I could give all three an Oscar, believe me, I would. 

Director Tom Hooper (The Dammed United) does a marvellous job here with the camerawork. Fantastic angle shots are shown here in such tiny spaces and Hooper does a fantastic job with the look of the film as well. The shots of Britain in the 1930's are absolutely breathtaking. The look is just as great as his directed mini-series "John Addams" did. Hooper, you've done good. 

The script, written by David Seidler is marvellous and will hopefully get nominated for an Oscar. His perfect pacing and work with incredible balance on humour and drama is incredible. The dialog, well, lets just say its some of the best I've seen in a while. Seilder, your script equals one hundred percent perfection!

The cinematography by Danny Cohen is beautiful. His cinematography is surly a pure achievement a beauty to look at. The cinematography will hopefully gain itself an Oscar-nod (and win), as well. 

All and all, "The King's Speech" is a film that deserves plenty of Acadamy Awards all across the board. From the performances to the direction to the wonderful script and finally, to the breathtaking cinematography, everything about this film is a pure-achievement! "The King's Speech" is a very rare kind of gem that doesn't come around to often, so, do yourself the favour by seeing this now. You'll be amazed just as I was..and the whole audience. Don't you just love when an audience roars after a film?

Geoffrey Rush is the unconventional speech therapist who helps Bertie become the strong unifying voice for the nation during WWII, and the film milks the odd couple comedy of manners with some hilarious, yet also many touching, scenes. The script should be praised for hitting a perfectly British tone of both some degree of reverance and respect for the monarchy, as well as pointing out its any absurdities and emotional deficiencies. Also quite an achievement is mixing the personal story with the larger historical context. Fine use of wide angle lenses throws us right into Berties face in both the uncomfortable and triumphant moments and also emphasises both the literal and metaphorical claustrophobia, and loneliness, of power and privilege. One of those films easy to pass over before it's award hype set in, but definitely all deserved in this case.
