The King's Speech is one of those movies that's really hard to dislike. The reason for this? It has a lot of heart in all the right places. No one can look at this movie and say it isn't being sincere or heartfelt.
The King's Speech stars Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush as King George and his speech therapist (respectively). The king is a stammerer and he needs to be able to speak well in order to keep up his nation's spirit during a time of war.
Firth and Rush share an enormous amount of chemistry together. The way they play off each other is magnificent fun to watch. They seem like good friends, and that's why this movie works. As a matter of fact, their chemistry is so wonderful together that when they have scenes with other actors, the movie starts to drag. The chemistry among the supporting cast simply is not as strong as it is between Firth and Rush. Do not misunderstand me, the acting is not bad anywhere, but it is possible for a great actor in a great role to not have chemistry with his fellow actors on screen.
But that's really the only complaint I have. The story is really engaging and I loved the screenplay. I got to love the characters and how the king had to make some agonizing decisions between duty and friendship. There is a lot going on in a film like this, and that's why it's so great to watch.
All around Oscar-worthy performances and Oscar-worthy cinematography kept me investing in every moment of this movie. It goes deep into its characters and is unafraid of taking a couple unsettling turns for sake of keeping the story together. Bottomline: The King's Speech works because of its strong characters and some great chemistry between Firth and Rush. This is one of the best films of 2010.

With movies like this, there are a few things you can take for granted. Yes, the costumes and set dressings are rather extensive. Yes, the script has that oft-irkful air of pompousness. Yes, the acting from the leads is terrific. What isn't always guaranteed is just how entertaining the film may be. While theres a lot of interesting history and monarchal drama, The Kings Speech greatest success is perhaps giving a feel similar to very good sports movie in a strange way rather than a slow-moving period piece, something refreshing to both genres. While fans of period pieces will enjoy it either way, fans of general dramas or even the odd buddy comedy may find themselves surprised by one of the best story-telling films of the year.

The Kings Speech documents the rise of King George VI in the late 1930s. While not the focus of the film, it covers a great deal of incredibly interesting history. Perhaps the single most interesting piece of royal history  is the abdication of King George's brother King Edward VIII, covered in detail yet not laboured upon. Of course, the events are also all building around the threat from Nazi Germany. While not a WWII movie, war buffs will indeed get something out of the film from a more political angle.

While the history is actually incredibly interesting, the film is about King George VI himself, or Bertie as he is called by his family. Despite being expected to help lead the nation, Bertie is crippled by a stammer, making him incredibly socially awkward. After trying numerous doctors, an unconventional method is attempted with speech therapist Lionel Logue, who uses bits of psychology to attempt to find the roots of the problem. Theres an excellent scene where Bertie and Lionel discuss his relationship with his near-tyrannical father and bullish older brother.

A film about a stammer doesn't seem that interesting though, so thankfully there is another level to it. The stammer is a representation of Bertie's nervousness toward responsibility, progressively improving in time with his acceptance of his position. Its not pure coincidence, as much of it is due to Lionel, who acheives an excellent rapport with Bertie. This is where the film begins to feel like a sports drama or buddy comedy: montages of vocal exercises and light jabs (at a Prince, getting points for guts) produce more laughs than expected and the relationship between teacher and student is written extrordinarily well. The final speech has a similar vibe to the final football game in ye standard sports flick.

Most of the weight lies on the cast in this film, and they deliver in spades. Colin Firth gets the most attention, and does indeed deliver his lines incredibly convincingly with the stammer and adds numerous subtle layers to his character. It should not be understated how great he is, but he gets all the attention, so lets shift to perhaps the real star of the show: Geoffrey Rush. While Firth is the emotional center, Rush is the reason to rewatch the film. His performance as Lionel is believable, entertaining and animated, yet never feels like acting. 

Helena Bonham Carter goes decidedly non-crazy as she who became The Queen Mother Elizabeth, portraying a much warmer character than I thought she could. Guy Pearce does very well with a smaller role as King Edward VIII, as somewhat of a spoiled brat who somehow maintains sympathy even as he shirks responsibility. The only misfire in the cast is Timothy Spall as Winston Churchill. Perhaps I have trouble dissociating him from Wormtail, but he seems to try to steal every scene he appears in and gets tiring quickly.

While it starts off slow and will definitely bore some, for those who appreciate dramas of any kind, The Kings Speech is a great film. Well acted, well scripted and surprisingly funny, as well as seemingly quite the crowdpleaser, The Kings Speech is the best awards bait in some time.

A good screenplay or, indeed, any screenplay that actually includes dialogue instead of endless descriptions of special effects is a rare find in films these days. Even rarer are actors who can make the script come to life. Films have become exactly what Steve Martin suggested they were at the Academy Awards several years ago: great ideas for posters and nothing more. Thankfully, The King's Speech is not just a great idea for a poster. In fact, it's probably not even a good idea for a poster. It is a great idea for a film, an honest to goodness film, where actual characters have actual personalities and they actually manage to move the audience. The fact that it also contains Timothy Spall doing a damn good impersonation of Winston Churchill - a man I have taken to affectionately referring to as Churchy - is just a cherry on top of the cinematic equivalent of what I might walk back to my table with at an endless-supply-of-toppings-sundae bar where the ice cream is actually just concentrated, frozen awesome. Colin Firth is fucking spectacular. He plays the Duke of York so brilliantly, so pitch perfectly, that there are moments where he ceases to look like himself. That kind of thing happens when an actor truly loses themselves in a performance, and I wish I could say it happens often. It doesn't. Firth so embodied this character that he moved me. He made me swell with pride and brought me to tears, and he made me believe in something grand and epic despite the claustrophobic camera angles Hooper utilizes throughout the entire film. Firth is nothing, however, without his fellow cast members. Helena Bonham Carter is virtually unrecognizable, showing a kind of posh restraint as the Duchess of York that it's easy to forget that she typically plays all kinds of batshit insanity on film. She grounds Firth's performance, keeps it centred, just as the Duchess is shown to keep her husband grounded and centred. Equally impressive is Geoffrey Rush as the Duke's speech therapist Lionel Logue, a man brave enough or crazy enough or both to challenge the King of England and force him to confront his greatest fear: himself. Rush is, like Carter, perfectly restrained in his performance, playing Logue with a kind of well-bred candor. He's easy to like, which, I suppose, makes his more intense behaviours so forgiveable. Oh, and Timothy Spall is Churchy, and it's amazing. I must mention the screenplay just once more in this review though, because the screenplay is what really brings all these actors together and lets them shine. Every word is so precious here, because every word is a struggle. More importantly, The King's Speech really elucidates the power of words. There is a scene - my favourite scene, actually - where the Royal Family sits watching the coronation and a clip of Hitler speaking begins to play. "What's he saying?" Lilibeth asks, to which her father, now King George V, replies, "I don't know, but he seems to be saying it rather well." Despite not understanding the German language, the King recognizes that it isn't the content that matters so much as the way it is conveyed. It is a person's ability to speak and the way they speak that matters, not always what they say. A screenplay like this finds every word precious, and so I can't help but find every line of dialogue, every stuttered syllable, precious and endearing and lovely.

Wow... this really is one of the better films to come outta 2010. Where was this film when I compiled my top ten movies of 2010 list?! It's that great. First: time to blow off some steam. I hate the MPAA. These fuckers always blow their ratings out of proportion. The King's Speech is rated R for language. How bad is the language? Well, the King, played by Colin Firth, has a bit of a fit in which he spews out a couple of F-bombs due to his frustration with his stammering during one of his classes with speech therapist Lionel Logue, played by Geoffrey Rush. It's a brief minute or so, even less, out of the film's entire 111 minute runtime. Should audiences under 17 be barred from watching a film that is otherwise harmless yet historical, informative, and perhaps even inspiring? There's definitely not a whole lotta movies about this topic, and the way it blends with a historical narrative is also quite invigorating. But no, it gets slapped with an R rating because of a few naughty words. Anywho, The King's Speech looked like another case of Oscar bait. It's got all the praises and rave four star reviews and Oscar buzz. It's strictly a talkie. And it stars Colin Firth. However, I connected with the poor chap a tad more than Mickey from The Fighter. Maybe a lot of us can, especially when it comes to public speaking however for King George the VI (or, The Duke of York, take your favorite name), it's more than that; it even interferes with his personal life, like stammering when he's trying to tell his daughters a story. He's so insecure and frightened of the world, but the world (more appropriately his country) is counting on him especially as World War II is just over the horizon (almost literally). How this movie succeeded was to bring towering figures down to our level, or treated as equal. Like Mickey from The Fighter, Bertie has just about lost hope in "curing" his impediment after failing sessions with past speech therapists (one of which is kinda funny), at least until he meets Lionel. Bertie and his wife Elizabeth (played to perfection by Helena Bonham Carter) meet Lionel and one of his rules was to treat his client as his equal, not always acknowledging him as a royal figure or saying correct introductions, just calling him by his nickname "Bertie." A friendly approach to make his subject more comfortable and willing to open up, which will come in handy especially as Bertie's royal/political world begins to take shape, culminating with the ensuing conflict with Nazi Germany. And like The Fighter, Bertie's family relationships are quite... shaky, so to speak, as he reveals in a rather tear-jerking revelatory scene that resonated strongly with this viewer. This time, the spotlight shines on him as he reluctantly moves up the ladder towards the crown. And having a royal background, there are certain cultural practices forcefully implemented. Bertie isn't being instructed because it was best for him (unlike what Mickey's family was doing), he was forced all his life because that's what was expected and soon his self-esteem lowered and was being mocked and criticized for it, leading up to him constantly at battle with himself because he feels unfit to be king. As he assumes power, he feels even more alienated. This is the story about a man who's been treated like shit all his life, is this close to losing all hope, but because of his position he can't let his weakness perspire; his whole country is counting on him. He has the whole world on his back. The King's Speech is a surprisingly damn good film. Yeah, plenty of youse guys, especially me, may think, "Oh it's just about some guy trying to deliver a speech." Nah, it's much more than that just for all the reasons mentioned above. And that it's about speech as well only adds a tinge of uniqueness. I have no qualms if Colin Firth walks away with the top prize come Oscar season. It's a major step up from last year's overrated borefest entitled A Single Man. I apologize for all the needless comparisons to The Fighter, but I couldn't help but think how similar the themes and main characters are to each other. Both main characters in each film have a voice, and both men are afraid to use 'em. Are the two movies worth it? Fuck yeah... but I think The King's Speech is the stronger film. The Fighter is still worth checking out.

"The King's Speech" gave us the story of a man who shouldn't have been King but staunchly rose to the position. Colin Firth plays King George VI who had a deeply-rooted, severe stuttering problem and his struggle to overcome it. Helena Bonham Carter in the role of the (young) Queen Elizabeth is priceless, giving a fully-dimensioned portrayal of the woman behind the crown seeking someone to help overcome her husband's stammer. She finds Lionel Logue (played by Geoffrey Rush), an Australian with seemingly good credentials for the task but who uses unorthodox methods to get results.
Colin Firth succeeds in making you feel Bertie's shame and anger at not being able to speak forcefully and fluently; not being able to do what his father, especially, but also his brother did so well. This film has such a wonderful message about how one person can overcome adversity and another seemingly ordinary person can make an extraordinary difference in helping him overcome it. Geoffrey Rush is  magnificent and his talent shines with all its glory. He makes it look so effortless and yet the expressions he portrays in the movie are so subtle.
Needless to say this film held me spellbound every moment, from the very beginning to the end. The film is always engaging, interesting with fantastic acting, great dialogue and brilliant costumes. Highly recommended!

THE KING'S SPEECH is a textbook example of how a film can be nearly perfect in every way but still fall short of greatness.  It's a wonderful movie, but it's missing that spark that the greats possess, that intangible quality that bequeaths a film to the ages.  Perhaps it's just my own personal preferances holding it back. I tend to respond to films that don't just engage me intellectually, but emotionall as well.  THE KING'S SPEECH is resplendant with the former but sadly lacking in the latter.  It's stimulating, but rarely stirring.
One thing is for certain, though: this is an actor's film, and the actors on display deliver some of the best performances of the year.  Central to the film's success is Colin Firth, an actor I've long admired who gives the very best performance of his distinguished career as Prince Albert, second son of King George V.  Afflicted his whole life with a terrible stutter, "Bertie" is now faced with the prospect of ascending to the throne, after his gadabout older brother David (Guy Pearce) leaves the royalty in scandal.  On the cusp of war with Germany, it is vital that the new King be able to speak to his people and impart a sense of confidence, but his stutter is poised to stand in his way.  Enter Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), an Australian expatriate and speech therapist renowned for his unorthodox and controversial methods.  Taking a more psychological than physical approach to speech therapy, Logue believes that his high-profile patient will benefit from speaking to a friend more than a doctor, and all but forces his friendship and affection on the hot-headed king.  
If the plot I've described above sounds a bit dry, that's because it is, but it's unexpectedly engrossing and funny.  A lot of the credit for this goes to Rush, giving his best performance in over a decade.  When he's onscreen, the film crackles to life, and his chemistry with Firth is a joy to behold.  He's so good, in fact, that the film suffers from a dip in energy every time he's not on screen.  Firth is a likely Oscar frontrunner for his performance, and it'll be well deserved.  What initially seems like a performance coasting on an affected stutter grows deeper and richer as the film progresses, as Bertie's insecurities and inherent strengths are pulled to the surface.  In a smaller but substantial role as his wife, Helena Bonham Carter proves the old addage that there are no small roles, only small actors, infusing her regal character with a level of sweetness and genunine affection for her husband.
Like I said, it's a wonderful film.  Director Tom Hooper has a great eye for detail, and the period is recreated flawlessly by some exceptional art direction and bravura camera work.  I still don't think it'll be remebered among the greats, but that's simply a matter of personal preference.  It's well worth the price of admission, and is a wonderful showcase for some of our best actors.

Colin Firth's Bertie is a satisfyingly flawed character; he strives to be utterly composed and strait-laced then his frustration bubbles to the surface in wicked rages. In the 1930s, Bertie, the real Queen's father, has been landed with the job of King of England, despite the fact he's ill-equipped to do it. But with a plucky wife, he finds a speech therapist who, with some very unorthodox methods, gives him back his voice, something he desperately needs to lead his country in time of war. The British royalty is a delightful thing. Especially if they happen to suffer from some terrible embarrassing problem, so the poor unprivileged commoners can pity them. Well, it seems even kings aren't immune to stammering- or at least that's what Tom Hopper's Oscar-nominated-film is about.  Unexpectedly, Edward VIII(Guy Pearce) abdicates in order to marry the flamboyant American divorcee Wallis Simpson(Jennifer Ehle), scandalizing his dying father king George V (Michael Gambon) in the process, and opening the way for his unsuspecting and seemingly inadequate brother Albert(Colin Firth) to ascend the throne as George VI. Too bad he ends up with a job involving a lot of speaking in public, since he suffers from a severe stammer which doesn't want to go away. His wife Elisabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) tracks down Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), an unusual speech therapist that, in the end, manages to solve the king's problem and win a life-long friend. 

The best thing about "The King's Speech" is that it's unpretentious. It's rather an anecdote then a big story(though it is based on a real story) and it deals more with what goes on beyond the curtains of history. In this sense, it was a brilliant move from the director to move the limelight from the oh-so-scandalous Edward VIII and the Wallis plot to the awkward Lionel and the events in his office. This was Geoffrey Rush's coup de force and if it was up to me I wouldn't hesitate a moment to give him the best supporting actor Oscar. The way how he forces the Windsors to treat him as an equal is just fantastic. He doesn't hesitate to underline the importance of his techniques and finally manages to make Bertie's stiff royal ass relax and let go. Helena Bonham Carter took her usual Burtonian quirkiness down a notch for this one which is why she makes a rather dry impression. Of course, you can't do Queen Elizabeth and The Queen of Hearts in the same way, and she was very aware of that, which is probably why, for the whole screen time, she couldn't decide which way to go character-wise. Timothy Spall's Winston Churchill was as far away from the popular perception of this great man as can be, safe for the cigars. He just didn't have it, and Hopper probably thought it wasn't necessary anyway since he was not the key character. Guy Pearce did a wonderful job with his love-deluded Edward VIII, whose arrogant ways and infatuation with Wallis Simpson do seem very credible. Jennifer Ehle's Wallis, on the other hand, doesn't deliver satisfactorily. A woman who made the king of England renounce his throne should have much more juice and charisma in her, which is not the case with her. Colin Firth's royal stammer was very convincing. You almost choke with him as he struggles to complete the sentence. His initial conduct with Lionel is full of auto-irony and helplessness hiding behind the title. Gradually, he lets "Bbbbertie" out of his cage and opens up to the good-natured therapist. Firth is quite a sure Best Actor at the upcoming Oscars, I think. 

Oscar Wilde wrote that history was nothing but a calendar of war crimes. This little film begs to differ by talking about that fun, more interesting side of history which is rarely mentioned in school books.This seems to be a trend. In the future, we will probably see much more historical films that aren't biographical in the traditional sense but address a particular episode from his/her life, like "The King's Speech".

Although the King's Speech is aimed primarily at an American audience, like The Queen, it doesn't shy away from its subject matter in order to preserve the mystique of the British monarchy. In Tom Hooper's old skool interpretation of royal events leading up to the 2nd World War, no expense has been spared in conjuring up a believable nostalgia which is both entertaining and informative. As the stuttering King overwhelmed by his brother's abdication, Colin Firth is superb at conveying the unmentionable origins of his impediment whilst Geoffry Rush (as his erstwhile companion and elocution coach) cements his reputation as one of the best character actors in the business. Visually stunning, TKS's sumptuous period interiors will have Anglophiles drooling while the costume department's 1940s realisations earn it an extra star. Entertaining and wittily-scripted, TKS, while not a warts-and-all biography, is the sort of Sunday afternoon movie you thought had disappeared decades ago.

The power of determinism, the power of friendship, the power of social support, the power of speech, and the power of a king. This film shows that no matter who you are, life's misfortunes and problems don't have boundaries and everyone are equally susceptible to them. 

In this case, through this real historical drama, King George VI, Duke of York or "Bertie" (Colin Firth) suffers from stammering due to past trauma which let him grow into an insecure, clumsy, with low self-esteem man. Of course he could afford therapists but non of them succeeded in treating him. Thankfully the love of his wife Elizabeth and later on Queen (Helena Bonham Carter) helped him to begin working with a speech therapist called Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush).

The movie goes about a miraculous transformation. Starts with a hidden child within a man that needs to resolve troubles of the past and move on, a man who gradually gains self-awareness through anger, sadness, and love, and learns that there is hope even if he can't see it clearly. Eventually that scared child becomes a determined man, and when that man embraces his destiny a king is born who is ready to lead his country and his people and speak encouraging and wise words to them.

Colin Firth in an amazing performance, truly convincing through out the film with no loose edges or boring moments. Geoffrey Rush, a man behind the man, like a true friend through thick and thin added humor, intelligence, and was really satisfying to watch. Lastly, Helena Bonham Carter as the loving mother, wife, and companion has a great supportive presence.

In conclusion its a film worthy of your attention, money, and time, easily likable and so highly recommended ;)

Although it will probably have limited appeal to mass movie going audiences, this is the best movie of the year so far and certainly the finest acted. "The King's Speech" is based on the real life Duke of York that became King of England at the onset of WWII, after his brother, the rightful next in succession abdicated the throne to marry an American divorcee. The drama comes from the fact that this reluctant crown barer had a crippling speech impediment with a stammer so bad, it was painful to watch him struggle to get out every word. Can you even imagine, being the figurehead of a nation, in a time of war, where 85% of your duties involve giving speeches and radio addresses to your entire nation and the world? Now imagine that you can't speak publicly without stuttering.  Just great actors all around in this one. Colin Firth as the king, Geoffrey Rush as his speech therapist who teaches the king more than elocution. The guy who played the rat in Harry Potter as Churchill and my pic for a Best Actress Oscar, Helena Bonham Carter, another Potter alumnus. Normally I dislike her wild eyed, crazy hair, over the top characterizations and god forbid you put her in the same film with Johnny Depp. Here she plays the wife of the future king and does so with a reserve and genuine quality, while still invoking tremendous empathy as you watch her suffer for her beloved husband and his affliction. This amazing story/character just got overshadowed by the time and the larger than life leaders of the day. The history books, literature and film ran out of room after they addressed the likes of Churchill, Roosevelt, Stalin and Hitler. Somehow you get the feeling that was perfectly fine with King George VI. Excellent film.

Every now and then, there's a feel-good film that comes along and what should be a cliche, dull movie, is far from that; "The King's Speech" is one of these movies; it excels in every form and does it with brilliant results. Amazing. How did "Inception" win best cinematography, I do not know... but I know "The King's Speech" deserved it in every way. Other stand out achievements include the terrific acting of Colin Firth's character, George VI as one who has a speech impediment, the rich, intricate screenplay, and a narrative that's so alluring that even though the audience may understand what will transpire within the plotline, they can't help but to be sensitive to the characters' developments. 

"The King's Speech" is a success in every way. It may be a little too Hollywood for some folks, but this is a Hollywood film reaching the highest caliber of blockbuster filmmaking with tip-top, best-of-the-best ensemble attributes.

This film seems pedigreed for the Academy: a story about the British royals, a period piece, encompassing WWII, a character with a physical ailment he must overcome, class confrontations and an unlikely friendship. And it really happened.Yet thanks to a marvelous cast, witty and heartfelt writing, and sure-handed direction this film emerges as one of 2010's very best films. The movie tips us to its brilliance in the opening scene--a masterfully tense sequence where the stammering Duke of York must make his first speech to the British Empire in 1925 on the radio, which consisted of approximately a fourth of the world's population. The fear perfectly conveyed on Colin Firth's face, the fear and sympathy pouring out of Helena Bonham Carter's loving wife, all aided by director Tom Hooper's gliding camera and crisp editing, results in a heartbreaking moment of terror and hesitation. Firth has always been good, but delivers a true Oscar-worthy performance as the stuttering prince who would be king and lead his country through a key time in Europe's history. Bonham Carter is so warm and caring she reminds us why millions fell in love with the woman who would go on to their Queen Mother. Geoffrey Rush brings a great dose of fun and laughs as the teacher who must help this man overcome his diability, by any means necessary. The film also features wonderful casting flourishes in smaller roles: Guy Pearce as the self-absorbed and cowardly Prince Edward VIII, Michael Gambon as a bluff King George V, Timothy Spall as a wry Winston Churchill, Derek Jacobi as a flustered archbishop. It's a magnificent cast, with not one bad performance. The film is also a triumph of style, with divine period details and cinematography, as Hooper shot this with big lenses that make interiors look overbearing, long and narrow, visually representing the King's psychosis involving his closing throat and fear of inadequacy. Thanks to everyone involved, this is a fascinating, engrossing, emotional and inspiring true story that is worth seeking out for your immense viewing pleasure

"The King's Speech combines well-balanced elements of comedy, tension, romance, history and drama and provides the best movie in 2010"

What an extraordinary piece of filmmaking. Tom Hooper took the interesting story of King George VI of Britain (Colin Firth) struggle for regaining trust in his own voice. Knowledgeable of King George's stammer, his wife, Queen Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) appealed to some local and relatively unknown speech therapist by the name of Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). As a short history brief I could add that the Duke of York by the real name of Albert Frederick Arthur George became King of Britain not after the death of his father (King George V) but because of his brother's (King Eduard VIII) discharge or abdication of the duties as king and emperor. The story itself is well proportioned, the narrative linear structure is intelligently mannered and the dialogue is just captivating. I loved the pacing in this movie because it doesn't get slow or dull nor quickly and forgettable. It's a perfect achievement in terms of filmmaking and it's definitely one of the best pictures of 2010 if not the best. As the movie tag is saying, it takes leadership to confront a nation's fear and It takes friendship to conquer your own. King George has to regain not only confidence in his own voice and personality but also has to regain a lost friendship. A friendship he didn't had since his childhood days. He finds that special friend in his speech therapist who is a brilliant psychologist and a great human being. Although the story may sound for some people to be another royal-drama this is obviously not the case. The King's Speech combines well-balanced elements of comedy, tension, romance, history and drama. It succeeds by not focusing too much on just one character but let all of them be more than just screen-puppets. Be relevant pupper-masters that could steal the audience in any scene. Great craft, intensely intelligent and gallantly mannered, King's Speech is one of the finest products of comedic-biopic ever made.

Of course, for a movie to be brilliant you need brilliant acting besides brilliant screenplay and dialogue. And I admit, sometimes the screenplay, the story, could build a character more than his acting but this movie is one of the exceptions. Colin Firth does an outstanding job portraying the hardly King George VI. He looses himself completely into the king's personality. He somehow manages to both interact and disagree with his own character. His mannerism, his tonality, his impeccable eloquence and elegance is by far the outstanding piece of acting this year and Colin Firth deserves his Academy Award after his first nomination last year for "A Single Man". The secondary roles however are not to be forgotten. Helena Bonham Carter as Queen Elizabeth and Geoffrey Rush as Lionel Logue are both dueling with his majesty in terms of acting and they greatly succeed. A great complementary casting in these two wonderful and talented actors. Geoffrey Rush is more of a comedian than a serious therapist and manages to make the audience enjoy his character while Helena Bonham Carter represents the aristocratic fanciness in that period of time.

The entire staff should get recognition for the beautiful and imposing cinematography. It's a perfect combination between two contradicting feelings within King's personality: claustrophobia and liberation. The anti-thesis in this movie is perfectly shown thanks to the beautiful shots and even the chosen contrasts. The decors are also part of this sublime description of our main character by combining complexity with simplicity. Elegance with rustiness. Although all these technical details are pretty good and help to create a worm and comfortable atmosphere, the most incredible thing to me is the music I'm hearing while watching the film. Alexandre Desplay is guilty for providing the best original score this year. I'm sorry for The Social Network or Inception but this is pure music. This piece of astonishing and captivating music is on another level for me as a solid cinefile that I like to believe I am. I had goose bumps just listening the melody in the first 2-3 minutes for the movie and I was already amazed and dazzled.

What more can I possibly say?... The King's Speech is, if not the best, then definitely one of the best movie released in 2010 and one of the best comedic-biopics ever. I still judge this movie as being more a drama/comedy type of movie than being strict and choose just one genre which would be drama.

It is essentially a powerful 2-hander with Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush as, respectively, Bertie/George VI and his speech therapist Lionel Logue, but it has the backing of a superb ensemble cast, including turns by Guy Pearce, Anthony Andrews, Michael Gambon, Derek Jacobi and notably Helena Bonham Carter, who, for me was the best of the lot.
The only disappointing performance in the whole film was Timothy Spall's Churchill which seemed to be a complete caricature, but his contributions were blessedly brief. 
Given the much deserved hype about the film I doubt that anyone in the English speaking world will be unaware of its premise and there isn't actually much to give away if you have any knowledge of 20th century British history, even without knowing much about Bertie and his attempts to conquer his speech impediment. Some have criticised the film for deliberately whitewashing anti-semitism in the Royal family (unlikely given that members of the writer's own family died in the Holocaust) and painting George VI as a plaster saint, but that's not the point of the film. It isn't a documentary, and is factually incorrect in places, such as with Churchill, who was actually a friend of Bertie's brother David/Edward VIII, seeming to support the idea of abdication in this film. But, taking the general principle applied to history by Hollywood of never letting the truth stand in the way of a good story (although to be fair William Shakespeare also played fast and loose with historical fact when it suited him... see Macbeth for example) this is really a simple study of the relationship between 2 people- one a person of immense privilege yet aware of his limitations in the face of an undesired position of responsiblity, the other a person who looks beyond class and status to see and help the person beyond. The political backdrop is simply that, the scenery against which two actors at the top of their game work with an excellent script, crafted beautifully by David Seidler. As a child Seidler too apparently struggled with a speech impediment, which he believes was brought on by the trauma of the early years of WWII in London, and more recently he has been struggling with throat cancer, while George VI himself died of lung cancer after years of heavy smoking, prompted in part (according to the film) by physicians suggesting that the smoke would help relax his vocal cords. At the BAFTAs it was said that George VI's speeches on radio were a great inspiration to the young Seidler, but apparently he didn't know, until starting to write the screenplay, that his uncle, who was also a stammer, had also been sent to Logue by his grandfather. How much of the dialogue reflects the real interactions between Logue and Bertie (informed by the notebooks that apparently came to light only a few weeks before filming began) is unclear, particularly the "swearing scene" which nearly had the film classified as a 15. However, the interactions are compelling and the relationships entirely believable and deeply moving.

A superbly executed account of the reluctant succession to the throne of King George VI & his speech impediment, "The King's Speech" is sure to win a host of accolades at this years various awards ceremonies. And rightly so. 
Colin Firth will naturally receive much recognition for his efforts as King George/Bertie, but - from a personal perspective - Geoffrey Rush stole the show with his portrayal of Lionel Logue, the King's  unconventional speech therapist.
In fact, Firth & Rush play off each other to stunning effect as we are treated to a visual & aural exploration of how the pair work together to overcome the King's stammer. The onscreen relationship is both believable and intriguing - maintaining the attention of the audience from the very first meeting to the conclusion of that famous wartime speech. Indeed, it's fair to say that the film explores not only the King's stammer, but other issues that impede him from becoming the man he feels he should become. The friendship that blossoms between Lionel & "Bertie" unveils the psychological monsters faced by the prince as he aspires o be everything that is expected of him, to the point that it is quite believable come the conclusion of the film that Logue was very possibly the first true friend Bertie ever had.

The film is superbly cast, with cameos for the likes of Timothy Spall as Sir Winston Churchill and Michael Gambon as the ailing King George V. Helena Bonham-Carter takes leave from the standard work directed by her husband to take on the challenge of a young Queen Mum, and does the role justice. 
A sumptuous score penned by Alexandre Desplat accompanies the visual element to great effect, with additional use of Beethoven's 7th Symphony enhancing the dramatic delivery of the speech.
Anyone who has an interest in historical drama will not be disappointed with The King's Speech. It is surely the first overwhelming success story in theatres for 2011.

I always like a film based on true events, it seems that real life has just as many amazing stories as pure fiction. This is a case in point. A man who stammers has to rise above his affliction, with the help and support of those around him, to speak for a nation. It's quite a remarkable film. Here's a short summary first before I give you my thoughts (summary haters please wait outside while I get through the next speech... sorry, paragraph).

King George VI, known as Bertie to his friends and family, was not born to be king. That honour went to his older brother David, or King Edward VIII, after their father George V passed away. Unfortunately, David finds he cannot carry out his duties due to events in his private life (quite a scandal actually) and so Bertie has to step in. A long time before this he had started seeing an unorthodox speech therapist named Lionel Logue. He had always stammered and found it particularly hard to speak in public. With the help and support of Logue, his wife, Elizabeth and his daughters another Elizabeth (later to become Queen Elizabeth II) and Margaret; this film depicts how he overcame his problems to give a very important speech live on the radio to the entire British Empire (as it was then) just after the outbreak of World War II. It also gives an insight into the reasons for Edward's abdication and the effect it has on the nation. But I think that's enough summary for now.

I found this a totally engaging film from start to finish. As a Brit, I was taught about the abdication of Edward VII in school, but I never knew about George VI's stammer or the work of Lionel Logue. Of course, the film is most noted for the performance of Colin Firth as King George VI (Bertie to his friends), which is totally justified, he is outstanding! Also worthy of note are both Geoffrey Rush as Lionel Logue and Helena Bonham Carter as Queen Elizabeth. Honourable mentions go to Derek Jacobi as Archbishop Cosmo Lang, Michael Gambon as King George V, Guy Pearce as King Edward VIII, Claire Bloom as Queen Mary and Timothy Spall as Winston Churchill.

Apart from the performances, I thought it was an excellent screenplay by David Seidler. Nicely directed by Tom Hooper, it depicts the period perfectly. This is a film with many laughs, more than a lot of modern 'comedies', IMO, which serve to lift the mood of what is, after all, rather serious events in world history. Over all, brilliant performances, a great story and a few laughs along the way... who could ask for more? Very highly recommended.

The King's Speech a drama surrounding the stammer Duke of York and his therapist is getting a lot of award attention lately. You cannot argue about the fact that this is a good piece of filmmaking, but it lacks some essentials in the entertainment sector, which is a bit of a downer coming out of the theater.

For a historical drama it is always a fine line to walk between the repetition of historic facts and the refreshment with new creative parts. Sad thing about The King's Speech is, that it walks this line well from a script perspective, but it is rather unentertaining when it comes down to the historic facts. Every scene that is outside the room of Lionel Logue is a bit of a letdown, because you get the feeling that it is only there to provide a bit of additional drama. It sure tells the historic background a bit and the urgency of a strong and stammer-free King, but it feels short sometimes. 
The entertainment in this movie is provided by the great chemistry of Firth and Rush. Their scenes, that they have together are strong in the dramatic department and they are giving this film the award spark. Firth, as the stammer Duke of York, who later becomes George VI, the King of the Kingdom of Britain, and Rush, as his therapist are doing a great job of playing their characters in an entertaining and interesting way. The thing between this two is, that the power is reversed, which makes for an interesting look at a Prince, that is working out of his comfort-zone. Logue as an authority works with the King with very unconventional methods. The King can argue about the way these methods are working, or about the way his therapist is treating him, but he cant argue with the results.

This look at a odd couple is great, not only because of the therapy but also because of the character development. George is opening himself to his therapist and those stories are really a strong dramatic act in the film. Colin Firth is getting a lot of attention because of his performance, but it might be for the wrong motives. He surely delivers a great acting performance with his stammer, the way his face is doing the stammer, how he keeps it up and only slightly improves his speech throughout the film, when his therapist is not available. That is a great performance, but he also delivers a human Highness, he is able to walk the thin line between a Royal Highness, that should demand respect out of every person, and a human being that really needs the help of a therapist.
Logue as the counterpart is a demanding and autherity thriven person, who is the only "doctor" around, who can treat the King because of the lack of respect for his social position. That is a social image that is hard to deliver, but those two are working as a cohisive unit that brings across this fact perfectly.

At the end of the movie, where the therapist has to leave his safe castle, to really help his patient out of the house in the real world, the relationship between those two is great and as an audience you really get the equal level of these two. The only thing that makes underlines the social difference between the two right there is the great camera work. The speech George delivers, The King's speech, is done in a small room, and Logue and George are treated as equals, only the fact that the camera is looking upwards to George and down to Logue manifests the difference between the two at the end. With these small things Tom Hooper was able to get the equal relationship that should exist between a therapist and his patient, but still showing the different social levels.

Other than that The King's Speech is a good film, that deserves the award spotlight, but is not entertaining all the way through. What still remains is a great performance by Firth, Rush and also Helena Bonham Carter, she plays the "first lady" the proper attitude and also is performing the equal relationship at the end of the movie. It´s a well-rounded cast with a good story and great performances, that are elevating this movie to a hot candidate for any award!

Tom Hooper's The King's Speech was nominated for 12 Academy Awards, and won four, including Best Picture and Best Director. In a way, I really wanted to hate this - the fact that this won the Best Picture award over such masterpieces like Inception and Black Swan was astounding. I hate to admit, but I loved The King's Speech. I don't think it should've won Best Picture, but it's still a terrific and rather fascinating look into King George VI. SUMMARY:

Most of us are familiar with the story of how our present Queen's father was forced to take on the throne when her uncle Edward VIII (Guy Pearce) decided to opt for life with American divorcee Mrs Wallace Simpson rather than staying on as King. What is less known is that Bertie (Colin Firth)- that's what the new King's intimates called him - had a speech impediment which made public speaking of any sort an agonizing embarrassment. He had tried various cures, all of them failed, until his wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) dragged him to see an Australian elocutionist Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), and that's when the fun and games begin between the down-to-earth Australian and the man before whom the world bowed. REVIEW:

The screenplay was written by David Seidler, who won an Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay. It's a fascinating account into how this man overcame his stammer. Though I don't if everything was accurate, there were a lot of interesting elements to the plot. Yes, I'm not familiar with King George and his battle with his stammer, but I absolutely took a lot from this film. Seidler's screenplay is charming as ever, with sophisticated dialogue that really works with the film's target audience. There's a touch of very tamed yet very funny humour as well. The King's Speech is a tad long, as it follows the whole relationship between Bertie and Lionel. That relationship is possibly the very heart of the film. The friendship that forms between the two men is touching, and Bertie's speeches are absolutely inspirational. While there's a truly grim and depressing side to The King's Speech, it's also very uplifting. The film ends quite similarly to most British period dramas these days, but it doesn't make the film any worse. Colin Firth, who won an Oscar for his role, is a revelation as Bertie. You can not fault his performance. He brings off that stammer as if he actually had one. I haven't seen him in a role quite like this, as it requires a lot from him. It's quite an emotional role, but he pulls it off with skill. Geoffrey Rush, who was nominated for an Oscar, is sublime as Lionel Logue. Rush works well with Firth, and the two create a significant and believable friendship. Helena Bonham Carter is finally in a film where she doesn't have to act all spazzy and crazy - she's here as a classy woman, and she does it perfectly. She can tackle almost any role. Actors in support are also fine - Guy Pearce is brilliant as King Edward, and Michael Gambon is impeccable as Bertie's father. On the technical side of things, The King's Speech is terrific. Shot by Danny Cohen, the film is marvelous to look at. It's a very beautiful looking movie. Alexandre Desplat composed a truly sophisticated score, suiting very well with the classy material of the film. The production design is also a highlight - the creation of 1930s London makes you feel like you're there, and the sets are simply breathtaking. In terms of pacing, The King's Speech has its ups and downs. From the get-go, the film moves along at a terrific pace, but towards the middle, the film does tend to drag for a while. Though it's not boring at all, you get the feeling that it isn't going anywhere. The costumes however are superb. Sophisticated and detailed costumes that really work well to keep the context convincing - it's nice to see Helena Bonham Carter dress like an actual lady for once rather than her being Tim Burton's Barbie doll. I do think that The King's Speech is a tad bit overrated. I don't think it should've won Best Picture. Still, it's an amazing effort. Every element is top-notch, with the music, the cinematography, the script, and most of all, the performances. They're the best thing about the film. Watching this for the performances wouldn't hurt, as the acting from the stars is definitley worth it. Colin Firth, Geoffrey Rush, and Helena Bonham Carter are sublime.

When I first went to see this just over a week ago I was struck by just how packed the cinema was, and with very elderly people, some of whom appeared not to have been to 'the pictures' for a decade or more. One gentleman carefully made his way down the stairs about half way through the film to go to the toilet, and walked right up to the wall where the toilets' entrances used to be in our former local cinema, which I believe was closed down back in 2003. The film's success, other than the Awards Season buzz for both it and Colin Firth's much ballyhooed performance contained in it, does seem in part to be down to a groundswell of nostalgia coming from people who either lived through the period in which the film is set or at least through the war-time aftermath. In a way this is backed up by the fact that of the two screenings I went to I was the youngest person there by a good 30 years on both occasions. Then there were the people I went to see the film with, both pensioners; firstly I went with my dad, who was a kid when George VI was the nation's king; and after seeing how much the audience had enjoyed the film (and how much myself and my dad had for that matter) I convinced my 88-year-old nan to come along with us for another viewing; and she talked of how she could not only remember George VI's reign but also his brother's and father's before him. Any historical inaccuracies this may have (and I believe there are many) clearly don't get in the way of making it a good film, as I heard no complaints from any of these people knowledgeable of the time; some people have pedantically stated that the king would certainly not have swore in front of his therapist, but the scene in question drew some of the biggest laughs of the entire film. The film obviously wants you to side with George VI and he is made out to be the 'hero' as opposed to his brother Edward VIII's 'villain', and all the 'good guys' in history like Churchill side with the former, which is all very probably largely exaggerated or not true at all. But I think it's important to remember that this is primarily (perhaps entirely) a piece of entertainment, and it is very entertaining. A film like this is more likely to get people to take an interest in the real history and find out the facts for themselves. Those who don't choose to do so after viewing the film will be misguided but so be it; if films purely stuck to THE FACTS then they would not be escapism and would not work in the way cinema was essentially designed to do so. Personally I think the screenplay is brilliant, encapsulating almost 15 years of great change seemingly with ease, and full of wit and clever dialogue that does a very good job of summarising the characters of all those real people involved in the story. The cast is arguably one of the best assembled for some time; there isn't really one actor you could say wasn't well suited for their role. Colin Firth is of course worthy of being singled out for praise, his performance being funny, poignant and inspiring, and he is almost a dead cert for this year's Best Actor Oscar, but Geoffrey Rush and Helena Bonham Carter would also be worthy of winning Best Supporting Actor and Best Supporting Actress respectively. Frankly I'd be quite happy for The King's Speech to clean up at this year's Oscars, as despite not being a huge fan of royal dramas I found it highly interesting and engaging.

It's clear that Albert has a speech disability and worst of all it's more frightening for him, since most of the British Empire and other parts of the world is honing in on his speech. Albert's brother becomes King after their father has passed away but decides to step down since he wants to marry an American who was twicely divorced. Well if this isn't Oscar bait I don't know what is. A movie about the British monarchs that comes out in December. The only thing that is holding it back from pure gold is that it is actually doing well in the box office, people are going to see it.

It seems that come award season a couple movies always make it across the pond and infiltrate the system. This movie follows the same formula as the ones before it. It humanizes the monarch while still telling a story of perseverance. Already nabbing a couple awards it is sure to win a couple of Oscars as well. Had it not been for the suburb acting in this movie I'm sure this would just be another British film nabbing awards that no one would see.

The title of the film references two things. Both the slammer that Albert Fredrick Arthur George (His Majesty to you) possessed since an early age. It is this stammer he must overcome to deliver his most important address to the nation at the dawn of World War II with Hitler knocking on the doorstep.

But Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush make it worth it. Firth plays the stammering king who lives in the shadow of his father and brother, hauntingly played by Michael Gambon and Guy Pearce respectively. He once again dives into the role that calls for quiet restraint. He has become known for this type of role and continues to flourish with it. But his best moments are when he steps out of his quiet demeanor and stands up for himself. He is a shoo-in for best actor this year.

Firth's strong performance of the damaged son lacking confidence allows for his supporting cast to step out and excel as they try to raise him up. Helena Bonham Carter does well as the Queen Mum, her strong personality fits well as she interacts with some of the commoners. Her role is more limited in this story so most of the accolades not given to Firth will likely be given to his other costar. Geoffrey Rush steals every scene as the eccentric speech therapist who believes in his king. He delivers most of, if not all the laughs in the movie (Timothy Spall has some as Winston Churchill but I'm not sure if that's the writing or the fact that Timothy Spall is playing Winston Churchill). There is little to no nuance to the performance and while it may be the big named actors that get you in the theater it will be Rush who keeps you in your seat.

That seems to be what the problem with so many other English movies, they are often so serious that they keep fun loving American movie goers away from the theater. The performances and writing in the movie will keep the viewer engaged. All the characters are believable and it isn't until the final sequence that all the king talk really hits home, it is less about the monarch and more about the man looking to fulfill his duty.

Writer David Seidler had been looking to make this film for some time. And although he didn't need to, he asked for permission from the Queen Mum to make the movie. She in turn asked him to wait till after her death as the memories were still to fresh for her. After she passed away at the age of 150 he was finally able to tell the story of a man who fell by the wayside with so many larger personalities during this time period.

The story is an interesting one, but the execution is what brings the movie down a peg, it is formulaic. Fortunately the formula is how to win a lot of awards so it is a good path to follow. Even more fortunate are the male leads in the movie as they take the this story over the top which will have one of these men (though both deserve it) walking away with gold in February. A-

This film is very British. Properly so, I might add, as its a film about British people (and an Australian) concerned with British matters and all are dealt with in the traditional British way. If you're in the mood for a period piece/biopic, you really can't go wrong here, and really its a refreshing break from Superhero/Action movies, Romantic Comedies and the latest CGI extravaganza. This film doesn't rely on any sort of trick aside from solid acting jobs from the entire cast. Indeed, the film stands on their shoulders and elevates itself to greatness at the hands of a solid script and capable director.

   There's nothing too outlandish about the plot, it follows history very, very closely, with King George VI's ascent to the throne set against his own struggles with a debilitating stammer. While Colin Firth brings a perfect blend of gravitas and self-effacement to his portrayal of the king, and he never crosses into melodrama or overacting, Geoffrey Rush is usually the clearly dominant personality whenever the two are onscreen together. Rush provides the catalyst to what might have been a lifeless partnership and is able to fully embody his role without outshining his costars. He manages great presence and is definitely a standout in a whole cadre of great performances. Helena Bonham Carter is great in a role that is strangely reserved (for her).

   Even though the film takes place in a buttoned up era and carries a somewhat drab color scheme, it has moments of well-timed levity and although a sense of despair and tension is apparent as war looms closer, from the perspective of a modern audience, the whole event comes off as an empowering tale of triumph and friendship, and it can be downright inspiring. 

 It perhaps could have done with stricter editing at certain points, as the movie loses a little bit of focus and we are sort of left wondering about the certain characters until the film happens to bring them up again. It barely detracts from the proceedings, and only the most jaded cimeagoer might label this a 'flaw.'

  All in all, this movie is a solid achievement for traditional film making in an era where special effects and grandiose set-pieces tend to override character development and pure, solid writing. If you need a break from such shallow Hollywood fare,this is exactly where you should look.

The King's Speech is about as good as period dramas come. Bertie, the Duke of York, has a terrible stammer and has tried every doctor and cure in the book in order to overcome it. His profession is most unforunate, as he is given to making large public speeches, such as the disasterous closing message at the 1925 Empire Exhibition. When his brother King Edward VIII abdicates after being determined to marry divorcee Mrs Wallis Simpson, Bertie is forced onto the throne as King George VI. The need for him to speak publicly becomes even more pressing as the Second World War beckons, and so on the advice of his wife Elizabeth (the Queen Mother), sees Australian speech therapist Lionel Logue. Logue's unconventional style of diagnosis alternatively infuriates and amuses Bertie, with whom Lionel eventually develops a friendship. The King's Speech is a masterclass in acting from all fronts, notably Colin Firth. Certainly his best role to date, his portrayal of George VI is sympathetic but not ridiculous. In the hands of another actor the constant stuttering could have become unfortunately comic, but Firth brings a resilience to the role which is poignant and very convincing. Praise must also be given to Helena Bonham Carter for her rendition of Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon, being both friendly and supportive of her husband's condition. The film is not without a few faults, notably Timothy Spall's performance as Winston Churchill, who at the point the story is set was not an important enough person to be privy to the inner-workings of the Royal Family. Nonetheless, for a dialogue-heavy production, very few liberties are taken to twist the facts, such as the admirable decision to end the film on 3rd September 1939, at the outbreak of war in Europe. Funny, romantic and ultimately uplifting, this is a sensitive historical drama which treats the subject matter with the gravitas it deserves. Enlightening.

Will be better remembered for its performances than for its excellence. The King's Speech will almost assuredly bring home awards for Actor (Firth) and Supporting Actor (Rush), and will likely get some attention for ensemble cast in the ceremonies that observe such awards. They smash through their roles with precision and fervor, and never for a moment do we perceive them as the people playing the characters. There is also a great deal of talent in the cinematography, as the peculiar angles and shots give a sense of claustrophobia not unlike what must be going on in the king's mind. The story, however, can't keep up. There is no measurable progress in the main story, no indication that his speech is improving, or that we are gaining a further understanding as to why he is impeded in the first place. It gets boring for brief periods, only to string together events that only serve to get us to the end, rather than enhance our viewing experience or offer us insight into much of anything. That's not to say it was a terrible plot - rather, it's simply an obvious weak link that keeps the movie good rather than potentially excellent.

Make no mistake -- this masterful film is worthy of its many accolades!!   As its basic premise, Elizabeth -- the future "Queen Mum" -- engages the services of eccentric speech therapist Lionel Logue in an attempt to cure her husband, Albert ("Bertie"), of his pronounced stuttering, even as kingship (King George VI) is suddenly thrust upon him in a vacuum of English leadership on the eve of World War II.   These historical events are given new life by means of a deft, well-written screenplay which follows this personal journey with an stunning abundance of pathos, drama, and yes, even comedy.   As a note, even with its serious nature, good humor flows throughout this story, with genuinely funny moments that break the tension.   Colin Firth is superb in his riveting, must-see performance as Albert!   Likewise, Geoffrey Rush animates the role of Logue with palpable vigor.   It is fascinating to watch Firth and Rush at work as the dynamic, high-stakes interplay of friction and friendship unfolds between "Bertie" and Logue.  Helena Bonham Carter displays considerable talent as she brings a caring, steely (and even playful) gravity to her role as Elizabeth.   This trio is supported by a myriad number of capable performances.   Technically, cinematography is always appropriate -- especially when "moody".   Art direction deserves special mention, as does the musical score, which draws from a number of classical composers.   In short, given the combination of these elements (and more), "The King's Speech" makes for a royal film experience!!   Content: Colorful, R-rated language.

On the eve of War, Bertie sang: "One of the highest distinctions is service to others." For the record, everyone else may know him as King George VI but for all of us in the inner audience sanctum of the 'The Kings Speech' he is very much 'Bertie'. 

Maybe it's my staunchly Catholic Family or more likely my mother's dislike of the Royal Family that has kept me away from really becoming familiar with the profiles and personalities behind the British Royal Family. Thank God for the Top Hopper's and Stephen Frear's of this world - it might not be absolutely 100% 'you can bet your bottom dollar accurate, but it's a historical depiction, a suggestion, an insight and in the two films that have driven my interest, compelling portraiture. 

This social and political background is woven beautifully into the tone, setting and dialogue of the film. Desperation in the Depression, the fear of War and the rise of Fascism and Stalinism all mirror beautifully the personal, private struggles of those suffered by the newly appointment Head of State. That desperation is a small nuance and overtone should not be overlooked - in the colour of Lionel Logue's Consulting Room walls, in the Mist surrounding the King and his therapist, in the Rain that poured on the Queen's Motorcar, in death, in abdication, in frustration, in triumph, still, desperation lurked. 

The film offered a slow journey filled with humour, friendship, commitment, courage, compassion, duty and honour but did not creep into the realms of sentimentality or propitiousness. So you could leave the Kleenex in your cabinet at home, but still feel immensely satisfied that your life had just become a little bit richer. That had an awful lot to do with the superior performance of Geoffrey Rush, laden with impeccably timing, witticism and humanity; the humorous and puckish Helena Bonham Carters spin on the Queen Mother and Derek Jacobi's autocrat Archbishop. 

I do not agree that the film is mainly Firth's triumph - without Rush the film would not hold the same pleasure. It was Rush's Australia against Firth's Britain and the bridging of that social gap that allowed the film to transcend to something extremely moving. What I do agree with however is the recognition that Firth has already had, and will certainly continue to get with the Oscar's just around the Kodak corner. As an avid movie goer, this is possibly the first convincing role that Firth has ever held to warrant a nomination and possible Academy win.

The following are a number of reviews and comments I have come across that I generally agree with (I'd scroll down to the final comment to sum up my general opinion of the film):

"Working from the British-royalty-biopic template perfected by Peter Morgan (The Deal, The Queen), The King's Speech provides a cute, complication-free portrait of the Duke of York (Colin Firth), who would eventually become King George VI of England, and his difficulty overcoming a lifelong stammer. Opening in 1925 to the sight of George addressing a Wembley Stadium crowd with halting bits and pieces of words, Tom Hooper's film proceeds to chart the future king's failed efforts to deal with his problem through kooky speech therapist sessions (one has him stuff marbles in his mouth), all while his father, George V (Michael Gambon), lambastes his younger son-after one of the King's famous, eloquent Christmas broadcasts via the newfangled radio-to just speak, "dammit!" 


As embodied by Firth, George VI is emasculated and debilitated by his disobedient tongue, which has made him at once a reticent figure prone to retreat into silence, and a furiously angry man driven half-mad by his handicap. Firth's high-pitched stuttering voice only infrequently plays as an affectation, but even in those rare moments, the actor's well-modulated, pent-up performance refuses to devolve into caricature. That makes it something of a triumph considering that, from its fundamental narrative building blocks on up to its particular one-liners, The King's Speech remains a decorous bit of middlebrow mush. 


Having previously worked with Morgan's writing on The Damned United, director Hooper proves a competent fit for David Seidler's Morgan-knockoff script, shooting the action in austere hues and with low-angled compositions in order to create a superficial sense of period-piece solemnity and significance. However, no amount of surface classiness or historical-bigwig cameos (hey, there's Timothy Spall as Churchill!) can mask the contrived nature of the film, which pivots around the relationship between George and Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), an "unorthodox and controversial" Shakespeare-adoring speech therapist and failed actor who challenges George to not only train his body, but, more crucially still, to confront the root emotional causes of his stammer. These can be boiled down to "It's the fault of my demanding daddy, bullying brother, and mean nanny!" 


Yet despite such simplistic psychologizing, The King's Speech barely buys what it's selling. No sooner are these explanations introduced than they're discarded, all so the proceedings can eschew true character development in favor of the jokey sight of George learning to enunciate through singing and cursing, the romantic shenanigans of his older brother, Edward VIII (Guy Pearce)-who assumes the throne and then relinquishes it to marry a twice-divorced American hussy, Wallis Simpson (Eve Best)-and the buildup to war with Hitler, whose threat to the U.K and, specifically, George, is epitomized by his mesmerizing oratory skills. 


Through it all, George and Lionel develop a combative but respectful friendship that, following romantic-comedy dictates, starts out unevenly, then blossoms, and is eventually destabilized by a foolish act of betrayal and then saved in time for a heartwarming finale. Rush exuberantly expresses Lionel's confidence and taskmaster bossiness, but, from an early lesson involving a phonograph recording to his assertive poise in the face of the Church's archbishop (Derek Jacobi), who functions as the story's nominal kinda-sorta villainous presence, he remains a two-dimensional cipher of impeccable virtue and noble intentions. The same holds true for George's loyal wife Elisabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) and, ultimately, George himself, whose intermittent furious outbursts mask such pedestrian-and easily resolvable-hang-ups that he comes across as more petulant than deeply pained. 


No leaden symbolism à la The Queen's stag further weigh down The King's Speech, a merciful development given how sluggish and reductive the material is to begin with, epitomized by both its eventual, one-dimensional conflation of George's speech issues with the WWII effort and its glossed-over address of the radio's role in transforming the ruler-ruled dynamic. Straining to elevate its real-life footnote of a tale into a meaningful fable about a man, and nation, "finding their voice," the film manages to spit out merely high-minded sitcom uplift."

REVIEW NO 2 (Notice how it also mentions 'sitcom' in its criticism)

"The King's Speech isn't the worst of the recent films to receive a gluttony of Academy Award nominations, but it is quite likely the most boring. There are films that win Oscars and there are films that are made with the intent to win Oscars, and sometimes those two overlap, but for the time being (nominees were just announced this morning) Tom Hooper's film is most definitely in the latter category. As dolled up and self-consciously serious as to count as something of an epitome of the glamour-hungry Weinstein Company's distinctive output, this dramatization of Prince Albert's (later King George VI's) journey to overcoming his speech impediment would like to think of itself as a moving, soulful character study, but such are the clothes of the naked emperor. In actuality, this high-minded exercise -- pretty looking and paper-thin -- utilizes the same template as any number of crowd-pleasing biopics, but whereas a film like Walk the Line embraces the simplifying nature of historical caricature (and Hollywood-typical manipulation), The King's Speech foolishly tries to pass off connect-the-dots psychology as profundity and sitcom mechanics as high art.

It speaks to the strength of Colin Firth's lead performance, then (as well as his shared chemistry with Geoffrey Rush, who portrays the speech expert who tries to cure the King), that the film almost gets away with it. Alas, personality has been washed from the cloth of The King's Speech with a heavy starch, and save for a few humorous sequences concerning Bertie's (as his family and friends refer to him) diction lessons, the effect is not unlike being straightjacketed for tea. A scantly-used Rorschach device typifies the wasted potential here; instead of a legitimate psychological inquiry, we're given a lavish movie of the week with lip service, and for every idiosyncrasy there are a half dozen lame concessions to sutured, unimaginative screenwriting -- it isn't long before the film feels thoroughly "safe" and insignificant. Emotional heft is traded in for tidy resolutions and pat history lessons (Hitler, the ultimate challenge of his kingship, is presented as a daunting Great Speaker and then promptly forgotten), and they all lived happily ever after. Ultimately worth watching for Firth, who finds nuance amidst what might otherwise be cartoon slickness, Helena Bonham Carter, who puts on a great fashion show as Bertie's wife, the Duchess of York, and Rush for his particular refusal to devolve into complete two-dimensionality, but only just. The pleasures are minimal, but at least the pain is, too."

I'm noticing a recurring theme in this year's prospective Oscar nominess:  the perils of public performance, either in the realms of ballet or politics.  As in Black Swan, we see the anxiety in meeting the expectations of the audience and of thyself to be emotionally and physically crippling, and it matters not whether you're an aspiring ingenue or part of the aristocracy.  Colin Firth gives a bravura performance as one, the to-be-named George VI, who struggled to put two words together that anyone could follow.  The King's Speech, which has a double meaning that is fairly obvious based on what I've already described, shines the spotlight on the stigma of stutterers and stammerers unlike few films before, this time not for comic relief or caricature, but to reveal how commonly it afflicts those of all backgrounds and affects the credibility of many who underneath may even possess a brilliant mind and a will to lead.  Geoffrey Rush is to be equallly lauded for offering a sympathetic portrayal of a speech therapist who subs as a counsellor, competently and masterfully.  Watch the two act together; you can actually see and feel the other listening while one speaks or at least attempts to.  These are the fundamentals of great acting, two sharing a scene and engaging in a dance (sounds as if I'm reviewing Black Swan again).  The only questions I have about this fine period piece is what its intentions might be besides presenting the stuttering community to the world.  Oftentimes in recent years, historical dramas implicitly allude to issues that are pressing on the world of today.  Politically and culturally, I don't see any specific parallels being made (perhaps my Facebook friends may enlighten me).  Maybe it doesn't have any such intentions, which may leave it struggling on Oscar night in the face of The Social Network.  I also think the film won't earn too many fans of those expecting a fair assessment of the Edward VIII/Wallace Simpson affair; the two look like aloof nincompoops in this movie that could give two hoots about the monarchy and its sense of tradition.  After the multi-layered portrayal of The Queen a few years ago, this one may actually get an appreciative thumbs-up from her Majesty, not to mention other pro-monarchist folks out there.  How fitting as the newest generation of royals heads up the aisle.  My my, have I hit on a hidden agenda?

Although the subject of a future king who has a speech impediment doesn't seem very interesting on paper, The King's Speech manages to pull it off with grace. This is mainly due to an appropriate decision to focus the movie around the well-staged relationship between a teacher and a student who happens to be a monarch. Colin Firth is excellent as Bertie (the future King George VI) making the struggle with his stammer palpable, while Geoffrey Rush as the teacher proves to be the heart of the movie delivering a stunningly vibrant performance. This being said, director Tom Hooper tends to overdramatize the movie on numerous occassions. It's evident that The King's Speech was about to be a highly inspirational movie, yet this fact doesn't excuse the trite dramatic tricks such as some overly exaggerated scenes or the use of overexposed music. In addition, some sequences that don't involve the interaction between Firth and Rush simply don't work very well and thus unncessarily slow down the pace of the movie. Consequently, The King's Speech doesn't quite live up to its reputation of being one of the best pictures of the year. It's still an enjoyable watch though chiefly on account of superb acting. 7.5/10 (B)

Some films, sad to say, are sorely lacking in Hollywood. With special effects and fancy editing it is underwhelming for a filmmaker to "lower" him or herself to the level of simple period drama.

Here we have a film that, like Black Swan, has no pretenses about being anything other than it is. Some of the best films of the year have displayed similar symptoms. It is almost too much to ask nowadays for a film to simply be true to itself. However, unlike Black Swan, the story is compelling and understandable, just like we expect it to be. The story is also simple, just like we expect it to be.

While the story is simple and some would say routine, the tremendous British (and Australian) talent on display here carry the plot with such weight that it doesn't matter. Collin Firth's King George VI is a well acted, and believable king, whose stutter never once causes even the most immature audience member to laugh. His figure is one of inner strength, but also incredible outer weakness, from which immense sympathy arises in the audience. Helena Bonham Carter has risen from oddball Tim Burton performances to a nuanced character as the wife who just won't give up for her husband's problem. Geoffrey Rush plays an actor/speech therapist who may or may not be qualified to treat the King's problem. These three alone could have (and did at some points) carry the film alone, but an ensemble of supporting characters, including Derek Jacobi, Michael Gambon, and Guy Pierce provide a strong backdrop for England on the eve of WWII.

The cinematography of this film is not exemplary, something that makes their nomination somewhat stunning, but never mind. Many of the scenes are handled with single takes which provide the actors enough room to act without being restricted by angle. There are plenty of Steadicam shots in this film, which reminds us that the story is following George in his struggle with his problem.

So many times nowadays I notice that films have increasingly negative messages. The King's Speech has one of the best feel-good endings of the year. The writing for this film is incredible. Supporting the great actors, we have incredible wit and heart in this screenplay. While the construction was nothing new, if there is an academy award for dialogue alone this film would get it.

Overall, a well scripted period piece with the best British Cast of the year. Two Thumbs Up!
