"The King's Speech" refers to the climax of the film, when King George VI is forced to deliver a speech to a large portion of the world. He has to tell everyone that his country is now at war with Germany, and that everything will be okay. Oh yes, he also has a problem speaking, having a stammering problem that he has just spent 90 minutes attempting to overcome. There, I just gave away the majority of The King's Speech. It's okay though, because the title already did that, I just contextualized it for you. Now all there is to do is find out how well this speech goes, and what happens to the characters after he delivers it. And you'll likely also want to look back on the last hour and a half of film that you just watched and think for a moment about what you've just seen. That is to say that you'll likely really enjoy yourself while watching it, and also come to appreciate it after it concludes. There aren't really a lot of plot points that will surprise you, nor are there any that intend to do that. The story is single-minded in nature, and this simplicity helps the film hold the attention of its audience. The majority of The King's Speech centers on The Duke of York (Colin Firth), soon to be King attempting to deal with his stammering problem. It's been an issue he's had to deal with since around the age of 4, and it has recently been hampering him in his public engagements. His wife (Helena Bonham Carter) finds a speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), who claims that he'll be able to help the Duke. This is what the majority of the film centers around--the Duke's constant problems with his stammering, the therapist's attempts to cure him--and there isn't a whole lot else going on. Everything that occurs leads up to the final, climactic speech that is to be broadcast worldwide. So, yes, it is about a man overcoming an obstacle in his life, and that's just about all the film is about. Yes, there are some sub plots, but they generally don't matter. The Duke has a brother, who is actually first to inherit the throne, but for reasons that I'll leave as a surprise, ends up passing the job onto his younger brother. Lionely Louge also has children, who mock his failed acting career, something else that doesn't actually end up being important. In fact, everything that wasn't focused on propelling and furthering along the main story can actually be ignored, because it holds no bearing on the finale. One could argue that these side points help develop the characters, but I didn't see that. The characters do get significant development, I saw that, but it wasn't at these moments. No, when characters did change and show depth, it was during moments where they would have intimate interactions with one another. The dialogue exchanges and the actions that the characters perform say more about them than anything else, and are especially telling in moments that actually advance the plot. The script is incredibly well-written and well performed by the actors. Most surprising about the film for me was how funny it ended up being. There was more genuine laughter in The King's Speech than many other comedies I've seen, and I'm very grateful for that. While the plot was interesting, integrating humor into it kept my eyes transfixed upon the screen with even greater intent. Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush both do an amazing job with their roles. I wonder how difficult it is to play a stammering politician, but Firth does a great job with the role. Rush seemingly makes things way too easy, both stealing every scene he's in, while also somehow fitting in perfectly with the rest of the cast. He stands out and is noticeable, but also blends in. I'm still not quite sure how that works, but that's what happens. Helena Bonham Carter also does a good job, but in a far smaller role, not actually appearing in the film all that much. Despite not liking history much myself, films like this are incredibly enjoyable, because they focus on a single part in time, and don't try to make me learn about the history behind it. They make you feel like you are there, in the time period they are set in, and draw you in. The story is simple, but captivating, the acting is great, and you will care for the characters by the end. The King's Speech was really enjoyable, and most surprisingly, incredibly funny.

Historical narratives in cinematography are usually perceived as slow-paced if not boring, especially if focusing on events not packed with actions such as war. The King's Speech, while depicting the grey years of the declining British Empire and the unstable political climate in-between world wars, totally defies that assumption with a witty, tragic, funny and semi-realistic accounting of Queen Elizabeth II's father, George VI, and his struggle with stammering.

Colin Firth, who plays George VI, reveals once again a hidden jaw-dropping talent in providing an even stiffer image of British royalty as well as a strong representation of how being a king can be a stressful burden. For the first time, I see a film which portrays the weakness of British Royalty and the fact they are normal human beings like the rest of us. Geoffrey Rush (playing Lionel  Logue) and Helena Bonham Carter (playing a young Queen Mother) perform as brilliant support actors, bringing a lot of humour and common sense to the sad, pessimistic  times in which the story unfolds. Such eclectic mix in story-telling tried to keep the story as real as possible with some hints of dramatization that would make the story more interesting and more appealing to the wider public. The writer has been clear on this and I think awareness of the matter makes you appreciate the film even further. For the historians out there, you might find some small discrepancies from history, such as Churchillâ(TM)s alignment with George VI, the reasons of Baldwinâ(TM)s resignation, and so on. Such elements within politics can never be confirmed and we should remind ourselves the Kingâ(TM)s Speech is not a historic film or a bopic. It is the story of how man had to learn how to speak to his country, speak for the people and for what he represented to them.

Photography was simple and marvelous, with de-centered close-ups in key dialogues between George VI and Lionel Logue. The close-up showed a great part of the image as empty, as if you were expecting thought bubbles at any moment. The musical score was good and appropriate although not striking at heart; I believe most of the emotional moments come from the dialogue struggles as well as Colin Firthâ(TM)s impotency in getting his message across until the very moment where he must lead his country to war. My favourite was the stand-off between â~Bertieâ(TM) (the friendly name of George VI) and Lionel in Westminster Abbey â" you will see great resolution and also see the clash between royalty and common man.

Overall, Kingâ(TM)s Speech is an outstanding film, teaching us about key events in history but above all the important of leadership and what it means to recognise it, whether a king or not.

To quote another classic film... "The King's Speech" is practically perfect in every way. A deeply emotional film that manages to be personal, FUNNY, and beautifully filmed the whole way through. Colin Firth's performance is indeed masterful, and will go down in history as one of the best, alongside performances such as Marion Cotillard in La Vie En Rose. The King's Speech is deserving of, and will receive, a multitude of awards this awards season.

It's hard being British during awards season. Seeing British films nominated is great; seeing people win just for playing monarchs is frankly quite depressing. But unlike The Queen or Shakespeare in Love, the acclaim for The King's Speech has a lot more to it than simply baiting the Oscars. Stripped of all its ploys and generic concessions, it remains an enjoyable, well-made film that will outlive most of its competitors. 

There was a time, not so long ago, when British period dramas about royalty (and by extension the aristocracy) were very tight-lipped affairs. Merchant Ivory and their derivatives handled their stories with an emphasis on repression, creating scenes where humour was seldom tolerated and private anguish emphasised almost to the point of tedium.

What makes The King's Speech such a breath of fresh air is the complete absence of this suffocating stiff-upper-lip. The film does more than its fair share of exploring British pleasantries and social graces, but it never takes itself too seriously in doing so. David Seidler's script is closer to the work of Alan Bennett in The Madness of King George, or to some extent Julian Fellowes in Gosford Park. There is a sense of playful mischief at the heart of it which prevents the film from becoming self-important.

To this end, the moments of humour in The King's Speech are a balance between subtle one-liners for the costume crowd and more raucous elements that will pull in a mainstream audience. One cannot help but titter during George's arguments with Edward, involving the latter's attempts at "kinging" and letting Wallis Simpson sleep in their mother's suite (to which Edward remarks: "Mother's not still in the bed, is she?"). But the really laugh-out-loud moments come when George is made to swear therapeutically, delivering Anglo-Saxon vulgarisms with both reserve and abandon.

The King's Speech is at heart a character piece, carried not by its storyline but by the talent and charm of its performers. And you couldn't have picked a better cast. Colin Firth is great in the lead role, delivering a performance almost on a par with his work in A Single Man. He shrinks into the role, slurring his 'r's and staggering his gait in a deeply empathetic manner, taking us right inside the strife of a man beset not just by a speech impediment but years of insecurity brought on by his brother and his father. Not only is he a reluctant king, he is naturally withdrawing, using even the most dated traditions for much-needed support.

Geoffrey Rush is brilliant as Lionel Logue, nailing the character so early that he can be serious and well-meaning one moment and camp it up as Caliban the next. Helena Bonham Carter makes a successful return to her costume drama roots, carrying herself with just the right mixture of grace, pomposity and cheek. Elsewhere there are good supporting turns from Michael Gambon and Derek Jacobi, himself no stranger to stammers through his work on I, Claudius. But most surprising of all is Guy Pearce, who brings a real complexity to Edward VIII. The film makes no bones about his Nazi sympathies and skewed devotion to Wallis, but we really feel a lump in our throats when he is forced to decide between her and the throne.

But although the performances dominate our memory of the film, The King's Speech is a great deal more than a gallery of famous British actors talking in rooms for two hours. All accusations about the film being televisual are complete and utter balderdash. Tom Hooper is a director who excels at putting personal conflict up on screen, even behind closed doors. Through meticulous sound design and an excellent choice of camera angles, he manages to make the drama both personal and expansive. We hear every hesitation in Firth's throat, and when he can get the words out the world he is addressing stretches far beyond the four corners of the screen.

The film's ambiguous title hints at the three main issues tackled by the film beyond its conformance to generic conventions. Firstly, there is 'The King's Speech' as in 'King's English', the form of standard English against which all dialects are compared, contrasted, weighed in the balance and found wanting.

Although it doesn't touch on it in great detail, The King's Speech raises an interesting issue about how social hierarchy is ingrained even in language. The King is the head of both the imperial and the lingual family, and the hierarchy of accents below him is every bit as old-fashioned and restrictive as the insistence upon people's breeding. If the King cannot speak, then this entire system of hierarchy based on comparison threatens to collapse, putting the whole empire in jeopardy.

Secondly, 'The King's Speech' refers to the actual stutter or stammer and the various stigmas attached to it. Aside from the stammer, George VI suffered from a number of other problems, some congenital (knock knees), others nurtured (being forced to write with his right hand, despite being naturally left-handed). In his big scene, Michael Gambon (playing George V) shouts at Firth every time he stammers, demanding that he get it out of his system. This was an age where stammering was seen as something which could be cured by parental discipline rather than caused by it, and in which fear was the natural basis of a father-son relationship.

Thirdly, the title of The King's Speech refers to a momentous event, whether the state opening of Parliament, the Christmas address or in this case the declaration of war. After recording his Christmas address, Gambon complains that the invention of the wireless has reduced the monarchy to little more than actors, and later on Firth is wrestling with his exact role as King. Since he has no constitutional powers, he can only be an emblem - he speaks for the nation not as a legal representative, but as someone whose persona and moral values reflect the nation as a whole. His role as King is not just to hold ministers to account, but to feel his way through the ether for some common ground or position of national empathy.

There are a couple of faults with The King's Speech. Being a film about the triumph of the human spirit, and based on a true story, it is massively predictable. This doesn't stop us rooting for the characters, but with all the interesting ideas running alongside we can't help wishing for something more adventurous as the story winds to a close. Even if we accept the various dramatic devices which Hooper puts in place, we still have to suspend disbelief quite some way to believe that the relationship between George and Logue was as informal as depicted. And there are small inconsistencies surrounding the passage of time: as in A Beautiful Mind, many years pass but the girls don't get any older.

In the end, however, it is very easy to overlook such problems, because The King's Speech is a damn fine film. Taken purely as an actors' piece it is a delight, with a gallery of fine performances anchored by Firth who fully deserves his Oscar. Hooper's direction is intelligent and restrained, and the film never feels manipulative or melodramatic in the way that crippled Shine. While not a perfect film, it is a very fine piece of work which everyone should readily embrace.

I thoroughly enjoyed The King's Speech, which is based on the true and fascinating story of King George V and which includes a stellar cast including Geoffrey Rush, Colin Firth, Guy Pearce and Helena Bonham Carter (to name just a few).

This film portrays a man who in his own way brilliantly illustrates the successful use of strengths (especially as a way to overcome adversity)...it is about King George's attempts to overcome a disabling and distressing stammer (quite an occupational hazard if your "job" requires frequent public speaking!), which he ultimately triumphs by using his admirable courage and perseverance (two signature strengths).  

Colin Firth's performance is exquisite; his ability to show the uncertainty and fear yet underlying resolve of the King is masterful. It is heartbreakingly good. Helena Bonham Carter is also adept as Elizabeth. She nails each of her scenes with tender facial expressions capturing the love and support she has for her husband. The film also highlights the touching social intelligence and  the hope instilled by his teacher and the use of humour by many. The flick is an intelligent drama that puts flesh on the bones of historical figures.

While there are different elements to this movie, it's the special relationship between King George VI and therapist Lionel Logue that makes it most compelling. They are filled with inspiration, heart, and plenty of laughs! The only real shortfall here is that you know ultimately how it will finish - a significant, but rarely infuriating reality. And although the script is a little rough-going in spots, screenwriter David Seidler has done fine work here along with the art direction crew. This one is quite worthy of all of the awards it has won!

Generally speaking, all the films that have been raved about have always left me perplexed of their success and generally speaking were a disappointment to me. Considering I am not at all a royalist, this had all the early signs of a 2 hour bore trip at the cinema.
I have to admit that I was pleasantly surprised and was truly taken in by the story. 
Even though the movie is the dramatization of King George the V life, I loved the way the film explores the humanity, quirks, fears and failings of the main character. It is a story of a man first and then the burden of being a King later. It shouts at you "Well it isn't all it's cracked up to be!" This is why this film is universal. We have all suffered and at some point in our life had to deal with our demons, the pressure to fulfill other people expectations or simply were thrust upon us huge responsibility unexpectedly and had deal with it, and for this, I believe it is almost impossible not to feel emotionally involved!
We feel, we laugh, we get upset and cheer with "Bertie" not because he is the King but because he is a man!

What about the cast? 
Firth, Bonham Carter and Rush were superb! This film boasts three huge acting talents and to watch them in action was a joy. I can only imagine that the understanding, real respect and appreciation of one another is what created this scintillating chemistry and you need to trust me when I say it shines through the screen. 
Bonham Carter - Firth could easily pass as real life married couple. They captured the essence of married life exactly right. The dynamics were spot on! There was the complicity, deep affection and respect there, just I imagine a happily married people feel after a few years. The relationship portrayal seemed natural and believable!
Geoffrey Rush as Lionel was superb. I cannot fault his performance. Firth and Rush bounced off each other wonderfully! 
The Director Tom Hopper was able to give the movie the perfect rhythm. Just when the movie starts to drag on and maybe starts become a little flat, there are some comedic, witty and funny intervals which manage to recapture the audience attention and involve them into the story again. 
Overall I think that this film deserves to be seen, if you are not convinced about the feel good, human story, at least watch it for the opportunity to see three great interpretations. Three consumed professionals loving their craft and giving a masterclass into what acting should be about.

Directed by Tom Hooper (The Damned United), this is the amazing true story of how our last monarch became King, and how he overcame a stammer, and was able to speak publically. It's a very inspiring and warm film, with a power that holds your attention throughout. Prince Albert, Duke of York (Colin Firth) is son of son of King George V (Michael Gambon), and second in line to the throne, but he has a terrible stammer, and goes to pieces when speaking publically. In 1934, his wife Elizabeth, Duchess of York (Helena Bonham Carter) meets a maverick Australian speech therapist Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), who believes he can cure the Prince of his malady. The sessions are slow at first, and the Prince chooses to acquiesce to defeat easily, but Logue won't give in. However, when George V dies, Albert's brother (Guy Pearce) becomes Edward VIII, and is forced to abdicate after his affair with Wallis Simpson (Eve Best), and Albert becomes George VI, now the new king relies on his speech therapist more than ever, especially with a war looming in Europe. It's a powerful and inspiring film, Firth makes a good King, but Rush absolutely steals the film as Logue. It's a story that focuses on one piece of the life of George VI, but a very crucial moment in his life, and one that made him beloved.

To consider it part and parcel with 'The Social Network' would be a grave mistake, but considering that they came out in the same year and both lead the Oscar race, the similarities are unmistakable. Both feature strong scripts based on historical fact and have been perfectly edited, but the differences are just as vast.

For one, this film features some of finest acting on display in the last several years, and though I'm talking about Firth's performance as the titular king, I could just as well be speaking about the rest of the cast. What could have been a boring historical film is brought to life by Firth's protagonist, who walks, moves, and looks like British royalty, but who, through a life of shyness and taunting, has a worse speech impediment than a gaggle of Looney Tunes. The complexity of Firth's portrayal is simply astonishing, as we can watch him march around the room, lividly shouting a string of obscenities, and still see a scared little boy. In another sequence, his speech therapist has him singing to enunciate a story, but what could be comedy rends tears as he recalls an abusive nanny who used to starve him and make him cry in front of his parents, the king and queen. In another actor's hands, this would have been mere exposition, but Firth thatches this anecdote with the rest of his performance in a way that can be seen throughout the first 3/4 of the film.

Never one to step aside and let someone else take the spotlight alone, Rush is brilliant as Logue, the speech therapist who eventually manages to control the king's stammer. Again, in the hands of another actor, his role would merely be comic relief fused with an exposition tool, but Rush fills his character with sympathy that bleeds through his eyes as he tries to help and brilliantly insists upon his own methodology, allowing us to watch as he both helps and hurts the king.

Around this, Pearce is nearly unrecognizable in his performance as the first heir to the throne, Gambon comes off with effortless elegance and fury, Jacobi is reliably prestigious, and Carter is acceptably loving without being too remarkable.

Director Hooper proved he could juggle characters and actors well in his 'John Adams' series and delivers from an acting standpoint, but his directing occasionally has too much in common with his previous work; choosing to cut off character's eyelines, repeatedly show us the size of the room a character enters, and insist on handheld work where a dolly would be more appropriate are stylistic choices that do not suit every work, and this film often suffers for it. Almost everyone else behind the lens does an excellent job without distinguishing themselves. In a film like this, where the performances are God, that's not a terrible thing.

One of the first people whom I spoke with about this film before seeing it praised its watchability, and that in itself is a striking achievement; while the pompous nature of other historical films and the heady languor of most dramas would limit this to one laborious viewing, it's easy to imagine watching and loving it more and more each time.

This is a well crafted film. The King's stutter stumbles all over the King's English, until a uncommon commoner, after an entertaining tug-of-war, has him speaking in front of a microphone inspiring the nation as England enters World War II. That's the gist. There is humor, some tensions, misunderstandings, as there are in all relationships. And that's what this movie is: a relationship movie. I admit that it being a king and a commoner, instead of a struggling husband and wife, or any other ordinary couple, gives added interest to the movie.  I like that it's told in a straight forward style, which I prefer to the quick cutting, jumble of confusion, of a lot of recent films I've seen. The swan is a graceful bird, The Black Swan was not a graceful movie. It's style confused the substance, and that's lousy storytelling. The King's Speech on the other hand tells it's story plainly and well. It looks like it'll win the Oscar over The Social Network. I liked both films, but preferred The Social Network. Maybe if they rename it The Nerd Who Would Be King, it'll stand a better chance against The King's Speech.

Maybe Oscar got it right this year. The film with the most nominations is a stunning feat -- it takes a cold, ill-tempered nobleman and makes him sympathetic. This is what "The Social Network" was unable to accomplish with its similarly stunted hero. Both films are skillfully executed and extraordinarily performed -- but in the end we never really care for Zuckerberg. We do, profoundly, for King George VI.

I remember taking speech classes as a kid. I struggled to pronounce certain sounds distinctly ("r" and "w"s still give me trouble). Never being certain of how words will sound when they come out of your mouth, whether those you are intoning them to will mock you for your flaw, is an incredibly powerful and stifling self-antagonist. It's no wonder Bertie (the King, as his family calls him) has become a man withdrawn into himself. Fear has paralyzed him, and ridicule has made him cold. That he arises suddenly and unexpectedly to the throne does not help matters. Which is when he enlists the aid of the unorthodox speech therapist Lionel Logue.

And thus begins a courtship, if you will. Two men, becoming friends, both from very different backgrounds. This central relationship is rich and fascinating, made more so that the story has placed it at the center of nothing short than the outbreak of World War II. The stakes for both men are deeply personal and extremely high -- I dare say the fate of the world rests on it, but the movie makes a solid case for this argument.

Which leads me to the performance of Colin Firth. Take away Tom Hooper's flawless direction, David Seidler's keen and witty script, Danny Cohen's bravura photography, or Eve Stewart's sumptuous production design, and you're left with one of the great performances of the new millenium. Nothing Firth has done thus far could prepare you for how deeply this character infects him. The nuances of his vocal impediment, the emotion that so often is swallowed inside of him but at others comes bursting forth, the way his Bertie registers the weight of the crisis around him; recognizing that he is no longer that boy who was taunted, but a man who must rise to the occasion -- this is acting of the highest caliber. He finds the humanity in a man who doesn't seem to know what it's like to be a real human: the kind of privileged modern royalty we tend to write off as arrogant, frivolous, and impotent.

Geoffrey Rush is, per usual, brilliant, and the supporting cast is pitch perfect. A triumph of character study and cinematic entertainment, "The King's Speech" is one of those must-see films, and quite possibly the best of the year.

Simply a wonderfully acted film with a strong cast and an excellent score underneath it all. Period pieces always can be dangerous because if they don't grab you and take hold of you quickly, they lose you for good. This movie grabs you right away by jumping into the plot's main issue: the future king's stammer, at an event well before he becomes king. Watching the opening scene is difficult if only because seeing someone fail so miserably and so publicly can be hard to watch when they are trying so hard. Colin Firth is masterful as King George VI aka Bertie. The stammering is one thing to nail down as an actor, but his portrayal of the internal strife he experiences with this debilitation and how his upbringing and past memories are brought out is just plain amazing by Firth. And then to challenge him with Geoffrey Rush's Lionel Logue, the man who helped him with his speech, is just plain genius. Rush brings energy, power and simplicity all at the same time when he is on screen. And when the duo are together, it is cinema magic with some great screen writing propelling them along their linguistic journey. The banter that flows back and forth between them as they start off as adversaries (in a sense) and then become lifelong friends is superb. I also liked the director's use of framing between the two of them. In single person shots, one of them was always on the right, the other on the left or vice versa; never did the shot have them on the same side when bouncing back and forth and, not until the end, were either of them ever centered in a shot (and I am only referring to the scenes that had them together). In this typically English tale, Colin Firth plays a convincing introverted stuttering monarch-to-be.  As the next King George VI he is the British monarch with an over bearing father and stiff upper lip is unable to vocalise when the nation needs him to.

With the advancement of radio technology he is called upon to  speak to the nation through radio, expect he has a terrible nervous stammer. 

We live through his tension as he is required to lead the nation through the difficiult thirties by giving speeches on radio. 

Two supporting actors help him through this difficult phase plus two that are more of a problem.  Helena Bonham Carter is George's wife Elizabeth (the future Queen Mother).  In an understated way she is very supportive seeing him through it by finding a suitable speech therapist.  Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) is an Australian without the stifling formality.  We are taken through the pain that "Bertie" goes through to adjust to his unconventional methods.  

Bertie is caught struggling with the scandal of his brother Edward's abdication of the throne and ominous warnings from Nazi Germany and how it may impact on him.

His distant father (Michael Gambon), expects backbone and is shown to be demanding.  His wayward brother joins by mocking his stuttering.  

Firth singlehandedly demonstrates Bertie's fear and inability to speak publicly and how he recognises the importance of his friendship with Logue over the more traditional sources of advice from the church.

A traditional British film industry covering a difficult period in history, the suffocation inside the monarchy, a few fickle attempts at humour and a gentle portrait of stammering.

Britain's Lottery Dollars at Work  

As is so often the case, the history on this one is not exactly spot-on.  The woman with arguably the most stake in it, given her father is the eponymous king, has given her royal approval, though the descendants of the other main character have actually gone on record with a few of their objections.  (I'm most confused by a claim that the king can't speak German, given how soon it follows on the heels of mention of Cousin Wilhelm.)  Historians are arguing back and forth the details most moviegoers, probably including most British ones, barely even notice.  There's almost a formula for these, and it wouldn't do to have talk of appeasement, even when historically accurate, clutter the stiff-upper-lipness of the characters.  I'm sure that would cause rather more stir among those with a more vested interest.  Just as they aren't going to discuss the weird psychosexual relationship which leads to the man's becoming king in the first place.  Call it love; that's safer.

At the beginning of the story, he is not the king at all.  He is Duke of York, then as now the title given second sons in the British monarchy, and he is called Bertie (Colin Firth).  His job as a royal is to be a public figure.  It's what they do now.  As he himself later says, it's not as though the family really has any power anyway.  What he does have is a dreadful stammer.  He and his wife, Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter), have sought out just about every speech therapist in all of England, and none have worked.  Finally, it is suggested that they seek out Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), who has unconventional means but tends to get good results.  Unusually, he tries to seek out the root of what causes Bertie to stammer.  Things become rather more pressing as Bertie's father, George V (Michael Gambon), gets even worse in health.  Bertie's brother, called David by the family (Guy Pearce), is to be Edward VIII, but he would rather run off with Wallis Simpson (Eve Best), a not-quite-twice-divorced American woman.  Lionel must prepare Bertie for things no man with a stammer should face.

I must admit, I got distracted by the fact that Guy Pearce is younger than Colin Firth.  Only seven years, so a great deal less than I'd thought, but he still looks substantially younger.  This is apparently an accurate look.  In the movie, at least, Bertie is a serious, thoughtful man, one more inclined to look after what needs done.  David bursts out in frustration once that he seems forced to choose between what's best for the government and what's best for himself, and I couldn't help wondering how much thought he'd given to what was best for the people.  When his father died, he burst into tears about how Mrs. Simpson, as they persist in calling her (also Queen Wallis of Baltimore), will take it.  The discussion of how David is wrong for the throne can arguably be considered sedition, but I think everyone engaging in it knows that they are right.  They probably also have a pretty strong suspicion that David wouldn't prosecute them anyway; he'd agree with them.  He really abdicated because the woman totally dominated him, but I doubt he regretted it much.

The actual filming of the movie was quite well done.  Director Tom Hooper has won the Directors Guild of America award, and will therefore almost certainly be getting an Oscar at the end of this month.  However, he will actually deserve it.  Yes, this has the ever-present problem of prestigious British movies; the Queen is Bellatrix Lestrange, Winston Churchill is Wormtail, and George V is Dumbledore 2.0.  The Archbishop of Canterbury is Brother Cadfael.  A lot of the others were familiar out of the corner of the eye, and I have to tell you, I still call Guy Pearce "Felicia" in my head.  On the other hand, there is also one shot which reminded me how much I notice about film.  Bertie and Lionel are arguing in a foggy London park, and when Bertie has had enough, the way they are held in frame is striking.  At the end of the scene, we get a shot of each man from fairly close up with the other small and out of focus.  The set design also said a great deal about Lionel's standing at any minute, starting with that horribly battered room with the lovely windows and enormous fireplace.

In the end, though, what I took away from it was not necessarily the history lesson.  Remember, even had David not abdicated to run off with the Queen of Baltimore, Bertie still would have been in the public eye the rest of his life.  His wife and younger daughter were until 2002, when both the Queen Mum and Princess Margaret (Ramona Marquez) died; Princess and then Queen Elizabeth (Freya Wilson) obviously still is.  But Bertie's problem was different.  No matter the root causes, it plays to the average person as a disability.  We first see Bertie speaking to an entire stadium of people and on the radio to the entire Empire.  But no pressure.  Later, his father yells at him to try giving a speech and relax!  Ignore that he's being yelled at.  We see him trying to talk to his advisors after he's been made king, and the portraits of his ancestors all seem to be staring at him.  And when he speaks in front of Normal People, most of them wince away in pity.  And so Lionel Logue took the King's Shilling and did what he could.

Three thoughts on THE KING'S SPEECH:

1) Colin Firth is great, but Geoffrey Rush steals the movie. He's brilliant. And it's nice to see Helena Bonham Carter not looking like a witch or a goblin or a monster for a change.

2) It's very engaging. I had to go to the bathroom about ten minutes in, but I stayed in my seat because I was enjoying it too much. I have no doubt it's going to win a ton of Oscars. It's just that kind of movie: British, period piece, funny in the right spots and serious in the others, having some sort of physical ailment to get over. As long as you have a handicap or a stammer or write with your feet, you're pretty much guaranteed an Oscar.

3) About the historical inaccuracies which I think really swirl around King Edward VIII's depiction. I've read some things (ie Chris Hitchens) railing on how the filmmakers sugar-coated Edward's Nazi sympathies. I find that part superfluous to the story here. It's still a movie...it's entertainment, and it's a movie about a friendship between a king and a commoner working together to overcome the former's stammer. A film about a man trying to overcome a speech impediment? Can't be too good, the subject matter isn't exactly riveting is it. Well, that's what I thought before seeing The King's Speech anyhow; before witnessing a performance by Colin Firth that must put him in good stead to finally win himself the illustrious Oscar for Best Actor; before seeing Geoffrey Rush at his absolute best; and before scribe David Siedler and director Tom Hooper demonstrated that a film about a man trying to overcome a speech impediment can be bloody riveting.

Hooper is a very British director; not in the sense of where he was born, rather that he has excelled working on projects that concentrate on the majestic and regal way of life and that exclusively deal with archetypical high class British characters. He's obviously keen on period pieces - his "John Adams" and "Elizabeth I" miniseries attest to this - and he's now developed that avidness and prior experience into something very special indeed. Dramatic period pieces are often renounced as ostentatious, overly-flamboyant pictures that feature pompous, plum-mouthed characters hard to care for. When done right - hello, Elizabeth and The Young Victoria - they're anything but; they're enthralling, exciting and transcend the multi-generational gap. Hooper has achieved this with near perfection, for his recount of the Prince's battle with a stammer is unequivocally gripping from start to finish without even a hint of pretension.

At its heart The Kings Speech is a buddy flick in its finest form. The relationship between Lionel and Bertie - as the quirky Australian would call him, much to Prince Albert's dismay - is funny, sad, touching and engaging, with their friendship blossoming in a natural and compelling way. They complement each other akin to Matthau and Lemmon did in The Odd Couple; Albert uptight and apprehensive thanks to his secluded life within castle walls where the butlers and nannies counted as friends, Lionel carefree and slightly off-kilter due to his acting background. However Lionel's abrasiveness - and more specifically his determination to treat Bertie like a common person - was exactly what Albert required, and quite probably, yearned for. 

It goes without saying that the standard of acting on show is second to none. Firth has garnered critical acclaim that has many thinking he is a shoo-in for the Academy Award, and honestly, he should be. He embodies the insecure Albert with the ideal balance of strength and vulnerability, making him relatable and likeable despite his many human flaws. Rush on the other hand is an affecting delight as the idiosyncratic and often facetious Logue, investing him with such depth and charisma that should see him also nab an Oscar nom. Somewhat against type as Queen Elizabeth, Bonham Carter is marvellous as the sturdy and even-tempered constant in Albert's life, prompting thoughts that perhaps she should stray from husband Tim Burton a little more often in her career. 

The King's Speech is sumptuously photographed, powerfully acted, captivatingly scripted and brilliantly directed. Simply put: it's mesmerizing.

Without the outstanding performances of Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush, the King's Speech would certainly not have recieved as much praise as it is currently getting. They carried the film, and I wouldn't be surprised if they get Best Actor and Best Supporting Actor respectively at the Oscars. Firth portrays the repressed English man, filled with anger and frustration, as he did in Fever Pitch, extremely well, and Rush plays the caring, perseptive therapist equally well. 

The film is very gentle as a whole. There are no 'on the edge of your seat' moments, but instead a lot of slow moving character development and long stretches of dialogue. While this did help to craft such believeable and multi layered characters, there were patches in the middle of the film when I was getting a tad restless, waiting for the story to move forward more quickly. Also, the relationship between the King and his brother (played by Guy Pearce) could have been delved into further. If the rivalry and tensions between the brothers had been explored more closely, i suspect it may have been a better film, because it would have added an extra dimension to the drama.

However, despite its flat moments, this film really was all about the acting. It wasn't only Firth and Rush who were good. Helena Bonham Carter, Guy Pearce and Michael Gambon all did well with their roles as members of the royal family. An all star cast lived up to expectations and helped to make a film that certainly had many merits, even if there was still some room for improvement.

Uniformly brilliant in every way.

This is no lavish, pretentious costume drama. Historical details are made accessible; although at times liberties may be taken slightly, and the script allows for an inviting atmosphere rather than the usual boredom that comes with the subject matter. These aspects are helped by wonderfully crisp direction, assured pacing and marvellous performances.

From the outset King George VI's struggle with his stammer emerges with a full and nervous intensity. From then the film draws the conflict by pushing together the grandeur and station of royalty with the informality and humour of speech therapist Lionel Logue. Within these scenes Firth and Rush are outstanding - supported too by a slightly understated yet still brilliant Helena Bonham Carter   and the depiction of their growing friendship makes the film.

It's refreshing to see a film to no enemy; no true antagonist from which the drama and conflict derives. Instead you end up sympathising with almost every character and their personal issues; non more so than Firth's King who has duties and leadership thrust upon him and all he wants to be able to do is speak.

A wonderful feel-good film that doesn't lean on your sympathies, but draws them out quietly with intrigue along with a layered and ultimately touching lead performance. Firth deserved a Best Actor Oscar, and Rush may be the only one who can snatch the Support statuette from Bale (The Fighter).

by Ken San Nicolas

Director: Tom Hooper

Time: 1 hour and 51 minutes

Genre: Drama

Starring: Colin Firth, Geoffrey Rush, Helena Bonham Carter, Guy Pierce

We saw many brilliant movies in 2010 -- "True Grit", "Inception", "Black Swan", "The Social Network" and "The Fighter" are all worthy of high praise. However, after watching "The King's Speech" this weekend, there are two thing that I'm positive will happen when the Oscar's come around in February: 1) Colin Firth will earn the award for Best Actor 2) "The King's Speech" will win Best Picture.

The film is set during the crowning of King George VI of England. The King, also known as 'Bertie' (Colin Firth) by his family, must be the icon that his country can look up to during this tumultuous period in England's history. But Bertie has suffered from a serious speech impediment since his childhood which will clearly jeapordize his appearance to the country. He accquires the help of Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), a speech therapist with very quirky techniques. Will the King overcome his impediment and be the figure that England needs or will he stumble upon the microphone and forever be defined by his stammer?

"The King's Speech" is the culmination of a heart-warming story combined with an unexpected acting duo. While not all of us have had a speech impediment, we all can relate to having an embarassing fault that perhaps prevents us from attaining our respective goals. Seeing that with King George brings the story closer to home and gives the King a much more human appearance -- even royalty is affected by the problems that the common man must face.

The other factor that makes this film truly standout is the on-screen chemistry between Firth and Rush. Credit the dialogue or the actor's themselves -- whatever it is, they bring out the best in each other. There is such a visible difference between their characters' perceptions that each shines much brighter because of the other. The polarity between the characters helps emphasize one of the story's smaller themes as well. (The social separation between the royalty and the middle class).

 Geoffrey Rush is so strong in his supporting role that the biggest shame here is that he will probably lose the Oscar to Christian Bale for his work in "The Fighter". Nonetheless, Rush gives a powerful performance and quells any doubt about his acting prowess that may have arose from his performance in "The Warrior's Way".

But Colin Firth steals the show. It must be very difficult to sell a stammer as an actor the way Firth does. It is so believable and Firth goes even deeper into character and truly portrays the vulnerability and impatience that the impediment has on his persona. Firth does something very special with this role and deserves much praise for his work.

The Oscar's are in February and "The King's Speech" is going to win Best Picture. If you want to know what all the hype is about, catch it tonight at the Tango Theatres. It lives up to all its praise and is also a fun film filled with drama, inspiration, laughter and success. For a movie filled with so much stuttering, I find it ironic that I cannot stop talking about it.

When it comes to subject choice in movies, one of the most well-explored areas is royalty, which raises the question, do we really need another one? We've been through everything from butlers to monarchs with results varying from good to terrible. However, The King's Speech is not just another royalty flick. It stands tall among the very strongest of its genre through the strength of its script, direction and especially its performers.

The King's Speech is the story of King George VI, Bertie (Firth) to his friends, and his ascension to the throne after the death of his father (Gambon) and his brother's (Pearce) abdication. The only problem is his stammer. Bertie can barely blurt out a sentence without st-stuttering through every word. In order to overcome this impediment, his wife (Carter) enlists the help of a slightly unorthodox speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Rush). This may seem a thin premise to hang a film on, but the themes explored with admirable confidence are more than enough to fill two hours with.

The entire cast, bursting at the seams with talent, put in oscar worthy performances, with the fiery yet burdened Colin Firth incredible as the King, the demure yet commanding Helena Bonham Carter as Queen Elizabeth and the inimitable Geoffery Rush as Lionel Logue. Leading the cast is Firth whose entire career is littered with brilliant performances, and he outdoes himself yet again with a beautifully restrained, utterly human performance which you cannot help but feel for. He also pulls off some welcome flashes of humour and brings on the fire and brimstone with fantastic conviction, all the while maintaining a perfectly imperfect stammer which pervades, but never gets in the way of, his towering performance. And the chemistry which he finds with his co-star Geoffery Rush makes for one of the more believeable and exciting male partnerships in years. Rush's own performance matches Firth's in terms of subtlety and nuance as well as the same level of perfectly judged restraint, yet the two never seem at odds, finding a rhythm with each other in their slowly building friendship which is at times flat out hilarious and at others brilliantly intense. It is an breathtaking display of two top-class actors working seamlessly together. Helena Bonham Carter plays the ever-supporting Queen Elizabeth who, in the hands of a lesser actor, could have turned into a stereotype but is instead a strong, quiet character in her own right. She is able to command a room with a look but also able to guide her husband through some of the hardest days he has had to face, showing a beautiful light and shade in an entirely selfless performance. Guy Pearce, though lacking a lot of the screentime his co-stars are given, makes and incredible impact in every one of his scenes. His slimy Edward is the unofficial villain of the piece and he manages to be spitefully real at every turn. It's one of his finest performances and, in comparison to his co-stars, he barely graces the screen.

The script which all these performances hang off is a thing of beauty. It manages to combine reality and creativity seamlessly with never a moment devoid of the reality it deserves whilst never missing out on an opportunity for the humour and intensity which the film is strewn with. Unexpectedly, the film also quite a bit of abbraisive language, but the context which it's in means that even the most sensitive of viewers won't be turned off. But its greatest achievement is the very real characters it helps create and the relationships it helps to extend.

Tom Hooper nails the direction, despite the tremendous leap forward in terms of content and responsibility. His biggest venture before his latest is 2009's The Damned United, so it's quite a step up in exposure, yet he never seems to show it, taking bold risks with confidence. His use of fisheye lenses is reminiscent of Kubrick and he uses the effect sparingly and effectively. He also pushes the rule of thirds to the extreme, making for some eye-catching shots which are either genius or annoying depending on your point of view. I'm for 'genius' by the way.

But the greatest part of the movie is the tangible connection created between characters and audience and the pounding in your chest when Bertie takes the microphone or Lionel oversteps his bounds on a morning walk as every part of the film works together in a beautifully restrained piece of filmmaking.

Defining Scene:
Any scene where Colin Firth and Geoffery Rush are onscreen together. But more specifically the ending speech, conducted by Logue.

Quotes:

King George VI: I'm not... -here to discuss... -personal matters.

Colin Firth is deserving of all the praise for his portrayal of King George VI, as he not only conveys the tortured and repressed nature of a reluctant head of state, but also brings the only dramatic element to a rather predictable and low key costume drama.

It sounds harsh to criticize what appears to be, on the surface, such a triumph of the spirit film, but "The King's Speech" is, in the context of British film dramas concerning the Monarchy, more like "Rocky V" than the original "Rocky."

That original film would be, "The Madness of King George," which contains many of the same elements as "The King's Speech," but develops them into a far more interesting study of the importance of the Monarch during a period of State crisis.

It is difficult not to compare the two films, as there are so many familiarities between them: The failure of the established medical community's ability to treat the problem (with comic results); the non-establishment practitioner who demands the King be stripped of his royal standing as part of the treatment; the ensuing tension between the King and his healer; the loving and loyal royal consort; the re-establishing of the status quo and the avoidance of potential social and political chaos by the success of the King's triumph in beating the illness.

Where "The King's Speech" pales in comparison to "The Madness of King George," is that it lacks the dramatic core that lifts the central issue of the King's problem to the level of great social significance. The constitutional crisis that is portrayed in "The Madness of King George" is at the very center of the drama and fuels all of the politics and personal decisions that result: It is crucial that the British pull themselves together in order to confront the ideology that the Colonialists' revolt implies. 

In "The King's Speech," the British government's concern over Edward VIII's politics was very lightly addressed. In reality, there was serious consideration of how to bypass his accession completely. Even after his abdication, Edward, (then the Duke of Windsor), flaunted his Nazi connections across Europe and was known to have passed important state secrets to the Nazis. There is some speculation that he even passed knowledge of Allied troop deployments to Hitler resulting in the Germans altering their invasion plans of the Low Countries and France. 

The British needed a Monarch who could counter the symbolic power of Hitler and Mussolini and who could also unite a country that had experienced its own social upheavals since the end of the First World War. This was the Establishment's pressure on the reluctant George VI and he was well aware of it, but it is rather passively portrayed in the film. Instead, we are treated to more Commoner/Royal sparring and peering at each others lives ("It's 'Your Royal Highness' and then, Ma'am, like 'Ham'...").

All of the ability is there with the cast and technical ability, but in the end, "The King's Speech" chooses to turn itself into a kind of biographical guided tour rather than a powerful drama.

King George VI was a symbol of strength and unity during World War II through his radio broadcasts. What is barely discernible in the broadcasts His Majesty's profound stammer and that is thanks to Lionel Logue, his speech therapist. This friendship is the core of the movie The King's Speech.

Colin Firth plays Albert, Duke of York called affectionately by his family, Bertie. His birth name was Albert Frederick Arthur George. He couldn't be called King Albert, as that was too German, but George was his father's name and lent to itself a nice continuity. 


His wife, Elizabeth, Duchess of York (Helena Bonham Carter) found speech therapist Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) and enlisted him to help her husband with his public speaking engagements. The two did not hit it off right away. It is quite entertaining to watch. 


Albert was the second son of the King, making his brother David (Edward Albert Christian George Andrew Patrick David) first in line to the throne. David (Guy Pearce) has an active social life that includes the twice divorced Mrs. Wallis Simpson. (scandalous.)

Tom Hooper (the director) had beautiful shots in the film. It was just gorgeous to look at. Alexandre Desplat provided the music. That was truly a joy to listen to. Although there were moments where I was listening and I heard Beethoven. It through me for a loop the first time. :)

Mr. Firth gives one of the most poignant and affective performances ever by a male movie star. Where, inside himself, an actor goes for a performance like this, is beyond my comprehension. 

In the movie, "A Single Man", Colin Firth served notice that he was an actor of depth and subtlety, the surface of which he had only just begun to scratch. Now, he's more than scratched that surface. He's gouged a chasm through it. He plays the tormented, soon to be King of England, George VI, and does so in a way that very early in the movie buries his hooks in you and doesn't let go. I can not ever recall, while watching a film, having to choke back tears for over an hour and a half. The suffering portrayed by Firth as George VI is subtle at times. In your face at others. The point of The King's Speech is to illustrate the importance of having compassion for those with disabilities and how it is possible for the disabled to overcome them. This is a supremely worthwhile message that should not be overlooked or minimized. Yet it is important that such movies maintain their credibility by being accurate in their depiction of historical facts when they hold themselves out to be historical dramas. The King's Speech makes a few blunders in this regard. Moreover, it is being hailed for being a great cinematic masterpiece, and we are being told that we must accept it as such. While The King's Speech is a wonderful movie, it is not a cinematic masterpiece, and this is unfortunate given the social significance of its theme.
THE KING'S SPEECH (2010) WRITTEN BY: David Seidler DIRECTED BY: Tom Hooper FEATURING: Colin Firth, Helena Bonham Carter, Derek Jacobi, Robert Portal. and Richard Dixon GENRE: DRAMA PLOT: King George VI retains a roguish speech therapist to help him overcome his disabling stutter. COMMENTS: King George VI was good natured fellow who followed the advice of his advisors and was a popular figurehead. He was a great guy! The King's Speech is a shining example of contemporary humanism in that it is a sensitive treatment of a likable character who took great strides to overcome a very real disability, one which caused him and his family tremendous and genuine distress. The KIng's Speech is an important film because it inspires compassion and empathy for those less fortunate in their functioning. It illustrates for us just how real and distressful disabilities are, how challenging it is to have them, and how it is possible to triumph over adversity and overcome obstacles. The KIng's Speech is, despite its noble purpose and effect however, rife with historical inaccuracies, and it is a typically formulaic movie in that it is meant to manipulate our emotions and in so doing, qualify for an instant Oscar. I will forgive it for this because it serves such an important social function., I LOVE THIS MOVIE. IT IS WONDERFUL AND IMPORTANT AND COMPASSIONATE!!!! I have a few criticisms however of certain types of similarly formulaic movies in general, ones which do not teach us compassion for people with disabilities, and I shall use The King's Speech as an illustration of certain formulaic conventions. The King's Speech is well produced, but cookie-cut for an obligatory Oscar. It is tailored to stroke the masses into feeling like cinephiles for seeing it in a way that is akin to how liking actor Sidney Poitier could make otherwise socially apathetic audiences feel "cosmopolitan." This is NOT because The King's Speech is a film about disabilities, but because it is allegedly a must-see, importantly historical portrait of pivotal past events. In fact, sadly, many of the facts portrayed in the picture make it a bit insulting to historical film enthusiasts. This is a shame given the importance that the film's message not be undermined through a loss of credibility. Emotional cliches and formulaic ploys at audience manipulation abound in this plaintive appeal for an obligatory Oscar award. Yes, it's the family-friendly, warm-fuzzy, feel-good movie of the year. Unless you wish to be socially ostracized at the water cooler, you had better agree with Jeffrey Lyons and Roger Ebert that The King's Speech is not only uplifting and inspiring, but the best darn movie everyone must see since your parents flocked to watch Gandhi so they could report that they fulfilled their herd mentality, conscientious duty to society. Replete with whimsical, (and at the climax, inspirational) classical music to summon elation during cinematic moments of mounting triumph, The King's Speech is a bit of a tease because it is set amid historically compelling events in an historically interesting setting. Yet the substantial context is only the backdrop for a story that is trivial to all but the participants. In The King's Speech, King George VI employs the help of a colorful speech therapist to improve his stuttering defect in the interest of achieving greater public credibility. George VI develops a friendship with the therapist who eventually coaches him through a rhetorically significant radio address announcing England's entry into WWII. In a nutshell, that's it. That's the plot. There is some minor depiction of King Edward VIII's abdication of the throne, which in my opinion, would have been the more interesting and entertaining primary subject matter. George VI however, was not a particularly important person politically. Nor was his speech announcing Britain's entry into the war of any great consequence other than for the minor rhetorical significance of it's supposed rallying effect, though despite the cheering subjects shown in the film, these were somber times. In fact, King George's speech impediment was not a matter of particular national importance in light of his limited political role compared to Churchill's. Had he been unable to speak at all, it would have had little different historical impact. Moreover, contrary to the film's triumphant message, George VI's speech didn't improve that dramatically by the end of the film. It was much better, but still quite strained. In real life, his speeches were recorded and edited to cover up his lingering stutter. He always required Logue's assistance and this is even noted at the end of the movie. The King's Speech is a well produced, but sentimental, overly-simplified lie, rife with historical falsehoods. There are some very important inaccuracies that are quite problematic. For instance, counter to the film's portrayal, it is historically well established that King Edward VIII was a Nazi sympathizer, and George VI was privately all for Nazi appeasement. For a quick synopsis of the more significant historical revisionism, suitable for the MTV-absorbed, unread beginner, I suggest you click on this link to Christopher Hitchens article: Churchill Didn't Say That The King's Speech is riddled with gross falsifications of history, by Christopher Hitchens (LINK) The reader might also be interested in Royal Mess 'The King's Speech' is an ugly distortion of history, by Isaac Chotiner, published in The New Republic (LINK) In the meanwhile, I shall illuminate several other travesties of the record. In the film, Churchill dotes on George VI in the most unlikely situations, and denigrates his brother. In real life, Churchill did not rub elbows with George VI, nor was he a critic of Edward . In fact, he encouraged Edward VIII not to abdicate, contrary to what we see in The King's Speech. The story depicts accounts of The Nuremberg Rally and George's coronation as reported in the same newsreel. These events did not occur in close enough temporal proximity to make this likely. The King's Speech depicts Prime Minster Stanley Baldwin resigning, ashamed of and repentant for resisting rearmament. In actuality, public perception that he had a role in Britain's military unpreparedness did not occur until after the onset of WWII. At the time Baldwin retired, he was so popular that diplomat Sir Harold George Nicolson said of him, ''No man has ever left in such a blaze of affection.' (Harold Nicolson, Diaries and Letters, p. 113.) In The King's Speech, George VI mutters,"I was told that my father's last words were, 'Bertie has more guts than the rest of his brothers put together.' He couldn't say that to my face." In actuality, King George VI suffered from ill health and was described as "easily frightened and somewhat prone to tears" (Wheeler-Bennett, Sir John (1958), King George VI: His Life and Reign, New York: Macmillan, pp. 17-18.) Less importantly, Helena Bonham-Carter is perhaps a bit too curvaceous and alluring to convincingly double for the formal, conservative Elizabeth. But now I jest. In an interview, royal adviser Hugo Vickers highlighted how historical details were altered to preserve the essence of the dramatic story. The high ranking officials, for instance, would not have been present when the King made his speech, nor would Churchill have even been involved at any level, "but the average viewer knows who Churchill is; he doesn't know who Lord Halifax and Lord Hoare [sc. Sir Samuel Hoare] are." (Henley, J. "How historically accurate is the King's Speech?" www.guardian.co.uk, 9 January 2011.) Yes movie-goers. The writer, director and producers of The King's Speech have pegged you as being stupid and/or uninformed. And perhaps many of you are, based upon the fact that your collective praise for frivolous historical fairy tales in general, (i.e The Patriot [2000],Titanic [1997], etc., etc.) indicates your enthusiasm to accept revisionist history. The problem with movies playing fast and loose with the facts in the interest of profit is that they distort the way we understand the past, in the present case, for instance, the way we look at politics and understand power. This has a deleterious effect on our skepticism and thus our knowledge of how the world really works. Of course that only matters with regard to those off us who are willing to turn off MTV and put down that can of cheap beer long enough to stagger along the lonely walk to the polls on election day. In short, The King's Speech has the prima facie look and feel of one of those historical movies in which command performances give us an inside glimpse of compelling personalities who shaped the past, such as Waterloo (1970), Les enfants du siècle (1999), or even Bright Star (2008). But it isn't. Not only is the material superficial, set against a more significant backdrop, it isn't even wholly truthful. At the end of my viewing experience, I feel tricked. And so film buffs, if you don't mind being historically duped and emotionally manipulated in a cheap sort of way, by all means go see The King's Speech. The cinematography is well done, and the performances are adequate. Oh, and the message is very important. We must all learn to have compassion for those with disabilities. Those so disadvantaged are challenged and can overcome adversity with determination. We must not forget this. (All the more reason why we should not tolerate the use of film industry hype, or the presence of historical inaccuracies in movies with such a message to overshadow it.) If however, you should hunger for a more substantially impressive tale of handicapped royal triumph over adversity, dust off the BBC's 1970's era series, I Claudius. It features a much more substantial performance by Derek Jacobi than his bit part in The King's Speech, and if you aren't careful in viewing it, you might learn something of true historical value.

I had the pleasure to finally watch The King's Speech this week. I saw the trailer in theaters months ago and thought it would just be another inspirational movie. The acting was phenomenal, with sporadic surprises throughout. In addition to expecting the film to win Best Picture, I hope both Colin Firth and Geoffery Rush walk away with Oscars. I can only imagine that Firth spent months preparing for this role, as that was evident in his compelling portrayal as King George VI. Helena Bonham Carter, whom I have always felt typecast as rather peculiar (Harry Potter, Fight Club, Alice in Wonderland) has redeemed herself in my book after playing a genuinely caring and comedic take on Queen Elizabeth. I was pleasantly surprised to see Michael Gambon playing the patriarchal role of King George V. His acting has not died with his character of Dumbledore, but continues to thrive and demand respect in the British acting realm. Last, and certainly not least, Geoffery Rush beautifully executed his role as speech therapist to the King. He crafted years of experience into this role, and truly came out of the screen and into our hearts. The cast as a whole truly delivered and deserve respect and praise.

What's a fantastic film without a superb screenplay? History was blended with determination. Sympathy with redemption. Rage with comedy. From beginning to end, my eyes could not be averted from the screen. One criterion for a decent film is its ability to remain with the viewer long after the closing credits. This script gave me the peace of mind that effective narrative has not ceased to exist in film, but rather is possible to transpire with an excellent story and talented cast. All hail The King's Speech!

This art house drama stars Guy Pearce and Colin Firth as King Edward VIII and King George VI of England ruling over a country on the brink of war. Oh, and his wife Queen Elizabeth is Helena Bonham Carter and his eccentric speech therapist is played by Geoffrey Rush.

Ironically, this real-life historical drama about a royal speech impediment is the most articulate statement of the awards season thus far, speaking volumes through its amazing performances and captivating story. It helps that a gifted visionary gave the true events such a forthright voice. Though director Tom Hooper's (2009's The Damned United) name wasn't previously known to many American audiences, his latest project should be considered kingly filmmaking on either side of the Atlantic. Working from a brilliant screenplay by David Seidler, Hooper captures an important moment in history with a meticulous eye for consistency of character. Perhaps, it is not a spot-on historical recreation, but the film's voices certainly ring true.

After his brother's (Guy Pearce) abdication, Britain's King George VI (Firth) seeks the help of a radical therapist (Rush) to overcome a harrowing speech impediment to lead his nation through WWII in the R-rated historical drama The King's Speech.

Chalk it up to the Pearce factor. The talented actor seems to be a lucky rabbit's foot, starring (LA Confidential, Memento, The Proposition) or doing supporting work in (The Hurt Locker) some of this reviewer's favorite films of the last 20 years. He, Rush and Helena Bonham Carter (as the queen-to-be) give remarkable depth to their historical counterparts. The King's Speech, however, would be a stammering mess without Firth's awe-strikingly gripping turn. Capturing humor, wrath, warmth and resolve and in one fell swoop, the actor gives filmgoers nothing less than the absolute truth ... a true performance WITH a dead-on stutter to boot, that is. 

Bottom line: Worth a king's ransom.

I know this movie is currently the golden child of the Academy Awards, and Colin Firth's performance definitely deserves the Best Actor nomination, but I have to say it wasn't as amazing as I had hoped. And maybe that is why it didn't really resonate with me- it was exactly what I assumed it would be.  A well-done movie with all the cleverness you expect from a good British film, and delivering an ultimate message about over-coming adversity. Yet instead of being absorbed into the story, I felt I couldn't break away from appreciating it from purely a technical standpoint.  When I watch a good movie, I get lost in it, and love that feeling.  There was no getting lost in this movie, but a constant awareness that I was watching Colin Firth and everyone else do a good job with a good script, and that was all.  Still, I do hope Colin Firth wins for Best Actor.  And, speaking of which, why aren't people going on about Geoffrey Rush's performance??  I thought it was just as exceptional as Firth's, and I feel like he is being unfairly overlooked. (which just goes to show the ridiculous politics of the Academy Awards.  But I will restrain myself on that topic.)  In summary, The King's Speech is a well-done and uplifting movie driven by top-notch performances, but still somehow lacking the connection and punch to, in my opinion, make it truly superb.  Nevertheless, it's worth your time.

There are many jewels left from December (and November) scattered across the garbage that's been heaping up within January and February, and The King's Speech shines the most. The film, following the tale of how King George VI got beyond his stammering issue to take his rightful place as the voice of England, mostly benefits from some of the best performances I've seen in a long time. Everyone loves to see elegant performances out of a film taking place in 1920s England, but The King's Speech manages to go even beyond that. There are many people out there who are forced into stammering due to some disability, but for an actor to stammer on purpose in order to fit into his character and make it come off as natural is the accomplishment of the century, and Colin Firth pulls it off perfectly. I also love Geoffrey Rush's performance as George's doctor attempting to pull him out of this stammering state through strange and over-the-top, yet surprisingly effective methods. His performance is greatly elegant, yet strangely goofy at the same time.

On the whole, if you haven't seen The King's Speech yet, be sure to check it out while it's still in theaters, as it's definitely worth the ten bucks you put into seeing it.

The King's Speech has been nominated for twelve Academy Awards this season and is worthy of every one. I really enjoyed this film.  It's brilliant, delightful, remarkable, and any other hyperbole you might want to throw into the adjective casserole.  I'd even say it's compelling.  I've heard reports of many people saying they've connected with Prince Albert's struggle as it parallels some barrier in their lives.  That's the power of storytelling.  That's mainly why I love film.  Personally, I just didn't feel that way about this one.  I loved his journey and his internal battles and the story it told -- and the fact that it's all true -- but I didn't find any attachment to his character.

I think ultimately what makes this movie great to me in spite of my complaints is that it's so much more than just what is shown on screen.  There's a larger story at play.  There's a man who has greatness inside him but a severe impediment that restricts his ability to fulfill his passions.  Its significance is only enhanced by a world at war and a nation in need of leadership.  When I think about this movie and all that is surrounding the story of a man with a stammer, I like it even more.

Akin to Firth's Oscar-worthy performance is Geoffrey Rush as Lionel Logue, the King's speech therapist.  Without his role and delivery Firth would not have the nomination he has.  Their relationship is the best part of The King's Speech and there are countless memorable exchanges between these two that range from funny to poignant and sometimes both at the same time.

While it can seem a bit slow in the middle as the momentum starts to sag, it's probably more appropriate to deem this pace "deliberate" rather than lethargic.  Overall, it's an amazing film that deserves all the credit it will continue to receive.  My only hope was that I had felt more from the story and that it had relied less on its restrained and cerebral style.  As I've said before, great film doesn't just tell me what to think about what I'm seeing, it tells me what to feel.

The total concentration on George VI's stammer relegated the abdication crisis and the onset of WWII to "little local difficulties", rather than the huge challenges they offered to George VI, precisely because of his speech impediment.  And, according to the Internet Movie Database (imdb.com) Logue never swore in front of George and never called him "Bertie". Some historical leeway must be allowed, as it is not a documentary, but the film made a "big deal" of Logue calling the king "Bertie" which, if untrue, unbalances the relationship.

The strength of this film is undoubtedly in the quality of the acting throughout. Some of the casting surprised me: Mike from Neighbours as King Edward VIII, the little girl from Outnumbered as a young Princess Margaret, and Timothy Spall as Winston Churchill! They are all very good, but Geoffrey Rush and Colin Firth are tremendous, with Firth particularly deserving all the plaudits sent his way. The screenplay may take some liberties with the truth but a little artistic licence shouldn't stop people from appreciating what a good film this is.

Firstly, I find it reprehensible that this movie should get 12 Oscar nominations.  I cannot rationalize such outstanding recognition, because The King's Speech is not outstanding at all.  It's been engineered for the kind of accolades it's been receiving (Royalty!  Nazis!), and it operates on one single emotion, being a muted joy.  This is one half of director Tom Hooper's faults, the other being his irking, almost grotesque aesthetic, a troubling mixture of Wes Anderson and the Coen brothers that rarely works.  It plays its Oscar bait so carefully that there is really only one risk present (and, consequently, only one payoff), being Colin Firth's lead performance.  He lends his fragility and his sophistication to the role with great skill, but he's done much better (A Single Man), and it's actually a very technical role with all its stammerings and awkward deliveries, rather than one with great depth or emotion.  Not to say that it's less than commendable.  But it doesn't save The King's Speech from being horribly transparent in its charity to the audience; if anything, it makes it watchable.

Or is it about the speech itself, given at the outburst of the Second World War, and the story that leads up to it? Any of these three topics could have given a consistent movie, but the film dangles between the three, each in turn, and ends up having no actual story thread that is gripping. The film starts by showing that Colin Firth, the second son of King George V, future King George VI, stammers, and canâ(TM)t speak to a public audience. For one, you know that by the end of the film he will deliver the all important speech, so there is no surprise, no drama, nor climax.
