So I finally got around to seeing The King's Speech.  My thoughts, I was very surprised.  It was a great movie, one of the years best, and not at all boring like I thought it would be, but is it really at all deserving of the praise it's been getting as being as good or better as The Social Network?  Not at all.  If you've read an overload of King's Speech reviews lately like I have stop now and thanks for reading, if not here we go.

I think everybody knows the plot by now.  The Duke of York, and later on King George VI has a lot of trouble giving speeches.  He stutters and can barely get through them without people leaving.  His wife hires an odd speech therapist to help him.

On paper, this plot looks stupid.  Even in the movie the plot is pretty stupid.  In all honesty I can't believe studios agreed to make a movie based on this.  The screenplay however is excellent.  It's not very unique but the dialogue is great and ives the writers something worth praise.  In the end I still think the plot is stupid but it's the great characters and sub plots that make it worthwile.

Colin Firth plays King George VI, aka Bertie, and I think everybody is aware that he is amazing in it.  Bertie is a very interesting guy.  When you start learning about stutters you start realizing that they are all psychological, and that really makes you wonder why he has one.  How could someone in the royal family, the most powerful in the world, be so traumatized and unhappy that he stutters.  It's also interesting that he stutters more around certain people really helps you understand his relationship with them.  Geoffery Rush plays Lionel, the speech therapist and he's my favourite character.  He's quirky and weird, but he brings the otherwise tragic movie it's lighter moments and his pure dedication makes you like him.  He's willing to defy the law, defy the order of the king, and the order of the church just to make the king stop stuttering.  Rush does an amazing job with him and I think he gives the more under appreciated of the two performances, but then again when you've got Colin Firth opposite you it's hard to get the attention.  Helena Bonham Carter plays Queen Elizabeth I, which is out of character for her but she still does a goodjob.  I don't really understand why she is getting so much praise for this movie.  She's barely in it and barely has anything to say.  I don't even think supporting role could define it.  There are several other great performances, especially from Guy Pearce and whoever was playing a spot on Winston Churchill that really make this movie great.

As I mentioned the movie has some great little subplots going on.  The whole story of Bertie's brother, and later the king, falling in love with a two times divorced everywomen and leaving his post for her was great. I remember learning about this in school but there it was prtrayed as a happy, romantic occasion.  Here I see that he was actually just an asshole who no one respected.

The movie is also, like most biopics, very interesting.  It's just little facts that make it so great.  I find it incredibly fascinating how because no one had television at the time, The King could walk the streets and be left alone because no one realized what he looked like.

If there is anything I really have against this movie is that it takes a really boring approach technically.  The music is dull and sounds very stock.  The camerwork is also very average.  There are a few interesting shots, particularly the ones of The King looking at people through the radio microphone, but in general it doesn't take any risks.  The direction as a whole from Tom Hooper is pretty average. A movie about a self-employed speech therapist helping a to-be King overcome his impediment may not sound like much at a glance, but, largely thanks to solid performances from the likes of Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush supported by a strong plot and plenty of factual historical research, this is definitely going to be a difficult film for other directors to contend with in 2011. Dashes of humour and sprinklings of suspense and expectation complete the recipe to this wonderfully-written and fantastically-performed drama, which truly demonstrates how even the most powerful of monarchs can be brought crashing down to reality by the most common of problems. In spite of the fictional importance of the lead character, one feels sympathetic for King George VI on a somewhat personal level, and largely thanks to this fact, viewers will walk out as the credits begin to roll with a new and more optimistic perspective on persevering to achieve your goals. It takes a lot to pull of a two-hour movie which manages to keep the audience's interests while being both inspirational and humorous at the same time, but director Tom Hooper nailed it perfectly. The only possible downside I can possibly think of is the unexpected burst of swearing mid-way through, which may deter younger audiences or parents thereof.

"My dear dear man" utters Helena Bonham Carter's character to Colin Firth's King George VI in a scene where a stately regal man is reduced to a hapless sack of nerves. This scene perfectly embodies Firth's exquisite humanizing portrayal that endeared himself to the audience and is most like the tour de force drive in garnering this movie it's very well deserved 12 Academy nominations.  Who amongst any of us cannot identify with having to display our most embarrassing and thus closely guarded personal Achilles heel to the public? - In this case, a speech impediment, which must be overcome against a ticking clock as the monarchy fights to stay relevant in the face of modernization and to the inevitable terror that is Hitler.  Yes, I shuddered and shirked along with Firth at every speech broadcast opportunity, at the mention of mental and psychological during his childhood, and even when he was still being berated as an adult by both his father and older brother.  

The cast of Rush, Bonham Carter and Pearce were all strong, but the triumph of "The King's Speech" belongs entirely to Firth. The script most likely won't appeal to a contemporary audience that prefers action with the typically formulaic ingredients of things getting blown up with a scantily clad Megan Fox running around, but this period piece was incredibly very well done taking it's time to develop the characters along a very familiar historical backdrop for a very satisfying full bodied cinematic viewing experience.

"Courage is the first of human qualities because it is the quality that guarantees all the others." Winston Churchill so eloquently said this in sometime before the Nazi's stormed halfway across the Europe. In "The King's Speech" we're brought back into that time, where England is on the brink of war and the king's thrown in a state of precariousness. While Churchill's character has just a minor role in this film; his message of courage is powerfully conveyed. 

This is a film about courage,  leadership, inspiration and friendships of the most unlikely kind. Tom Hooper's powerful and elegant take on King George's (Colin Firth) tumultuous battle to overcome a dreaded stammer that he's fought for as long as he can remember is just about as inspirational and as heart-warming as films get. Set in the gravest and most timorous of times when Britain is on the brink of going to war with Hitler's Germany, it is up to George - who reluctantly assumes the thrown after his brother abdicated - to unite and inspire the country by delivering a critical speech.With the help of an unorthodox speech therapist named Lionel, George slowly but surely improves his articulation while at the same time forming a unique friendship with the man. But when it comes time to deliver the most important speech of his life, factors that trigger the stammer such as nerves, anxiety and emotional stress get in the way. 

Colin Firth is magnificent in the role of a lifetime as the short-tempered, warm hearted, sympathetic King and Geoffrey Rush is equally brilliant as his amiable speech therapist, Lionel. Lionel challenges George in ways George isn't accustomed to and it takes him some time to warm up to Lionel's personal and unconventional approach. In the end it's Lionel's desposition to dare George to be great that leads us to the climatic final speech. In it you'll find yourself wanting to guide George through the speech and cheering for him as he says each word. Helena Bonham Carter is superb as his supporting wife a film that is beautifully directed and has received twelve well deserved Oscar Nominations. 

This movie is a must see. You will be moved. This is not merely a movie about a king's strife with his speech impediment. It's a film about the bond of friendship and grace and discovering the unexpected gifts each of us have to offer if just given the chance.

It was the late 1930's. Europe was on the brink of all out war. Adolph Hitler, Germany's charismatic, highly influential leader was pushing his powers to the limits and only a few nations were going to push back.

"The King's Speech" is the story of how King George VI (Oscar front runner Colin Firth), "Bertie" as he was known to his closest family members, ascended to the thrown in an unorthodox way and became the voice of his nation during the long, dark years of World War II.

"The King's Speech" focuses on how "Bertie" needs to overcome a speech stammer that has completely derailed his ability to make public speeches. Queen Elizabeth (current Queen's mum, played by Helena Bonham Carter) goes to several speech therapists before being directed to seek the help of Lionel Logue, played to brilliant perfection by one of my favorite screen actors, Geoffrey Rush.

King George VI has quite a temper and finds that he and Lionel have a friction that is immediate upon  their first meeting. Lionel has unusual methods that he brings to his craft while "Bertie" is a stickler for what is considered "proper". "Bertie" wants nothing to do with delving into his private life and he finds it beyond irritating that Lionel insists on calling him "Bertie" which is a name only close royal family members ever use.

However, it is in this friction, in these unusual methods where "Bertie" finds the most success.

When King George V dies, Bertie's older brother Edward (Guy Pearce) takes over as Edward VIII. However, Edward is a hopeless romantic who has fallen in love with a divorced American woman who is currently going through her second divorce when Edward proposes marriage. This type of scandal is too much for a King so Edward abdicates the thrown so he can marry his American divorcee thus relinquishing the throne to his brother Albert who becomes King George VI.

There is so much depth to this story that really gives this film layers of drama so deep that if it was a pool, you could safely dive in head first. The great thing about the script is that it blends perfectly timed humor into the rich, juicy story.

On top of all of this is a cast filled with unending talent including Michael Gambon as King George V and Timothy Spall as Winston Churchill among many others.

All in all, a brilliant period piece focusing on one of the most importantly periods of time in the past half century. "The King's Speech" is the best film I have seen this year.

The King's Speech delivers on every level.  It tells the fantastic true story of King George VI, the father of the current Queen Elizabeth, and his unlikely rise to power.  The greatest struggle he faces isn't the daily duties or responsibilities of being King as most would think.  In fact he seems to be quite politically gifted with his mind.  His problem is with day to day speech and even more so, public speaking.  Prince Albert suffers from a stutter that, as we learn in the opening scene, immensely hinders his ability to communicate with the people around him, a chore that is very important for a king.  Upon learning that his father is most likely on his death bed and that his brother is perusing around with a woman who is twice-divorced he decides, or rather his wife does, that he needs to nip this speech thing in the bud before the throne is thrust upon him.  They seek the services of many speech therapists that all fail.  Finally they give their last fleeting efforts to a Lionel Logue, played beautifully by Geoffrey Rush.  Through his stubborn yet effective methods Prince Albert and Logue form an unlikely friendship and help battle his stutter, culminating when he must take the throne due to his brother's abdication.

This film is honestly surprisingly nice.  The acting and scenery are truly beautiful and the writing is wonderfully written to draw the audience into the frustration that the prince is feeling as well as letting us laugh quite often.  The chemistry between Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush is magnificence and their personas on screen play off of each other so well that the audience is left almost feeling they're watching a bro-mance rather than the story of a king's rise to power.  Some might think that having to listen to someone stutter for a whole movie could get very tiresome and most likely annoying.  However, Firth accompanied by the wonderful writing do a great job of making the character feel real and the while the stutter might hinder the prince on screen it doesn't hinder Firth's performance.  They are also joined on screen in an unusual role by the always wonderful Helena Bonham Carter.  She is one of my favorite actresses out there right now and normally plays a darker role than this but she plays Queen Elizabeth beautifully.

As mentioned previously the scenery is magnificent as we are shown the contrasting backdrops of the pristine palaces of the monarchy followed by the dirtier grittier street view of the life Logue lives.  We see sprawling rooms filled with art and majestic cathedrals, and then we are taken into a small office building with an elevator big enough for one fitting two members of royalty rather uncomfortably or a small apartment with dusty chairs.  It's a very humbling sight for both the audience as well as the figures on screen.

As stated before, this film comes off as a film that is very nice.  It's not grand in its scope, as a film about royalty could easily be, and the acting and writing is neither too gritty nor too strong.  It's a fun ride and surprisingly hilarious.  I went and saw this with my mother and felt no apprehension to do so either before or after so you can consider it a good family film (aside from a little cursing).  I highly recommend it if you are looking for a good-feeling film that you can laugh at without fear of facing the anything too painful in any sense.

There's something about this crowd-pleasing character driven drama that leaves one feeling satisfied, but ultimately empty. It's an interesting true tale, brought to the screen by Tom Hooper and released at just the right time to conveniently sweep through awards season. In all fairness, this is a pleasant enough visit that begins during 1925 era England and ends on the brink of a world war in 1939. It's a period piece of a time that wasn't too long ago, but largely ignores the political and social problems of a country struggling to recover from one world war moments before being plunged into another. Instead, the focus is on the royal family and the responsibilities that come with the throne. In examining a higher class of life, Hooper conveniently sidesteps any contemporarily relatable challenging content to instead focus on award-baiting issues such as disability and friendship. Admittedly this film is very successful at achieving what it sets out to do - which is to provide a nice movie experience that will undoubtedly please an older generation who perhaps don't wish for intellectually stimulating cinema.

'The King's Speech (Hooper, 2010)' introduces us to Prince Albert, Duke of York (Colin Firth) who is second in line to the throne. Despite his father King George V (Michael Gambon) falling ill, the throne is succeeded by his elder brother and Prince Albert is quietly confident that he will never have to take on the responsibilty of kinging. He has a fear of such duty for he suffers from a stammer, and in a world where radio is becoming the primary form of communication, good diction is expected from the country's leaders.

Upon the death of King George V, Prince Albert's brother is crowned King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce) - but struggles with the responsibility. His new-found love is a married woman who is already a divorcÃ (C)e, and is planning to divorce again in order to marry the newly crowned King. Yet the church will not stand for such a marriage, forcing King Edward VIII to step down and hand the role to his younger brother.

The majority of the film deals with Prince Albert trying to overcome his stammer, helped by an Australian speech therapist named Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). His methods are unusual but successful, and slowly the two bond. It's this unlikely friendship that forms the heart of the story, with the more dramatic plot points deriving from arguments between the two moreso than Hitler's marching army.

The screen truly does sparkle whenever Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush share the scene, which thankfully makes up most of the film. Firth especially deserves praise for his pained performance, which the film heavily relies upon. However, the glimpses into the life of the royals and the minor detour into the religious nonsense drags, with 'The King's Speech' dangerously teetering over boring territory at times. Thankfully Firth's performance keeps the proceedings on the right side of entertaining, but there are moments when one longs for Rush to return to the screen. The political aspect is also undercooked, with Timothy Spall delivering a truly woeful Churchill impersonation.

There are moments when the film feels terribly over-directed, with the cinematography thinking it's being clever when really it's distracting and soon becomes grating. It's a simple story, and it requires a simple method of being told. Despite this, 'The King's Speech' is an enjoyable enough movie, and despite predictability creeping into the conclusion it is a fascinating story. Astutely aware of its target audience, it hits the right notes at the right points and is a satisfying piece of cinema - although it would be quite forgettable if it wasn't for a stellar performance from Colin Firth.

Aside from the terrific work on the cinematography and overall mise-en-scene , "The King's Speech" also worked perfectly both as a period drama(which portrayed the stirring anxiety of late 30's England about to collide head-on with the Second World War), and as a dynamic display of acting talents, particularly Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush, whose exchanges, ranging from the most subtle to the most intense, overwhelm the visual scope of the whole film. 

Yes, it is about a piece of royal history, which of course is impossible to tell without wallowing a bit into the majestic and exquisite corners of the Buckingham Palace or the Westminster Abbey. Or touching a bit of Winston Churchill's presence(even though how insignificant he may be in the story). But beyond the external intricacies of the film's palaces and chambers is a humble story of human connection developed not by cinematic twists of fate, but by a verbal stammer under royal pressure. We get acquainted with the stuttering Duke and soon to be crowned King George VI(Colin Firth) with his initial embarrassment as he failed to properly deliver a speech in front of a crowd. His wife(a surprisingly radiant Helena Bonham Carter) then brought him to an unorthodox speech therapist Lionel Logue(Geoffrey Rush), whose peculiar personality initially clashed with the Duke's, but then soon evolved into a brotherly bond. 

I admired how the film looked upon the story with little intent on politics but more on the emotional atmosphere surrounding the monarchy itself: the prime minister's relationship with the royal family, the painstaking process of kingship, the pressure of being an heir to the throne, and finally, the most significant of all, the angst-laden anticipation and last minute rehearsals of delivering a speech on radio broadcast, which of course would mean the 'whole' of England.

All of us have unexplainable jitters towards speaking in front of many people. And with that, although how far up King George VI's social status is compared to humble viewers like us, we can connect with him, and at certain points of our lives, we ARE him. Different situations, but similar difficulty with enunciation.

His stammering could have easily served his head on a platter to his critics for endless bashing and one-sided scrutinies, but with the help of Logue's masterful effort gathered through experience and a firm belief that King George VI(or 'Bertie', as he preferred), amidst his outer imperfections, can be an able King, he inherited the throne prepared. Not just with how the way he talks, but also how he may think and feel.

And evidently, as he looked upon a footage of Hitler roaring with his Aryan speeches(ironic considering how brilliant a speaker Hitler was and how frail King George VI's ability to do so really is), he gathered his senses and stared at the Fuhrer with indifferent confidence; he is indeed quite ready.

The King's Speech is a sometimes corny, but emotionally rousing account of King George VI struggle with oratory. Colin Firth stars in the title role, giving an incredible performance as the stuttering Duke. Faced with the prospect of becoming King, George goes to an Australian speech therapist, Lionel, played by Geoffrey Rush. Together they work to both master the mechanics and the fears of a King, who is very uncomfortable in his new clothing. 
          This could have very well turned into an emotionally distant piece of Oscar bait, but most of the time that trap is avoided. Though it does unfortunately indulge in some moments of corn-ball self-importance, the film does sustain a strong emotional connection to George. 
             Director Tom Hooper (John Adams, The Damn United) has shown himself to be a master at getting at the heart of those in power. At examining the faults and triumphs of mythic figures in history. Hooper makes it clear that even though the King's troubles are very specific, stuttering is simply a stand-in for all the fears and insecurities of man. It is not just the examination of one man, but of the human condition. 
    The film works on that basis, and on the strength of it's performances. Neither Firth, Rush or Helena Bonham Carter make a single misstep in their roles. The film is beautifully and shot and crafted by Hooper, and he has simply made the best movie he could with the trappings of prestige and yearnings for attention at award time.

King George VI waged war with Germany. But before that, he was an inveterate stammerer. How he overcomes that is what the film is about. Hence, "The King's Speech." The King's a fragile person who shies away from people. There's a connection between that and his stammering. He doesn't stammer when he talks to himself or his family but when he's out there in front of people, he's conscious of what he says. As far as he can remember, he's been stammering.

At the age of four, some incident sparked his stammering. That incident is mentioned in passing and so is the world war. The film keeps these issues at arm's length and refuses to stray away from The King's Speech. His haranguing father is on his death bed and someone has to succeed him. His inability to live up to his father's expectations has made him want to be left alone. However, when his elder brother intends to marry a divorcee, (who acquired certain skills at an establishment in Shanghai), the throne becomes his to lose. Even his father had remarked, "When I'm dead, your brother will ruin himself, this family and this nation, within twelve months. Who's going to pick up the pieces?" The expectations pile on and he cries, "I'm not a King." Destiny however places the crown on his head and with it comes the royal responsibility of addressing the nation.

Colin Firth is both subtle and over-the-top in playing King George VI. The character is real but it is just one dimension of him that we're shown. Who would've expected to see the freak in Fight Club and Sweeney Todd, portray British highness with grace? Here, Helena Bonham Carter breaks stereotype. Just as her character, Queen Elizabeth stands by the King, Carter supports the film. Not entirely of course. There's Geoffrey Rush playing Lionel Logue, the unorthodox and controversial speech therapist. Logue has no diploma, no qualifications, and no credentials; yet he's a man with his head on his shoulders. Haven given people faith in their voices, he's mighty sure of his work and himself. Rush shines in the role and the scenes where he and Firth indulge in verbal sparring are a pleasure to watch.

David Seidler, (who probably used a lot of his own diary entries for research) a cured stutterer himself, gives heart to the film by laying the foundations with his slick screenplay, one filled with British banter.

The cinematography is beyond functional. It isn't just beautifully shot; it is effective enough to make the microphone look vicious and overbearing. There're wide angle and low angle shots capturing the audience who're actually at a lower plane but appear to be towering the King. As the last few long shots are shown minutes before The King's Speech, it is you who's going to feel the tension mounting with every "Good luck, your Majesty."

Every scene resonates with royalty thanks to the sublime direction of Tom Hooper, a master of his craft. Unlike its Oscar rival 'The Social Network', it may not stand the test of time; but for what the film is, it's flawless. The King's Speech is an inspiring, heartfelt film that is relatable to anybody wanting to be a somebody.

Rating - 10/10

It takes leadership to conquer a nation's fear. It takes friendship to conquer your own. Usually, a film regarding war and leadership involves a very grand story that reflects the impact of the situation in a wide scope. To mention a few, we have Saving Private Ryan, Gladiator, Braveheart and The Patriot. The King's Speech is a very different one. It is indeed a very difficult task for a ruler to suppress fear among his people. But how can you save others when you can't even save yourself? This is what The King's Speech is mainly about. When it comes to the screenplay, direction and cinematography, The King's Speech is surely over the top. However, the acting is something much more. Geoffrey Rush, Helena Bonham Carter and Colin Firth were all magnificent. I don't really think that everybody can portray their characters. I find their roles requiring perfection and classiness. And these three were flawless. At first, I thought of giving it five stars. However, the delivery of the speech made me change my mind. The speech was really powerful and moving but our lead just read it while trying his best not to stammer. He didn't feel it. All he cared about is that he wanted to finish the speech without too much stutter. What I treasure the most about this is how his friend never gave up on him when he himself already surrendered.

I FINALLY got a chance to see this the other day.

What can I say? I LIKED IT... but I didn't love it. I enjoyed watching it, but I don't think it deserves the excessive amount of hype it has gotten. Would I watch it again? Maybe once. Who knows, it might get better with a second viewing.

This type of story has been overdone, but I wouldn't necessarily hold it against the film. It was very well told. Despite this, the movie did not draw me in to the degree it was trying to. It was trying a little bit too hard to be inspirational, and moving, and whatever else films like this tend to be. I did not feel attached to the characters. That's not to say I couldn't relate to them. It's more that I didn't care as much about them as I should have. In addition, at times I thought it didn't take itself serious enough. I'm not saying I wanted the entire film to be deathly serious, I'm just saying that it veered beyond being merely comedic and into outright goofiness. Just watch the trailer and you'll see what I mean. 

The direction is what annoyed me the most about this film. Tom Hooper has some weird obsession with pushing the characters to the sides of the frame, and I don't understand why. He did it so much it became seriously distracting. At other times I felt like he was just showing off. There was one shot that very much stood out though. It honestly didn't even look like something you could pull off with a conventional camera.

By this point it sounds like I did NOT like the film, even though I already said I did. I merely find it more enjoyable to speak about the negative aspects. Let me try to be more positive.

Like I said, I loved the story of one man's struggle to overcome his disability. That is, with the help of his working class, quirky, and eccentric buddy, whom he does not trust at first, and slowly becomes closer to as the film progresses. Yes, stories such as this have been done many times, but it was executed well enough that I did not care. In my opinion, it's a story worth being told again and again.

I loved the score. I'd say it's one of the top five best scores of 2010. I say that because I generally don't even remember the music from a movie. In fact, the only films I saw in 2010 that I remember the music in even the slightest bit were Inception and How to Train Your Dragon. (I haven't seen TRON, nor do I want to, so don't whine to me about not mentioning its soundtrack)

Colin Firth is an acting powerhouse. More than anything else, he is what made the movie. If they had a lesser actor playing King George VI I guarantee that the film would not have held up nearly as well. Give him the Oscar, he definitely deserves it. The rest of the cast was great. Geoffrey Rush was awesome as always. The only person I wasn't impressed with was Helena Bonham Carter. I thought her character was bland, but that wasn't necessarily her fault. She didn't have that much to work with.

Overall, I'm still rooting for The Social Network to win the Oscar. It's definitely my favorite film of 2010. Seeing Black Swan take home the gold would be awesome too, but that DEFINITELY won't happen.

Oscar season has officially begun and January sees the release of a slew of potential award winners: 127 Hours, Black Swan, and True Grit among them. January is the month where cinemagoers, if they want to keep their finger on the pulse, start camping out at local multiplexes and learning how to pitch a tent on carpet.

The King's Speech is a certain contender to the Oscar throne, riding on the triumphal performances of its three leads. Leading the pack is Colin Firth in the role of King George VI, whose crippling stammer made every one of his public speeches just a tad embarrassing. A story of a man/woman overcoming a disability is already a well-worn Oscar path, plus in this case it chiefly involves watching Firth stutter for two hours, which isn't the most exciting of afflictions. However, he approaches the character with a real humanity; he is not the angelic tragic hero, but is flawed and ever so real.

Geoffrey Rush acts as his perfect counter part as the brash Antipodean speech therapist Lionel Logue. His disinterest in social protocol, although jarring to George at first, eventually allows the two men to nurture a deep friendship. The third element comes in the form of George's wife, and the late Queen Mother, Elizabeth, played by Helena Bonham Carter. Deftly dancing the line between aristocrat and caricature, Bonham Carter puts in a terrifically endearing performance as the loving, supporting wife. Plus, it's nice to what she looks like when she's not in one of her husband's films, following Johnny Depp around and covered in weird face paint.

However, don't make the mistake of believing that this is an actor's movie, just a stale but gorgeous frame for theatre luvvies to prance around within and pick up their Oscar on the closing credits. This is no ordinary period drama. The King's Speech has a beautifully modern grasp of cinematography; director Tom Hooper avoids endlessly panning across English gardens and country houses like they've never been shown on film before and denies the viewer the flurry of furs and dresses they are so used to. Instead the masterful use of focus and extreme close-ups assure us that this is very much a raw, human drama. Prepare to be practically engulfed by Colin Firth's face on numerous occasions as Hooper zooms in on George's every expression, as he struggles through his public speeches.

What is particularly interesting about the King's Speech is the angle it chooses to take on such a critical moment in the history of the monarchy, the abdication of King Edward VIII. It would have been far too easy to have told Edward's own story: his rejection of the monarchy to marry the twice-divorced American heiress Wallis Simpson. A man must choose between love and duty and of course, after many impassioned exchanges and staring out of windows into the rain, love wins. But instead, The King's Speech is brave enough in its originality to reject the easy route and to make such a dramatic event a side plot, important only in its effect on George's own character. Even more fearless is Guy Pearce's portrayal of Edward as a rather un-likeable arsehole. He is played as the spoilt older brother rather than the tragic hero, his motive seemingly driven more by a simple desire to get his own way, with love having only a minor role to play.

The King's Speech is a royal triumph, where powerhouse acting meets history through fresh eyes and beautifully-produced visuals. A must-see.

The moving story about King George VI and his struggle to overcome stuttering. Deftly written by David Seidler, once a stutterer himself, this movie brings on full emotion to the screen.

At a time when bringing the people of their kingdom together, united against the threat of Nazi propagation throughout Europe, the British Royal Family finds itself in a succession crisis when King George V died and Prince Edward, a socialite, is assigned the throne, clearly not wanting much to do with it. Due to Royal protocol, King Edward VII abdicated a year later so he could marry an american divorceÃ (C), leaving the throne to his younger, more serious brother, "Bertie".

Although Bertie's (later King George VI) stuttering is a very commonly overlooked piece of British Royal Family History, this story truly shows what's behind the curtains and the effort needed not only to break through the barricades, but at the same time, how such effort builds character. 

The movie-watching experience, for me, is all about rooting for a character and seeing him through thick and thin to jump every hurdle set against him. I believe the greater obstacle one can face is oneself, and as such, it is so much more gratifying to prevail, and this is what Bertie did. Although faced with doubt, his effort is relentless, and, no matter the outcome, the story takes us through his determination; we can actually say,  King George VI had "True Grit".
 
An Australian self-taught therapist, David Logue, goes one-on-one with Bertie to help him get through his speech impediment. This of course, stirs-up dissent amongst conservative circles, whom not only think that any Brit could be superior to an Australian, but also clearly more qualified. Nonetheless, after having taken Bertie to different therapists, his wife, Elizabeth (Queen Mum) finds Logue, which seems to work, against the odds.

I don't even know where to begin in this review.

For the past few months, I've definitely been rooting for The Social Network to sweep this year's Oscars, and for a while, it looked like this may have been the likely possibility. Then this film came along. After hearing so many times of Colin Firth's amazing performance, I knew that this was a film that I had to see and give my true opinion on. Then, just yesterday, I went, I saw, and I was truly blown away.

This film is basically a biopic about how King George VI of the U.K. attempted to deal with his stuttering problem. He is seemingly thrusted into kingdom when his father passes on and his older brother is forced to abandon the throne. This is all during the rise of WWII, when powerful speakers (Adolf Hitler, for example) are at an all-time rise. Thus, no one believes he is fit for the job; so he relies on the aid of Lionel Logue, a speech therapist, to help his find his voice and become a rightful leader for his people.

Honestly, I wasn't expecting too much when I walked into the theater. As many raves as I heard about how wonderful this film was, I also heard as many complaints about how overrated the movie was in general. I do admit, it was a bit slow to start, but as it picks up its pace, the film transforms into a wonderful work of art.

I could definitely see how Mr. Firth is gaining so much praise over this film, and I do believe now that all of it is rightfully deserving. His acting is just so wonderful, and he perfectly portrays the stammer and struggle emitted from it. I had a bit of a stuttering problem when I was younger, so in a way, I suppose I could relate to it. Even though he was acting the part, the emotional hurt was definitely present in his eyes, as if he's trapped in a dilemma from which he has no escape from; but he overcomes it with such courage, one can't help but completely fall in love with the character. He greatly deserves his Best Actor nomination, and there is no argument that he'll take home the award come Sunday night.

Helena Bonham Carter plays the Duchess of York, eventually Queen Elizabeth. I think she is wonderful in nearly everything she plays, and this film is no exception. However, she doesn't seem to have enough screen time for her Best Supporting Actress nomination to earn her a win. Geoffrey Rush, who plays the speech therapist, was absolutely marvelous as well. The screenplay truly plays justice to such a wonderful character, taking advantage of his and Colin Firth's encounters to create some unexpected moments of humor. The dry British humor fits in excellently, and create some of the most memorable scenes of the film.

My personal favorite scene of the movie comes near the very end. As King George VI gives his repeatedly rehearsed speech to the public via radio broadcast, Lionel remains at his side and skillfully "conducts" the entire thing. This climax is wonderfully played out with Beethoven's 7th Symphony in the backdrop, and I was at the edge of my seat the entire time. It was really one of the most beautiful things I have ever watched, and I admit there was a lump in my throat near the end.

This film is undoubtedly one of the greatest films of this past year. I believe that it is very much deserving of all of its nominations and wins thus far. Though The Social Network still holds a special place in my heart, and I'm still hoping for it to win big at the Academy Awards, I will not be surprised if The King's Speech succeeds in this feat, nor will I be disappointed. This film is a classic tale of overcoming one's fears and disadvantages to become a true hero, and the ending doesn't leave any disappointments. Nearly every bit of this film is absolutely fantastic, and I have mighty high hopes for it this Sunday night.

I don't want to offend any of my friends in the great UK, but this is definitely a British film. I say this because The King's Speech is quite unlike any film I've seen.

Bertie, soon to be known as King George VI, is entering into a time where he has to do a lot of public speaking. There's only one problem: the guy has a serious stammer and can barely talk at all in front of people he's not comfortable with. With World War II approaching, and with his father dying, he decides to seek help from a common speech therapist named Lionel Logue after seeing numerous other physicians with little results. At first, he is resistant to the man's unorthodox methods, but must persevere in order to overcome his problem when he becomes king.

Two months ago, I had never heard of this film. Then all of a sudden, praise upon praise was heaped on this film, and it is even believed that it might steal the gold from previous Academy favorite The Social Network. I can easily see why. This film is Oscar bait at its best. And that is by no means an insult.

It's a historical piece, which the Academy always likes. Many have accused it of being unoriginal, but that is unfair. It's a historical film, and therefore has to follow a certain series of events that really happened. This ain't Inglourious Basterds, you can't just rewrite history to make it more interesting. Even though it is predictable, the story told here is quite interesting. It's one that is not typically given the spotlight in historical films, and I actually learned something in this movie.

The film is made all the more interesting because of the performances. Colin Firth blew it out of the park on this one, giving one of the finest performances I've seen in the past decade. He will be getting that Oscar, and he deserves it. His stammer is so realistic, and you can see in his eyes that he is trying, that you would believe Firth actually stammered, and you feel for the guy. Equally impressive is Geoffrey Rush, giving an excellent performance as Lionel. Helena Bonham Carter plays a normal woman for once, and she is excellent at it too. So this is easily a winning film in the performance category.

One thing I found interesting about this film is the style. At times, the film has a very artistic feel to it, with each shot feeling very fluid and artistic. It's very cool, but at times it becomes too artsy to the point where it just feels pretentious. Still, Tom Hooper does an impressive job directing what could have been another boring biopic. Not to mention that a number of scenes are actually entertaining due to the interactions between Firth and Rush.

I was set to not like this film. I didn't want to buy into the hype, and I didn't think The King's Speech would be as good as everyone said it was. But damn it, it got the best of me and won me over. While a predictable piece of Oscar bait, it's superbly acted and directed. The film never bores, but keeps you interested with it's not so well-known story. Most average filmgoers will only see another history lesson in this film, but this is one lecture that deserves your attention.

Whether or not Colin Firth is the shoo in for best actor at this year's Oscars or not he is without doubt superbly good in this magnificent movie. There can be few who by now don't know the premise of the film so I won't go over the details. At the heart of the story is an unlikely friendship between two outcasts, one with a deeply rooted need and the other having an extraordinary gift and deep humanity. This is a period of history that us Brits feel very proprietorial towards so everything has to be just right, from Queen Mary's iron rod posture to pea-souper fogs in London and here, everything is just perfect. The main stars, Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush are just the diamonds in a coronation crown of acting talent. Helena Bonham Carter and Jennifer Ehle as two very different spouses, Derek Jacobi, Anthony Andrews and Timothy Spall as the British establishment, the wonderfully regal Claire Bloom and delightful Freya Wilson and Ramona Marquez, all cast perfectly and acting their cotton socks off. Of particular note in the supporting cast are that on screen chameleon Guy Pearce and the pantomime wicked queen Eve Best as the boo hiss pairing of Edward VI and Wallis Simpson. Indeed, I hope that if any director takes on the task of telling the story of this truly odious couple of social parasites, this pairing could be seen together again. Frankly, I don't care if in typical British style we fail at the Oscars They've seldom been a sign of quality and frequently miss the mark. If this movie doesn't however pick up more than the odd statuette, I'll simply be satisfied knowing that we was robbed and this is one of the best films you'll see this year.

I confess that I went to see "The King's Speech" more out of necessity than anything else.  I felt obligated; it leads the pack of Oscar nominees with 12 nods, and it's reportedly the front runner for Best Picture.  Colin Firth is said to be a lock in the Best Actor category.  Plus, I'd already seen the nine other Best Picture hopefuls, so I felt like I had to round out the list.  The premise just didn't sound all that interesting to me: a prince with a speech impediment seeks help so that he can confidently address his nation at a time of great need.  Truthfully, I expected this movie to be a boring period piece.

I couldn't have been more wrong.

It is a period piece, to be sure, but it's about as far from boring as a film can get.  In fact, it's just as rousing and entertaining as "The Fighter," or any other sports or action themed movie out there, and it rightfully deserves its place on the list of best films of the year.  At the end of this movie, if you aren't moved to the point where you want to cheer or applaud, you might want to check your pulse.

Firth stars as Prince Albert, Duke of York.  As the movie begins, he is about to speak at the close of the 1925 British Empire Exhibition at Wembley Stadium.  His eyes express great fear and inner turmoil as we see him making his way to the microphone, and as soon as he begins to speak, we realize why: he suffers from a paralyzing stammer, and now the entire nation will be aware of it.  Seeking help, Albert enlists the aid of Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), an Australian speech therapist whose unorthodox methods irk the prince at first, but then slowly begin to charm him.  Eventually the two become friends and confidants.

These two actors are simply amazing.  All due respect to James Franco in "127 Hours," but Firth deserves the Best Actor trophy.  He plays Albert (or "Bertie," as he's affectionately called by Logue) as a man tormented by his past, the pressures of his title, and of course his stutter.  As is directly stated in the movie, it's not like he can simply get another job, one that doesn't entail public speaking.  This is something he simply must deal with.  And Firth is more than capable of taking on the difficult role.  As hard as it must have been to portray a man with such a noticeable stammer, it must have been even harder to have to ADJUST the stammer as the movie progressed.  And Rush is just as good as Logue, creating an eccentric but effective and very funny character.  The sessions between the two men are wonderful to behold.

And the big climax, in which Albert must address his nation prior to England's entry into World War II, is, simply put, riveting.  That a climax involving nothing more than two men in a radio booth can be as labeled as "riveting" must surely sound as strange to you reading it as it does to me typing it, but I assure you, it is true.  For anyone who has ever doubted the power of words, this scene serves as a testament that you are gravely mistaken.

What a great film.  "The King's Speech" contains very little "action," in the traditional definition of the word, but that does not stop it from being captivating and downright entertaining.  Go see this movie.

The King's Speech is simply remarkable. In every facet of the direction, the acting and the writing, there's an irremovable sense of majesty. Fitting a theme considering what the film is about, understandably. The film is a beautiful tale of courage, adversity and friendship which transgresses social traditions. Tied with Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush's standout performances, The King's Speech is a film that is a continuous joy to watch.

Colin Firth takes on the role of the late king George VI, who before his inauguration was known as Bertie. For as long as he could remember, Bertie had been beset with a debilitating stammer. This didn't make him prime royal material in the eyes of his father, George V, which lead to Edward VIII the next person in line for the crown. However, after a scandal (a scandal for that era, at least), Bertie will have to take a huge step forward in his life, work on his stammer and become the next king. To achieve that goal, he must rely on the Australian voice coach Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), who has some unorthodox methods to cure his ailment.

The chemistry between Firth and Rush is simply divine. For every rash outburst from Bertie,    Rush responds in an aloof matter completely unaffected by the fact that he's helping royalty. As the bond between them grows stronger, a friendship is struck up that is both convincing and likable. Firth is clearly in the best role he's been in since he started out in the film business and is stunning in his role of Bertie. Not only does he emulate a stammer perfectly (this reviewer knows someone with a stammer, as a reference), but his performance is amplified by how accessible he proves to be in the confines of privacy. One cannot forget Geoffrey Rush either, however, who is, for lack of a better word, adorable as the nonchalant voice coach.

There's a very sturdy supporting cast as well. Helena Bonham Carter plays Bertie's wife admirably while Guy Ritchie is perfect as the loose Edward VIII. Special mention goes to Timothy Spall for his portrayal of Winston Churchill, the inspiration for bulldog names all over the world.

The film's director, Tom Hooper, puts the film together with the utmost care. When the film looks like it's going to be overly dramatic, you get a ranting Bertie throwing around swear words like rice. Adversely, Hooper keeps the drama present to emphasize the difficulties of Bertie, shown prominently in the inner conflicts of Bertie, where he battles with his duties and responsibility. The ending is particularly powerful, and shows just how well Hooper built up the narrative. In that respect, the film's writer, David Seidler, of course deserves heaps of praise. Every character feels natural and the pace, as mentioned earlier, is simultaneously easy to follow and surprisingly entertaining given the subject matter.

The King's Speech is a lot of things. One of the finest examples of British cinema, proof of Colin Firth's deserving place in the upper echelons of acting pedigree, a wonderful combination of common values like friendship, determination and will. However, The King's Speech is first and foremost a sign that films can touch an audience of incredible diversity, all from the youngest to the oldest. This reviewer's theater was filled with people of all ages, all walking out with a smile on their face. That's an accomplishment that few have ever managed to achieve.

I resisted watching this because felt it was over-hyped and assumed it would be full of cliches.  However I was won over, as although there is familiar territory; the icy reserve of British royalty, the looming threat in Europe, the young princesses, naughty Mrs Simpson, and profligate David etc, the area of the King's speech defect and personal battle is new and interesting material.  Colin Firth, I feel, does deserve all nominations and awards conveying the quadruple agonies of his inability to speak clearly, abusive childhood experiences, dysfunctional family life, and his sudden and overwhelming destiny as King, and Head of a nation at war.  He does so superbly, his vulnerability and struggle is painful to watch and I wanted to kill the ghastly nanny who had pinched and starved him.  Geoffrey Rush brings a touching melancholy as failed actor turned speech therapist turned King's advisor and the key to the film is their relationship which was highly engaging.   I did question how much dramatic license is in the film, and if they really were that close and that informal, the swearing etc to release the voice and the way that Logue sometimes addressed him but, hey, it made good drama.  Also David and Mrs S were a bit over demonised perhaps.  There are no really good substantial female roles in the film but Helen Bonham Carter is elegant and divine as the young Queen mum, supporting her man.  It is a bit unnerving to see actresses of Jennifer Ehle calibre in tiny supporting barely-there roles as Logue's wife, but it didn't really matter as it was the men's story and that was ok.  Touching too were the affectionate scenes of Bertie with his daughters.  I will confess to an embarrassing feeling of patriotism as the King finally delivers the speech on the eve of war to the people of GB and every stop was pulled out for this in true Brit war film fashion.  Also Tim Spall is pitch perfect as Churchill.   So I have no complaints, a very high calibre film. For me thought the most heartbreaking scene was when David (Edward VIII) breaks down at his father's deathbed in his mother's arm and she is completely unable to respond or hold him or comfort him.  I actually felt sorry for the royals for a moment.

Although it is difficult to see past Firth's performance, Geoffrey Rush adds another incredible performance to his resume (including Shine, Shakespeare in Love, and the Pirates franchise).  Helena Bonham Carter also breaks loose from her character role reputation as she brings emotion and chemistry to the relationship between herself and King George VI.  Amidst other amazing actors on this cast list is Guy Pearce who once again thrives in a despicable role.  In addition to the incredible story and acting, The King's Speech boasts 12 Oscar nominations including best score, best picture, and 3 nominations in acting categories.  This film will not soon be forgotten.

I'm not sure of this, but it is highly possible that with the wrong actors and the wrong director, The King's Speech could've easily been forgotten as a boring, melodramatic snooze-fest.  Thankfully this isn't the case.
There are several things that make this film great, and worthy of the Best Picture Oscar it recently received.  The first, and most obvious, is the acting.  Helena Bonham Carter plays Queen Elizabeth as a lovely, supportive wife.  She plays her part with beautiful reservation.  I'm very used to seeing Carter basically eat up the screen in most of her performances (which is fine, she is excellent), but this role needs to be supportive because that is the nature of the character.  She needs to be there when we wish we could be there for King George VI, or Berty as she calls him.  She does her job very well.
Secondly there is Geoffrey Rush, who once again shows his excellence in one of the finest performaces of his career.  Rush plays Lionel Logue, the speech therapist who takes on the task of helping Berty by unusual but effective means.  Logue, in a sense, is the hero of this film.  Yes, King George has his speech impediment to overcome, but it is Lionel Logue whom he must lean on.  It is important here to point out what is truly outstanding about the two main performancing, starting with Geoffrey Rush.  Usually, we would see caricatures of people like Logue in a film.  His methods would be exploited to make him appear to be an unconventional, mad genius.  His character is considered somewhat unconventional, but the film doesn't intentionally draw our attention to this or overly glorify Logue as a genius who happens to care.  He's just good at what he does, and he does care.  He ends up caring a lot.
This brings us to Berty, or King George, whichever you want, played by Colin Firth.  I don't know how well-known he was to the common movie-goer, but he is almost certainly now, seeing as how he just won Best Actor at the Oscars.  I've seen several of his films, and always thought highly of him, but this film shows him at a level I wasn't aware of.  He's superb, and it's not just how well he depicts the speech impediment of King George.  In fact that is secondary.  His excellence is in showing his fear, his self-loathing, his anger, etc.  Colin Firth's character is angry at his personal brokenness, and yet cannot stand hoping for it to change.  He wants to give up, but no one and nothing will let him, not even himself.  After seeing The Social Network, I didn't think anyone could have done a better job than Jesse Eisenburg, but I stand corrected.  
Once again, this character could've easily been exploited due to his deficiency.  Take Forrest Gump, for example.  The character has a low level intelligence, and it is exploited by putting him in situations where we wonder how the two (the low IQ and the situation) will mix.  Forrest Gump is an excellent movie, but this approach would be bad for The King's Speech.  Instead, the approach is to present a man who has trouble speaking but is forced to speak due to his charge.  This was a real person and it is presented realistically.  We know how the speech impediment plus the situation will mix, so what happens is we sympathize with Berty and want to help him.  Credit for this approach, both with King George and Lionel Logue, goes to the excellent direction of Tom Hooper.  He effortlessly portrays these members of higher society as people.  People like anyone else, and that is perhaps the masterstroke of this film.  For someone with so few films under his belt, he is proving to be a remarkable director.
The King's Speech is a masterpiece of story, writing, directing, and acting.  Everything about it is wonderfully made and it is a very worthy Best Picture winner.

From its opening frame of a vintage radio mic this film reeked of Oscar success. While not a particularly experimental or thought provoking film, this fantastic feel good number is well worth the hype. 

	In a year when many of the best films focused on complex narrative structure where in time, plot and character were often subjective definitions prone to dissolving at a moments notice, (or the gentle spin of a top,) it is almost refreshing to find a film that lives so whole heartily in the world of one main character, moving through time in a linear fashion. The Kings Speech, from its onset, has the unique qualification of feeling like both a 1920's-30's period piece as well as a product from the mid 90's. Few special effects, heavy-handed dialogue, ornate production pieces and an all start cast, all contribute to making the King's Speech feel like a classic film you missed the first time around and are now catching in wide release. 

	Based on the life of King George the 6th (both before and after his ascension to the throne.) the film focuses on the King's speech impediment. Taking place during the lead up to and beginning of World War 2, the film focuses on the King growing concern that his inability to speak is a rather large issue for a prince. A matter of personal pride motivate him to over come his speech impedement, though the attempts are often feeble and half hearted. Yet as the opening of factories and speeches at horse races taken on a more serious note with the cloud of war beginning to brew along the horizon, his inability to speak articulately takes on a more serious edge, as the King fears that he will be unable to motivate the masses against Hitler. The film unsurprisingly culminates in the King's first wartime speech which is delivered rather flawlessly. 

	The acting in this film is singularly sublime. Wonderfully traditional feeling character acting where the actors, for a rare change seem to give themselves whole heartedly to the plot leaving behind there many rather larger then life characters and own personal egos. Helena Bonham Carter for instance shows for one of the first times in her career that she is a rather exceptionally talented actress who can do more then scream and rip her hair asunder. Geoffrey Rush is sublime, which is rather to be expected and yet unsurprisingly, as the film does really hinge on his performance, it is Colin Firth who manages to shine brighter then all the others in this film. Colin Firth's performance as king George is intoxicating to watch and beautiful to listen to. He is sensational as a man crippled by his own voice and manages to infuse all of his scenes with a sense of un-abandon gravitas. 

	Ultimately I felt this film was very refreshing. Simple, logical and linear, with wonderful direction and exquisite sets it is always a joy a watch in the most traditional of sense. Granted at times it felt heavy handed, if I saw one more sequences where the king's mouth was obscured by a radio mic for instance I was going to write a rather angry letter to some one.

"The King's Speech" is about a man's stammer. The man happens to be King George VI (Colin Firth) but it is impressive how the movie never loses focus of its main subject - the stutter - and turn into a biographical tale or a history lesson. Even more impressive is how the movie manages to hold our attention and entertain for nearly two hours given its subject matter. It is undoubtedly one of the most uplifting movie-going experiences of 2010. 
We first meet the king in 1925 as Prince Albert, the Duke of York as he is about to give his first public speech at the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley Stadium to drastic results. British TV director Tom Hooper ("The Damned United") succeeds in making us feel the constraints in this scene as well as many others through the effective use of a wide lens. His wife Elizabeth, the Duchess of York (Helena Bonham Carter) stood beside him all the way as she consistently tries to cure his stammer. She approaches an unorthodox Australian speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), to help her husband. The two get off to a rocky start and the therapy ends. 
He then returns back to Logue and the two start an unusual friendship. The second half of the movie mainly focuses on Bertie's accession to the throne. When his father (Michael Gambon) dies, his brother Edward, Prince of Wales (Guy Pearce) is the natural successor but his desire to marry a twice-married-before American socialite leads to his abdication making Albert the new king. Now he needs Logue more than ever. 
Firth, the great actor he is, delivers the performance of his career portraying the sometimes tough-tempered king and perfects the stammer. More importantly, this is an emotional performance -you will be easily drawn to his character. Rush is also superb here providing sometimes comic relief aided by a pitch-perfect script by David Seidler ("Tucker: The Man and His Dream") that is smart, dramatic and funny without drifting into a satire. Carter makes a career shift playing one of her most non-eccentric characters as the woman who stood by her husband all the way. 
It is hard to pinpoint something wrong with this movie (I probably just wanted to have myself loving this movie more). Hooper is a revelation and proves himself as a highly talented filmmaker aided by top notch "support functions", namely production design, cinematography and editing. The movie is mostly filmed in interior locations (a rarity among period movies) but the pieces never cease to impress. Winner of 4 Oscars: Picture, Director, Actor (Firth), Original Screenplay. Nominated for 8 Others: Supporting Actor (Rush), Supporting Actress (Carter), Art Direction, Cinematography, Costume Design, Editing, Original Score, Sound Mixing.

For all the technical merits of a film, this one is astounding. The script feels organic and real. The art direction and set decoration evoke London in the first part of the 20th century perfectly, and even occasionally aid in your understanding of character. The direction is subtle and at times sublime, and the (Oscar winning) director has a unique and interesting eye. He frames his shots in unusual ways that are often artistic, occasionally slightly jarring, once or twice bordering on avant garde, but always interesting to look at, and often quite beautiful. (The king and his therapist walking through a park, the camera tracking in front of them, and everything vanishing behind them in the brightly lit, starkly white London fog as they walk. It's one of my favorite moments.) The acting is absolutely perfect all around, especially Colin Firth, whose performance not only deserved the Oscar it won him, but deserves to be remembered as one of the finest performances of the early 21st century. I'm not exaggerating. A friend was impressed with his stammer, how real and organic it was, rising and falling with his emotions. For me it was far more than that. Watch his eyes. I've always thought the best performances happen in the eyes. He is completely earnest. As a whole, though, this movie was not greater than the sum of it's phenomenal parts. Between moments of great drama and moments of surprisingly high humor, it seemed to drag, and I found my attention starting to wander. It would always come back around, but the very fact of it prevents me from giving the film a full 5 stars. I should note however by the end I was wholly absorbed again, and the film finishes with an emotional wallop. It's nice when a movie honestly brings out happy tears.

Let's take a moment to consider the atypical career of Colin Firth. He became a superstar in his native Britain in his mid-thirties thanks to his definitive portrayal of Mr. Darcy in Pride and Prejudice, a role that made him so iconic there that he spent many years parodying or acknowledging it in films like Love Actually and Bridget Jones's Diary. Sure, he worked in other capacities -- a talent as versatile as his is almost guaranteed steady work in British film -- but it was his turn in Tom Ford's 2009 drama, A Single Man, that brought Firth international acclaim, as well as his first Oscar nomination in the United States. Just one year after that, with Tom Hooper's The King's Speech, Firth solidifies his status as one of the best actors of his generation.

Playing the future King George VI, Firth takes the kind of part that stereotypically wins Oscars -- a powerful man with a physical handicap -- and makes him a three-dimensional human. Bertie, as the man is known to close friends and family, has suffered from a stutter his entire life. When his older brother, Edward (Guy Pearce), abdicates the throne just as World War II becomes eminent, Bertie must not only overcome the emotional pressures of ascending to power, but control his stammer as well in order to address and inspire his people on what was, at that point, the most widespread form of mass communication -- radio.

To that end, he hires Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), a commoner who has worked in the nascent field of speech pathology long enough to offer some relief to the self-doubting Bertie, and to force the future monarch to consider the deeper psychological issues that lie at the core of the problem.

That description, however, doesn't come close to doing justice to how entertaining The King's Speech is. David Seidler's juicy script is packed with dialogue that alternates between belly laughs, witty retorts, and dramatic revelations with such deftness that each scene -- like the one where Bertie and Lionel first meet -- feels like its own mini-movie, with the character arcs all advancing steadily but surely toward the big day when the king must tell his people that they are at war with the Nazis.

Given such an airtight script, director Tom Hooper delivers the goods. His ability to hold a shot -- especially close-ups -- for just the right amount of time is uncanny; he knows where the dramatic or comedic beat is at every point, and he focuses on it with minimum fuss. The King's Speech is old-fashioned in the best sense of the word.

Firth is outstanding in the lead role, playing a man with a disability as opposed to simply playing a disability. An actor always capable of indicating the emotions boiling inside a repressed person, he brings out Bertie's neuroses in the subtlest of ways -- hand gestures, eye squints -- as well as in his speech. He makes us feel the near-constant physical frustration of not being able to express yourself.

Firth is the biggest reason to see this movie, but he's far from the only one. Rush offers flawless support (and gets the vast majority of the best laugh lines), and Helena Bonham Carter, as Bertie's wife, Elizabeth, reminds everybody that she can handle much more than just Harry Potter movies and her significant other Tim Burton's films. In fact, a scene where she meets Lionel's wife stands as one of the most astoundingly layered exchanges between royalty and a commoner that's ever been filmed.

Inspiring, funny, touching, and delivered with craftsmanship and artistry, The King's Speech is a testament to the greatness of King George VI, the talent of Colin Firth, and the joys of quality filmmaking.

What do you do with a king who is from that royal family who established a great empire where the sun never set? What if the king, Duke of York at present, later to become King George VI (Colin Firth), comes from that nation where verbal and written articulation reached their great heights and yet the king falls short of perfect verbal articulation and stammers, in spite of the efforts of many speech therepists? Well, fiddly problem, wouldn't you say? A nagging thorn in the ass is what a lifetime of losses and pains are to the hoi polloi. Great enough a problem to bring tears in the eyes of the king's wife, to-be Queen Elizabeth (Helena Bonham),  and embarrassment to the listeners.  The movie doesn't let us to sentimentalize over it while it shows this human face of the royals. The opening scene shows the King botching up his speech at an occasion and the the movie  glides us soon after opening in medias res to this Australian therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), who tells the lady-the Duchess who has come under the alias of Mrs Johnson  and who uses the royal 'we'-to make her "hubby pop by"  and for whom it is "my  game, my turf, my rules" and has guts enough to call the previous therapists "Idiots" and to call the King "Bertie" (as in a Wodehouse novel (and in a Wodehouse novel a person with a stammer is advised to sing by the therapist just as in a scene in this movie too))  and not "Your Highness" after the treatment starts (and its not Mohamat going to the mountain but vice versa) as he wants  to be on equal terms with the King in the therapy sessions in his "palace". The treatment is as unorthodox as the therapist and it is a case of the treatment of the person through which the speech defect  is cured. "Physical exercises and tricks are important," he says. Many of his methods are shown by a series of short shots amalgamated in one scene. This makes us get a feel of fun rather than tedium of the treatment. In the meantime, the father dies. The elder brother who gets the throne doesn't much enjoy "Kinging", as it is, and is infatuated with Mrs Wallis Simpson from America. And the king, as the Head of the Church of England, can not marry a divorced woman. Bertie, on the other hand "is afraid of his own shadow" as Lionel rightly assesses. After Bertie becomes the King, and a minor estrangement, Lionel assumes his job before the coronation. His job is to break down the stammer, but more than that, the fear, that generates it.  He does that. The King is now not only a more vocally fluent man, but a surer man.  The movie ends with the king's speech. The speech of King George VI.  What the audience care for,  and are on tenterhooks, is not the occasion of the speech nor the content but the delivery.  Tears again in wife's eyes but of joy this time.  Congratulations from all and one. You can call this a movie of the comedy genre. It is also a movie about friendship that can exist between men of different stations and destinies, as also about good human values, about family, and about a man assuming the responsibilities that are alien to his nature but which he must. "Let Courage Reign" seems somewhat bland as a tag line but so it works in the movie. The therapy lessons turn through intimacy and friendship towards personality development too. 

Don't look for too many historical facts. Even the portrayal of the  person, the Duke who suffered ill-health, is in contrast: Firth is shown as straight, healthy and in robust health really; the way he climbs up stairs after his brother after their father's death shows him anything but that. And then, how many of us knew all this? We remember from History, those happening times and Churchill, Hitler etc etc  but not the English King. It's art that catches that little something forsaken on the paths of time, brings it forth in a new livery and puts a shining crown on it. 

Tom Hooper seems to have done a good job. The script is good too with wit carrying on the movie where it could have become dull. For the most part, the focus of the camera is on the faces of Firth and Rush. At times, the moving camera shots-- long shots many, some at waist level-give a documentary kind of feel when one can feel the state of mind of the character.  Local colour is maintained but no special attention is given to it, which is good and keeps the movie on the right focus. In fact, the acting is so good you may get tempted to try stammering yourself. Don't carry it too far, though. Firth has done a good job of showing the progressive lessening of stammer the credit for which goes to the director and the script writer (David Seidler) too. He has done well in emotional scenes showing animation, anxiety, nervousness, love, anger and also in scenes showing composure. Helena Bonham has done well too, as a confident, supportive wife. Darek Jacobi, a great actor, doesn't get much chance to show his talent in his role as the Archbishop. Kids, Hitler, and Shakespeare have been well brought into the movie. All this fills even this period drama with life.

I'd love nothing more than to expose this movie as shameless Oscar Bait and enlighten the public as to why they're being duped into thinking this movie is good but I can't in good faith completely write this movie off. See I get the feeling Tom Hooper was in earnest in making this film, he has a history of good but obscure political dramas including the fantastic John Adams television series with Paul Giamatti and watching the charade that was the Oscars where he thanked his mother for recommending the script to him after watching a play adaption I feel like he was just trying to make a good historical film about a little known story. But those responsible for the script were obviously out to get an Oscar as this is one of the most reprehensibly cliche buddy movies in a while, with strange and questionable moral basis and most annoyingly a healthy dose of melodrama. Still I'm reviewing this movie on its own merits not on how ridiculously over hyped it undeniably is so is this truly a good movie or merely manipulative tripe? Let's take a stammering l-l-l-look.

As our story begins we see our protagonist Prince Albert "Bertie", Duke of York (Colin Firth who gives a pretty good performance I'll admit if a little...aspbergery) who is attempting to speak at the 1925 British Empire Exhibition at the wish of his father King George V (Michael Gambon, I swear half the cast of this is from Harry Potter as well). Unfortunately he has a pretty awful stutter and can't get a word out and so we get some brief scenes of intellectual and scientific people trying to correct his speech with now laughable and "primitive" treatments. None of these work until his wife the Duchess (Helena Bonham Carter, see you can act when you're not trying too hard to be weird) persuades him to see "eccentric" new age Australian speech therapist Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush who is intermittently funny and annoying) and this seems providential as on the brink of WWII King George dies and his son, Bertie's older brother David (Guy Pearce, who is not at all developed and they half-heartedly and without real conviction or balls try to make him seem like a dick at one point) shamefully abdicates the throne and this leaves B-b-b-b-bertie to take the throne. Can he overcome his speech problem in time too...give a speech that will have no real consequence on the war? Well of course, not that you genuinely care.

Herein lies my major problem with the work, more so than the predictable story where he and Lionel fall out and reunite by putting aside their differences just in time, more so than the criminally unfunny "touching" scenes you're supposed to laugh at and even more than the revolutionary speech therapy techniques the movie glazes over to focus more on the sense of duty Bertie feels I hated the focus on the importance of British Monarchy. I'm not British so no one asked my opinion, but honestly why does the monarchy exist and why does this movie act like Bertie's ability to speak in a full sentence without stuttering is the reason we socked it too Hitler? Furthermore how the hell am I supposed to feel sympathy for a character who will never have to worry about money, loneliness or feelings of self-worth from the beginning to the end of their life? Especially during this time period when so much of their riches were garnered from their fucking colonies in India and Africa, I mean seriously fuck white people. And finally I was very underwhelmed by the Direction especially since everyone else clearly was not and Hooper won Best Director. This was about the same quality as a TV movie, an HBO movie maybe but Hooper is certainly nothing special behind the camera. Seriously what scenes really stuck with you in regards to camera work? The part where Geoffrey Rush sticks his head sideways through the door? Having your actor stick his head through a door oh wow what an innovator.

I suppose I'm forced to admit this movie is successful even if it's not very good it's some highly elusive Oscar Bait, a story of a character with a dignified British accent, overcoming some obstacle, but not one that will make him seem unattractive (like autism or a stutter), during the "Greatest Generation" for good measure since most of the Oscar voters are members of this generation or baby boomers and making it seem like the obstacle being overcome somehow helped in defeating Hitler. But here's the thing about Oscar Bait sometimes even if I don't like it it's alright. Titanic is shameless Oscar Bait and I hate that movie but Cameron had some pretty solid and damn epic camera work in it. Schindler's List could be called Oscar Bait but it was gritty unsparing film and is one of the most heartfelt movies I've ever seen if nothing else for the fact that Spielberg's Jewish, it feels like an artist mourning the trial and tribulations of his ancestors. But the King's Speech has none of these things, it's certainly not bad and Firth is great and it's very watchable but don't get too wrapped up in it, it's not without some fundamental flaws.
