The King's Speech.
Slow and polished, but comical and gripping.
First off, don't bash me for being one of those "Well it won best picture so I guess I'll see it people", that's a perfectly reasonable reason to watch a movie. Second, The King's Speech is probably one of the greatest commentaries on WWII England. What I appreciated most was the way it combined the monarchical drama of The Queen with the satire on British aristocracy of The Remains of the Day (that's a mouthful). Does it seem without emotion at times? Yep. Is the humor sophisticated and underplayed? Naturally. Do they wear the most luxurious tweed suits and pea-coats the entire time? Most definitely.
The Colin Firth performance was captivating, Geoffrey Rush was, well, Geoffrey Rush, and Helena Bonham Carter looks great when she's not dressed up as a witch (let her out of the house every once in a while Burton). The trifecta of heroes worked great together.

Why 90%?
Because while it's not as held back as The Remains of the Day, this polished story of a forty-year old kid facing his greatest struggle head first is funny, emotional, and satisfying. Though ever-slightly forgettable (The Oscar should help though).

Extra: Did you guys notice Colin Firth's neck veins? They were crazy at times. I felt like I could see his neck veins more than James Franco's arms veins in 127 Hours, and he was slicing through it with a dull pocket knife. So maybe I'm exaggerating, people do that. I'm just saying the guy knows how to make you feel for him.
The whole thing was marvelous. I am back in love with Colin.

I wanted to see this movie before the Academy Awards but I just wasn't able to get around to it. So I went into the theater knowing how many awards and for what this movie won. I also knew that there was a divide of some kind between the people who thought this movie didn't win enough awards and people who think it's drastically overhyped. I tend to agree with the latter although I will not deny this is a great movie.

	The plot is straightforward and neat, with almost no bumps or surprises to drive this movie an extra few yards. This movie is performance driven, and without the strong cast this movie would be forgotten in a pile somewhere. There is nothing about the story that would suggest this movie would be as successful without the fantastic Colin Firth or Geoffrey Rush behind it. Bland and predictable this movie was often slow but throughout the film there was never a point where you weren't very far away from some amazing dialogue.

	Colin Firth may have won for Best Lead and it was well deserved, but the real performance of the film for me was Geoffrey Rush. He was consistently funny and made an excellent counterpart for Firth to continually perform. Firth's part was obviously the more difficult one, having to stammer as King George VI, and his award was one of the few I think this film deserved. Firth's onscreen wife, played by the always great Helena Bonham Carter, was the last member of this trio of award deserving performances.

	While this movie was really well done and enjoyable to watch I don't think it was the best movie of 2010, but that's just my opinion. I can think of three movies just off the top of my head I enjoyed more than this one, but that doesn't mean they should have won it just means that I liked them better. Tom Hooper, the director of this movie, did a great job but I will come out and say he was given a gift in the Best Director award, David Fincher deserved the nod for The Social Network, without a doubt. 

	So while the movie was definitely enjoyable I think it's more than a little overhyped. The trio of Colin Firth, Geoffrey Rush, and Helena Bonham Carter all deliver strong and fantastic acting performances to make this movie great.

THE KINGS SPEECH= THE EMPEROR'S NEW CLOTHES
 
            As I watched the highly touted movie "The Kings Speech" I felt like I was living through the "Emperor's New Clothes". I had gone to this film expected to be enthralled with its cinematic magic only to have left feeling like my wallet was stolen. This film depicts the compelling true story of Prince Albert (later King GeorgeVI's) rise to power during one of the most difficult times in England 's history, World War II. What makes this story so fascinating is that King George was responsible to motivate his nation through his oratory skills yet suffered from a major speech impediment. This story had so much to offer yet much more was missing. It was like the King was half dressed or dare I say naked.
    I had anticipated seeing Prince Albert 's development but was left with a rather flat dull character. Most of the characters in the film lacked the depth that I saw in other Oscar Nominated films like the "Social Network" and "The Fighter".  I believe that if they had included flashbacks to the times of the Prince's youth, that his character would have seemed more rounded and fleshed out. Instead we only learn about the Prince's earlier life through dialogue that lacks the emotional depth that would have us feel for this character.  There were no compelling characters that I truly cared for and as such I lost interest in this film before it even ended.
     The film also lacked the cinematographic aspects that I expected when dealing with this subject matter. The landscape of England and its royalty was never truly utilized in this film. The film just touched on the subject of World War II through dialogue, not the images of the horror that this war was about to bring on England . The closest we got to truly observing the world around this character was a vintage newsreel of Hitler speaking  and  King George observing his oratory skills. I can understand the Directors need to let the viewer feel the very insular world that the king lived in but at times I felt claustrophobic.
     The film had a fine musical score, beautiful costumes, fine acting, and an historical story that the world should know about, but the flaws were just too much. Although this might hurt me with the royalty, I still must say this film is not in the same class as the other films nominated for best movie of the year. I guess I won't be invited to the Royal Wedding this summer. . I'll give it **  1/2 stars a half more after I finish my tea and crumpets.

The film tells the true story of King George VI, who had a pretty bad speech problem. The movie follows him from when he's the Duke of York, all the way to his ruling. He has tried everything to fix his speech but nothing seems to work. His wife, played by Helena Bonham Carter, decides to take him to a different speech therapist for once. This new therapist, played by Geoffrey Rush, has a completely different method to his madness, but his uniqueness and un-orthodox style envelop this beautiful chemistry between him, and the king. This in turn creates a friendship for them that last a lifetime. It's a wonderful story, and I'm glad it was made into a movie. A perfect movie as well. 

The performances in the movie, are absolutely perfect. Everyone is astounding. Colin Firth gives the best performance of his life in this movie. I knew that he was finally getting serious when he made "A Single Man" the previous year, and this movie just proves that he really meant it. He was amazing, and he definitely deserved the Academy Award for Best Actor. I loved his development as a character, going from a man in denial, unsure of himself, to a man with confidence. Geoffrey Rush was also fantastic. He had this brilliant and satirical style to his performance which really drew you into the film. He was absolutely wonderful. The same goes for Helena Bonham Carter. Even though she wasn't amazing as these two, she was still excellent,doing everything that she needed to do, and then some. 

But without a doubt my favorite thing about the movie was how it was shot. This to me, was amazing. Because the film is all about vocalization, and stuttering, the cinematography focuses completely on emotions conveyed by the mouth. When Firth or Rush are talking to one another, the cameras focus in one what's being released orally, in a sense that we have this interesting view of what's going on. It's a brilliant tie between a films premise, and a film's presentation. It's quite astounding if you ask me. Also, there are various beautiful landscape shots that recur throughout the movie, and you'll find yourself gazing at it's beauty. 

The soundtrack is astounding as well. Alexandre Desplat creates beautiful compositions that go on throughout the movie, and they definitely help the film's tone. He did a wonderful job. 

Every component in the movie is perfected. Everything is just superbly wonderful. I have no other way of describing it. It just all seems dead on amazing. 

"The King's Speech" is one of those films where I don't really have that much to say, because it just needs to be seen. It's a phenomenal, wonderful, beautiful movie. The day before the Oscars, my wife and I checked out The King's Speech.  The movie retold, in a movie kind of way (i.e. facts were artistically adjusted), the story of the British King George VI who had a speech impediment.  He rose to power just prior to World War II; a time when a strong voice from the king was needed.  The story revolves around the future king, played by Colin Firth, and his speech therapist, played by Geoffrey Rush.  Helena Bonham Carter plays the future king's wife.  

Like Oscar contender The Social Network, there is zero action in the movie.  It's all about story and characters.  It's all well done.  Excellent acting and an interesting story.  The sprinkles of light comedy was of the dry British style, which I usually like.  

The audience was mostly over 30.  Overall, a good movie.  Personally, I'd give the edge to The Social Network, though the royal flick would probably appeal to the much older Academy.  I always give Oscar contenders a tougher standard when I rate them.

[b]The King's Speech (2010) [/b]

[b]Starring:[/b] Colin Firth, Geoffrey Rush, Helena Bonham Carter, Guy Pearce, Timothy Spall...
[b]Directed by:[/b] Tom Hooper

[b]Synopsis:[/b] Price Albert, "Bertie", Duke of York (Colin Firth) is King George V's younger brother, who suffers from a serious problem of stuttering, hence not having the abilities to speak in front of large audiences or appearing in public. When his father dies, and his older brother Edward (Guy Pearce) abdicates months after he is given the throne, Bertie now faces himself with the seemingly impossible task of becoming King George VI. His wife, Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) then finds him an unusual and unorthodox speech therapist (Geoffrey Rush) to help Bertie find his inner voice to speak out to England in the beginnings of World War II.

[b]Thoughts I Had Before Watching:[/b] I watched it before it took home the Oscar for Best Picture. Of course I was attracted to it because of all the Oscar buzz. Without it, I might've been slightly interested in it, but I wouldn't have forced myself to watch it like I did. Yes, I had relatively high expectations, especially on the acting part (which didn't let me down at all), but I was a bit disappointed when it comes to the freshness and originality of the script...

[b]Storyline/Script:[/b] This was probably the weakest point of the movie for me. Don't get me wrong. The film was splendidly written, with near-perfect dialogues and character development, and it was very entertaining throughout its entirety. However, I found it extremely predictable and often way too conventional. I don't think it brought anything new to the film table (except for outstanding performances, but that's another topic...). It was well done, but the story, at the end, fell a bit flat. Nothing remarkable. Did it deserve to win the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay? Regardless how well it was written, no. Inception or The Kids Are All Right were way more deserving. [b]24/30[/b]

[b]Acting:[/b] The King's Speech is what it is because of its performances. Seriously. I bought each and single one of them. Colin Firth gives the performance of a lifetime as Bertie, the prince that the situations forced to become king, who suffers of serious insecurity problems due to his stuttering. The type of character that is usually loved by the Academy (historical character with an impediment that manages to overcome), and was loved by me as well. Firth didn't show me a king. He showed me a human being. Helena Bonham Carter, one of my favorite actresses, also does an equally good but more subtle job as Elizabeth, Bertie's wife who shows unconditional love and support for him, and she deserved that nomination to its fullest. Not the best performance I've seen of her, but she managed to show us a whole different side of her, aside from the madness and darkness typical of her Tim Burton and Bellatrix roles, and prove that she can do just as good. But the person who steals the entire film is Geoffrey Rush as Lionel Logue, Bertie's unusual speech therapist slash friend slash confident. He was the comic relief, and the dramatic basis, and the character that put the whole movie into motion. I'm still debating whether he deserved that Oscar more than Christian Bale, but, in my opinion, his performance wsa the best of the movie (yes, over Firth). [b]30/30[/b]

[b]Behind the Cameras:[/b]Very classical. Very according to the rules. Very clean. Very traditional. Almost a manual on how a movie should be made. This can be good, as it worked perfectly here, and delivered an almost impeccable film, with all of its elements being carefully planned (music, costume, cinematography, edition...). However, just as it was with the screenplay, it felt way too conventional and conservative. There was no effort to think outside the box, and the result was a perfectly made classic period drama. But that's it. Also, I am totally against Tom Hooper winning for Best Director. I didn't feel like the direction played a strong part in the effectiveness on the movie, but rather on its performances and the way all of its parts were assembled. As crude as it may sound, I feel like any other could've done it with a not much different result. But, hey, the movie came out really good at the end, and that's eventually what matters. [b]15/20[/b]

[b]Entertainment/Fun Factor:[/b] Yes, it was very entertaining and interesting to watch. You laughed, you cried. The performances captivated me completely, and I was most of the times amazed by the cleanliness and detail with which it was done. It was a visual experience as well. But, still, that didn't keep it from being slightly predictable at times, a bit repetitive, and even (for some slight moments) dragging... [b]16/20[/b]

[b]Highest Point:[/b] The magnificent speech therapy sessions (all of them), which probably captured the essence of the entire film, and the climax of the film, when Bertie is about to speak to a nation in need of the voice of a leader.

[b]Lowest Point:[/b] Actually, I don't think there was a low point as such. I just think it was a bit of a disappointment that a movie with such a high potential and expectations left me with a slight feeling of "they stayed safe..."

[b]Would I Recommend It?[/b] Yes, of course I would. I mean, it won the Oscar for Best Picture, didn't it? Did it deserve it? In my opinion, no, it didn't. The Social Network, or Black Swan, or even The Kids Are All Right were more deserving to me. But that doesn't take away merits from this movie at all. It was a good movie. A very good movie. Enjoyable for probably all types of audiences, and will be liked by most. Outstanding performances and a good guide on filmmaking. Just go in with the mentality that "The King's Speech" is by no means something transcendent...

[b]My Final Rating:[/b] 85%

This is a very small film in that it can almost be described as a two man stage play because Colin Firth (Prince Albert) and Geoffrey Rush (Lionel Logue) are in virtually every scene in the movie and almost always appearing together. I look at it as a stage play also because most of the story takes place in only a few different locations such as Logue's office or in the future king's apartment and the film is about one main specific topic which is to cure the Prince and future King of his stutter disability.

The film starts off at a slow pace and stays that way for awhile until it begins to build itself into a grand crescendo by its end. When the Prince's brother, King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce) abdicates the throne to marry his American fiance, Prince Albert becomes the new King of England and calls himself King George VI and the pace of the film begins to quicken and move more rapidly.

The new king is faced with an immense problem because he cannot deliver a speech without stuttering over every other word, something that would not give much confidence to the people of England who look toward the royal family as though they were gods. This is where the commoner Logue steps in as a highly regarded speech therapist who is not a real doctor but one who has learned his craft and honed his skills strictly from his experience in the field. The interaction between these two characters is basically the whole movie and they both make the most of it.

THE BOTTOM LINE?
Colin Firth is outstanding in this demanding role and Geoffrey Rush matches him with the exact same excellence. In fact, it is difficult to imagine one winning an award without the other although that's what happened at The Golden Globe Awards. I have only seen four of the ten nominated movies for the Academy Awards, The King's Speech, The Kids Are All Right, Inception and The Social Network.

Of these films, Colin Firth should be the clear winner of the oscar and, in my opinion, Geoffrey Rush should win for Best Supporting Actor. I'm not sure I would call it the best picture, however, and I think that honor may go to either Black Swan or The Fighter both of which I have not yet seen. I think that the other films mentioned above will come away with very few honors and I will be surprised, although it won The Golden Globe Award, if The Social Network wins anything at all.

The only potentially offensive scenes that involve profanity are therapy sessions that use language and emotion in order to address the cause of the king's stammer. The story of "Bertie", the man who was made King of England upon his brother's abdication, which happened not long after their father, King George V (Michael Gambon), died.  Deemed "unfit" to be king at an early age, Bertie has spent his lifetime in the shadow of his brother, the new King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce).

Thrust into the public eye an unwilling king, Bertie has to overcome his stuttering, a speech impediment he's had since he was a boy.  His wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) finds Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) a specialty speech therapist.  When he refuses to treat Bertie any differently than any other patient, he is at first offended, but slowly learns Logue's methods work.

This is all in preperation for a country on the brink of war with little faith in their King.  While all the technical aspects (cinematography, sound, costumes, and sets) are all top-notch, the story itself is a mediocre rehash of the themes of Forrest Gump.  Personal mental shortcomings can be overcome to do important things.  What does this say about the society of today, though?  It's uplifting just to fit the genre, there is no real heart or passion behind any of it, this is the dramatic equivalent to a popcorn action flick.  

Colin Firth stutters and gets blustery, and he eventually learns to like Lionel and that the source of many of his problems were his strange childhood and the fact that he had no friends because of who he is.  Indeed.  This theme has been mined in far greater detail, with much more passion and interesting filmmaking than on display here.

Despite being decent and well made, it brings nothing new or exciting to the table, an easily forgettable film.

If a motion picture can get Queen Elizabeth's seal of approval, you know it's doing something right. The King's Speech is a well-made and well-versed film about the true and historic challenges facing King George V and his vocal and speaking abilities. He's looked at as someone who must lead England with compassion and determination. The problem is, it's hard to get his point across to millions of his people because of a stuttering problem. 

Because of this, The King (wonderfully played by Colin Firth) enlist the aid of a quasi therapist/failed actor (played by Geoffery Rush). Together, they try to overcome his fear and bring about a King the people can be proud to call their own. Along the way, revelations are uncovered and friendships are tested. The cast as a whole is great, including Helena Boham Carter as his ever-loving and supportive wife. The main attraction, however, are Firth and Rush, who play off each other wonderfully and have great chemistry in their scenes. 

The King's various rollercoaster of emotions range from sadness to depression to failure and ultimately to triumph and victory. All are greatly conveyed by Firth and his ability to do that makes him the front-runner for an Oscar for a reason. Overall, this is a very feel-good movie about events that impacted royalty and showed what can happen if you take a chance on something (or someone)  you feel can change you for the better.

I'm just going to be honest and say that I don't always like to go see movies that make me feel stressed or sad. This may sound like a reasonable statement, yet people go everyday to see movies that are terribly sad and stressful and usually make you cry. These usually win Oscars.  You may be thinking, "what about feel good movies"? Well, these so called "feel good" movies are really a big sham. The make you feel so bad and depressed that you want to go home and eat an entire case of frozen yogurts while crying on the phone to your sister, and then they give you one tiny, little happy moment for the protagonist that you jump with joy that something finally turned out ok for that person. They basically punch you in the gut and then give you a candy. But sometimes I would rather just go and see a nice, relaxing film with interesting characters and not have to worry about having a heart attack from a shear overdose of drama in the middle of the theatre. The kind of film that you sit with your hands behind your head and a smile on your face while your watching. This is the kind of movie that "The King's Speech" is.

 

Personally, I think the world really needs a movie like "The King's Speech". These days people seem to think that throwing your emotions over a water fall is the only way a film can be considered excellent. People seem to focus on the events surrounding the characters rather than the actual development of the characters. "The King's Speech" changes that. You may think that there isn't enough story to be put into a film about a guy's speech impediment, but the story isn't really whats important  to the film. It's the characters that really make the film. Everything in the film is focused on bring the development of each character up a level. Rather than story being a series of events that distract from character, they are things that become parts of the characters and make them even more interesting. And these events aren't extremely stressful, they are actually interesting, something a few movies out now could learn a thing or to about being. But what really makes these characters interesting are the actors behind them. Everyone is talking about Collin Firth's Academy Award winning performance as King George the VI, but I think that Geoffrey Rush's role as Lionel Logue was just as good and maybe even better. he did a perfect job at portraying a regular everyday guy. The character wasn't anything special, but like every person he has his own special qualities. He also really brought out the interesting relationship between King George and Lionel. It made us ask questions about equality down to it's essence and what it really means to people. And of course, he was hilarious. At least 50% of the funniest lines in that movie came from Rush. He has fantastic comedic timing, but in a realistic sort of way that you usually don't find in comedies. It made the film generally interesting and pleasant to watch. Of course, Rush wasn't the only fantastic actor, the entire cast (which has 3 actors from Harry Potter in it, I might add) did a great job with the film. The only one I could think of being a problem was the guy who played Peter Petegrew in Harry Potter playing Churchill. He really overplayed the role, which somewhat surprised me because I didn't think that Churchill was a role you could overplay. But apparently you can. Still though, it hardly went noticed with the perfect formulation of the movie. Another thing I think should be noticed is the use of music in the film. In the final scene when they had the classical music playing, I found myself moving my hands like a  conductor with the flow of it. The scene was like a waltz, except with words rather than feet. It is truly a fantastic film.

I have heard people say that the film was a suck up for the Oscars. It was a period piece with British actors and based on historical events. But you know what, I don't care. I enjoyed it and thats all that really matters in the end. If you haven't seen it yet, then make sure to if you enjoy having a genuinely pleasant good time.

There are few films that manage to succeed in every--or at least, most--major category in the department of film. There are the areas of sound editing, film editing, musical score, acting, directing, and of course producing. Only one other film was released in 2010 that matched and exceeded the expecations of these categories, and that film was The Social Network. The film that succeeded in the same way, albiet with a tad less flair, was the phenomenal The King's Speech.

King George VI, after his father's timely death and the controversial abdication of his brother, King Edward I, is suddenly handed the responsibilities of an entire nation. Not only does he not want these duties, but he has a tragic immpediment; he has a terrible stutter, and as such, cannot give a proper speech.

And so, his wife--who has been constantly looking for help for her poor hubby--gives a visit to the last man on her list for help: Lionel Logue. Called controversial, unprofessional, and a little strange, Lionel is the man for the job: royaly just doesn't know it yet. Lionel agrees to help George--or "Bertie"--and the act of such sparks a friendship that will inspire confidence not only to the man without a voice, but to the world that was anxiously waiting for one.

Filled with antagionisingly good performances, fine writing, and a brilliant course of directing, The King's Speech soars above all the competition that it faced this year: even the critically acclaimed The Social Network had a hard time keeping up with it.

In short, a moving, astounding period picture of a man's last hope, and the troubles that he must go through in order to reach it. If you come for only Colin Firth's act of pure amazement here, it is only in the final act that you can truly realize all the commotion he managed to spark up.

When you go see a movie that's based on a true story, especially one based on a particular person's life, there's no promising the the story is going to have that fuzzy movie feeling. Real life doesn't usually have a classic three-act story arc. The ending of a biopic often peters out or just ends abruptly.

This is part of what makes The King's Speech so wonderful. It has all the touching gravity of a true story, but still moves along and captures your attention like a work of total fiction. This is probably because the writers made the wise decision to focus on a particular (and particularly volatile) chapter in the main character's life. And what a main character! Set in the 1920s and '30s, the film focuses on Berty (a terrific Colin Firth), aka Britain's King George VI, father of Queen Elizabeth II.

Having lived in the shadow of his brother Edward and his formidable father (a king, after all, makes for a pretty intimidating role model), King George V, Berty (as his family calls him) must overcome his lifelong feelings of inadequacy in his country's proverbial hour of need. This is not as simple a task as it may sound - the would-be king has suffered from a severe stutter for nearly all his life, and no Royal Speech Therapist or Vocal Doctor to the Crown of any type can seem to help. Having more or less given up hope, Berty's wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter, who, my dad observed, looked "prettier" than she has in many of her recent crazy roles) turns to an outsider, a speech therapist not sanctioned by the throne. Geoffrey Rush makes a typically spirited turn as Lionel Logue, the unorthodox specialist who breaks with the typical royal-subject deference guidelines and becomes a true friend to the future head of Great Britain.

The King's Speech manages to simultaneously tell a true story, make speech therapy dramatic and exciting, stir up the patriotic emotions tied to World War II and facing up to Hitler's Germany, all while leading up to a breathtaking climax disguised as a long, slow radio address. It succeeds beautifully. This one should serve as a lesson to biopic makers everywhere.

A slow yet compelling story which has taken the world of moviegoers by storm, the Kingâ(TM)s Speech claimed four Academy Awards and continues to mesmerize audiences with its stellar cast, exquisite time period design and story content. As the true story of King George VI and the help he got from a speech therapist to make one of the biggest speeches of his day is told with truth and dignity, we all should know we are seeing the best film of the year.
Starting in the mid 1930s and lasting until 1939 when England declared war on Germany, King George VI rises to the throne with wife, Queen Elizabeth and two daughters by his side. Though he should be thrilled (especially after surpassing his older brother who chose a relationship with a divorcee over being a king), he is completely consumed by his seemingly uncontrollable speech-stammering problem. When his loving wife (known today as the Queen Mum) discovers Australian therapist Lionel Logue to train him to improve his speech, the plan works amazingly well and a friendship develops. As trial and error lead to the kingâ(TM)s speech of the century, a remarkable tale is told with stamina and professionalism from all involved.
From Colin Firthâ(TM)s Oscar-winning performance to the filmâ(TM)s overall ability to hold oneâ(TM)s attention span (despite a lengthy runtime), the film is covered in potential from head to toe and plays it out dutifully. The film also sets itself up so the audience actually senses the tension Firth feels on the big day, drawing one in more than ever. Stay tuned after the ending as the rest of the story is told, which may be the most uplifting part of all. Film additionally won Oscars for director (Tim Hopper) and original screenplay. Helena Bonham Carter and Geoffrey Rush also would deservedly had won had it perhaps been a different year.

It's a fine, absorbing work, built with brilliance and without excessive showiness or flash. It feels, in fact, like a classic virtually upon its arrival. Tom Hooper's terrific, Oscar-worthy film is not merely a spot-on period piece; it's also a heartfelt study in the shadings of courage, a film about duty and friendship that's often warmly funny and sometimes painful to watch.Like Bertie's struggle, there's so much wonderment to articulate about this film that being mistaken for a stammering idiot is a risk. It is an intelligent, winning drama fit for a king -- and the rest of us. And this year, there were far too few of those coming from Hollywood. See it, then say it for yourself: The King's Speech is the best movie of 2010. Engrossing and moving story of a alternately warm and combative relationship. The King's Speech isn't just referring to a literal speech made by the king at the outset of war with nazi Germany, but also to the king's stutter: a speech impediment that can inspire or cripple a country in it's time of need.  

The film begins many years earlier, when Prince Albert (Colin Firth) delivers his first speech in front of a radio microphone with disasterous results.  Most of us would give up public speaking after such a nightmare but the royal family have a duty to uphold.  Albert's wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) persuades him to visit an Australian speech specialist named Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) whose unorthodox techniques at first repel the stuffy Duke of Wales.  It's only after Logue proves some success that the two begin to form a friendship.  When Albert's father, King George V dies, the crown is passed to his older brother, David, who accedes the throne as King Edward VIII.  David however, has fallen in love with an American divorcee, and amidst scandal, gives up his throne for the woman, leaving the monarchy to an unprepared Prince Albert.  It's "Bertie's" relationship with his teacher Lionel that helps him get control of his stutter and overcome his fear of his destiny.

As far as films about the Royals are concerned, "The Queen", starring Helen Mirren is probably the better film, but The King's Speech is more about the wonderous friendship between teacher and student/King and commoner anyway.  And perhaps it was the oscar-winning expectations that led the climactic titular speech to be well, anticlimactic, or perhaps the movie is much ado about very little.

Beautifully shot and superbly acted yet at times I thought the story was a little slow and at times boring.  The King's Speech stars Colin Firth as King George VI and Geoffery Rush as his speech therapist Lionel Logue.  The film follows King George VI's, or Bertie's, rise to become King of England, and his struggle with his speech impediment while also dealing with the life of being in the Royal Family.  All the while the beginning of World War II is lingering in the background providing for much of the political side of the film. 

The direction of the film was brilliantly done by Tom Hooper, especially during the scenes between Firth and Rush.  Most of the scenes are just simple conversations between the two but Hooper creates this beautiful environment, often in Lionel's office, reminding me a lot of a painting, or perhaps a portrait to more accurate.  He also excels during George's speeches to the public by really creating a sense of anxiety in the audience that George himself is feeling with his speech impediment.  Most of all, he captures the post World War II England beautifully immersing you into the environment.  

The most impressive aspect of The King's Speech by far is the cast.  Firth is at his absolute best as King George VI and won the much deserved Best Actor Oscar.  He brings out George's strong, stubborn personality while also showing his vulnerability while very realistically speaking with a stutter.  The best scenes with Firth are during his sessions with his speech therapist, Geoffery Rush.  They play off each other so well during these scenes and they are only strengthened by Hooper's direction.  Helena Bonham Carter plays Queen Elizabeth and as always is a strong presence on the screen that only aides Firth's performance as the King.  Guy Pearce also shows up a little during the film, as George's brother Edward, or King Edward for a small stint, and proves that once again (Animal Kingdom) that he can keep up with high caliber performers.  

The story itself is where I felt The King's Speech was faulty, and it may not be fair to just say it's the King's Speech or just any historical film in general.  The scenes between Firth and Rush are incredibly well done and pretty fun to watch on screen.  However the scenes that are in between are where I feel it slows down and I found myself just wanting Rush to come back on screen.  I do understand that those scenes are important to the character development of George because they mainly deal with the Royal Family, but I just found them to be too boring.  

Overall, The King's Speech is very well made film and in terms of a historical biography, it does it's job.  I just found it dull at times but luckily the direction and casting was enough to keep me entertained and interested in the characters.  I did enjoy the inside look it gave at the Royal Family, and especially what their role is in politics.  The pressure and stress that simply being born in to a family is a pretty unbelievable thought.  Being born into royalty and the pressure that not only comes from your family, but The Royal Family at that.  It's well worth a viewing even if it's only to just see the performances, but as a film on the whole I thought it failed with the overall story and it's not the production's fault, I just think the source material wasn't really there to begin with.  I felt like I was watching a history textbook and that's the kind of material I try to escape when watching a movie.

"If I'm King, where's my power? Can I form a government? Can I levy a tax, declare a war? No! And yet I am the seat of all authority. Why? Because the nation believes that when I speak, I speak for them. But I can't speak."

PERSONAL BLURB:
*clap* *clap* *clap*

THE PLOT:
The King's Speech tells the story of the man who became King George VI after his brother for the first time in history abdicated the thrown. Though his journey was not easy, he was a King unable to speak to his people due to a severe speech defect. In order to overcome his problem and deal with the matters at hand (a little thing called WWII) he calls upon the help of a rather unorthodox speech therapist named Lionel Logue. Through a set of unexpected techniques, and as a result of an unlikely friendship, the two are able to boldly lead the country through war.

THE GOOD:
WWII in the Background: 
Very few films that take place during WWII can have Hitler play a supporting role to a speech impediment, AND have jokes about Hitler's strong speech play so well. The film is able to balance the severity of the situation with a very honest and realistic perspective. At times they tread on some possibly dangerous ground, but because they handle the topic with such grace, what could be considered rude or offensive is actually quite interesting, important and even at times humorous.

Colin Firth: 
Not only does he have a stutter, a lisp, an accent different from his, he also has to sound like the real King himself who has a very distinct voice. Not only does Firth give an incredibly compelling emotional performance, but the way he physically transforms himself is beyond impressive. 
It's extremely complex and since his character is a stoic King he has very little room to express himself. A slight grimace or a tonal shift in his voice has to speak volumes and luckily, due to his grasp of the character, it does. 

Empathy for the King: 
It's hard to make people really side with a person they feel is so distant from them. This is one of the best representation of what a King really has to go through that has been put on the screen. You are able to find empathy for the man beneath the crown and somehow relate to the pressures that he has to face.

Supporting Cast: 
Geoffrey Rush and Helena Bonham Carter both give stellar performances that help to add to the films chemistry. Rush's great timing and Carter's endearing demeanor both help to round who King George VI is and more importantly the people who helped make him the great king he was.

The Score: 
This was a really beautiful, subtle yet powerful score that once again added to the grace of the film without ever distracting from what was taking place.

THE BAD:
The Trailer: 
DON'T watch the trailer for this film. Trust me, this might be the best package you see all year, its got it all and the trailer ruins some of the best moments in the film.

OVERALL: 
Easily a favorite of mine. The story is compelling, moving, with the perfect balance of uplifting, and humorous; the details of the epoch are recreated lovingly and precisely, but most importantly, it is a wonderfully told story of a human condition, of one man who wanted to overcome the obstacles on the way to accomplish his mission as the ruler able to reach out to the millions of people in the speeches that would make all the difference, and how love and support from his Queen, and the friendship, understanding and willing to listen from a "commoner" helped him to do so.

Sounded like a waste of time to me, yet time and time again i am wrong, first impressions aren't always right.

This film blew me away because it managed to be so powerful, considering its relatively tame story. The acting first and foremost was wonderful by the entire cast, i especially loved Geoffrey Rush's role as the man behind it all, who manages King Edware with all his might in order for him to succeed.

The movie is much more than a King with a speech problem, its about the bond of true frienship, the faith and support of a loving wife, the betrayal of family, the power of pressure and it addresses the question of self confidence, no matter what position you may be in socially. The film was very grey and dark, with typical stone colours throughout, the cinematography was beautiful for what it was and the choice of actors seemed perfectly fitting for the film.

The script was very gripping and powerful, my only complaint was that it did indeed start off slowly but after the first 30 minutes the film manages a great flow and you are behind King Edward the whole way. The music was charismatic and indeed triumphant especially towards the end as the story evolves into a more happy tune.

In the end, it is true the film doesn't have many physically gripping scenes, no intense fights, no blood, no sex, no rock and roll and not much that would stereotypically amuse "young" fans, but both mature and immature minds alike would end up loving this warm film (look out for the cussing scene). Hann dugir sera væl at stama uttan at gera tað irriterandi og fáa tað til at síggja realistiskt út - hann vísir eisini sannførandi pressið við at vera kongur og hava ta størstu ábyrgdina í landinum. British films are an odd one. For a number of reasons, I never know how to react to them. The chest-beating, patriotic part of me always wants to think that they are excellent and my other more curmudgeonly part wants to put them down as the cheap, illegitimate step-child of Hollywood. This dilemma - American screenwriter aside - was in full force when I went to go and see The King's Speech this week. For, that Colin Firth seemed a shoo-in for The Best Actor Oscar and the movie was nominated for another 11 gongs made me vicariously proud; yet I also thought it would be a cynical, trite royal story constructed solely to bother award ceremonies and please the British and American publics. In a way, both of my initial fears and feelings were confirmed.

As everyone will already know, The King's Speech is about Bertie, The future King George VI of England and his attempts to overcome his stammer before, during and after the abdication crisis. His final goal is addressing the nation by radio at the outbreak of WWII. Said in those terms, it shouldn't work; but it resoundingly does. What might initially be seen as a fairly pointless story about an uptight, unsavoury and unwilling monarch is granted a degree of universality through his unconventional relationship with equally unorthodox Aussie speech therapist, Lionel Logue. This 'bromance' (as Colin Firth has incongruously described it) is the source of much laughter and the human heart of the film. Bertie, or "His Majesty" as he insists on being called, must conquer his inhibitions to overcome his stammer and be King.

As has been mentioned, Colin Firth is magnificent as the stuttering king: convincingly stammering the audience into a visceral frenzy. The supporting cast, especially Geoffrey Rush as Logue and Helena Bonham-Carter as Queen Elizabeth, are also fantastic. So what was it that left me somewhat cold? The movie also seemed well-pitched and very well directed. There have been multiple reports of audience ovations in Dublin and elsewhere. But somehow it didn't click with me.

It wasn't really the re-writing  (or airbrushing, depending on your take) of a mildly unsavoury, Nazi-sympathizing chapter in British history that left me indifferent. Though, while I do find that slightly unsettling, one must inevitably bow to the spectacle in these types of films and provide entertainment, not existential angst. I think I simply found it too perfectly-crafted: a decent film about a human subject that held no interest for me at all. Shallow where it could have been profound, it seemed to skirt the big issues. Involving but pointless as it had nothing new to say about human nature, it was a very contradictory affair. Worth going to see if only to see what all the fuss is about, 127 Hours has my vote.

The King's Speech is not about a speech or a stuttering king, it is about finding the courage in each one of us through making peace with our fears and tolerating our shortcomings.
The movie was touching, witty (thanks to the unbelievably beautiful script) and sometimes incredibly funny!

Long live the King, but how long will he rule if he cannot even address his subjects?  The Kings Speech tells the story of Prince Albert(the man who would eventually become King George VI) who has a very pronounced stutter which makes it almost impossible for him to speak to the people. Colin Firth plays the titular character who must deal with his impediment. Any actor knows that portraying a character with a physical defect or speech problem is difficult and making it believable is an even greater challenge. Colin Firth achieves this with great skill and has you believing the whole time that he has this problem. The Prince tries many methods to cure his stutter(including using marbles which almost seems like an homage to My Fair Lady) but nothing works so his wife(played beautifully by Helena Bonham Carter) finds an unorthodox speech therapist Lionel Logue.(played by Geoffrey Rush) to help. Logue soon realizes that in order to help the prince he must get to know him and become a friend which considering the Prince's position was unheard of in his time and would still be unusual to see today on some level. Throughout the Prince's journey you feel his pain and you find that even the royals have humanity. The scale and scope of the shots helps to support the strength and intensity of the story and at some points its almost like you are seeing how the prince sees himself and the world around him. The most powerful scenes are the most simple and every word that is said you can believe in. The prince hopes to never become king for he believes he is not meant to be one which is not made easy by the actions of his brother(played by the often underappreciated Guy Pierce). The way Rush and Firth play off each other is fascinating to watch. To understand the guts that Logue must have had to try to reach the prince and through is actions we see that there is one way the two men are equal and that is in their insecurities. Through it all we see what this story is, it's the tale of two men, one trying to become the man everyone wants him to be, the other discovering that in order to help the prince he needs to help him see that the man he is is the man his subjects need .This movie is one of those stories that is destined to become eternal. This will grab and having you thinking about going back long after you have left the theatre. I believe that the King's Speech is a triumph and is destined to rule for many years to come.

Okay, so I've been inactive for a while (again), and have a lot of things I've been meaning to review, so I'm starting with the most recently watched, and will (hopefully) work my way back from there. Anyways for now here's my 46th review: The King's Speech.

       I'm a little late on this one, but I'd been meaning to see it long before it won Best Picture, and so I finally did. A little disclaimer: because I waited, I actually saw the edited version, so I didn't get the F-words, (oh well!). Anyways, just in case you don't know, The King's Speech is about Prince Albert, (later King George VI), who apparently had a bad stammer.

       I'm just going to go ahead and say it: The King's Speech is nothing short of an extraordinary film. It's not just flawless, I would say there's hardly a moment that isn't great. Such a film is certainly worth my time reviewing even if the verdict is already quite obvious.

    Colin Firth gives an incredibly authentic, vulnerable performance that was well-deserving of the award. Helena Bonham Carter does a wonderful job of being the supportive wife, princess and queen. Other supporting roles worthy of mention are Guy Pearce and Michael Gambon. But out of all the cast, the standout performance has to be Geoffrey Rush as the Albert's speech therapist, who is simply otherworldly great, and yet completely human and believable. This is actually the pattern for the entire cast: everyone is authentic. It's not often you get that in a movie all about royalty.
    
      There are so many great moments in this film, from the moving final titular speech to Geoffrey Rush playing Shakespeare games with his sons to one of the funniest swearing scenes of all time, (even in the edited version). You could watch any given five minutes of this film and instantly see why it's great.

        The King's speech is marvel of film-making. With phenomenal performances, and an incredibly satisfying overall experience. Certainly one of the best of the year, and a worthy best picture winner. 10/10

Almost immediately after The Kings Speech was released it was being touted to win every award under the sun. The film was surrounded by hype with many calling it one of the best British films ever made. It's nowhere near that level but credit must still be given to director Tom Hooper for managing to make a film about the British royal family not only tolerable but both interesting and entertaining.

The plot tells the part life story of King George VI, a man suffered terribly with a speech impediment from the age of four. It documents his rapid and unexpected rise to the throne and details the relationship between the King and his layman speech therapist who, despite his unorthodox methods, managed to greatly improve the Kings speech, so much so that he was able to make many radio speeches during World War 2 despite his debilitating condition.

What elevates The Kings Speech above the usual Royal Family dross is how well it's written, the script really is top notch and provides both drama and plenty of humourous moments. The acting from all is excellent but Colin Firth as King George is outstanding, not only does he portray the speech impediment to perfection but also the sheer frustration and anger at not being able to speak correctly no matter how hard you try. The relationship between King George and his therapist (Geoffrey Rush) is very well done and is the backbone to the film. The climax is quite touching as George finally manages to make a speech as unhindered as he could hope and is a suitable ending for an uplifting film.

Technically excellent and with an interesting story, The Kings Speech pulls of the incredibly difficult task of making a Royal Family film seem interesting. It's a good watch and quite funny but the actual plot isn't exactly thrilling and although provides entertainment it is not a film you will ever feel the inclination to watch again. It's certainly worth one watch though for Colin Firths excellent performance if for nothing else.

What a great film. More than that; it is a testament to the fact that a quiet, unasserting movie can both entertain us, and teach us valuable lessons, but only if we let it.

The Duke of York has a problem. Albert, who becomes George VI, is supposed to deliver a speech on his sick father's behalf (George V). In front of thousands physically, and millions via radio, he only manages to deliver what we would call a "fail". At first ejecting short groups of words, his confidence spirals down to uttering random vowels and consonants. Later we are shown how his current speech therapist is awkwardly attempting to cure Albert of his stammer. Unfortunately he is only one in a long line of unsuccessful therapists, when his wife, Elizabeth (future Queen Mother), secretly seeks out the assistance of a "controversial" specialist: Lionel Logue. 

Lionel demands total equality with his patients, even royal ones. For instance, he and George must be on a first-name basis.
"It's 'Your Royal Highness', and then 'Sir'."
"How about 'Bertie'?"
"Only my family uses that!"
"Perfect."
At first this disregard for social expectations comes as a shock to George, but he can only improve his speech when he lets go of his pride. A nice dose of reality for all of us; we often seek out the assistance of others, but fail to completely open up to them. Another thing to think about also comes from this sharp script. In their first session, George pulls out a cigarette to smoke.
"Stop that!"
"My physicians recommend smoking. It relaxes the throat."
"They're idiots. It only irritates your lungs."
"They've all been Knighted."
"That makes it official."
Just because a practice is endorsed by popular figures, that doesn't make it good for you!

But enough with the lessons, how is the rest of the movie? In a word, flawless. Acting is done by an ensemble of British masters; Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush are unsurprisingly brilliant. Helena Bonham Carter, well-known for her gothic presence in Tim Burton movies, does a nice U-turn here as the ever gentle and supporting Duchess of York. The cinematography is simple and functional for most of the film with conventional shots of famous England fog, but many segments are notable for their fluidity and use of wide-angle lenses.

Comedy is deftly integrated into the story. In one session, Lionel encourages George to swear like a sailor, as he doesn't stutter when doing so. This scene is a little unsettling, but also hilarious considering his upbringing. Again, culture shock is played very smartly.

One last lesson, but it's the most important one. Over the course of the therapy, Lionel tries to stamp out the fear and lack of self-confidence that has George by the throat, so to speak. George confers his painful child memories, including how his father George V even encouraged his siblings to taunt about his stammer. He has been given mental hints since a young age that his is not capable of being a king, and now he believes it. What England needed at that point was more than what he thought he could be. Lionel teaches George that pompous royalty will not get him very far. What matters is that you have a voice, and are able to use to influence millions.

The King's Speech may have been no-holds-barred, unmitigated Oscar bait, but the fact remains, the film was tasty Oscar bait that hooks the viewer with line and sinker in tow. In fact, it plays almost as successfully as other well done historical dramas, such as Apollo 13. The viewer already knows the ending, and yet director Hooper and screenwriter Seidler manage to pepper the proceeding with an element of suspense and infuse a story about a monarch's inability to speak without stammering with relevancy and urgency to a point where the viewer manages to forget, even for an instant, the possibility that an actual speech was made, stammer-free, by the king at the start of England's involvement in the second world war.

This carefully and effectively executed vision resulted in the bevy of Oscar nominations and wins for the film. There is no denying that Firth's performance contains an element of brilliance, as he portrayed the King of the title with quiet determination, subtlety, nuance, and sincerity. It cannot have been easy for Firth to take on a persona and character so close to a living, breathing Queen (his queen in fact), much less a man who struggled with his speech, and yet he did so with aplomb. Until his Oscar win, Firth may have been one of the most underrated actors of cinema today, but this role and his subsequent award are welcome validation indeed.

Similarly, Geoffrey Rush is phenomenal as Lionel. His chemistry with Firth, no matter how dramatized or fictionalized this relationship might ultimately have been rendered for the sake of the film, is the reason to watch this movie. This unlikely odd couple is what makes the viewer care. Similar relationships have been given the big screen treatment before, but seldom has such a friendship been executed so effortlessly and genuinely as it has been by Firth and Rush. Rush carried himself with such poise and offered so much depth to his speech therapist, his performance could only be characterized as charming.

Carter was also decent as the spitfire Duchess of York, and Pearce lent an edge to the pretty/playboy aspects of the King Edward VIII described in history books. The entire ensemble was terribly convincing and created the necessary suspension of disbelief that allowed the viewer to travel back in time and into the private quarters of the Royal Family.

Additionally, Hooper did a fine job. Perhaps, his style is not as fresh as David Fincher or as thematically bold as Darren Aronofsky, but he injected his own creative signature into the mix, aided by the superb skills of his technical designers. The art direction and costume design were exquisite, reflecting the extravagance and tenure of the few years depicted in the film and the level of society to which the viewer bears witness; the cinematography and editing were wonderfully creative, noticeably in Lionel's study, where camera zooms conveyed the passage of time, different lenses offered images equatable to constriction and tightness, and blocking created interesting emotional juxtapositions between the two characters in focus. The score was also lovely and might otherwise have won the top award, if not for Trent Reznor's cutting edge and original offering for The Social Network.

The King's Speech is not an exemplar of cinematic perfection - it's not a masterpiece. At times, the film feels a bit manipulative in obvious gambits by the filmmakers to reach for the heartstrings of the potential audience and to give a tug. This type of manipulative feel is common to historical dramas where facts are changed, exaggerated, or minimized for maximum dramatic effect, sometimes to the detriment of historical accuracy. Also, in an ironic reflection of its subject matter, the film's tone occasionally conveys a prim sort of stuffiness, accentuating the repressed and proper life of the royals at the forefront of the film but also carrying the tone of a dry documentary or the dustiness of old library stacks. Neither one of these sentiments last for any length of time; the film may betray this manipulative or stuffy tendency only in moments, but the moments are noticeable and tend to disturb the otherwise even and engaging pace of the film.

Still, what is offered is a good story that is well acted, well directed, and inspiring in its pedantically obvious way, and while some might be turned off by what can be regarded as mainstream sappiness, there is nothing wrong with a feel-good movie every now and again. Not all Best Pictures have to be wildly dramatic, edgy, and/or dark; if nothing else, Oscar has propped up a variety of motion pictures for the award of Best Picture, even if their choices were less inspiring than the films that were actually chosen. In any event, The King's Speech is nothing if not genuine in its aims and ability to inspire its audience.

The KingÂ´s Speech is a fine example of actor driven movie done right. The movie proves once again that sometimes it only takes great actors to make a simple movie fly. 

The movie is about English King Edward the VI's rough road to kingship. Becoming the king of Britania after the scandalous retirement of his brother, Edward VI inherited the throne of England on the dawn of World War 2. To make matters worse he suffered from from serious stammering preventing him from giving public speeches and quite simply rendering him unfit for the ceremonial role of the King. Enough said, Edward the VI had very little going fom him on his starting day, but with the help of an unorthodox speech therapeutist Lionel Logue, Edward VI managed to overcome his condition. Logue put the king through rigoreous training, both mental and physical, to overcome his stammering. The movie builds on these session and uses them quite cleverly to shed light into the Kings life. 

As said, The KingÂ´s Speech relies solely on the actors for resolution, luckily Colin Firth is up to the challenge and give a once in a lifetime role as the Stammering King. The other main actors are also topnotch, especially Helena Bonham Carter as the queen and Geoffrey Rush as the speech therapeutist shine bright. There is however no question who is the main star of the show, Colin Firth's role as the king is remarkable. He manages to brings the best and the worse out of the king Edward the VI. At times with his temper the king must have been a real bastard, on the other hand one cannot help but to feel symphatetic for the man; he is after all unwillingly put into a impossible situation. 

As no movie is perfect, The KingÂ´s Speech has a negative side to it as well. No matter how great the Colin Firth stage charm is, he cannot hide the fact that the movie is somewhat too long. The king's condition and the royalty's affairs sure are interesting but the movie loses it's strongest memontum around 1h 30min. Even with this nag, it does not change the fact the The King Speech unguestionably belongs to the best movies 2010 league and should be seen by everyone.

The King's Speech is amongst a genre of film I enjoy the most.  Historical dramas seem to prevail in my mind as a testament to the strength of a nation or an individual in this case. The King's Speech is not about the difficulties of King George VI's ability to speak in public but is about his inability to believe in himself. King George VI (Colin Firth) was never meant to be king, his brother King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce) was crowned after the death of their father King George V. As a child, King George VI also known as Bertie was abused and mistreated. No speech impediment is established at birth, every baby learns how to speak unless they have a mental disability. So to solve Bertie's problem meant uncovering his past to coop with the future. After many speech therapists and many failed attempts at change, Bertie's wife Queen Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) tracks down an unconventional speech therapist that focuses on the physiological aspect of King George VI's problem. This amazing role is played by Geoffrey Rush as Lionel Logue. While waiting in anticipation for this film and watching the previews I was expecting a story that solely focused on the therapy of altering Bertie's impairment but instead I was pleasantly surprised that the film focused on the dynamics of the Royal family, showing the problems that lie in any family and the frailty that can be created due to those unaddressed issues. The King's Speech comes at the precipice of the Second World War and when a country needed a fearless leader, King George VI felt like he could not deliver. Through the training of Lionel Logue and the spirit of King George VI this film shows us how an individual can overcome his biggest fear to become an inspiration to a nation. I see the perfection in this film, from the powerful camera angles, amazing dialogue and perfect delivery from every actor. This is a historical film that will stay in my mind forever and when it comes time for others to stand up to their enemies and show their true voice I recommend watching this film as inspiration. My only complaint is that I wished the movie continued throughout the War and showed us how King George VI led his people through their darkest hour.

The 2011 best picture winner "The King's Speech" will be released this Tuesday April 19th on DVD and Blu-Ray. Was it the best movie of 2010? Not really. Let's face it, the only one on par with his caliber this year was Javier Bardem. Firth certainly wasn't going to lose to Jesse Eisenberg or James Franco. Jeff Bridges was good but not good enough for consecutive wins.

Tom Hooper, this year's best director Oscar winner does a bang up job with the Actors but didn't really show us anything new as far as style and tone. As previously mentioned the wide angle lenses were a nice touch but in comparison to the masterfully directed "The Social Network" this one didn't quite hit the mark of more current cinematic masterpieces that have recently won the best picture Oscar like "The Departed", "No Country for Old Men" or even last year's winner "The Hurt Locker." I won't be adding this film to my collection but if I find it flipping through channels one night I'd give it a second viewing. My advice is if you haven't seen "The Social Network", "The Fighter", "Blue Valentine" or "Black Swan" then it'd be safe to skip this one until you do. If I were to make a top ten list of movies in 2010, this one would be towards the bottom. I didn't cry, I didn't get excited and I wasn't truly blown away by any of the acting or directing. Why did it win best picture over "The Social Network?" Who knows? I guess we can chalk it up to the Academy getting it wrong again, like they did with "Crash", "Ordinary People", "How Green was my Valley" and countless others. It baffles me how a movie like "Midnight Cowboy" can win Best Picture in 1969 but "The Social Network" loses to a glorified BBC costume drama in 2011. There couldn't be a better suited film to define the year then "The Social Network". A-lot of critics are writing it off as to say the Academy is just made up of old people and that innovation is lost on them. That can't be true. Remember three years ago when "There will be Blood" and "No Country for Old Men" were on the same ballot? Or the fact that they nominated Robert Downey Jr. For playing a black man two years ago? It's not political either. In the 70's when George C. Scott and Marlon Brando denounced their respective best actor oscars for "Patton" and "The Godfather" they were both nominated again the very next year. Clearly that decision was based on the quality of their respective performances in "The Hospital" and "Last Tango in Paris."
I guess we'll never know how the Oscar machine works and in that sense the broadcast will always be unpredictable albeit in a sometimes irritating fashion. 
All bitterness aside, "The King's Speech" is an undeniably good movie. Winning best picture wasn't it's only merit. It scored a 95% on Rotten Tomatoes and did something like 400 million at the box office. Which means both critics and audiences alike must've loved it. Just not my cup of tea, but whatevs.

The King's Speech: An Oscar-Winning Film For The Whole Family
The King's Speech, a 2010 British historical drama, won the Academy Award for Best Picture, Best Director (Tom Hooper), Best Original Screenplay (David Seidler) and Best Actor (Colin Firth). If you haven't watched this intelligent and witty film yet, do it. Not just to find out a bit more about British historical figures of the middle of the 20th century, but also to get amazed at the exquisite acting of the leading actors and the originality of the screenplay. You certainly don't happen to see royal figures swearing like rascals and making friends with ordinary speech therapists on a regular basis. Unlike many other films, The King's Speech is a striking demonstration of the fact that monarchs have the same weaknesses and fears as ordinary people do. 
 The action is set in 1920-1930ies when The British Empire was practically the most powerful monarchy including almost a half of the world's population. King George V (Michael Gambon) was on the throne having two direct successors: his older son Edward (Guy Pearce), an unreliable adventure lover, and his younger son 'Bertie' (Colin Firth), the Duke of York, always treated like a disabled because of his constant stammering. Quite fair given his disability even to tell a simple story to young daughters in the evening. Who would want such a monarch? As his crowned father claims, with the invention of the radio, a monarch should be able to do a little more than just 'look good in a uniform and not fall off his horse'. A real monarch should be able to boost the spirits of people with moving speeches. George V himself is very capable of making speeches in warm and sweet tones. Bertie speaks as if his mouth is filled with marbles he uses during lessons with regular doctors. The doctors who suggest that smoking is important to 'calm the nerves'. 
Struggling with his disability, Albert nearly gives it up when his caring and incredibly supportive wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) finds an unconventional Australian speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) who implements the methods of a psychologist in his practice. The relationship between the heir to the throne and Lionel is the heart of the film. Having grown up within a bell jar, Albert is not accustomed to being called by the first name or given friendly advice. Lionel, in his turn, is pretty firm in his decision to treat the patient as an equal. As Albert has a quick temper, he breaks with Lionel after the latter suggests that Albert would become a better monarch than his brother Edward who is going to give up the throne for the possibility to marry a two-time-divorcee Wallis Simpson. In the end, however, Alfred, a forced monarch, has to make a six-minute speech to declare war with Germany, the speech which is surely going to be heard by millions of people worldwide. A devoted friend, Lionel is there when Alfred approaches the microphone with all the delight of those marching toward a guillotine. That is the culmination point of the film. The scene turned out to be amazingly strong as the formerly tongue-tied monarch manages to make a historical speech to the world. 
In brief, The King's Speech is a history-based picture. The story tells the viewer about a stuttering royal destined to become King George VI and his speech therapist and life-time friend. It also gives a short overview of the historical background of the time. The King's Speech is a film for the whole family.

The King's Speech adheres quite closely to the propriety of most critics' darlings; it's warm, confident, inoffensive, funny, gorgeously designed, and sublimely acted. It's the kind of movie more than capable of garnering numerous nominations, but not substantial enough to win. It's the kind of movie that stays in people's consciousness for the perennial length of an Oscar race, enjoying a transitory success as "one of the year's best", but few will ever proclaim it "one of the best". It's the kind of movie that Geoffrey Rush does all the time.

Here is a true but surprisingly uncommonly told story, that of King George VI (Colin Firth) and his attempts to overcome a debilitating stammer that plagued him from his troubled youth. Remedying the hesitant monarch's lack of testimony is Tom Hooper, hot off directing the candidly satirical The Damned United. As portrayed by the filmmakers and Firth, George VI was a hot-headed, somewhat impetuous malcontent; well-meaning and humble, but crippled by anxiety, low self-esteem, and his frustrating idiosyncrasy. At first the Duke of York, and eventually King of England, he had responsibility and prestige thrust upon him; his modesty proved an undoing in a world that asked far more of him than he could offer. His feelings of misplacement in the Royal Family reflect the film's overall sentiment; for a movie that sounds as if it boasts a highly ambitious and pontificating concept, its agenda is instead one of far smaller a scale. It matters not that George is of royal descent, nor that many of the characters are recognizable heads of state today (his daughter Elizabeth, most noticeably), nor that while this man struggles with curing an oratory defect, Europe is gearing up for World War II. Historically noteworthy these facts may be, but they feature merely as grace notes in a deeply personal story about a man who happens to be King George VI. It's not quite Sofia Coppola material, but the woes of the over-privileged are rarely this accessible or free of condescension.

Still, it's not very clear what story Hooper and screenwriter David Seidler are trying to tell. The title is, of course, pretty indicative, and at first George's stammer-battling is the main focus of the film. Following one of the - intentionally - cringiest scenes of the year, wherein George tries and fails to deliver a speech to a crowd of equally-embarrassed onlookers (it's important that his predicament is often played for laughs, as it keeps George from becoming a maudlin boo-hooer, and gives a more balanced and realistic view of his handicap), he seeks out the help of Lionel Logue (Rush), a quirky Australian speech therapist (there far too many of those). This is at the the behest of his endlessly supportive wife, former Queen Mother Elizabeth (the divine and quintessentially British Helena Bonham Carter, who isn't given enough to do, but is more of a delight here than Tim Burton ever allows her to be).

George and Logue's sessions serve as the crux of the film, with both men building an unlikely camaraderie with one another. It sounds tried and contrived, but the oil-and-water dynamic and conversational cadence that Firth and Rush form is played with the utmost honesty and warmth, blending odd couple humour with far serious connotations of classism and hierarchy, without the segregation of tone ever feeling obvious. However, their scenes together aren't nearly as plentiful as one would have hoped, and an extended period in the film's second act sees Logue all but disappear, somewhat nullifying the significance of his and George's time together. The worst thing about the absence is being deprived of the lovable Logue, whose eccentricities the perfectly-cast Rush plays with theatrical gusto, in an incredibly fun performance. His departure is justified, but Firth alone cannot occupy the void they so pleasantly fill together. David Seidler's screenplay sparkles with wit and charm, allowing the movie's impressive ensemble to indulge in some delectable repartee, but the incoherent subplots, while individually engaging, never make the leap to entirely thrilling, partly due to the movie's calm pacing. By film's end, Logue's mission doesn't feel complete despite the film asserting the contrary, thus reducing what should be a triumphant ending to a merely satisfying one.

That the ill-defined purpose of the film doesn't make it feel inconsequential is down to Hooper's slick and assured direction. In spite of the conventionality, he keeps proceedings compelling, maintaining a tonal coherence by commanding focus out of Seidler's meandering screenplay. But by just composing the disparate elements into a solid whole, he leaves very little of his own artistic inflections on the finished product. Alas, he makes as much of an impression as he can in a movie mercilessly dominated by its actors. He breaks through the usual period film semblance in small ways, provided mostly by little visual motifs that consist of penetrative close-ups and, alternatively, askew angles that oddly downplay the human interaction in favor of the well-made scenery. These touches award the aesthetic detail the attention it deserves, but make it slightly hard to stay involved with the narrative content, even given the lack of density in the more-or-less straightforward story.

One exception is an encounter between George VI and his likable but chauvinistic older brother Edward (a great Guy Pearce, consecutively playing an ephemeral role in an Oscar contender - see The Hurt Locker). The two have an altercation while attending a party hosted by the latter, in which Edward, in a momentary lapse in correctness, mocks his brother's stammer. The suffocatingly intimate cinematography works wonders in relating the despondency that George no doubt feels when an extended period of success with his speech training is tarnished at the hands of his own brother. It marks the strongest detour from the far superior speech therapy scenes.

The performances consistently enthrall, working magic out of dialogue that is the stuff of actors' wetdreams. Heading the central trio (comprised of the aforementioned Rush and, to a lesser extent, Bonham Carter) is, of course, Colin Firth. He's certainly come a long way from working the hell out of sweaters in delightfully disposable romcoms, to now being one of the most exciting and in-demand dramatic actors in the industry. Last year, I was taken aback by his revelatory performance in A Single Man. It was a thing of aching beauty; he personified grief in such a devastatingly haunting manner, that it saddens me just to recall the performance. I'm confident that time will right how under-appreciated that acting masterwork was. Things did drastically change for Firth, though; as if his unmemorable filmography prior to A Single Man disappeared, people (including myself) immediately looked to this upcoming feature with the doubtless belief he would once again find himself in contention for an Academy Award. And sure enough, here he is, the topic of much buzz, and a reasonably safe frontrunner for the win.

While he doesn't surpass fellow hopefuls Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network or James Franco in 127 Hours, or his own nominated performance last year (then again, few performances do), Firth delivers another effortless embodiment of human tragedy; from overcoming loss and facing the future, he goes to overcoming physical adversity and conquering the past. He masters the challenge of imitating a stammer (no mean feat), and manages to rouse empathy for a dilemma few are able to directly relate to. Here is a performer who has once again gone above and beyond the call of duty, cementing his newfound status as an "event" actor.

The King's Speech is probably the best movie playing in cinemas right now (unless Somewhere is still out). It's an immensely entertaining movie, that will warm the cuckolds of your heart. Years from now, it will probably be like The Cider House Rules; a movie rightfully acclaimed in its time, and rightfully forgotten years later. So, for production values and superb performance craft, I highly recommend this little treat of a film; just try your best to ignore the incongruous plotting, and, of course, the giant "Oscar" sign hovering above it.
