The King's Speech has been given endless praise, and was the recipient of four academy awards. While this may not seem like a large number, they were best original screenplay, best actor, best director, and the best of all, best picture. It has a flawless cast from the three leads, the best pairing being both Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush as leads. And while I will admit I feared of perhaps being bored by the principal of the film, about 20 minutes in I was captivated. The story outside of the story, the styling of the film, the talents involved, and the shear brilliance throughout nearly all aspects make The King's Speech a marvelous film.
Set at the dawn of world war 2, King George the 6th, or Bernie, has suffered a speech impediment all his life. However, his wife Elizabeth may have found just the man to finally fix it, a mister Lionel Logue. They work together for years, and eventually develop a friendship, ultimately tested. Soon, he faces disaster when his father, King George the 5th, dies. When his brother, King Edward the 7th, resigns less than a year later, he must now take the throne. But with Hitler and his forces on the move, he must now find his destroyed voice and lead a nation in peril, all in one speech.
The King's Speech is one of the best films of 2010. It does an impeccable job in every area, with a slight blandness at times being the only criticism I can conjure. It also did a good job of capturing both the essence, but the accuracy of the time period, even in large locations such as Buckingham Palace and Westminster Abbey. Is it the best movie this year? No. Is it up there? You bet, gov'nah. The King's Speech is a phenominal movie, with speeches galore, each more royal than the last. It may bore those who were dragged to see it, or those who demand perfection, but it certainly pleases most everyone else. Except Germans, but we kinda guessed that up front.

What a long-overdue viewing this turned out to be. Besides meeting all expectations in terms of execution and acting, this British gem (who's director is currently helming the highly-anticipated Les Miserables musical adaptation) touched on deep themes in a way I did not see coming.
  Firth's lead role, seamless in facial nuance and precise in its distinct speech pattern, invokes instant sympathy for someone that many of us lowly peasants wouldn't expect to sympathize with. Equally breathless is Geoffrey Rush (Barbossa to fans of the Pirates films), whose balance of firmness, brutal honesty, and tenderness emits a glimmer of hope in a world of people who seek nothing more than to gain. The chemistry between the two rivals that of Paul Newman and Robert Redford in their iconic team-ups, or even (dare I say it) Jim Carrey and Jeff Daniels in Dumb & Dumber. As bizarre as it seems, it's true. This Oscar-caliber duo of Brits serve up the best buddy-based interaction I've seen in a long time, in both tear-jerking friendship and genuine humor.
   Technical points aside, what really sells the movie is its appeal to those who suffer in the act of communication, be it with strangers, associates, or even one's own family (that territory's all too familiar to me). I was thoroughly invested in seeing the central character overcome his impediment and his fear of failing those who depend on him.
   I had the good fortune of watching the film with my grandfather, whose ears are adjusted to British accents from years of BBC. With him at 68, myself 18, you can see just how wide of an audience the picture can reach.
    A great, inspirational film.

Seidler read about George VI's life after overcoming a stuttering condition he endured during his youth. He started writing about the men's relationship as early as the 1980s, but postponed work, at the Queen Mother's wishes, until her death in 2002. The King's Speech is simply Shakespearean. It is Shakespearean in terms of the complexity of its characters, in terms of its brilliant script, in terms of clever subtleties that may take several views to catch, even in terms of its factual inaccuracies (a common feature of Shakespeare's histories).

To obsess over the fact that the presentation of Winston Churchill is skewed to make him look more principled and noble would be an error. Nor does it do the film justice to pore over its hasty treatment of Edward VIII's well-established Nazi sympathies, which are given one fleeting mention in a clear effort to rush the viewer past an embarrassing reality. Yes, these points are worth mentioning; as history, The King's Speech is not entirely worthless, but it certainly is spotty.

Judge The King's Speech as a film, not a history, and its genius will become clear. There are too many scenes in which its phenomenal artistry flourishes. For example, whenever Bertie, frustrated, lapses into his old habit of stuttering, he also falls back on his old habit of smoking; the connection between the two is made clear by the incessant hiccup of his lighter as he tries to produce a flame to light his cigarette. The story of King Edward VIII's abdication, the accession of Prince Albert (who takes the name King George VI, but is still known to his family as "Bertie"), and the speech impediment that nearly cripples George VI's reign at a pivotal time in England's history is a fascinating one.

The King's Speech (2010)

Directed by Tom Hooper

Starring: Colin Firth, Guy Pearce, Helena Bonam Carter, Geoffrey Rush, Timothy Spall, & Michael Gambon

Okay...here's the thing...posting my review/thoughts on this movie I've gotta issue an apology to the director & the stars of this fantastic film...as if they'd be listening or caring...but if they were...you deserved every little statue that graces you mantle...but I still say Inception & Black Swan shoulda been right there beside ya.

Moving on...alright...so...a few months after the death of King George V (played artfully as always by Michael Gambon), the battle for the throne is fought and lost, or better yet, handed over from one Prince to the other. The only problem is...neither Prince is actually suitable for the job.

With England on the precipice of Hitler's war the new established King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce), neck deep in scandal with a thrice divorced harlot of sorts, hands the thrown down to his younger brother Bertie (amazingly rendered by Colin Firth) who has long suffered from a speech impediment all his life. With the crowning comes the pressure & with the pressure of the crown emerges a heightened sense of anxiety & thus worsens his stammer. 

Therein lies the problem of the newly crowned King George VI of England, with his position comes public speaking & being on the brink of war increases his need to strengthen his country. Bertie never seems strong enough on his own...but in the company & care of his wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) the Queen he begins a life rejuvenated by one selfless act. 

After being constantly belittled by every physician he sees, Elizabeth arranges a meeting between the King & a very uniquely quirky speech therapist named Lionel Logue (a brilliant Geoffrey Rush). The two mix like oil & water on their first few meets but the two develop an almost sweetly unbelievable bond as they get to the heart of the matter regarding the King's Speech. 

With the joint help of Elizabeth, Logue, & Winston Churchill (Timothy Spall) the King finds his voice...amazingly I might add...& well...I aint spoiling the ending for you...nor the beginning for that matter. 

I lie to you not people...this movie is a gut wrenching, tear bringing, fist pumping, laugh out loud drama that contains some of the most memorable performances of the 2010 Oscar roster.

It's a must see.

Like much of America, I was surprised to see a period film about King George VI's speech impediment become one of the biggest critical darlings of 2010. That said, while I wasn't quite blown away by it on the same level as many critics, it's still an undeniably excellent, enjoyable film.

There isn't a single poor performance in the cast. Colin Firth could carry the film if not for Geoffrey Rush's routine stealing of scenes throughout the film as speech therapist Lionel Logue. Where Firth effectively carries the weight of George VI's struggle with his speech impediment, Rush counters with Logue's good humor and unwillingness to coddle even royalty. Helena Bonham Carter also turns one of her most unselfconscious and enjoyable performances of her career as well. And not a single member of the British star-studded supporting cast disappoints in their performances either.

Tom Hooper's direction is strong, and the music is entirely period appropriate and befitting throughout the film.

Considering both the subject matter and the film's nature as a period film, your mileage will definitely vary with The King's Speech. If it sounds interesting to you, you'll probably enjoy it - if it doesn't, you may very well be bored to tears. But the critics definitely weren't kidding about this one - it's an absolutely excellent film.

I just finished watching The King's Speech  this morning.  I am a busy mother of three and honestly am behind on my movie watching, which is why I thought doing this with my brother would be fun!  Something to motivate me to keep current!  Anyway, my brother told me he didn't think it deserved Best Picture, and I admit I was surprised when I watched the Oscars that it won, even though I hadn't seen it.  However, I just read my brother's entry and I agree with all the positive things he said about the movie.  How can you go wrong with Collin Firth, Geoffrey Rush and Helena Bonham-Carter?  But I have to say that while I don't honestly know what movie I would have given the Oscar to, I think my brother has missed some of the genius that lay within this film.

First the obvious.  Collin Firth is fantastic.  He's so convincingly plays the awkward, insecurity of Albert that I was uncomfortable in places just watching him.  His restricted nature and reserved personality so painfully mirroring that of the royal family he belonged to that it actually made a person NOT want to be a prince or princess. His performance was incredibly emotional and I felt every word of it.  However, there were other aspects of the movie that lifted it above the pack.  I am not as well versed in the technical side of movies as my brother, but there was something about the visual effect of this movie that took me a while to get used to.  I am a huge fan of historical dramas, and this was an historical drama first and foremost.  The costumes and scenery were effective and brought you easily to 1930′s London.  However, the camera angle was different, and upon closer reflection (and feel free to correct me if I am wrong) I think it was director Tom Hooper's use of  interior rooms and narrow angles and passages that was unusual for an historical drama.  It had none of the pageantry that's so often seen in this genre.  I think this may have symbolized the constrictiveness of Albert's life, but feel free to debate that position.  For example the long walk he took as King to make his first address to the nation and the end of the movie, the viewer could feel every tense second of that walk with Albert.  It felt as though you were in the room, rather than watching from a distance.  Furthermore, I think the final scene where the royal family is waving to the public from Buckingham Palace was made that much more effective by the director's choice of visuals.  Because it was the first time that the viewer saw that side of Albert's life -  the majestic side.  It put his accomplishment is real perspective and you go - wait a minute....this guy is actually the King of England afterall!  I got weepy at that scene, because the importance of this person (family) in history suddenly becomes obvious, and you realize what a huge triumph his managed.

But on a more personal note,  I really loved this movie because I love this material.  I liked how the film glossed over the traditionally more juicy historical event of  Edward abdicating the throne for his American divorcee, and merely uses it as a catalyst to our principle character's development (which really was all it was).  After all, Albert is a more worthy character for our admiration!  However, it is interesting to us history buff's to see that story with a bit of context.  It was such a major scandal for that time. I remember studying the abdication in school as an important historical event of the 20th century.  Think of how it changed history.  George VI became a key character in WWII, his daughter Elizabeth too played an important role to the British people during that time, and went on to become a beloved monarch herself.  And thanks to those events, we all await the marriage of her grandson William to, ironically, commoner Kate Middleton!  Edward laments in the movie that the common man gets to marry for love, so why shouldn't he?  Too bad he hadn't been born 80 years later.

[b]"I've been terribly busy."[/b] 
[b]"Doing what?"[/b] 
[b]"Kinging."[/b] 

[b]The King's Speech[/b], a man at battle with himself a very unlikable man at that. Perhaps sympathy for one of the luckiest men to walk our mortal Earth is at times absent, yet The King's Speech manages to humanise one of closest things to a living God. Yes, you either love, or hate the reigning powers of the British Royals, but how satisfying it is to see one of us mere mortals (an Australian one at that) stand before him and say 'no'. The King's Speech is a surprisingly different movie, based upon the cloudy genre of aristocrats and the royal family; usually the genre consists of soft-core pornography and the misplacement of their aphrodisiacs. Yet we are served with great story telling of a true story, Oscar-worthy performances and quite interesting sets to keep interest in the commonly bland background. Despite being [b]MORE[/b] historically accurate, and having the best leading performance of the year, the results for best picture at the academy awards remains a mystery. 

[b]The plot[/b] is a simple one indeed. The King dies, so of course, David (Guy Pearce, strange casting that works surprisingly well) is to take the crown, but he decides to run-off with a twice-divorced woman, which is a big red flag in the Royal family. Therefore,George (Colin Firth) is to be crowned king. Worth celebrating one of the best titles, you can achieve. Well actually, this is harrowing for George as he has a horrible stuttering problem. Public speeches, patriotic rallies and defiant roars against Hitler (although he was pro-Hitler) are all a part of the job, which he cannot do. His wife Elizabeth (Helena Carter) talks to a non-royal speech therapist as the others failed to make a difference. Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) is the unorthodox and quirky 'doctor' who helps the rude King into speaking. 
The most common criticism for The King's Speech is it predictability. In a sense its true, like all based on true story films, you either do it perfectly accurate and risk predictability claims, or you go in another direction and are hounded for not following the story correctly. Therefore, getting into a true story will always have its let down. Surprisingly though, The King's Speech maybe predictable, and we may all know what happens in the end, but it's a fun ride getting there nonetheless. Perhaps we just need to accept the predictable aspects for a quality movie, which tells the story correctly. 

[b]The acting[/b] is superb. Colin Firth takes on one of the many fears of acting, stuttering is one of them. Although at one stage he looks like Al Gore choking on marbles, he takes on the role perfectly. The stuttering is not over-done, but done enough to see a clear problem. His character is not exactly a likable one, but we must remember he comes from royalty. He most definitely deserved his Oscar.  Geoffrey Rush is an Australian actor, playing an Australian character. He always brings such enthusiasm to his roles, and you can see how much fun he has in his role as an unconventional speech therapist. He really is a quality actor that gives his best for every movie he stars. Helena Carter finally casts away the shackles of Tim Burton, which is a nice change. She is one of the best female actors around, although it was hard to take her seriously as the Queen at times, after watching Fight Club. Guy Pearce would seem like the last candidate for this type of movie, but in his small appearances, he is fantastic. 

[b]So worthy[/b] of best picture and best director? No, The King's Speech is a charming and quality movie based on a true story. The Social Network is a near-masterpiece (or perhaps masterpiece in the years to come) which shows more creativity and risk in itself. The direction of Tom Hooper was 'clean' and very decent with no problems, but not daring. Hooper gives us a nice picture to watch, but nothing special. Fincher gives s absolute beauty in some of the most daring ways without creating its own 'style'.  The problem with The King's Speech as although it's a very well-made movie, it's a very grounded movie, which is not as memorable as you would expect an Oscar winning film. 

[b]Overall[/b], tastefully done movie, which has top notch acting all round which is enjoyable despite predictability, although that comes with every 'based on a true story' film. Although it is not bold or daring enough to deserve Best Picture and Best Director. Perhaps the main problem is I cannot imagine myself watching this again.

There was really only one right way to do this story, or at least one right way to do it conventionally, and that was to treat it like a sports movie. You know the film's going to end with the climactic speech, just like "The Big Game" or "The Big Race" so the entire structure of the film becomes about complicating that journey, building up the stakes, and setting up an entire crescendo of payoffs that rewards the audience for paying such good attention and leaves everyone feeling thoroughly denouemed. In other words, its a time-honored way to make a solid film, albeit a somewhat manipulative and archaic one. This is a good film, filled with many good elements, but it plays so safe that the constant comfort of an intimately familiar dramatic structure actually takes away some suspense. Granted, it's difficult to make otherwise uninterested people care about the royal family, or make speaking into a microphone compelling, but really there aren't any surprises here. If it's a good film it's because they carefully followed a proven recipe, not because they're brilliant chefs.

"If I'm King, where's my power? Can I form a government? Can I levy a tax, declare a war? No! And yet I am the seat of all authority. Why? Because the nation believes that when I speak, I speak for them. But I can't speak."

For what it is, The King's Speech is a brilliantly-crafted bit of cinema.  It doesn't necessarily do anything new (the therapist helping his student find his reluctant student find confidence in himself as a man doesn't exactly break any kind of mold...Geoffrey Rush is, in this film, the equivalent of a much less hairy Robin Williams in Good Will Hunting) but does it through the lens of war and in perhaps the greatest example of the importance of public image in the world-the British Royalty.  Hooper's directorial skills are in sharp display throughout the film.  The camera angles, blocking, and smart use of sound all indicate both the chaos throughout British politics in the 1930s, and the inner turmoil tearing Bertie apart.

The real praise, however, has to go to Rush and Firth.  Their chemistry makes a film that really breaks no new ground work on an astounding level.  From the first moment they share on screen together, as Bertie is withdrawn into the sofa in Lionel's office, through the shouting of profanity and the final regal image the film leaves the audience with, the two hold the attention of the audience exclusively.  So much so the film almost seems to lag when they're apart.  Guy Pearce does his best to hold up the political intrigue of the film, but The King's Speech is less about what is occurring in the world and more about what is occurring between the two men.  

Which can, of course, lead to a bit of a bitter taste in the audience's mouth at the end of the film.  There's a sense of triumph following the speech that is made possible through the affinity we build with Bertie and wanting to see him conquer his impediment, but it's a fake kind of happiness.  Hooper gives us images of Hitler and the air raid shelters in London which turn out to be lip service to the grander conflict that's occurring.  It's almost as if Hooper feels guilty for inviting us into a tiny world when so much is happening.  Newsreels and phonograph recordings alert us to the political reality of the film, but only briefly.  The film, then, leaves the audience in a funny state.  A climax of sorts occurs, and conflict is resolved, but only in a very limited way.  In bringing the formulaic to this era, Hooper almost runs the risk of trivializing the eponymous speech his hero delivers. Only through the compelling performances of the two stars (and they're doozies) can the film ultimately be redeemed.

Winner of Best Actor, Best Original Screenplay, and most importantly, Best Picture, The King's Speech is one of the best character pieces of the last decade.  We learn so much about King George VI from this movie, that even some history books will be tossed onto the shelf as maybe an edited version is put in the DVD player in high schools.  Maybe it was just me, but I thought that maybe The Social Network reflected our current generation, with kids being more on the computer than outside, with many new minds being ruined by the brain-squashing power of the internet, but I'm using it now, so I'll get back to that later.  But now, onto King's Speech.

With fantastic performances all around, including Helena Bonham Carter and Geoffrey Rush, both nominated for Best Supporting Actor and Actress.  These two alone are great on their own.  If the movie had mostly been about them, it would have been great anyway, but it wasn't.  Instead it was about Colin Firth, who won Best Actor for his work in this film.  His performance alone is among the best of the last few years.  There were many great performances throughout the year, but this one was undoubtedly the best.  Truly a masterful work in the acting department.  Any young actor should look to Firth and his work as an idol's golden time.

So, finally, the film is predictable, yes, and didn't need to be as long as it was, but it definatly was worth the watch.  Totally controlled by its great performances, nice direction, great cinematography, and an overall production of great quality, this is truly one of the best films of 2010, and will go down in history as a character piece of great skill and for Firth's gifted and somehow natural performance as the leader for the UK during one of our world's most troubled times.  Overall, an achievement for sure.

Now that I have seen this movie I still remain firm to my opinion that The Social Network should have received the Oscar for Best Picture of the year. It is a shame that the voting members selected this one although I thought the acting was extremely well and the plot relevance, no doubt, but we are talking about events that happened long ago regarding the fears and "problems" of a future King..yet Social Network deals with an issue that has transformed and impacted the social lives of 600 million people; how a nobody became a somebody pretty much on his own..Many of us CAN identify with that character (Zuckerberg)  yet in The King's Speech we have Colin Firth (playing Albert the Duke of York) showing some good  efforts to overcome his stammer in order to face his public. His father, King George V (Michael Gambon), is an emotional despot who mistakes chiding for medicine and every doctor or therapist he has tried has been unable to cure him from his speech impediment. His father makes clear to him that this is a new media age. It's not just a matter of looking frightfully regal on a horse, the monarch has to be able to master the radio microphone. 
 Despite growing up afraid of his father and older brother David, he is comfortable in his surroundings because he is part of royalty so everyone bows to him, everyone pleases him and takes care of his needs..but life or fate has a different plan for him. You see if you are familiar with history and this particular story, after their father King George passes away, the throne belongs to David- the older brother. Ironically I must point out that not long ago on Facebook I expressed my opinion about one of the ultimate sacrifices for love - abdicating the throne for someone you deeply love and I chose the example of King David who was forced to choose betweeen the crown of England or marrying the love of his life- a divorcee named Wallis Simpson whom the Queen detested. During the 1930's royalty was forbidden from marrying "commoners" and Mrs. Simpson had her share of lovers and enjoyed parties like many other socialites but her family was not part of royalty. Wikipedia will show you the speech that King David gave the nation when he abdicated, YES ABDICATED the throne in order to marry this woman. Incredible huh?? So once David gave up the throne, next in line was Albert or Bertie..
Some would argue that David (Guy Pearce) was unsuitable to be head of state claiming that he wanted to turn Balmoral into Charleston, throwing lavish and wild parties..I personally found him nicer and more personable than his brother Albert who was aloof, and so detached from everyone else. Anyways I don't want to digress... the abdication means poor, stuttering Bertie has to shoulder the ultimate burden while "Herr Hitler" is whipping up the stormclouds of war. The nation needs a king who can rally the forces of good in a clear, inspiring voice.
So in desperation, Albert and his wife (Helena Bonham Carter) seek help from an unlikely source: an unsuccessful Australian actor named Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), who is working in London as a speech therapist. To say they donâ(TM)t get on is an understatement. One is a commoner, the other a future monarch. One comes from Down Under, the other is accustomed to looking down at people as they bow before him. I disliked the way Albert treated Lionel, hence my feelings for royalty as you can suspect are not the nicest. I refuse to bow to a mere mortal; just because they were born into royalty does NOT make them special or unique in my eyes..I only bow to one King- and He is God or His Son Jesus- the King of Kings! Anyways, 
the tension between them is at least as much temperamental as it is cultural or economic. Logue prizes informality. He calls Albert âBertieâ?, begins one of their sessions by asking him if he knows any jokes, insists â" rather boldly â" âIn here, itâ(TM)s better if weâ(TM)re equals.â? Well as you can guess that did not sit well with His Royal Highness..Their encounters turn into therapy sessions..Albert is prone to self-pity, to lashing out, and to snobbish disdain. When he cries, âIâ(TM)m a naval officer, not a kingâ?, the effect is as resonant and it is blatantly obvious that he is not happy or comfortable in his new role as King but the entire nation is counting on him to lead as Head of state. The moment of truth comes when he has to give a speech to the nation regarding the impending war against Hitler (Germany)..can he do it? The Kingâ(TM)s Speech is a way of getting us to think about the Royal family less as an institution than as individuals weighed down by pomp and circumstance.
Not everyone's going to like this film: some may find it excessively royalist. Some may not even care about a King's stutter..I like how the writer's included information regarding David's abdication to the throne and some segments of Wallis Simpson (I was so curious to know about her; how she stole David's heart)..Bottom line is that despite the great performance and costumes, and a good plot regarding a true story, in my heart my vote if I could have voted goes to The Social Network..It made more of an impact to me than The King's Speech.

Conventional by any standards and less emotionally and psychologically complex than its closest companion, Steven Frears' The Queen (2006), The King's Speech is nevertheless an undeniably charming portrayal of the royal family during a time when England needed a leader. Colin Firth owns the screen in the title role as George VI, whose circumstances thrust him into the role of king while his shortcoming as a public speaker leave him unprepared for the job. Supporting cast members -- Guy Pearce and Geoffrey Rush and especially Helena Bonham Carter playing a human being for a change -- are quite good, but it is Firth's pure bravado that really shines through. He is brilliantly subtly in capturing the nuances of a stutter, and his journey to not merely overcome it but to do so in front of a nation is truly inspiring.

'm back, and I'm here to review the 2011 Academy Award Winner for Best Picture: Tom Hooper's THE KING'S SPEECH.  
It's very difficult to compare films that have been nominated for Best Picture.  The 2011 nominees were Danny Boyle's 127 HOURS, Darren Aronofsky's BLACK SWAN, David O. Russell's THE FIGHTER, Christopher Nolan's INCEPTION, Lisa Cholodenko's THE KIDS ARE ALRIGHT, Tom Hooper's THE KING'S SPEECH, David Fincher's THE SOCIAL NETWORK, Lee Unkrich's TOY STORY 3, Joel and Ethan Coen's TRUE GRIT, and Debra Granik's WINTER'S BONE.  I've seen only 7 of those films(THE FIGHTER, INCEPTION, THE KING'S SPEECH, THE SOCIAL NETWORK, TOY STORY 3, TRUE GRIT, and WINTER'S BONE), and I'm still having a difficult time comparing them all, and figuring out which one's deserved the Oscar more.  All of them are different, and all of them are good.  I almost have to watch my mouth at times because I never know who I'm going to send on their soap box about whatever film they liked the most.  Hell, I sometimes have to step back so I don't do the same thing about any film I liked.  Then again, I guess that's why we have professional critics like Roger Ebert, Bill Goodykoontz, and Gene Shalit to do the job for us.  This way we don't have to worry about unfair comparisons and we can all just enjoy the films for what they are.  
Onward!  THE KING'S SPEECH starts off in the year 1925 in England.  There we meet Prince Albert, Duke of York(Firth), the second son of King George V(Gambon).  One of his requirements is to give speeches, but there is a setback: He has a speech impediment that prevents him from getting words out -- he stammers.  So his wife, Elizabeth, Duchess of York(Carter), gets him to see Lionel Logue(Rush), a speech therapist to help him overcome the stammering.  After his father dies, and his older brother King Edward VIII(Pearce) relinquishes his throne, Prince Albert becomes King George VI, which throws more pressure on him.  
This is one of the most emotional films I've ever seen.  To see someone like King George VI going through the trials he went through is not just difficult to watch.  It's fantastic, and it keeps your interest all the way to the end.  Sure, there are parts of the film that are a tad slow, and some of what the actors say is hard to understand, but all of that can be forgiven.  
Colin Firth was just marvelous as King George VI.  He made my eyes watery a few times when he tried to talk and when he beautifully breaks down at one point saying, "I'm not a king."  The performance he gave was second to none, and he deserved his Oscar, as Jeff Bridges deserved his for CRAZY HEART, and Gregory Peck deserved his for TO KILL A MOCKINGBIRD.  Geoffrey Rush was excellent as Lionel.  The best parts of the film were the scenes that King George VI had with Lionel Logue.  They were funny, and they really brought out the formation of King George VI's friendship with Lionel.  Helena Bonham Carter's performance as Queen Elizabeth is one of her finest performances yet.  I am so anxious to see what she does next.  And yes, I still sort of have a crush on her, but what can I say?  A fine Method actress like her deserves as much praise as one can give.  
My interest in people overcoming their stutters has raised because of THE KING'S SPEECH.  It makes me wonder how people like Nicholas Brendon or James Earl Jones or anyone like that have overcome their stutters and have been able to lead lives that have been successful.  But getting back to THE KING'S SPEECH, I think this film deserved its Oscar.  It was a well-written, well-directed, wonderful film that has earned another watch or two.  Am I a little biased for INCEPTION?  Yeah, I am.  But I'm certainly willing to tip my hat to a film like THE KING'S SPEECH, because it's worthy that.  
The Reviewer approves.

"The King's Speech" could have very easily been just another period-costume drama that only appeals to a small demographic. I for one am not a fan of that genre as the majority of them are slow paced, uneventful and have all similar plots. "The King's Speech" however is a huge exception as it does not follow the norm as is adds witty dialogue and humorous scenes. The film therefore appeals to a much wider audience especially with the brilliant bromance Firth and Rush have on-screen.

The acting is absolutely outstanding. Firth instantly brings likability to King George VI and makes the audience route for him for the duration of the movie as he is very-much the underdog (which we British just love) as he is bullied by his father, King George V (Michael Gambon) and older brother- the abdicated king, King Edward VIII (Guy Pearce). Pearce is very clearly having absolute fun playing the egotistical, arrogant bachelor-catch. He is the villain we all love to hate. Geoffrey Rush is on top form with his quick witted one-liners that have great comic timing. He and Firth work off each other superbly with very funny banter. The always magnificent Helena Bonham Carter is to a degree underused here but still manages to have an elegant performance in all of her scenes.

You would think a film about the former king unable to deliver a publicly addressed speech would be, well, dull- especially with the climax being just that speech. But the pace of the movie brings suspense right until the final moment where you can't help but smile. The director Tom Hooper is to be praised for this achievement. He brings classic style movie-making to this project which is excellent.  The movie does show British cinema at its up most best. It is sad that this could well be the UK Film Council's final triumph. I'm sure this amazing triumph will bring a expression of regret and embarrassment to the face of Jeremy Hunt. At least the Council went out on a high I suppose.

The act of speaking to a large crowd is terrifying for many people. On most lists of common fears, in fact, public speaking ranks almost always near the top. It's a wonder more horror movies haven't been made about it, come to think of it. In The King's Speech, Tom Hooper's brilliant and beautiful film, the horror of public speaking is compounded by a stammer and by the sheer importance of the content of the speech.

The 2010 Academy Award winner for Best Picture explores the stammer of King George VI and the reactions of those around him. What can be done about such a powerful man who must, by the nature of his placement in life, speak to large groups of people? Worse still, the king must be the people; he must vocalize their wishes and speak on their behalf. What's to be done if the king cannot speak?


The King's Speech opens with the Duke of York (Colin Firth) speaking to close the 1925 British Empire Exhibition at Wembley. His wife, Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter), is by his side. We learn with some immediacy as to the severity of the Duke of York's stammer, as he cannot deliver a speech to the audience. Having tried several treatments without success, Elizabeth, as a seeming last resort, enlists Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush) to help her husband.

Logue is an Australian speech therapist in London and he carries with him an air of informality that tests the Duke's patience. But he does make progress. When the Duke's father, King George V (Michael Gambon) passes away, the throne falls to the Duke's brother, the Prince of Wales (Guy Pearce). The Prince of Wales wants to marry an American socialite, however, and eventually abdicates the throne. The Duke, called King George VI, takes the honour and must use his voice to help give confidence to his people in the shadow of war with Germany.

The King's Speech looks gorgeous. Hooper's cinematographer, Danny Cohen, uniquely frames each shot. Often the main subject of the shot is placed in a bottom far corner, with large swaths of background comprising the majority of the image. This effect, along with the use of long and narrow interior shots, give The King's Speech a sense of smallness that differs greatly from other historical epics. While the lush scenery and period style is often the way of things in period pieces, Hooper's decision to minimize its glamour is compelling and rewarding.

Because of this approach, the movie belongs to the characters. While context matters to some degree, the detail is found in the mannerisms and emotions in King George VI's speech impediment. Hooper is much, much more concerned with how the king and Lionel relate and struggle with each other than he is with setting a historical stage. While the import of Hitler's horrifying presence cannot be discounted, The King's Speech is much more concerned with how the king's impediment is tested.

I consider The King's Speech to be a personal drama set in a historical context. Some will quibble over the portrayals of certain characters or the accuracy of certain political positions, such as the role of Winston Churchill (Timothy Spall). But for me, this was a film about courage and about rising above fear to do the necessary thing. It is also about friendship emerging from what begins as a psychological struggle between two stubborn men.

Firth and Rush are absolutely spectacular. Note how they use space in their scenes and how Rush utilizes big, dramatic motions to offset Firth's smaller, subtler mobility. This approach goes beyond mere words and line delivery to show us how Lionel and Bertie feel about each other. In that respect, it would have been easy for Firth, the rightful winner of the Academy Award for Best Actor, to overdo it. But he downplays the struggle, elegantly distributing shame and fear to the corners of his mouth and to his eyes. The stammer, itself no easy feat to master, is an outcropping of what lies beneath.

The King's Speech is a wonderful film. It is about the formation of a lifelong friendship and about overcoming something seemingly impossible. It is about trying and succeeding. It is not about royal glitz and glamour or appeasement or Churchill's stance during this or that crisis. The externalities fly as distractions, I think, to what is the greater whole of The King's Speech: its rich, vibrant heart.

I know what you're thinking. "Five stars for a movie about a guy who can't talk properly and we all know ends up doing so later?" But it's about far more than that, my lovelies. The King's Speech is a testament to the human spirit and its ability to overcome odds when giving up is the easiest course of action. King George VI realizes this, and that most limits people have are self imposed, there is nothing you can't accomplish so long as you have the courage and confidence to do so.

As the Duke of York, George struggles with a terrible stutter which has afflicted him since childhood, inviting ridicule from family and peers. He is given the task of completing what are his brother Edward's (Guy Pearce) responsibilities, as he is too busy with the indulgences of life. We see first hand the pressure the Duke faces, as his father King George V (Michael Gambon) breathes down his son's neck as he fights the stutter to make a radio speech Edward should do. He begins to see a speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), though it is sporadic as patience is not one of his strong suits, and he has a short temper. Things escalate after George V dies, Edward renounces his royal duty to succeed him and the Duke of York is thrust into becoming George VI, necessitating the resumption of his speech therapy. Slowly, George gains confidence in himself and as a result, his subjects place theirs in him as well.

In the course of it all, George VI makes a dear friend in Logue, a man who refused to give up on this most important patient who needed more than speech therapy, he needed someone who could break down the barriers George had built up inside of himself due to insecurity, intimidation by his father and brother, and other emotionally traumatic instances during childhood. This is a beautiful movie and is an instant classic. Watch it as soon as possible if you haven't already.

The story was also very well-written, timing the pace of the king's personal struggles with the struggles of his country to keep you constantly engrossed in the dramatic suspense.

Overall, this movie is certainly a must-see, and you probably won't be satisfied with just one viewing after it's over.

3.5: This is not the best picture of the year.  It's not even close.  The story is a simple one and essentially follows the genre formula.  In some ways, it is this years The Blind Side, except it is about the British royal family instead of a southern football family, so it won.  It is simply a very moving historical drama that is brought down to a very personal level.  The relationship between Rush and Firth is what really makes it work, but it is not the kind of film that will be remembered decades from now, whereas a picture like The Social Network or Toy Story 3 will.  Firth's performance is outstanding, but I can't help but feel that his Oscar is at least partially due to his performance in A Single Man the year before as well.  He and Rush seem to have a real connection in the film, which is only amplified by the superb cast they have surrounding them on all sides.  Nothing about the film is new, different, or unusual; it is simply a well made picture done in the same vein that so many others are.  What sets it apart is the subject matter, the performances, and the quality of the filmmaking.  It will go down in the books as a Shakespeare in Love type film, which won over pictures like The Thin Red Line, Saving private Ryan, Elizabeth, and Life is Beautiful, all of which are arguably superior. Have him meet a man who helps him but comes from the opposite side of the tracks to get that social class humanity in there: check. Synopsis:  Britain's King George VI struggles with an embarrassing stutter for years until he seeks help from unorthodox Australian speech therapist Lionel Logue.

Though The King's Speech's script is essentially nothing more than the story of a man overcoming personal tribulations, which appeals to our base emotions without providing much in the way of real insight, it's a witty screenplay, and a joy to experience.

The film's brilliance is in it's visual design.  The director and cinematographer use a wide variety of different camera lenses to create optical effects that is not only unique and stylish, but also aids in telling the story of a man who's afraid to speak publicly.  Also visually intoxicating is the art direction, beautiful architecture and an obvious attention to period details create a visually remarkable movie.

And then we have the acting.  Colin Firth earned all the praise he has garnered, it's a vividly varied and heartfelt performance that will have you rooting wholeheartedly in his character.  Geoffrey Rush's performance is equally as lovable as a quick-minded self-made man with his own failed aspirations, he's sometime quirky, sometimes profound, always enjoyable.  and Helena Bonham Carter turns in what i believe to be her best performance, as the king's wife, a chipper lady who's often "glass half-full" personality is a wonderful foil to Firth's character's outlook.  The supporting cast shines as well with a fun minor role by Timothy Spall as Winston Churchill.

Though it's not a very insightful or subtle experience, it's one of the best experiences one could have had at the movies in 2010.

I'm pretty much dead set against monarchy, but it scored one achievement at least in the 20th century, and I admit that had he not been the son of a king, Bertie Windsor (ne Saxe-Coburg and Gotha), would in all probability not have been cured of his stammer. 'Course, had he not been born into such a dysfunctional family, he might not have developed it in the first place.There is some dreadful stuff here - poor Michael Gambon as George V has an awful spiel in which he summarises the 'plot-so-far-and-what-will-happen-in-the-future' at Christmas 1934. Firstly he delivers the Christmas broadcast to remind us that - one, we are in the radio age, and two, we are in the Great Depression and then, speaking to Bertie, his second son, he tells him that number one son, David, has affairs with married women and has now taken up with Mrs Simpson, who has 'two husbands living' and that 'no divorced woman can be received at court'. George then tells Bertie about Hitler and Stalin, who are intimidating half of Europe each. Er, actually, no they're not, not in 1934 anyway. Some of this might not matter, and this is a common enough device, but when inaccurate it provides just the sort of revised pseudo-history that fuels mythologies and blurs historical nuances even when the events are within living memory (or forgetfulness). It was after all, a speech impediment that Bertie had, not a hearing one. Maybe I'm too critical; maybe I'd like to have seen New York crime movies having stuff like "New York City (not to be confused with New York State) is a port metropolis on the east coast of the United States of America" or old biblical epics incuding explanatory lines like "God, sometimes known as Jehovah, was originally a middle-eastern deity, popularised in the later Roman period". Similarly, a chat between Bertie and his speech therapist, Lionel Logue, lays it on with a trowel -"does it feel strange, now David's on the throne?" "To tell the truth, it was a relief, knowing that I wouldn't be king." "But unless he produces an heir you're next in line. And your daughter Elizabeth would then succeed you." Oh dear God, these are the very lines. Thereâ(TM)s more stuff like this. Bertie, not unusually in his time, is a chain smoker "my physicians say it relaxes the throat" he tells Logue who all too presciently has said "I believe sucking smoke into your lungs will kill you." Really? If I'd made the film, just to make sure that this was not too subtle, I'd have been tempted to give young Maggie a line like "Oh, Papa, may have another of your nice ciggies please?" I might have put in the 1939 Christmas broadcast in which the king quoted "I said to the man who stood at the gate of the year 'Give me a light that I may tread safely into the unknown'" but that is just after the movie's end. 
And although royalty may have concomitant psychological pressures which are difficult to reconcile with normality, I also take exception to the psychobabble that is invoked to largely explain Bertie's problem. The film uses the old canard about George V's attitude to parenting, having Bertie say "I was afraid of my father, and my children are damn well going be afraid of me." This was not considered good parenting even in the pre Spock 19th century and this anecdote has its origin in a claim by the unreliable Randolph Churchill that George had remarked that "My father was frightened of his mother, I was frightened of my father, and I am damned well going to see to it that my children are frightened of me." This is entirely spurious and unjust. And what the hell is the older Churchill, Winston, doing in the abdication crisis? In the interest of self-serving populism (Oscar-bait?) we have a total reversal of truth here - so Churchill supports Bertie's accession when in fact his strenuous objections to the abdication were known to everyone at the time. In an absolute fabrication we even have Churchill suggesting to the still Duke of York Bertie, that when he becomes king, he should take the name George - "certainly not Albert, too Germanic". Exaggerated too is the importance of Bertie's stammer to England, the Empire and the World. Exaggerated, but it must be admitted, not without at least some foundation. And here is the central theme, not perhaps as well-executed as in 'The Madness of King George', a rather better movie but lacking the attraction of a recent setting. Bertie, Duke of York, the King-Emperor George VI, must be cured and the curer is a maverick commoner. In this trueish-story the commoner is the Australian speech therapist Logue.
Bertie can talk to himself ok, and is fine with his wife and two little girls, Betty and Maggie. But he is crap in public, and he has to be in public, and this is torture for him. Yes, there are lots of cringe-making bits, but it's difficult not to like this film, and I'm just not sufficiently curmudgeonly. Bertie is not to blame for his fate and must make the most of it. Lionel will help him.It is in short a first rate period drama which the English do so well and the Americans like so much (and give Academy Awards to). Michael Gambon's George V is just yummy (although they missed the bit when his doctor Lord Dawson, slipped the too-slowly dying king a lethal injection of cocaine and morphine, so that the death could be announced in the morning edition of The Times newspaper rather than 'less appropriate' evening newspapers). I enjoyed Helena Bonham Carter's Elizabeth (nee Bowes-Lyons) too, Gawd bless 'er. Fun, and a tad understated, you want more, yet rightly you donâ(TM)t get it, because the movie is about the relationship between Bertie and Lionel and the uphill task of getting, well yes, the king's speech sorted.S
o it's Colin Firth as Bertie and Geoffrey Rush as Lionel Logue who dominate the film and yes it works pretty damn well. The script, turgid in too many parts, can also rise and sparkle and sometimes works very well indeed as the pair work on both the stammer and their relationship. This presses all the buttons brilliantly, and despite my many reservations, yes, I succumbed. Very good film-making indeed.

History repeated itself, as it is often wont to do, at the 2010 Oscars. The two frontrunners, this and The Social Network, were just about as dichotomous as two films could be. The feel-good versus the feel-ehh; the classical versus the revolutionary; the old versus the young, if you want to break it down like that. These are simplifications, naturally, but the contributions of each film are pretty simply assessed. The Social Network was an incisive exploration of socialization, privilege, intellect, technology, and the role that all of these play in a rapidly-changing world. This...this was a movie about a king who gave an inspirational speech after overcoming adversity from his family. Even The Social Network, within a scope that admittedly could have stood some broadening, manages to feel bigger than a movie that takes place during World War II. This speech won no one a war; this speech didn't make a people's champion out of King George VI. Tom Hooper, in a move that earned The Social Network its fair share of detractors, is manipulating history in a way that suits his narrative. But where the blurry line between fact and fiction only seemed to play into The Social Network's mythos all the more, The King's Speech is unable to wrangle that line to the point where it seems like anything less than mistruth or conflation.

Handsomely crafted and wonderfully acted (Firth deserved that Best Actor trophy - if not for this, then as a career prize), this is nonetheless fluff, neatly packaged as "cerebral" yet "heartwarming." The latter, sure, but the former is pretty far from the truth. It wraps up its challenges about as neatly as possible, leaving the audience with very little to speak about other than how inspirational it was. The King's Speech more or less succeeds at its goals, but they aren't particularly lofty ones, which is a considerable disappointment given its subject matter.

Well the plot is that King George VI/Bertie/Colin Firth will become King George VI obviously. But he has suffered from a debilitating speech impediment since he can remember. So his wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter)hires a speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush). To help Bertie with his Speech impediment. 

The Kings Speech went on to be nominated for 12 Oscars and won 4 of them, for original screenplay, Best Actor, Best Director, and Best Picture! Is it deserving of all this awards? Almost! It for sure deserved 3 out of the 4 awards but which one did it not deserve?

Well lets start out with best screenplay. Before I saw The Kings Speech, I really wanted Christopher Nolan to win it, mostly because of how well written it is, that and because he got snubbed for his direction Oscar, even though if he did get nominated he wouldn't have won it (I'll get to that later). But I'm glad David Seidler won it. The screenplay is well written, makes great use of the actors, has excellent and witty dialogue and is actually really funny. I mean it this is one funny movie, in some cases it's hilarious especially from the excellent Geoffrey Rush who was  also nominated for his role.        

Next up the Acting. Best Actor Colin Firth. Colin Firth gives the best performance of the year and one of my favorite performances of all time, I'm really glad he won it, the most deserving Oscar that year. He gives a phenomenal performance of King George VI/Bertie, when he's pist of off, he is pist off. He's incredibly like able and inspiring. By that I mean I can relate with the speech impediment a little. When I was born my tongue was tied down to the bottom of my mouth (tongue tied) so the doctors had to cut it, not the tongue but the thing that kept it tied down, because of this I can't pronounce my th's and ch's well, and I can't blow a bubble with gum D: To be honest I don't mind it but I do sometimes stutter which I kinda mind. Seeing Bertie go through this I found out that I'm not the only one that has had a hard time with it and seeing him being resurrected and gaining his pride was very inspiring.

Now the excellent supporting cast. Geoffrey Rush, by god if I ever needed a speech therapist, I would want him. Geoffrey is hilarious in this whenever he is reciting plays or teaching Bertie how to speak, he is top notch in this, it's great to see him in this. Did he deserve the Oscar?   Well he won his Oscar for "Shine" Back in 1996 so I think he's good, but I will admit it was a tough choice. Bale won it for "The Fighter" but both of them were excellent.

Helen Bonham Carter plays Bertie's wife. She gives a fine performance, the best of the year, no, I wanted Hailee Steinfeld but she's a kid so I think that's why that and Melissa Leo needed her Oscar. But I didn't think her performance was that great. Anyways Helen did an excellent job as Bertie's wife and I'm glad she got nominated.
I should mention that I'm happy that Guy Pearce was in this. He's a great actor, he deserves bigger roles, Memento proves it. He was good in this (and also Animal Kingdom) why not give him bigger roles? He can handle it. 

Now Best Director Tom Hopper. We come to the Oscar in which it should not have won. Why? The Direction is excellent in this, but the thing is, is that it's what I expected it to be. "But Alex who should have won Best Director then?" David Fincher for the Social Network. The Social Network could have been so simple but David Fincher turned the Oscar winning screenplay (adapted) and turned it into a classic. That and that David Fincher needs his Oscar. The Direction is excellent in The Kings Speech especially during my favorite scene when Lionel is teaching Bertie and the camera flows in back and forth but Fincher deserved it way more through my eyes.

Before I saw the Kings Speech I was mad that The Social Network didn't win best picture, but after seeing it I was shall we say speechless? The Kings Speech may not be the best picture I've seen this year (that goes to "Exit Though The Gift Shop") But I'm glad it won best picture of the year, well deserved. This review does have spoilers, so be forewarned. After watching The King's Speech for a second time, I fell in love with this movie. This is the type of drama that will make you laugh and cry, and go through cycles of loving and hating the characters. The movie takes place in pre-WW2 England, where Bertie (Colin Firth), the Duke of York, struggles with his duties to make speeches due to a stutter. Due to the advancement of modern technology, the radio has increased the pressure on the royal family, making them give comfort to the people of England through speaking to them via the radio.
	One of the most heartbreaking themes in this film is the way it makes the audience confront Bertie's purpose; he himself complains that as King, he has no real power: he cannot declare war or change laws. But now the royal family needed to comfort a nation that was in fear of war, and if Bertie had no voice than what did he have? Through his anger, the audience is drawn into the real frustration of a man dealing with a speech impairment; because of his lack of a voice, he has a hard time knowing his identity. This point is accentuated by the film's setting: a cold and dreary England, gloomy and dark just like Bertie's emotions. 
	Ultimately, we find that what Bertie needed was someone to believe in him and encourage him, which is exactly what he found in his relationship with Lionel (Geoffrey Rush); throughout his life, Bertie's family had teased him and pulled him down, but Lionel saw his potential and drew it out of him. This film tells an engaging story about the importance of one's voice, but furthermore, it tells the importance of friendship.
	What I found to be an amazing aspect of this film is the use of sound, which is a beautiful technique given the plot of the film. Near the beginning of the film, whenever Bertie tries to speak or attempts learning from a speech therapist, there is absolute silence which makes the audience have to suffer through every single utterance that he makes. But as the king works with Lionel the music starts to play little by little, and by the end, when he makes his glorious speech to all of England, the music blares, drawing the audience into a proud euphoria.
	This was one of the best films of 2010, and it would be a shame to miss out on it. Director Tom Hooper does an amazing job of taking a story that is not easy to tell well, and drawing the audience in through so many venues, including the setting, the music, and the friendship between the lead characters. If you have not seen this movie, do yourself a favor and rent it tonight!

Inspirational films are not films which I typically enjoy; more often than not, they are overwrought and under-written, often relying on a solid performance to attain any acclaim in spite of less than compelling and glossed-over screenplays. However, The King's Speech proves that even a genre prone to such faults can contain great films, as here is a much better film than just about any of its type to come along in years. It's a drama to be sure, and it contains moments of true emotional heft, but it is also at times breezy and isn't at all profoundly depressing in the way many dramas of this quality are. It's a true crowd-pleaser through and through. What makes it work then? For one, The King's Speech is much better written than most such films; it creates believable characters and believable interplay as opposed to cardboard cut-outs and clichés. Its often very funny, but, while it would have been slightly better had it gone further into the King's internal conflict, it doesn't forget to explore the turmoil the titular character is facing throughout the film. Secondly, The King's Speech features not just a good performance in the lead role, but an amazing one. 
	
The film is the story of Prince Albert, Duke of York, later known as King George VI (Colin Firth), who has a problem in his pronounced stammer and the fact that  such an office as his requires significant public speaking. Although he had tried to overcome his stammer multiple times, nothing had worked, and, still only a Duke, he feels as though the amount of public speaking that is required of him isn't worth a treatment which he doesn't believe will work. His wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter), felt differently however, and she, in spite of her husband's lack of faith, decides to give it one last try, consulting Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), a speech therapist known for his unorthodox methods. Initially reluctant, Albert reconsiders when his father dies and his brother, the new King, is forced to resign when he chooses to marry a divorced woman, an act which is condemned by the church which he is nominally the head of. Because of this, Albert is forced to accept the role of King as next in line to the throne. With Hitler rising to power and war on the verge of consuming Europe, the new King has to come to terms with the fact that his speech's will serve as a voice of confidence and trust to the public, and he has no choice but to continue his therapy with Logue, forming a friendship in the process. 
	
Its been a weak year for films, but not so much for performances, and, amidst a solid handful of great ones, Colin Firth gives by far the best. For two hours, he truly is King George VI. It's downright absorbing watching his performance, which is at times heartbreaking. In his hands, King George is a man whose courage defies logic, frequently displayed by the speeches he gives. The opening in particular is a truly brilliant display of acting, as we watch him try with all his might to force the words out of his mouth and refuse to give up, only for his stutter (which is constantly a presence but never seems forced)  to hold him back. His face in particular is hugely emotive, conveying anger, sadness, and embarrassment within seconds of each other, and it's hard to imagine a more forceful, believable, and downright brilliant portrayal of the role. 
	
Its worth noting that, in spite of Firth's performance, Helena Bonham Carter and Geoffrey Rush are entirely capable of commanding the screen and even stealing scenes, as both are superb in their respective roles as well. Bonham Carter creates both a wife who loves her husband and a queen who understands what he means to his people. Rush is simultaneously emotionally involving and quite funny. Some of his lines generate big laughs, which keeps the film light when it needs to be, and the interplay between him and the stodgier King is entirely believable. The character has as much depth as Firth's though, as we come to view the struggle to mean as much for him as it does for the King. 
	
One of the biggest pleasures of the film is actually watching the way Logue is capable of both holding his own against the King and giving us a glimpse into his life. Around Logue, King George (or Bertie, as Logue demands to call him) sheds his pretenses of Kingship and opens up, which is much of the reason why we connect with him. His reluctance to be King but acceptance and understanding of how he must be King drives the character, and, through Logue, an everyman, he is able to simultaneously be fully aware of and forget that he is King and connect with him and the audience. 
	
In recent years, relatively predictable films seem to have gotten the shaft in the minds of many supposedly looking for something more off the beaten path.  A film can throw all the plot twists or inventive ideas at you that it wants to, but it all comes down to the execution when it's said and done. The King's Speech is an example for how this holds true for a more predictable film as well. There's nothing necessarily surprising in the narrative here, except for how well it is told, which is what matters. It's superbly produced, assuredly directed, funny, heart-warming, emotionally involving, exciting, and very, very well acted. The King's Speech has a soul, and thanks to the care clearly put into every aspect of the film, it's a truly rousing success.

This is a biopic about how King George VI, the father of Queen Elizabeth II, overcame his stuttering problem. Widely considered by all but his father unfit to be king, George is reluctantly thrust unto the throne and into the spotlight after his brother is forced to abdicate. Overshadowed on the global stage by powerful orators like Adolph Hitler and Benito Mussolini, the King relies on the help of a little-known Australian speech therapist named Lionel Logue to find his voice and courageously lead his people into the most devastating war humanity has ever faced.

This is a powerful, hilarious and deeply moving story, told against the backdrop of a critical juncture in modern history, of the emergence of a deep friendship out of a professional relationship between two men who would otherwise never have socially interacted. The screenplay, written by David Seidler (who also wrote Tucker: The Man and his Dream), is excellent. The dry British wit is hilarious. I was literally slapping my knee during some of the scenes. Tom Hooper (Elizabeth I) does a superb job directing this movie. The buildup to the climactic finale is skillfully executed and prompted the audience to erupt into spontaneous applause. (Apparently, this also happened at the Roy Thomson Hall premiere.) Geoffrey Rush (Elizabeth: The Golden Age) does a fantastic job as Lionel Logue and Colin Firth (A Single Man) is excellent as King George VI.

I saw the second public screening of this movie at the Ryerson Theater during the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF). Tom Hooper was present to introduce the movie. He was joined by Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush after the movie ended for a brief Q&A.

It turns out that David Seidler also had a stuttering problem as a child and drew inspiration from the king's struggle. Early in his career he wanted to write a screenplay about it. He dutifully asked the Queen Mother for permission. She agreed but told him "not in my lifetime". Little did he know she would live to be 101 and he would have to wait another 30 years.

Another interesting tidbit we learned was that near the end of the shoot, the crew finally located one of Lionel Logue's grandsons, who just so happened to live about 10 minutes away from the director. They got access to Lionel's diaries and correspondence and managed to incorporate some of it into the script.

This movie is an unqualified must see.

The King's Speech is not the best film of the year, but it's still a well acted, well directed, and overall great film. It really keeps you interested in the characters and story, and it has a memorable quality to it. It's not perfect, but it mixes sophistication with entertainment very well. The story is about George VI, played by the wonderful Colin Firth. After his father, George V, dies, George VI is crowned King of England. The problem with this is that is George VI has had a speech impediment all his life, and as king, he has to make important speeches publicly. So, as the country is at war and in need of a leader, his wife arranges for her husband to see a speech therapist, played by Geoffrey Rush. I won't say anymore, as I just described the first half hour right there. So yeah, the plot is really simple, which can actually be one of this film's downfalls. The films accomplishes so little in such a long time, and even though that often leads to more atmosphere and character development, which it does here, it leaves time to be bored, which is a flaw. The characters are hit and miss. The 3 main characters, George VI, the speech therapist, and Queen Elizabeth are all very well done, but the rest of the characters are uninteresting and most of them seem pointless. However, most of those characters only get about 2 minutes of screen time, as most of the screen time involves the 3 main characters, so it's not much a problem, so I'll let it slide. The acting is... hard to explain. Most of the actors do good, but not great. Helena Bonham Carter, who plays one of the three main characters, Queen Elizabeth, also did good, but not amazing. Nobody does bad, but only two people actually do amazing, and I think they were the best actors of 2010, Colin Firth, and, especially Geoffrey Rush. Colin Firth get's a lot of emotion across, make his character feel like he's not Colin Firth, but his character, George VI. Also, the best of the movie, if not the best of the year, Geoffrey Rush. He's so interesting and when you watch the film, you don't see Rush, you see the speech therapist character. That's how good he was. Now, it's time for "The Best and Worst of The King's Speech". Even though it's obvious Geoffrey Rush was the best part about this film, I already described how good he did, so, to bring up something I didn't mention yet, the best is Tom Hooper's direction. He really knows how to keep us interested in such a simple plot as "A guy trying to speak in front of people", and he does it well. With awesome cinematography and camera work, Tom really brought light to a simple concept. The worst, in my opinion, is that, for a film that act's very important and even won Best Picture, it really isn't that revolutionary. This wouldn't be a problem, but if you're going to make a film that acts like it's a modern classic, it doesn't introduce any new and interesting ideas. Even films like 127 Hours and Black Swan, film's you'd expect to be similar to other films of the past, introduce new ideas that you'd like to see in other films, but this film doesn't do that. So, what's my final opinion of this film? It's flawed, I know that, but it's very entertaining, very memorable, very atmospheric, and with 2 of the best performances of the year (Though James Franco would argue), this is a great film. Worth the watch any day, just don't expect the best film ever. 4/5.

Colin Firth really makes you sympathize with Prince Albert and what he is going through. Prince Albert soon reluctantly finds help in the form of a speech therapist named Lionel Logue, played by Geoffrey Rush. He is absolutely perfect as Lionel Logue. However, Prince Albert has the throne of England thrusted upon him, and it is through his friendship with Lionel Logue that he acquires the courage to make himself worthy of the crown. Albert not only has to summon the courage to take the throne but also restore faith in himself. Colin Firth and Geoffrey Rush have a good chemistry that makes their characters friendship seem believable and intriguing. Helena Bonham Carter, who plays Queen Elizabeth, also gives a very fine performance as her character unconditionally supports her husband even through the darkest times. The settings in this film are fantastic and very historically accurate to the 1930s England time period. This film is filled with witty humor but at the same time it has a heart that makes the film a joyful and fulfilling experience.

The film opens with Bertie, Duke of York (Firth), the younger son of King George V, making a speech and becoming embarrassingly tongue-tied. Hearing the echo of his words in the outdoor stadium is enough to thwart his efforts. He looks desperately unhappy as the audience watches, some with expressions ranging from sympathy to impatience - clearly this has happened before.

Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), is an Australian speech therapist known for unorthodox methods. The moment we see his home, its eclectic decor tells us he is an unusual character. Logue has a happy and active family. He and his wife (Jennifer Ehle)have 3 sons, ranging in age from early adolescence to late teens. Evidence of the boys' activities is seen around the somewhat messy house - schoolbooks, model planes, etc.

Into this home comes the Duchess of York (Helena Bonham Carter), clearly out of her element. Presenting herself as "Mrs. Johnson," she tells Logue her husband stutters and is called upon to speak in public in his line of work. Logue replies that perhaps he should find a new job! She says that would be impossible, to which Logue inquires if he is an indentured servant. "Yes, sort of," she replies. After she reveals his true identify, Logue only agrees to take him on as a patient if the therapy is conducted in his own office (no house calls, even for royalty) and tells her it is "my castle, my rules."

A reluctant Bertie is coaxed into a first appointment, which ends badly. Logue records him reading the "to be or not to be" soliloquy from Hamlet while wearing headphones blasting Beethoven so that he can't hear himself speaking. Bertie has little patience for these "tricks" and ultimately rips off the headphones and storms out, but not before Logue presents him with the recording as a "souvenir." Some time later, Bertie plays the recording, in which he perfectly enunciates the Shakespearean passage , as Elizabeth, unseen, stands in the doorway listening.

So back to Logue he goes.

Their sessions are filled with pathos and humor. An unlikely friendship begins between two men from vastly different worlds - Logue insists on equality, calling the duke "Bertie." Logue knows that in most cases, stammering results from traumatic childhood experiences, although Bertie scoffs at this assertion. "I was always like this," he insists, Logue replying that no infant begins talking in a stammer. Gradually, his harsh treatment as a child - what we would consider child abuse today - is revealed, sometimes in song at Logue's insistence, when it is too painful to relate in speech. This breakthrough is one of the most powerful scenes in the film, and made me cry both times I saw it. At one point, the two men have a nasty argument and a disruption of their relationship. Bertie makes some cruel comments, mocking Logue's background and questioning his motivation. You can clearly see the hurt on Logue's face as Bertie walks away.

We all know what is going on in the background: the abdication crisis. Edward VI (David) and Wallis Simpson are unsympathetically portrayed. In one scene, David mockingly mimics Bertie's stammer, accusing him of wanting to steal his throne. In truth, Bertie dreads becoming King, breaking down in tears when he realizes his fear is about to become reality. When GeorgeV dies, making David the King, David abdicates when not allowed to marry the twice-divorced Wallis.

Bertie rekindles his relationship with Logue, trying to apologize without saying the words. Logue understands that royalty does not apologize, and begins readying Bertie to speak at the coronation.

The Archbishop of Canterbury does not approve of Logue's influence on the King, and questions his credentials. In a pivotal scene at a Westminster Abbey "rehearsal," the King supports Logue, who admits he is not a doctor and does not have impressive credentials, but never misrepresented himself to clients. After the Archbishop leaves, an amusing "rehearsal" scene takes place at the Abbey.

The film takes a serious turn as Hitler comes into power. Bertie, Elizabeth and their daughters (Margaret and Elizabeth, the current queen) watch a coronation newsreel, followed by footage of Hitler inciting the German people. Bertie's comment? "I don't know what he is saying, but he says it well," envying Hitler's oratory power.

Bertie is an affectionate, hands-on father, in contrast to his own childhood when he and his brother were brought to their parents for a "daily viewing." After he becomes king, the princesses hesitate, then curtsy, upon seeing him. Bertie's face changes as he realizes how completely his life will change, but immediately gathers them into his arms.

As WWII approaches, preparation begins for "The King's Speech" to the nation. The end of the film is brilliant as Bertie speaks live on radio, with Logue there to coach him. We see shots of his subjects - soldiers, people in pubs, his mother, even David and Wallis - listening to the stirring speech. It is a resounding success, but realistically portrayed, as Bertie hesitates several times, following Logue's non-verbal cues to get through it. Afterwards, Logue tells him "you still stammered on the W's" to which Bertie replies, "I had to throw in a few of those so they 'd know it was me." Director Tom Hooper revealed at the Q&A, that that response was taken from the king's own diary.

The film ends with the royal family on the balcony, waving to their subjects as Logue watches, having, for the first time, addressed Bertie as "Your Majesty." It is noted on screen that Bertie and Lionel remained friends for the rest of their lives and that Lionel was awarded a CVO for "personal service to the sovereign." I highly recommend this absorbing drama with masterful characterizations by its two principal actors.

Title: The King's Speech

What It Is: The story of how England's King George the VI (Colin Firth, in an Oscar-Winning turn) works to overcome a terrible studder that he's had since he was a young child. When he first meets Australian actor, turned speech defect therapist Lionel Lough (Rush, also in an Oscar turn) the then Duke of York is under the impression that a.) his defect cannot be fixed, and b.) that this man is an ACTUAL doctor. Turns out both a and b are wrong. Mr. Lough, or Lionel as he prefers uses various methods in order to helps "Bertie" fix his impediment. What the two men get in return is a lifelong friendship. Now George VI is dealing with the death of his father George V, as well as his brother King Edward the Veii's  (Guy Pearce) affair with a married woman. All this while trying to get over the hump he's dealing with. To make manners worse Hitler's Germany is on the verge of war with the King's nation. This means that our bumbling monarch must make his first of what  would be many wartime speeches.
 
What We Think: Simply put this is an incredible piece of cinema. Before seeing it I didn't buy into all the Oscar hype it received, nor did I understand the reasoning for it winning so many. I have now, since seeing this movie respect it. And the academies decision to call this  the Best Picture of the year. Firth was in  full form much as he was in his Oscar turn last year (for which I felt he should've won the Oscar.) I feel as though this years win was a makeup for last year. For me however it was Geoffrey Rush that absolutely dazzled. He didn't win the Oscar, but I'll be damned if he didn't make a great argument. Helena Bonham Carter also shines as George's wife Elizabeth. In addition to the principles their were many other brilliant performances by Timothy Spell as Winston Churchill, and Michael Gambon as King Edward V. 
 
Our Grade: A+, When it comes to brilliance The King's Speech goes above and beyond just about everywhere. Tom Hooper's direction is subtle enough to leave a fingerprint but not overbearing. He instead allows his brilliant battery of actors to do exactly what they do... marvel us. While not too many films can claim to be perfect and this one certainly isn't it is as close as we've gotten this year. So every Golden statue The Weinstein Company has from this film is a well deserved homage to a delightful cinematic experience.
